items.title: Rachel Whiteread punctures 2027 Brit Award trophy
paragraphs: Artist Rachel Whiteread has revealed her design for next year’s Brit Awards trophy, a silver sculpture covered in holes to “expose the interior of the statue”.
Since 1992, a different creative has been selected to design the handheld trophy for the UK music industry’s annual Brit Awards.

Essex-born Whiteread has designed the statuette for next February’s ceremony, which is her interpretation of the annual trophy depicting Britannia, a helmeted warrior that is a traditional symbol of Britain.
The result is a minimalist silver statuette cast in resin and covered in holes to draw attention to the inside of the trophy.
“I exposed the interior of the statue, as an artist would do with their music,” said Whiteread.
The artist then handpainted the nickel-plated trophy in a silver hue.
Whiteread is known for casting everyday architectural forms, such as staircases or sheds, in materials including plaster and concrete to showcase their negative space.
She explained that when designing the Brit Award, she wanted to put her own spin on the recognisable trophy.
“I saw this as a natural extension of my work – to continue to celebrate and recognise British art and creativity,” said Whiteread.

“Art and culture are under very real threat,” she continued. “So I was grateful to be able to take a tangible role in highlighting the importance of safeguarding creativity through the design of this year’s trophy and standing together as artists, whether from music or the visual arts.”
The Brit Awards will take place on 27 February 2027 at the Populous-designed Co-op Live arena in Manchester, where the ceremony was held for the first time at the start of this year.

To mark the awards’ departure from London, where it was held consecutively before 2026, British fashion designer Matthew Williamson designed an amber trophy to reference Manchester’s worker bee city logo.
Other former trophy designers have included British architect Zaha Hadid and British-Indian artist Anish Kapoor.

items.title: People are making their own art from GTA VI, and it's really quite beautiful
paragraphs: We've seen the GTA VI Easter eggs, we've admired the best GTA VI brand reactions and we've dived into the history of the Grand Theft Auto logo. Today, let's turn our attention to the artists.

I don't mean the artists who made the game – we've already interviewed Rockstar Games' art team about GTA VI's environmental storytelling and the building design in GTA VI. I mean the players who are turning their passion for the game into art of their own.

I hesitate to say "turning GTA VI into art" because it already is art. But there are players who are using the game's vast world as a creative medium for their own expression, whether through in-game virtual photography or capturing scenes from the game in other media.
There's nowhere near enough space here to mention all of the people who are making art from the game, but here are just a few examples.
GTA VI's Photo Studio, available from the pause menu, provides adjustable camera settings such as aspect ratio, aperture, and depth of field and lighting controls for in-game virtual photography.

Players can frame shots, hunt for the perfect lighting, compose scenes, and capture images that resemble fashion, street, documentary or landscape photography. Photo Studio even has filters and post-processing effects, so you don't need to take your shots into the best photo editing software like Photoshop.

The dedicated PlayStation in-game artist Photo.in.game (above) shows that creating art in photo mode is about much more than taking a simple screenshot, demonstrating their editing process for a shot of Jason and Lucia at sunset.

The Cone Studio has been sharing multiple daily shots from GTA VI taken not with the in-game Photo Studio but with a real-world Sony Alpha Nex 5n. Using a low shutter speed and some curves and hue filters in post, they're creating some evocative shots that feel drenched in nostalgia.
There are phones in GTA VI, and phones can shoot hyperlapses. So Fons de Haan has done just that: a hyperlapse made only using Jason's in-game phone.

Australia-based Kindred Cameras (above) has been bringing in-game shots of the GTA VI's stunning environments into the real world by printing them as Polaroids. Anyone unfamiliar with the game might never connect this piece of art to a controversially violent game franchise.
I made an oil painting of Jason stealing a mobility scooter in GTA VI https://t.co/ei0axkXs72November 25, 2026

The artist Cayde (above) is painting scenes from GTA using oil paints. Again, the use of physical media brings the game into the real world. His subjects so far have included Jason stealing a mobility scooter and Cal and Jason snuggling. He's been painting some scenes live on Twitch. Check out his website.

GTA VI is an incredible achievement that sets a new bar for game graphics, and it also has a very distinct aesthetic, so it's perhaps only natural that it would inspire players to create their own art.

As I said, this is just a sample of how people are finding inspiration int the game. There's also the traditional fan art, design and brand concepts, which perhaps deserve a post all of their own. Let me know in the comments if you've spotted some more good examples.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: 'I wouldn't be here today without you': Student's praise for man who stopped train attacker
paragraphs: Meeting after the guilty verdicts were delivered, the two train passengers hugged.
Astrid told the Nottingham Forest fan, who had been travelling home from a match: "It's brilliant to meet you... now we will know each other for a long time."
Crean said: "It means the world to me to meet her. Meeting her was the best thing, it was worth waiting for. I'm just so happy."
Astrid, who did not want to use her last name, said Crean was a hero for his actions that day.
"I just owe him everything," she said, before adding: "I wouldn't be here today without you, and to put your life on the line for someone else, a complete stranger, is just complete bravery."
She said Crean had a "split second to make a decision" and she owed him her life because of that.
"So I'd just like to say thank you," she said.
Crean praised her for alerting him to the danger of Williams as she ran past.
"You can be proud of yourself, and your parents will be proud of you," he added.
During the trial, Crean told the court he decided "to try to stop" the attack and "launched himself towards and at" Williams.
Crean and Astrid both faced terrifying moments as Williams rampaged down the train.
Crean said Williams asked, "Do you want to die?" as he stabbed him several times.
Crean then managed to lock himself in a toilet and call 999 telling them what had happened and that he was covered in blood and scared.
He said he remembered seeing Astrid crying with makeup running down her face.
The fashion student said she remembered seeing Crean throw himself at the attacker and put himself between her and Williams so she could escape.
"I was able to shut the door with the rest of the people behind me. If you hadn't been in between us... I have no idea what would have happened if you weren't there, literally in that second."
Astrid had seen an interview with the 62-year-old on the BBC two days after the attack and contacted the BBC to say he was the man on the train who had helped protect her and others.
Only now the trial has finished have they been able to meet.
Crean said he is pleased the jury found Williams guilty of attempting to murder him as he did not believe he should be allowed to get away with the vicious attacks on him and the other passengers.
On Thursday Cambridgeshire police apologised for failings in stopping Williams after another assault the month before the Huntingdon attack.
As well as the train attacks, Williams was found guilty of attempting to murder four other people in separate incidents and will be sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on 4 and 5 February.

Crean believes more should have been done to prevent these further offences. "I think they should have had him before. He shouldn't have been allowed to go running around like this. And if they'd picked up on it, we'd have had him before."
Having survived the attack, Astrid is running the London marathon for Crimestoppers as part of her efforts to turn around the harrowing situation she found herself in.
She can, she says, because of Stephen Crean's actions. And he has promised to be there for her again: this time on the finish line.

items.title: Australia's sandpapergate probe to also include 2017-18 Ashes against England
paragraphs: Cricket Australia's fresh independent probe into the sandpapergate scandal has been widened to include the 2017-18 Ashes series against England.

The terms of reference for the independent forum have been published and the scope will include "ball-management practices in the Australian men's team during the 2017–18 season", which includes the Ashes series Australia won 4-0.
Also included are all four Tests of the subsequent South Africa tour and the investigation which followed when the ball-tampering scandal emerged.
Cricket Australia has pledged to publish the full independent report and recommendations within 30 days of receiving them.
All those involved in Australia's 2018 tour of South Africa will be invited to speak to the independent forum, though none will have to do so and no retrospective sanctions will be handed out.

The scandal was reignited by the release of former batter Usman Khawaja's autobiography. In it, Khawaja claimed the entire team knew about ball-tampering in the third Test of their series against South Africa in Cape Town.

The four frontline bowlers in that 2018 team - Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon and current Test captain Pat Cummins - have always denied knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper on the ball.
Cummins has called Khawaja's recollection of events "nonsense".
However, former team-mates David Warner and Cameron Bancroft - two of three players who were banned for their part in the scandal, alongside Steve Smith - have backed Khawaja's version of events.

"All participants in Australia's 2018 tour of South Africa, including players and support staff, will be invited to take part in the Independent Forum, as will CA management and directors at that time," Cricket Australia said.

"While all involved will be encouraged to participate, there will be no compulsion to do so. All materials supplied will be treated as confidential unless otherwise stated by the participant and no sanctions will be retrospectively applied.
"Participants can choose to attend the Independent Forum in person, online and/or provide information via written accounts or through relevant documents and materials."

"This is an opportunity to provide their accounts in a safe environment and to provide the CA Board with relevant information including about the events of that tour and resultant investigation," CA chair David Boon said.
"We are acutely aware of the enormous toll the renewed focus on this tour eight years ago has had on those involved and their welfare remains our main priority.
"This forum is the best opportunity for people to speak and be heard, and for CA to listen and learn.
"Publishing the report in full is part of our commitment to transparency, and to be open with cricket fans about what we learn.
"It is also very important to understand that it will not seek to sanction or recriminate."

Writing in his autobiography in 2019, former England opener Sir Alastair Cook - who captained England in the 2017-18 Ashes - alleged Warner admitted during post-series drinks that he had previously used strapping on his finger to tamper with the ball.
The final Ashes Test in Sydney was just two months before the start of the South Africa series.
"Our suspicions had been aroused in Perth, when they managed to get the ball reversing an inordinate amount when the outfield was still wet, following three hours' rain," Cook wrote.
"When the series was complete, and we had lost 4-0, the teams shared a beer in the dressing rooms at the SCG.

"Warner, a couple of beers into his celebration at the time, mentioned to a group of England players that he had used substances attached to the strapping on his hand to accelerate the deterioration of the ball during a first-class match.
"I looked at Steve Smith, who shot a glance that said 'ooh, you shouldn't have said that'."

items.title: My self-care ritual is a meal at a fancy restaurant - on my own
paragraphs: Self-confessed foodie Catherine has booked tables for one in the UK and abroad

Catherine Smith is perusing the menu at a high-end Mediterranean restaurant she has been excited to try. She has a new outfit on, and as she sips her rosé, she looks across at the empty seat opposite - bliss.
"I think what is so special about solo dining is that you don't have to wait for people to make those plans. You can go out and do them yourself," says the 23-year-old.
The self-confessed foodie is part of a growing trend of people booking tables for one - not because they're away with work but as a treat.
As food trends analyst Charles Banks puts it: "[Eating alone] is becoming an intentional act, a little pocket of independence, indulgence and self-care."
We spoke to solo dining fans and hospitality industry experts about how the trend is shaping the restaurant experience and asked if you would book a table for one.
Solo dining: Would you book a table for one?
Catherine, from Yorkshire, began dining solo at university and now does it at least once a month, choosing high-end restaurants she would not usually go to with friends and family.
She has been to a range of places both in the UK and abroad, doing "lots of research" to find new spots, typically spending £100 to £200 per meal.
"I think because a lot of my friends are vegan or vegetarian, I find that difficult sometimes because I'm quite a big meat eater," she says.
"I find it nice to be able to go out and pick a restaurant where I haven't had to scour through the menu to make sure that it's suitable for them."
Catherine says the sense of freedom she gets from picking where and when she eats "feels empowering".
"It definitely feels like not only a form of self-care but also a form of female liberation."
While solo dining Catherine likes to read, journal or simply enjoy the peace and quiet

Online booking platform OpenTable says it covers more than 5,000 restaurants in the UK. It says solo dining makes up the smallest proportion of its bookings in the UK but it is the fastest-growing category.
Figures from 1 January to 31 August this year saw a rise of 23% in solo bookings compared to the same time period a year ago. It did not provide the data to the BBC to verify.
Nishi Singh was an avid solo diner when she lived in London, but found it wasn't widely accepted after moving to Delhi.
"Someone approached me and said that they assumed I'd been stood up," she tells BBC World Service's The Food Chain podcast.
"It sparked a conversation about the culture around solo dining in Delhi and I was really shocked to hear that it's not really something people do."
A couple of days later, she started documenting her solo dining experience on social media.
"Quite a lot of people have reached out and said that this is something they'd like to do and they're too scared to do it themselves," she says.
Ruth Alexander hears from solo diners - some who find peace and joy in a table for one, and others who would much rather not be alone

Banks, joint managing director of The Food People, a food trends and ideas agency, says that while solo dining isn't a "new consumer behaviour", changes in society mean it has become "almost aspirational".
But he notes that not every restaurant has welcomed the trend.
"A single diner could therefore feel like an inefficient use of a table rather than a customer the restaurant actively wanted."
SoloTable, a website that helps identify restaurants suitable for solo diners, found that one in eight of 178 restaurants it surveyed in London did not accept online reservations from solo diners.

Catherine says she has previously been turned away. "There are a lot of restaurants that I've wanted to go to before where they don't actually allow solo diners. And I've always found that to be really disappointing."
Yousaf thinks solo diners could produce another useful business stream for restaurants
However, some restaurants like Jungli, an Indian restaurant in Newcastle upon Tyne, is working to attract solo diners.
Co-founder and director Yousaf Khalid has included high tables and bar seats in his recently opened restaurant. They also have charging points for laptops and phones.
"We want people to feel comfortable in these sorts of environments, being able to walk in on their own," he says.
He has hired staff with "bigger personalities" to engage customers in conversation but they also know when to leave diners alone if they want a more solitary experience.
Catherine urges anyone who fancies solo dining to give it a go.
"Food is a great way to bring people together, but it's also a great way to have good experiences on your own.
"I think with time, people will see and will start to accept it as something that's more normal."
Additional reporting by Jemma Crew and Emma Jackson.
Do you treat yourself to meals out on your own?
The Food Chain examines the business, science and cultural significance of food, and what it takes to put food on your plate. Listen to The Food Chain on BBC Sounds

items.title: Natural England objected to a datacentre. Weeks later ministers threatened to abolish the agency
paragraphs: Natural England objected to the building of a large AI datacentre near Bristol weeks before the government threatened to abolish the independent environmental adviser.

The nature adviser made a significant intervention to urge Bristol city council not to grant planning permission for a 40MW datacentre at Avonmouth, because of the threat to protected wildlife and habitats at one of the UK’s most important sites for migratory birds, which is within 600 metres of the site.

The Environment Agency – which is also threatened with abolition by the de facto deputy prime minister, Louise Haigh – objected in addition to the flooding risk at the site, which is on a high-risk flood plain, expressing concerns people would not be able to take safe refuge in the event of a deluge.

Haigh this week blamed quangos, including Natural England, for blocking development and indicated both bodies could be scrapped with their responsibilities handed to ministers or devolved. Ministers are pushing for the construction of AI datacentres across the country as key to growing the UK economy.

Hundreds of AI datacentres are planned, with more than 300 waiting in the queue to connect to the electricity grid, representing 73GW of demand – almost double the peak winter energy demand for the entire UK. But they face considerable environmental and sustainability issues over their high energy use, pollution, encroachment on protected habitats and emissions from fossil fuel power stations many want to install while waiting for grid connections.

To side-step local democracy, the government is allowing datacentre developers to use the nationally significant infrastructure projects (NSIP) regime, with the secretary of state acting as the decision maker.
But Natural England has expressed concerns to ministers about the rollout of datacentres, urging caution and a precautionary approach.

In a response to the government’s draft datacentre national policy statement, Natural England said AI datacentres were a relatively new development type whose full environmental impacts were still being understood.
It highlighted the potential impact on rare and vulnerable species from overabstraction from waterways to meet datacentres’ demands.

Government sources denied the objection to the datacentre at Avonmouth or Natural England’s stance on taking a precautionary approach to their widespread construction had influenced Haigh’s announcement of their possible abolition.

But Craig Bennett, the chief executive of the Wildlife Trusts, said the government’s threatened abolition of Natural England was a worrying sign of an attack on environmental regulation. “Regulatory arm’s-length bodies like Natural England are set up to implement the law of parliament,” he said. “If we want decisions made about nature on the basis of science rather than the very last private corporate or vested interest that a minister has spoken to, then we have independent arm’s-length bodies like Natural England.”

Earlier this month Natural England advised Bristol city council that the datacentre could cause “disturbance and displacement” to rare and vulnerable bird species within the Severn estuary special protection area, just 600 metres away. Another protected site, Hallen Marsh, was only 270 metres away but had not been accounted for by the developers when assessing noise pollution, Natural England said.

As well as the flood risk, the Environment Agency said the developers had not provided any information on the level of water use, and the risk of pollution from land contamination to controlled waters. More than 4,000 people have objected to the datacentre’s construction.
Bristol council said the proposal was “likely to give rise to significant environmental effects” and it wanted the developers to carry out a full environmental impact assessment.

Mary Stevens, an AI campaigner at Friends of the Earth, said: “Natural England was doing its job brilliantly here as an independent adviser. I would have no confidence if this was a government minister doing the work because they would not be acting independently to protect nature.”

Rivington Energy, which is developing the datacentre, said: “We acknowledge the feedback received from the Environment Agency and Natural England and welcome the opportunity to continue working constructively with all consultees throughout the planning process.

“While substantial environmental and technical assessment work has already been undertaken, additional studies are being prepared in response to comments received and will be submitted as part of the ongoing planning process.
“We … are now preparing a detailed environmental statement to support the next stage of project assessment.”

The Wildlife Trusts have launched a petition to save Natural England, saying the current body and its predecessors have been vital protectors for wildlife, land, water and sea across England since the 1940s.

A government spokesperson said: “Datacentres are essential to our economy, but their development must protect the environment and benefit local communities. Developers must meet planning requirements, with local authorities assessing environmental impacts, and then deciding on local applications.”

items.title: ‘If the bot gets it wrong, who’s liable?’ Retailers enter the unknown with AI shopping assistants on Black Friday
paragraphs: They promise to find the best Black Friday deals, source Christmas gifts and find the ingredients for a romantic dinner.
This week’s UK launch of the Muse AI assistant by the owner of Facebook and Instagram promises to transform how we shop – and how retailers make money.
Meta has teamed up with high street names including Marks & Spencer, Sainsbury’s, JD Sports and Currys for what the Silicon Valley firm claims is a seamless, secure and time-saving tool.
“From doing the Christmas shopping and searching for a cheaper energy deal, to sorting the school calendar … Muse can get it done for you,” Meta said.

But for companies that have painstakingly transformed from bricks-and-mortar retailers into online emporiums, AI agents pose risks as well as opportunities. Will AI agents kill window shopping, ignore vast online ranges and send shoppers straight to the checkout? Will retailers be forced to discount heavily to stand out? How do they avoid being steamrollered by Silicon Valley tech titans in commercial negotiations?

John Roberts, the founder and chief executive of online electrical goods retailer AO.com, said the impact of AI agents – at present – was “relatively low” but their use as shopping assistants was clearly “a direction of travel”.

He said AO was positioning itself to get recommendations from AI agents in the same way it generally attracted customers, by offering decent prices and good service, which was winning good online reviews on sites such as Trustpilot.
“We need to work out how we are the best option for whichever AI agent you use,” Roberts said.

Working out where to invest is a challenge. Some smaller firms are almost ignoring the developing channel, waiting to see how and where it might go. However, holding back on involvement with the developing technology – such as online shopping in the early noughties – has killed off brands in the past.

Sharon Iles, a senior apparel analyst at the analytics and consultancy firm GlobalData, said those brands that have chosen to partner with Muse would get an early view of how people shop, what they bought through an AI agent and which products got recommended, which could help brands make their listings more visible.
But she said retailers “must continue to prioritise their own channels to protect what an AI agent cannot replace”.

If agents bypass retailers’ websites, said Iles, this could mean companies “miss out on the impulse items that shoppers often add while browsing”, while those selling more complex items such as apparel could find issues with the choice of fit and sizing, “which could lead to higher return rates”.
“Retailers’ own channels should remain the core of their business, and they must give consumers more reasons to shop directly,” she said.
Retailers including Sainsbury’s and Tesco have used their loyalty schemes and websites to build sizeable businesses that monetise customers’ data and sell advertising space to brands.

However, retailers cannot ignore the agents. Muse has proved successful in the US and is ranked first and second respectively on Google and Apple’s free app store, having been downloaded millions of times.

UK residents may be more cautious about agentic technology than those across the Atlantic, but the technology is entering the mainstream. This year, a third of people planning to shop during Black Friday sales intend to get help from AI – up from 19% last year, according to a recent YouGov poll.

To fans, the likes of Muse or rivals such as Google’s Gemini or ChatGPT’s Dots can be a personal secretary helping organise the boring details of life, but to others they are an untenable busybody, parsing their personal data and monetising it.

For Muse to work as Meta envisages, it not only needs access to your email, calendar and shopping apps but details of relationships on apps such as WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, your preferences and even your financial and health information.

Sainsbury’s suggests its customers can “tell Muse about their week” and the AI agent will help build a shopping list to provide for dinner parties, different dietary requirements or suggest menus and recipes.
Mark Given, the chief technology and marketing officer at the supermarket chain, said the retailer was “starting carefully, listening to customers” and using what we learn to keep making it better”.
“AI can be genuinely useful, taking on routine tasks like checking offers and building the basket, and helping customers find great value and inspiration more quickly,” he said.
In the UK, Muse must ask for your approval before making a purchase or sending an email, while a separate “security agent” checks the AI tool’s actions against the permissions you have granted.
Meta said Muse had no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods, and it did not share users’ conversations with advertisers.

However, almost half of shoppers using AI (48%) are concerned about biased or sponsored recommendations, according to YouGov. Rival research firm Kantar found only 23% trusted a chatbot’s recommendations.

Meanwhile, some retailers are territorial about which AI agents get to trawl their data. Amazon has blocked AI agents from its store, although it is reportedly in talks with Meta about allowing access. Last year, Amazon sued the AI company Perplexity over its shopping feature that automates placing orders for users.

Research from the advisory firm KPMG highlights consumer caution. It found just 12% of those planning to shop during Black Friday – a largely online sale event in the UK – intended to use an AI tool (such as prompting ChatGPT or Gemini) specifically to find deals, slightly lower than the 15% using it last year.

Linda Ellett, the head of consumer, retail and leisure at KPMG, said trust would remain an important factor for shoppers and, while some would be happy to give access to their data to “make life easier” and enjoy the ability to “have a chat with an agent” to organise tasks, others would be much more cautious.
With about 70% of shopping still taking place in stores, and more than that in many categories, AI agents have some work to do to kill off the high street.
Brands made familiar through advertising, a store presence or social media content will continue to be important.

Most consumers use AI as only part of their search, to compare prices on kitchen equipment, home electronics or food, for example, or seek recommendations on complicated products such as electronics or supplements.
The advisory firm OC&C said: “For now, AI often helps shoppers validate a choice rather than create an entirely new preference.”

Mark Howell, the director of European retail at Rithum, an e-commerce firm that works with Asos, M&S, Aldi and Shein, said: “Retailers aren’t going to be comfortable handing checkouts entirely to bots until questions around responsibility and liability are resolved.

“Agentic commerce is both real and overhyped. The technology is clearly going to become part of retail, but the legal and commercial realities are much more complicated than people acknowledge. In Europe especially, retailers are asking a simple question: if the bot gets it wrong, who’s liable?”

Retailers and brands said that AI agents were having only a tiny influence on shopping behaviour but most larger businesses already had teams ready to support “generative engine optimisation” (GEO) tactics. These include: making sure they appear in Reddit forums, an important source for some platforms; ensuring AI models can access correct and more detailed product information in text as well as photographs; and responding to reviews on Google or Trustpilot.

While some have suggested that the use of AI agents could diminish the power of brands and loyalty schemes built up by companies with advertising and paid-for search, Roberts suggested agents might well be influenced by these factors.
The AO boss said that if an agent could see there were better deals via a loyalty scheme, then the technology could act as “an accelerant to membership not something that bypasses it”.
In future, industry insiders believe, ChatGPT, Amazon, Meta and Google are likely to try to monetise their AI platforms with some form of paid search or featured ads.
“I am pretty sure agents will start clipping the ticket from an advertising perspective,” said Roberts.

items.title: Grace Tame calls out ex-Murdoch media executive who said she ‘must be looking to be raped again’
paragraphs: A former Murdoch media executive has admitted he said Grace Tame “must be looking to be raped again” at an event, after the former Australian of the year overheard the comment and confronted him.

Tame, a child sexual assault victim survivor who was Australian of the year in 2021 for her advocacy work, revealed in an opinion piece for Crikey that she heard Matt Handbury make the comment to another man at a function last week.
“That’s Grace Tame,” Handbury said, according to Tame’s piece published on Friday.
“Look at her with her tits hanging out. She must be looking to be raped again.”
Tame wrote that she didn’t realise that the man was Handbury until a bystander told her. He introduced himself as “Matt” after she confronted him.
The 77-year-old is Rupert Murdoch’s nephew and the former owner of Murdoch Magazines and Murdoch Books. He is now on the board of The Sydney Retreat, a rehab centre.
Tame said Handbury conceded at the UNSW event – where former military lawyer David McBride was presented with an award – that he had made the comment.
The following day, Handbury sent an email to Tame, seen by Guardian Australia, in which he also admitted he said “she must be looking to be raped again”.

Tame was 15 when repeatedly sexually abused by her 58-year-old maths teacher, Nicolaas Bester, who was later convicted and jailed. In 2019, Tame won a supreme court exemption which overturned a Tasmanian law that had until then gagged her from speaking about her experiences of assault.
“He didn’t say she must be looking to get raped,” Tame said of Handbury’s comment.
“He said she must be looking to get raped again. Therefore evidencing his prior knowledge of what I have been through.”
Tame said that the comment “activated really deep seated trauma and there are consequences to that”.
“It’s really destabilising and disorienting because your body is essentially your abused self and it is in total survival mode,” she said.

Handbury said in the email to Tame: “I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up. It was meant to be in appreciation in a male-to-male exchange. I can see that might be offensive in the context of suggesting a woman is making herself attractive to men in some titillating fashion.”

“I also said: ‘She must be looking to be raped again.’ This was certainly meant for no one’s ears but my friend. However it was in poor taste. In fact in highly objectionable taste and I regretted it as soon as I got out into the fresh air. Thank you for calling me out.

“Some men, obviously including myself, are prone to finding suggestive humour in the wrong places. I deeply regret my letting such bad habits get in the way of common courtesy, respect and decency. Please accept my humblest apologies.

“Thank you for opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink on Friday. But no one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous that night.”

Tame wrote in her Crikey piece that “what makes this provocation especially egregious is that Matt didn’t reference an imagined harm, but a very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about.
“It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?
“This isn’t about Matt personally; it’s about a broader culture of normalised violence. However, part of that culture is the self-censorship that protects people like him.”

Tame referred to research that showed 35% of Australian men believe women’s rights have come too far, adding that “research has repeatedly shown that misogynistic attitudes are a broad predictor of violent extremism and prevalent among men of all ages.”
Tame said she often faced re-traumatising behaviour from men.
“I’m tired of the maltreatment. I’m tired of the gaslighting. I’m tired of being baited, and then have people be shocked why I would be angry or re-traumatised.”
Tame thanked bystanders at the event who supported her following Handbury’s comment.
The chief executive of Full Stop Australia, Karen Bevan, called on people to speak up if they heard similar comments because “we all have the power to shift this”.

“If one of the most recognised survivor advocates in the country can be spoken about like this at an event honouring a whistleblower in a room full of people, you can be assured this behaviour is normalised,” Bevan said.
“Things like this do get said in workplaces, pubs, group chats and boardrooms across the country, where no one is recording, and no one writes about it afterwards.”
Handbury was contacted for comment, as was The Sydney Retreat.

items.title: How Fury and Joshua changed British boxing forever
paragraphs: Tyson Fury (left) has 36 wins, two defeats and one draw as a professional, while Anthony Joshua has 30 wins and four defeats
They have conquered the world, filled stadiums and transformed British boxing.
Now, after more than a decade of lingering tension and endless debate, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua are finally preparing to share a ring.
They are from different worlds, with contrasting personalities and wildly different journeys to the summit of heavyweight boxing.
Fury is the unpredictable showman who dethroned a seemingly unbeatable champion. Joshua is the Olympic golden boy who became a global superstar.
Who is better? Who has achieved more? The arguments have raged in pubs, boxing gyms and across social media.
We may soon get our answer, but whatever happens when the first bell sounds in Cardiff in the early hours of 12 December, their greatest achievement may already be secure.
Together, Joshua and Fury have taken British heavyweight boxing to new heights, attracting wider audiences and inspiring the next generation.
Britain had produced heavyweight champions before, but for years many of the division's biggest fights took place overseas.
Lennox Lewis fought some of his defining bouts in Las Vegas and Memphis. Challengers travelled to Germany when the Klitschko brothers reigned.

In November 2015, Fury outpointed Wladimir Klitschko in Dusseldorf. Less than five months later, Joshua knocked out Charles Martin at London's O2 Arena to win his first world title in his 16th professional fight.
"Bosh, that's it. The revolution starts in that six-month period," said BBC Radio 5 Live boxing pundit Steve Bunce, who was interviewed for the BBC documentary Rivals: Fury v Joshua.
Joshua's former trainer Rob McCracken saw an early sign of his appeal in Birmingham, where a show sold out with Joshua on the undercard.
"I'm from Birmingham, and it's hard to get a big crowd that sort of size," McCracken says. Promoters soon realised Joshua was bringing in a different audience and could sell tickets almost instantly.
By 2017, Joshua was fighting in front of 90,000 fans at Wembley Stadium, where he stopped Klitschko, while Fury's trilogy with Deontay Wilder made him a box-office draw in the USA.
"The two of them have been in eight massive stadium fights over an eight-year period," Bunce says. "That's reshaping British boxing history."

Yet for all the domestic ground they broke, both men eventually helped export the division's biggest nights back overseas - trading British stadiums for Saudi Arabian paydays, with even this Cardiff homecoming bankrolled by Turki Alalshikh's 'Riyadh Season' and timed for an American streaming audience.
Will Tyson Fury v Anthony Joshua be 'the most defining fight' of their careers?
Fury and Joshua's reach extended beyond boxing. Joshua became a familiar face on chat shows, while Fury stepped into a WWE ring and welcomed Netflix cameras into his home.
Derek Chisora, who lost three times to Fury, could see that wider appeal in the crowd on fight night.
"You've got a guy who's running a hedge fund for £2.5bn having a drink with a guy who works for the local council," Chisora says.

Crossover contests - both faced former UFC champion Francis Ngannou, while Joshua fought YouTuber Jake Paul - reflected a sport increasingly blending competition with entertainment. But a lot of boxing fans viewed those fights as lucrative, low-risk detours that stalled the division.
Even so, that mainstream visibility turned Fury and Joshua into household names - and sustains Britain as a major centre of the division for another generation.
Today, a new wave of British heavyweights - Daniel Dubois, Fabio Wardley and Moses Itauma - are stepping into a landscape Joshua and Fury helped create.

Seven years after Joshua stopped Klitschko at Wembley, Dubois beat Joshua on the same ground. "Two legends of the sport," Dubois says. "What they've done for the sport in the last few years has been great."

Highly rated British prospect Leo Atang was 10 when he watched Joshua beat Klitschko on television at home in York and decided to give boxing a go. Seven years later, he won gold at the World Under-19 Championships.
Wardley remembers Fury's win in Dusseldorf as the night that "re-sparked a lot of people's love for boxing".
Yet for all Fury and Joshua have achieved, one question has followed them both throughout their careers is: what would happen if they met in the ring?
After failed negotiations, lost titles and shifting circumstances, some believe their bout is arriving too late. Chisora describes it as "getting the last drink in the barrel".
For years, promotional politics, rival broadcast deals, and mutual risk aversion kept both camps protecting their commercial brands rather than risking undefeated records.
In the time it took to make the fight, both men lost twice to Oleksandr Usyk and Joshua was beaten by Andy Ruiz Jr and Dubois.
Fury's father John Fury did not even want the fight to take place.
"Both men are bigger than boxing, both men [are] bigger than the event. Leave them, they're both multi-millionaires. They don't need to fight," he says.
But former world champion Natasha Jonas believes legacy ultimately comes down to what fighters feel they have achieved.
"Legacies are a huge thing. Once you walk away, you want to be happy and satisfied with what you've done and what you've left behind," she says.
The reality is that - barring a late withdrawal - Fury and Joshua will put their reputations on the line in front of 80,000 fans in Cardiff.

But, whether their rivalry is settled in 12 rounds or a single punch, Fury and Joshua's wider legacy has been built over more than a decade of filling stadiums, drawing new audiences and making British heavyweight boxing a global attraction.

items.title: Man City owners should be forced to sell, say rival club chiefs
paragraphs: The independent commission has yet to decide on a sanction that could range from a fine, to a points deduction, the stripping of past titles, or even expulsion from the league.

But speaking on condition of anonymity, one executive claimed they are among a group of clubs who feel that City's punishment will be irrelevant unless the owners are also forced to sell. They added that anything less will make them question why they are funding the regulator through a levy.

In comments that reveal the level of anger felt by some of City's rivals, another claimed the rule breaches had undermined the league's credibility, and that they would not be able to draw a line under the scandal and move on if the owners were allowed to stay. The club were found guilty of inflating revenues and disguising losses by £900m through "sham" commercial arrangements.
Manchester City's owners are Abu Dhabi United Group - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy Prime Minister Sheikh Mansour.

The executive who spoke anonymously said that clubs had been asked by the Premier League to refrain from publicly revealing their views on sanctions, and let the process run its course, although some are said to have privately made their opinions clear to IFR officials. They acknowledged that some clubs were less opinionated about a punishment.

Other clubs the BBC approached declined to comment, or said they were willing for the independent commission panel and IFR to reach their own conclusions following the publication of the commission's ruling in September.

But the fact that some clubs want the unprecedented sanction of a forced sale will put pressure on Kogan to mete out the harshest penalty possible in what is being seen as a defining test of the watchdog just over a year after it was established.

It also comes amid mounting questions over whether wider UAE trade and investment in UK projects could be impacted by such a move. In September, Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" if the scandal led to City's owners selling the club, adding that "they have been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester".
When approached, the IFR declined to comment. But Kogan has consistently said that the IFR will not be influenced by any political pressure.
Earlier this week he told a parliamentary committee that the watchdog would not be afraid to investigate City's hierarchy and take action, depending on the outcome of the appeal.

"Forget the name of the club, forget the size of the club, forget the scale of the issue. We cannot simply ignore our statutory duties in relation to a club because it happens to be of a certain size," Kogan said.

"We absolutely will have to take the appropriate action as laid out in the legislation, depending on the circumstances as they come to us, which are the evidence that's been presented and collated by the independent commission of the Premier League and by any judgement that takes place on that evidence through an appeal.

"But in one sense, the evidence has already been judged by those cases having been found guilty, so we will absolutely have the stomach to do so... assuming those circumstances are triggered, if we don't act, what is the purpose of having a football regulator?"

When asked how any potential legal battles with Manchester City would be paid for, IFR chief executive Richard Monks told MPs that a litigation reserve of £2m was to be built up over the next two years via the levy charged to clubs, which would be paid back if litigation was successful.

"Now clearly - and I'm not talking about a specific case - clearly, there could be a very large legal case of any particular club that would require us to spend more than £2m in terms of litigation costs and barrister costs in particular", Monks added. "So if that happens, we have agreed with government [that it] will effectively lend us the money in terms of cash flow.
"We'd expect to win that litigation, to claim costs and repay government. If we failed in that massive litigation, then ultimately it would be added to the levy and we'd repay government that way."
Last month it was revealed that the IFR would cost clubs in the top five divisions of English men's football £20.3m annually.

Last week, Premier League clubs voted to cover legal expenses for its five board directors if any of City's sponsors sued them. Two UAE-based commercial partners - Etihad and Etisalat - have both said they are considering legal action against the Premier League.

The IFR has the authority to force a sale within section 34 of the Football Governance Act which allows it to investigate whether an owner meets the required suitability standards around honest, integrity and financial soundness. If an owner fails this assessment, the regulator can direct them to take reasonable steps to relinquish ownership within a specified period before issuing an ownership removal order.

City have been approached for comment. The club previously said that the commission's ruling contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe", adding that they filed "a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence [that] exists in support of all of its positions".

items.title: ‘Absolute jerk’: police investigating after 500-year-old ‘King Jarrah’ tree chainsawed in WA national park
paragraphs: Western Australian authorities say they are considering “all options” in their race to save a beloved jarrah tree they suspect was vandalised with a chainsaw in a national park south of Perth.
Police on Friday said they were treating the vandalism of “King Jarrah” as an alleged criminal damage incident, as they appealed to the public to help them find the person or people responsible.
The tree, in Wellington national park near Bunbury, was damaged on 21 or 22 November when someone attempted to cut it down, police said.
The WA environment minister, Matt Swinbourn, said an “absolute jerk” had damaged the “iconic” tree with a chainsaw, in an act he described as “appalling, senseless, and heartbreaking”.

“It’s hard to fathom how shocking it is that someone would do this to a tree believed to be about 500 years old, particularly in a national park,” he said in a statement on social media on Thursday night.
“Western Australians love this tree. Our community will be heartbroken, and they have every right to be angry.”

Experts, including an independent specialist arborist, were assessing the tree’s condition, but the immediate priorities were giving it every possible chance of survival and finding those responsible, Swinbourn said.
“Whoever did this has damaged something precious to all of us,” he said.
Swinbourn said surveillance cameras have been installed in the area, which had been closed to the public.
“If you know anything, come forward,” he said. “Anyone capable of such a deliberate and callous act should be held accountable.”
The jarrah tree, Eucalyptus marginata, is a towering hardwood native found only in the forests of south-west WA, which plays a vital role in the local ecosystem.
Visitors travel to the state to see the jarrahs, known for their towering foliage and longevity, as well as their rich red timber and honey.
The state’s biodiversity, conservation and attractions department said a member of the public reported the damage to the parks and wildlife service on Tuesday.

A chainsaw had been used around the base of the tree, one of the tallest in the national park at 36 metres, which is the “focus and drawcard” of a small day-use recreation site, the spokesperson said.
They said a consultant arborist and relevant government staff travelled to the national park on Wednesday to assess the health and safety of the tree.
Formal technical advice from the consultant arborist on whether King Jarrah could be saved was expected next week, they said.
“All options are being considered to save this iconic tree,” the spokesperson said.

They said vandalism of this nature was a potential breach of several sections of the Conservation and Land Management Act 1984 and, if found guilty, court penalties for the person or people responsible could include a fine of up to $10,000 and one year’s imprisonment.
Police said a silver Jeep was seen in the area in the days after the incident and they believed whoever was in the car may be able to assist with their inquiries.
They encouraged anyone with information to contact them via crime stoppers.

items.title: Strobe Talbott, former Time magazine reporter and deputy secretary of state, has died
paragraphs: FILE - Strobe Talbott, President Brookings Institution, speaks during a news conference in Berlin, July 16, 2008. Franka Bruns/AP hide caption
Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.
His son, Devin Talbott, confirmed he passed away peacefully after a long illness in his East Hampton, New York, home.

The elder Talbott was educated at Yale and Oxford, where he bunked with Clinton. While at the British university, after interning for Time in Moscow, the magazine asked Talbott to help translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former first secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union who was ousted in 1964.
FILE - President-elect Bill Clinton and Strobe Talbott of Time magazine talk privately as they walk along the beach on Hilton Head Island, S.C., Jan. 2, 1993. James Finley/AP hide caption
Talbott did, and it gave him some notoriety as a young man and a job at the magazine.

After 21 years at Time, where he focused on Soviet-American relations and held positions including Washington bureau chief and a foreign-affairs columnist, according to his U.S. State Department biography, he received a call from the newly elected Clinton.

Talbott joined the U.S. State Department in 1994, swiftly becoming deputy secretary of state. In that role, he was the architect of the Clinton administration's approach to Russia and other formerly Soviet countries and conducted negotiations between the U.S. and India after the latter's nuclear tests in 1998.

"Strobe was a good and brilliant man who made our world more peaceful and secure," said Clinton in a statement after Talbott's death. When Talbott was translating Khrushchev's memoirs while at Oxford, it was Clinton's job to make him breakfast every day, he said, adding, "somehow, I got the better end of the deal."
Both he and Hillary were "deeply saddened" by the passing of "a wonderful friend, and a world-class human being," he said.
Afterward, he served as the president of Brookings from 2002 to 2017. In that time, he also chaired the U.S. State Department's Foreign Affairs Policy Board.
Talbott also authored over a dozen books. His last book was titled "Our Founders' Warning: The Age of Reason Meets the Age of Trump," which was published in 2020.
He was born in Dayton, Ohio, in 1946, and is survived by two sons, Devin and Adrian, and six grandchildren.
His first wife, Brook Shearer, died in 2009, and he later married author Barbara Lazear Ascher.

items.title: Chris Mason: Immigration stats are down but will that be the end of the issue?
paragraphs: Net migration falling to the tens of thousands is a landmark moment in our collective national conversation about immigration over the last couple of decades.
There is a simple reason for this. We have had years and years strewn with the litter of politicians promising to cut net migration to under 100,000 annually.

In the latter decades of the last century, net migration was broadly net zero. Sometimes more folk left than arrived. But, around the time that I first arrived as a reporter in Westminster in 2004, the story was changing and would change rapidly.
I have followed every twist, turn, argument and campaign since, both from Parliament and from Brussels.
On 1 May 2004, the European Union expanded hugely, from 15 to 25 members, the biggest expansion in its history.
The bloc's population grew by 74 million people overnight as countries including Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia and what was then the Czech Republic signed up.
And remember, a core plank of EU membership is freedom of movement: the right to travel, live and work anywhere in the club.
Transitional controls on workers from these former communist states could be applied at the time, but the then-Labour government led by Tony Blair chose not to.
The consequences of that decision were as substantial as they were consequential.
Ministers had predicted a minimal impact. But net migration cranked up.
Crucially, this began to ground arguments about sovereignty in the swirling debates about the UK's membership of the EU.
At the time I was a Europe correspondent based in Brussels and a frequent visitor to the European Parliament in Strasbourg.

The UK Independence Party, led by Nigel Farage, were on the rise. But Eurosceptics would tell me privately that their deeply held concerns about the loss of sovereignty, of power, to EU institutions had been a hard sell to many back home. It was an argument, regardless of its merits or otherwise, that felt theoretical and intellectual to many, rather than practical and grounded in day-to-day concerns.
But that changed for many given the scale of immigration people could see.
Plenty of places, particularly beyond the big cities, felt the rapidity of change. Immigration took on a greater political salience.

Should all control over migration be re-imported to Westminster? Such was the growing strength of feeling among many, a sequence of prime ministers began promising to reduce net migration to the tens of thousands.

David Cameron made the promise. The Conservative election manifesto in 2010 harked back to those numbers before the turn of the century. "We will take steps to take net migration back to the levels of the 1990s – tens of thousands a year, not hundreds of thousands."

Five years later, Cameron renewed the promise, in the Conservative manifesto of 2015. The party would "keep our ambition of delivering annual net migration in the tens of thousands, not the hundreds of thousands," it read.

By 2017, Theresa May was prime minister and while the UK had voted for Brexit, it hadn't happened yet. In the Conservative manifesto that year, she promised "controlled, sustainable migration, with net migration down to the tens of thousands."

At the 2019 general election, Boris Johnson was in Downing Street. He didn't repeat the tens of thousands promise, post Brexit, instead arguing for an "Australian-style points-based immigration system" and, crucially, that "overall numbers will come down."
They didn't. Instead, they soared by almost a million – a giant spike on the graph of recent net migration, branded by his critics as the "Boriswave."
Johnson argued that Brexit would mean Westminster would take back control of migration, as leaving the European Union would mean the end of freedom of movement among the member states.
And yes, Brexit did repatriate that power. But this delivered choices, not a guaranteed outcome that the numbers would fall. And Johnson's choices led instead to a spectacular rise.

It took Rishi Sunak's government and the then-Home Secretary Sir James Cleverly to substantially change the rules and so limit the number of visas granted. The incoming Labour government in 2024 inherited these rules and kept them.
The question now, with the net migration number now in the tens of thousands, is whether immigration will now shrivel as a topic of widespread worry.

How migration feels can be influenced by world view and wealth, politics and geography. Let's take just one aspect of it: the number of asylum seekers being housed in Scotland has increased by 20% over the past year, despite a fall in numbers across the UK as a whole. Glasgow remains the council area with the largest number of people in asylum accommodation in the UK, and there have been increases in areas from Aberdeen to North Lanarkshire which buck the UK-wide trend.

And a lower net figure also does not necessarily mean that the scale of immigration and emigration are low. Large but similar numbers merely serve to almost cancel each other out, numerically. The underlying official statistics set out that an estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June, while 661,000 emigrated.

But just as previous political choices still have consequences now, a persistently low net migration number, depending on who is coming and going, could have consequences in the future. Take Andy Burnham's desire to shake up social care in England, a sector traditionally reliant on arrivals from overseas for much of its workforce. How might it cope? It's one of many potential questions for the future.

For now, as we examine this latest set of statistics, many will reflect that we have collectively as a country – if not everyone individually - exuded an anguish, sometimes an anger at the scale of immigration. It has been one of the standout demographic, social and so political issues of recent times. Perhaps now that conversation turns to a new chapter.

items.title: Council to set London's highest littering fines
paragraphs: People caught littering or illegally dumping waste in a north-west London borough are set to face higher fines as the council steps up its efforts to tackle persistent fly-tipping.
Harrow Council has approved plans to increase penalties for littering, breaches of Public Space Protection Orders (PSPOs) and the most serious fly-tipping offences.
Penalties for littering will rise from £500 to £750, with a reduced penalty of £300 available for early payment - the highest to be introduced in the capital under a new national maximum cap.
The penalty for breaching a PSPO will increase from £100 to £500, while a new £5,000 penalty will be introduced for the most serious fly-tipping offences.
The changes follow an increase in the maximum penalties available to councils under government rules.
The highest fly-tipping penalty will only be used in cases involving "aggravating factors", such as hazardous waste or repeat offences.
Other factors include the dumping of multiple bags, whether the waste affects vulnerable people, and whether it was dumped by a business for financial gain.

Speaking at a cabinet meeting where the proposal was approved last week, councillor Pritesh Patel said: "The reason for these changes is that the government has increased the maximum penalties available to councils. This gives us an opportunity to strengthen our response to environmental crime.
"Most people do the right thing, but there is a minority that don't, and it is important that the consequences are meaningful and encourage prompt compliance and resolutions."
