items.title: "We wanted to avoid the idea of tropical modernism" says curator of Geoffrey Bawa exhibition at Vitra Design Museum
paragraphs: As the Vitra Design Museum hosts Geoffrey Bawa: Architecture for the Senses, the first major retrospective of the Sri Lankan architect in over 20 years, co-curator Johan Deurell explains why the ‘tropical modernist’ label has confused Bawa’s legacy.
Geoffrey Bawa is one of Asia’s most prolific 20th-century architects, known for projects such as the Bentota Beach Hotel, the Kandalama Hotel and his own houses, Number 11 and Lunuganga.
Bawa’s work is often described as tropical modernist, as it is seen to blend Western modernist principles with Sri Lankan vernacular traditions and materials.
But Deurell said he and his co-curators deliberately stayed away from this label, which was coined by Western architects and scholars and is closely associated with British colonialism.
“We wanted to avoid the idea of tropical modernism,” he told Dezeen.
“It comes with so much baggage. But it’s also not the most useful tool to discuss Geoffrey Bawa’s work with.”

As one of the Vitra Design Museum’s in-house curators, Deurell oversaw the show with Shayari de Silva, chief curator for the Geoffrey Bawa Trust, and Ikko Yokoyama, a senior curator at M+ in Hong Kong.
The exhibition offers a broader understanding of Bawa’s legacy, highlighting qualities that set him apart from the modernists.
For instance, it highlights how his buildings worked with existing landscape conditions.
“He built with nature rather than against it,” Deurell said.
“Modernist site planning often involved clearing the land, rather than having buildings like Kandalama Hotel, which snakes its way around a rift.”
The show also spotlights the sustainability of Bawa’s designs, in terms of both ecology and socioeconomics.
His buildings harnessed the skills of local craftspeople and were built with locally sourced materials. They also featured climate-conscious strategies for shading and ventilation.
This approach is particularly relevant today, said Deurell, as the building industry faces the reality of a climate crisis.
“His ideas on landscape and ecology was really at the forefront,” the curator said. “He had a holistic approach to architecture and he built with nature in mind.”

The exhibition features a scenography designed by Lina Ghotmeh, who was named Dezeen Awards’ Architect of the Year 2026. It contains over 250 exhibits, including drawings, models, archive photography and furniture.
Among the highlights is a new photography series by Iwan Baan, capturing 11 of Bawa’s buildings as never seen before.
Drone photography offers a look at Bawa’s Number 11 house and University of Ruhuna from above, while other shots show people occupying the Lighthouse Hotel and Bentota Beach Hotel.
Furniture on show includes a mix of original Bawa designs and versions of well-known modernist pieces remade with local materials.
As Deurell explains, these were not intended as copies. The originals were not available in Sri Lanka at that time, so Bawa simply commissioned replicas for use in his interiors.
Standouts include a version of the Barcelona Chair by Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich, with a welded iron frame and stripy upholstery fabric designed by Sri Lankan designer Barbara Sansoni.
“Bawa collaborated with artists throughout his career, ” said Deurell, pointing to long-standing collaborations with Ena de Silva and Laki Senanayake as well as Sansoni.

“All of these artists ran their practices as social enterprises, so they would employ villagers and train them in a craft,” stated the curator. “It shows the social consciousness within his practice.”
Drawings bring another dimension to the exhibition. Highly detailed maps, floor plans and sectional drawings emphasise the relationship between building and landscape.
Although these drawings were mostly produced after the buildings were completed, they offer an insight into the architect’s mindset.
Deurell points to a quote by Bawa, where he talks about landscape elements as being part of “the total picture”.
“They are just as important as the architecture itself”, he said.
All archive material is courtesy of Geoffrey Bawa and Lunuganga Trusts.

Geoffrey Bawa: Architecture for the Senses is on show at the Vitra Design Museum in Weil am Rhein, Germany, from 26 September 2026 to 28 February 2027, before a run at M+ in Hong Kong from June 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design exhibitions around the world.
Photography is by Iwan Baan unless otherwise indicated.

items.title: Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson launches last-ditch High Court appeal
paragraphs: Australia's mushroom killer Erin Patterson has launched a final legal bid to overturn her murder convictions and avoid dying in jail.
Erin Patterson, 52, was last year found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023.

Last month, in Victoria's Court of Appeal three judges dismissed an appeal against her convictions and threw out the possibility she could be released on parole – saying her crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms".
She has now made a last-ditch application to the High Court to look at her case.
Patterson had 28 days to file an application for special leave to appeal to the High Court, a deadline which expired on Friday.
She wants the country's top judges to examine both her conviction and sentence - but the court does not have to agree to look at the case. It only hears appeals in about 10% of cases.

After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms which she had tracked down, foraged and prepared.
Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.
He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.

Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.

Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face. This glimmer of hope of freedom was thrown out by the appeal judges, who ruled she should never be released.
She had argued her conviction was unsafe on seven grounds - including a hotel booking mix up which saw the jury stay in the same place as the prosecution, a key police witness and the media.
Her lawyers said this was "catastrophic" and undermined the integrity of her trial, but the appeal court judges dismissed all the grounds for appeal.

items.title: Erin Patterson launches high court appeal bid over mushroom murder convictions
paragraphs: Erin Patterson has applied to the high court seeking leave to appeal after a failed bid last month to overturn her triple murder conviction.
Patterson, 52, was found guilty last year of the murders of her estranged husband’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, and his aunt Heather Wilkinson, after she hosted them for lunch.
She was also convicted of the attempted murder of Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who survived eating beef wellington laced with death cap mushrooms after spending weeks in hospital.
On Friday afternoon, her lawyers filed her application to try to overturn her convictions and life sentence in the high court, a source confirmed to Guardian Australia.

Victoria’s court of appeal last month ruled Patterson’s appeal against her convictions should be dismissed. But it granted an appeal by the director of public prosecutions against Patterson’s sentence, finding that her original sentence of life imprisonment with a non-parole period of 33 years was too lenient. She was resentenced to life without parole.

“This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated and stands to be denounced in the strongest terms,” court of appeal justices Lesley Taylor, Stephen McLeish and Peter Kidd found in their judgment on 30 October.

“Necessarily, we have given the question whether it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period anxious consideration, in light of the gravity of such a conclusion and the different view to which the experienced sentencing judge came.
“But the features of the offending … lead each of us to conclude that this is a case of such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period.”
Patterson had 28 days from that judgment to apply for special leave to appeal to the high court, a period that ended on Friday.
Her written application for leave to appeal is expected to be determined by all seven high court justices.
If they cannot make a determination based on the written application, the justices can refer the application to a hearing for oral argument.
Applications are typically referred to the justices the week before a sitting period and considered that Monday, before decisions are published the following Thursday.
The high court’s last sitting period of the year runs from 30 November to 11 December, meaning Patterson could know the fate of her application within the next fortnight.
If not, the court does not sit again until 1 February. The court would not comment on the application.
Patterson’s lawyers had previously argued in the court of appeal that her convictions should be overturned on seven grounds, all but two of which were dismissed without leave to appeal granted.

The two grounds for which Patterson was granted leave to appeal, but were also dismissed, related to the sequestration of the jury during their deliberations, and the telephone cell tower and iNaturalist evidence presented during her trial.
The court heard that the jury in the case stayed at the same motel as the police informant and DPP staff while they were deciding on their verdicts in the trial.

Patterson argued that this represented “a fundamental irregularity … that has fatally undermined the integrity of the verdicts and requires the quashing of the convictions and an order for a re-trial so that justice can not only be done but be seen to be done”.

The second ground was that cell tower evidence, which suggested Patterson could have been in Loch and Outtrim after death cap mushroom sightings were reported in the towns on the citizen science website iNaturalist, should not have been adduced in her trial as it was either irrelevant, or its relevance was “outweighed by its unfair prejudice”.

items.title: UK papers: 'Scores' of Labour MPs oppose Rosebank and 'Shameless Huw'
paragraphs: The Guardian reports that Labour's internal divisions over the Rosebank oil field have "spilled into the open", external, after nearly 100 MPs signed a letter opposing the project. One frontbencher - who is said to be considering resigning - tells the Times that, for some MPs, tackling climate change is their "number one reason for being Labour"., external But a colleague supportive of the project is quoted as saying that "the anti-crowd are resorting to internal party politics".

The "participation fee" the UK has to pay to the EU as part of the post-Brexit reset deal is described in the Financial Times as a "pay-to-play" charge, external. The details of the deal also include what the paper calls a "Farage clause", which EU diplomats say is aimed at deterring Reform or the Conservatives from "ripping up" the agreement.

The governor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, tells the Times that banks are likely to pass on the cost of higher taxes to customers., external Last month, the Chancellor John Healey used his first Budget to hike levies on banks. But the paper says they could respond by offering more expensive loans or less generous interest rates on deposits.

The front page of the Daily Telegraph features the news that the military cannot track down half of the reservists it may mobilise, external - because the Ministry of Defence has lost their addresses. The Liberal Democrat chair of the all-party parliamentary group on rearmament tells the Times, external: "The government has launched its Be Ready campaign, asking us to be ready. It would be nice if they were ready".

And "Shameless" is the headline in the Sun, which says that Huw Edwards is being allowed to "explain away his horrific crimes" in a new "poor me" interview, external with Channel 4. The move is also criticised by the charity, Victim Support - which tells the Daily Mirror, external that "giving such a platform to a convicted sex offender will cause significant distress to victims and survivors". Channel 4 has insisted it holds Edwards to account in the documentary.

items.title: Alan Jones defence opens and closes in space of a few hours as indecent assault trial draws to a close
paragraphs: Alan Jones’s defence in his indecent assault and sexual touching trial has lasted only a few hours, with closing submissions in the long-running case due next week.

Jones’s barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC opened the defence case on Friday by stating, “I am not calling the defendant,” ending months of speculation about whether the former broadcaster, 85, would give evidence.
Jones has pleaded not guilty to 19 indecent assault and two sexual touching charges brought by five men who allege the offences took place between 2003 and 2020.
On Friday afternoon, after a break for the crown to read the defence submissions, Bashir presented two medical reports and a restaurant receipt, along with a corresponding bank statement.
After half an hour of objections to the documents by the crown, Bashir said: “Your honour, that closes the defence.”
No witnesses were called on Friday although some defence witnesses were called by the crown during the four-month trial.
The prosecutor Georgina Wright objected to the restaurant documents on the basis they carried no weight “whatsoever” – but judge Glenn Walsh admitted them.
Bashir argued the documents were relevant to the “credibility and reliability” of complainant C, who alleged he was assaulted by Jones at an end of year lunch at a north shore restaurant.

The alleged victim, a former driver for Jones, earlier told the court that Jones had instructed him to sit next to him and then spent the entire lunch with his left hand under the table either on his leg or on his penis over his pants.
The defence has argued the end of year lunch took place at a different north shore restaurant and presented a receipt for that establishment for $1,247.
Jason Morrison, a former 2GB colleague of Jones, earlier told the court he recalled a different name of the restaurant to complainant C and other witnesses.
“This has been a big trial,” Walsh said. “There are something like 290 or so exhibits and about 5,000-odd pages worth of transcripts.”
The judge gave the parties four days to prepare closing submissions, which are scheduled to begin on Thursday.

The judge-only trial has sat for 70 days at Sydney’s Downing Centre local court and the defendant has been present for all the evidence. Jones has sat in the front row next to his solicitor Bryan Wrench.
The youngest complainant, known as complainant A, alleged that Jones touched him on the bottom when he stayed overnight at Jones’s Fitzroy Falls farm when he was 17.

The trial has heard from a prominent athlete, known as complainant M, who told the court Jones would welcome him with a hug and a kiss on the cheek and use flattering terms like “champion” and “beautiful man”.

M told the court the defendant kissed him and pressed his genitalia against his thigh causing him to shout out “OK mate” and flee Jones’s harbourside apartment. He alleged that on another occasion Jones kissed him on the side of his mouth at an awards night.
Jones has denied all wrongdoing and said the allegations were either baseless or distorted the truth.
Bashir has said the alleged victims were egged on to complain by media rivals, and that their reliability and credibility were questionable.
Media rivals, Bashir alleged in her opening statements, included shock jock Ray Hadley and Sydney Morning Herald columnist Peter FitzSimons.

items.title: Race hate exploded in this Spanish town last year. Now its residents are bracing for more
paragraphs: Sitting on a park bench, taking in the sunny day, Naima reflected on all that had seemingly changed since she moved to Spain three decades earlier.

Back then, the Moroccan national had felt warmly welcomed by Spaniards. “I had never, at any point in my life, felt like there was racism,” she said. “But now things are changing. And the blame lies with rightwing politics.”

Over the years, she has steadily watched as a growing crop of politicians sought to win votes by demonising migrants, minorities and Muslims. The impact reverberated deeply in places such as Torre-Pacheco, whose fertile fields and constant demand for farmhands has long attracted workers from around the world.

“They peddle racism, and lots of people end up suffering,” said Naima, 53. “Here everyone knows me, but others speak of being treated differently, looked at in a certain way, or having gestures made at them.”
On Sunday, Spain is set to gain a glimpse of how deeply engrained these divisions have become as voters cast their ballots in a snap general election.

Most polls suggest the government of the Socialist leader, Pedro Sánchez, will be replaced by a rightwing coalition led by the conservative People’s party (PP) and supported by the far-right, anti-immigration Vox party. If so, it will be the first time that a far-right party has governed Spain since the return to democracy after the death of General Franco.

The possibility has left many in Torre-Pacheco, where migrants make up at least 30% of the 42,000 residents, worried about what comes next, according to cafe owner Allal Abourayane. “A lot of people are afraid of Vox,” he said. “They’re worried about what the party will mean for their children’s futures.”

In the lead-up to Sunday’s vote, the far-right party has pointedly targeted people from north African countries, announcing plans that include revising the nationalisation of more than 300,000 people of Moroccan origin and limiting the number of pupils from “other cultures or with insufficient command of Spanish” in classrooms.

Other Vox initiatives have more broadly targeted all migrants, such as a promise to impose a tax on remittances similar to the one launched last year in the US by Donald Trump’s administration. Last year, a party official briefly floated the idea of deporting up to 8 million people of foreign origin, including the children of immigrants, before the party backtracked. In September, another official reportedly told the country’s major corporations of plans to lower the cost of housing by expelling 1.5 million migrants.

The PP has responded by hardening its discourse, with promises to bar the burqa and niqab in public spaces and expand the process of residency renewal to include Spanish language tests and constitutional knowledge questions. This sparked wider questions as to what this could mean for some British or American pensioners and digital nomads living in Spain.

On the tree-lined streets of Torre-Pacheco, many were swift to point to the risks of this discourse. They speak from first-hand experience: the Murcian town made headlines last year when extremists from across Spain arrived, intent on exacting revenge after reports of an assault on an elderly man.

The pensioner had told local media he believed his attacker was of north African origin. This sent racist messaging on social media rocketing by 1,500%, according to tracking by the central government.

In Torre-Pacheco, locals watched in shock as the hatred leapt off social media platforms and on to their streets. As baton-wielding groups roamed the town for two nights, determined to “hunt” down people with foreign origins, the mayor called on migrants to stay indoors. Some refused, leading to clashes between the extremists and small groups of residents, at times carrying Moroccan flags.

At least 10 people were arrested, including three young men of north African background who were linked to the attack on the elderly man. Six Spaniards and a Moroccan national were also detained on accusations including assault, public disorder and hate crimes.

More than 16 months later, many are still coming to grips with those events. “The hatred came from the outside,” said Antonio León, a politician with the Independent party and mayor of the city from 2015 to 2023. “We’ve always lived together peacefully. People here didn’t take part in what happened, they understand the social and cultural diversity we have in this town.”

Even so, Torre-Pacheco had now become synonymous with extreme hate, he said. “The name Torre-Pacheco has been tainted. Everywhere I go in Spain, I say I’m from here, and they associate me with what happened.”

The Socialist-led central government was unequivocal in linking the events to the discourse of the far right. Its representative in Murcia, Mariola Guevara, said at the time: “We are normalising and giving space in institutions to radicalised, xenophobic, racist political organisations that constantly incite hatred and associate any kind of crime with immigration.”

As the blame game played out, those who had been targeted were left with lingering scars, said Abourayane. “Something has shifted here,” he said. “There are people who are still fearful or who don’t feel as comfortable here as they used to.”
It was a hint of how things could play out if Vox ends up securing a role in Spain’s central government, said Ousama Alalo, a political scientist from Torre-Pacheco.

The region of Murcia, whose economy is deeply reliant on migrant labour to sustain its global exports of fruit and vegetables, burst into the spotlight in the 2019 general elections after Vox emerged as the most popular party there. It soon became a prominent force in the region, transforming Murcia into what analysts have described as a “laboratory” for anti-migrant policies.
“The People’s party doesn’t have the necessary majorities to govern, so they look to Vox,” said Alalo. “So then what happens? Migrants become an easy bargaining chip.”

The result was a series of measures that have targeted Muslims and migrants in Murcia, from a ban on religious gatherings in sports centres that mainly affected Muslims in Jumilla to the scrapping of an extracurricular scheme that had allowed 350 children to learn Arabic and about Moroccan culture.

“They’ve been trying and testing things again and again – everything works here in Murcia,” said Alalo, who is among a group that has sought to counter these initiatives with the launch of the Platform for the Rights of the Muslim Community in Murcia. “To them we’re an easy target, we’re vulnerable and don’t have political power.”

The discrimination coming from the top levels of the regional government has added to the challenges for a population that was already deeply marginalised, Alalo added. “Right now we’re in the neighbourhood of San Antonio, where about 60% of the population hails from abroad and the average income is €10,600,” he said – less than half the average salary in the region.
“Many of them live in deteriorating houses, there’s a lot of school absenteeism and young people who can’t see a future for themselves, all while they’re being discriminated against.”
The result had left some migrants feeling as though they are waging battle on multiple fronts, according to Nabil Moreno, the president of the Al Manar Islamic Community in Torre-Pacheco.

Many were grappling with issues common across Spain, such as the soaring cost of housing, but with the added burden of being demonised by rightwing forces who seize on every conflict and every issue involving them, he said. “We’ve been in this city for 30 to 40 years, we have families, we contribute to the economy. Many of us have helped to grow the economy of this town. But of course, nobody talks about this.”

The view was echoed by Naima, who said the far right would probably do little to curb migration once in power. “We work in their homes, we work in their fields, we work in everything, they’re never going to throw us out,” she said.

Instead, she felt racism was being used to rally people behind a platform that would ultimately prove disastrous to many in Spain. “If the rightwing forces win the election, the middle class will be screwed. Retirees, schoolchildren – people will see their rights rolled back,” she said. “They’re not only going after foreigners. Hopefully people won’t be taken in by all of this.”

items.title: Former RAAF pilot convicted of murder after staging wife’s death as lawnmower accident
paragraphs: Former air force pilot Robert John Crawford has been found guilty of the murder of his wife after a jury accepted her death was staged as a fatal lawnmower accident.
Gasps and sobs could be heard in Brisbane supreme court on Friday after the jury returned a guilty verdict after deliberating since 10am on Tuesday.
Robert Crawford did not visually react to the verdict.
Frances Crawford’s body was found by paramedics at the bottom of a retaining wall near an overturned ride-on lawnmower at 4am.
Her husband was attempting to resuscitate her.
Robert Crawford was accused of murdering Frances Crawford by strangulation at the couple’s property, west of Brisbane, in the early hours of 30 July 2024, or late on 29 July.
Over three-and-a-half weeks, jurors heard evidence that included police forensic analysis of Frances Crawford’s injuries, texts between the couple and a UK forensic physician called by the defence.
They also visited the Crawfords’ hilltop home, surrounded by bushland in the Lockyer Valley.
Robert Crawford was described as a “love rat” who was motivated to kill his wife because he stood to lose financially in a divorce settlement brought on by his serial infidelity.
The former pilot faced the loss of his beloved $2m home and his early retirement plans if his wife followed through with divorce plans, jurors were told.
“He knew he stood to lose out,” crown prosecutor Chris Cook said.
“That’s why he was telling his lovers all about it.”
Referred to as a “master manipulator”, Robert Crawford embarked on a plan to make his wife’s death appear like a tragic accident, the jury was told.
“It was Mr Crawford who caused Mrs Crawford’s body to be at the bottom of the retaining wall of the property,” Cook said.
“It was Mr Crawford who also moved the lawnmower over the retaining wall.”
Robert Crawford’s defence had attacked the case against him as full of gaps filled in with speculation and wrongful suspicion.
“It is one of the weakest circumstantial cases you will ever see in a criminal court,” Robert Crawford’s barrister Saul Holt KC said.
The defence said he had engaged in multiple infidelities and lied about them but was trying to repair his marriage before his wife suffered an accident.
Robert Crawford had been busy with work calls and had let his wife move the lawnmower away from automated lawn sprinklers, Holt said.
But the prosecution said Frances Crawford would not have gone outside in her pyjamas in zero-degree weather to move an almost 250kg lawnmower that her children had never seen her use.
Robert Crawford, who was on bail throughout the trial, awaits sentencing.

items.title: MoD has no email addresses for about half of its reservists
paragraphs: The Ministry of Defence (MoD) is urging reservists to update their contact details, after it has emerged it does not have email addresses for about half of them.

The UK has an estimated 95,000 members in its strategic reserve force, which is made up of veterans who can be recalled in exceptional circumstances, but the MoD said it has only been able to send letters to around 50,000.
Open letters have been published on the ministry's website encouraging others to "reconnect".

On Thursday Defence Secretary Wes Streeting confirmed that the MoD had written to ex-military personnel to check their contact details and skills against the backdrop of a rising "threat environment".
His comments were made after The Times and the Telegraph reported that reservists who previously served in the Armed Forces had received letters telling them to prepare to be called up for war.

Streeting told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that this meant should they ever be needed "either for a national disaster here at home or for a more serious threat or conflict elsewhere" then they would "know where our strategic reserve is" and what their skills were.
"I want the country to be alert, not alarmed," he said.
The defence secretary also reiterated the importance of keeping "up to date" with reservists, and ensuring they had access to "further development opportunities".
On the MoD's website, the ministry said it was re-engaging with reservists due to a "more dangerous and unpredictable security environment."
It emphasised that the threshold for being recalled is high and reservists would not be used to fill routine staffing shortages in peacetime.
"It may be considered for serious national emergencies, warlike operations, preparations for war or a major crisis that requires additional military capability," it said.
Earlier this year, former Defence Secretary Lord Robertson said officials were failing to maintain records of military veterans who were entering the reserves.
"The Ministry of Defence at the present moment doesn't even know where most of them are," he said in April.
"So we need to round up those who are available and fit and willing to be able to do it."

Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton has made similar comments, warning in January that the UK did not have "an effective system of tracking and engaging" personnel after they had left the Armed Forces.

items.title: Watch: Truck hangs in the balance after losing control in wet conditions
paragraphs: A semi-truck carrying mail was left straddling an off-ramp and an overpass in Toledo, Ohio on Thanksgiving Day during severe weather in the US.

items.title: New Zealand election: final results show ruling coalition needs minor party to govern
paragraphs: The final results of New Zealand’s general election show the incumbent rightwing coalition will need the support of a centrist newcomer party to form a government, and to avoid sending the country back to the polls.

Preliminary results on 7 November handed the National party and its two coalition partners, the populist New Zealand First and libertarian Act parties, a slim two-seat majority, making the election too close to call until final votes were tallied.

On Friday, the electoral commission released the results from nearly 485,000 “special votes” – those cast from overseas or outside a voter’s electorate. National dropped two seats to 40, Labour stayed on 36 seats, the Greens picked up one seat to 17, Act had 13, New Zealand First 12, Opportunity seven and Te Pati Māori five.
The National-led bloc currently has 65 seats. In the 130-seat parliament, 66 seats are needed for a majority.

The revised results mean the National-led coalition has the only realistic path to power – if it can negotiate a deal with Opportunity. If it cannot, New Zealand will probably need to hold another election.

Three electorate seats changed hands after the special votes. Labour won Wairarapa off National with just 81 votes, and took Hamilton East from National with 173 votes. The Greens won Wellington Bays from Labour with 1,610 votes.

If National applies for a recount and wins back just one of those seats, it could return to power with a slim majority and without needing Opportunity. Applications for a recount must be made by 3 December, and results could take another five days.

Special votes in previous elections have favoured the left, and typically have cost the right one or two seats. Until Friday, a question mark hung over whether National would be able to govern comfortably alongside its coalition partners, or whether it would be forced to cut a deal with the Opportunity party – a newcomer centrist party that incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon had previously ruled out working with.
After the election, Luxon softened his stance on his initial rule-out, saying he intended to find common ground with the Opportunity party.
On Friday afternoon, Luxon said National will now begin formal negotiations with New Zealand First, Act and Opportunity, but he cautioned discussions would be “challenging” and could take some time.
“Getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly,” Luxon said. “Kiwis won’t thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart, or for sending them back to the polls.”

Lara Greaves, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington, said the prospect of New Zealand heading back to the polls was unprecedented, because negotiations between the four parties will be so complex.
“It’s not a 0% chance, it’s the highest chance we’ve ever had of it being another election,” she said.
Opportunity, led by Auckland businesswoman Qiulae Wong, has long said it will negotiate first with the party that secures the highest number of seats.

After the final results were announced, Wong confirmed she would speak with Luxon and that her party’s bottom-lines – which include climate and environment policies and capping political donations – were non-negotiable.
The party would focus on bringing New Zealanders a stable government, Wong told media, and she did not rule out heading back to the polls.

“Clearly stability is important. But setting that more hopeful and aspirational vision, where we can come together as much as possible as New Zealanders and move forward, I think is the priority,” she said.
Having Opportunity in parliament was a “pivotal moment” for the country, Wong said.
“I have every expectation that we will get in there and we will deliver, regardless of what shape the government takes.”

Previously, Wong has said its vision for a low-emissions future, and an inclusive New Zealand, will drive its final decision. Its five bottom-line issues include action on New Zealand’s supermarket duopoly, capping political donations, a 10-year cross-party plan for health, ending bottom trawling in the fishing industry and strengthening New Zealand’s climate commitments.

Negotiations with Opportunity could hit a snag with National’s coalition partner New Zealand First. On Friday, Wong confirmed she would not strike a deal if New Zealand First’s leader, the veteran politician Winston Peters, serves as foreign affairs minister – a position he has held on three occasions.
“We think that his behaviour over successive governments is not the kind of behavior that we expect of someone in that position,” she said.
In other points of tension, New Zealand First and Act have diametrically opposed climate policies, and Act are also unlikely to back Opportunity’s drive for political donation reforms.

Greaves said the Opportunity party will have to make difficult decisions over what it is prepared to gain, or lose. “For minor parties, it’s really hard to go into coalition, or be seen as being too close to a major party or propping up a government, and then turn around later and sell their brand ... as separate from that [major] party.”
Labour leader Chris Hipkins said he was proud the party had gained the highest share of the party vote, but was disappointed it could not deliver a change of government.
It is the second election Hipkins has lost, raising questions over his political future. Hipkins said a decision over his leadership would be made after a government had been formed.

New Zealand could be facing weeks of negotiations in what could become its first ever four-party coalition. In 2023, negotiations took five weeks. With Christmas just four weeks away, New Zealand may need to wait until 2027 to know the shape of its next government.

items.title: Threat from China looms large over Taiwan’s local elections
paragraphs: Taiwanese voters go to the polls on Saturday in closely watched local elections that will shape the fortunes of the ruling Democratic Progressive party (DPP) as it navigates an increasingly precarious set of relationships on the global stage.

Saturday’s vote will choose mayors, council members and other local leaders across 22 districts. Unlike the presidential elections, in which foreign policy is often a key issue, the local elections, held every four years, are largely focused on bread-and-butter issues such as housing affordability and wealth distribution.

Nevertheless, China looms large over the vote, which takes place against the background of intense military pressure from Beijing. China claims Taiwan as part of its territory despite never having ruled the self-governing island. Taiwanese officials have raised the alarm over thousands of incidents of suspected misinformation or election interference, and certain candidates have been subjected to harassment from the Chinese authorities. There have also been reports of hundreds of China-linked AI-generated videos spreading disinformation about Taiwanese politicians disliked by Beijing.

Beijing calls the allegations of election interference “completely fabricated”. Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for China’s Taiwan affairs office, said the allegations “stir up anti-China sentiment to win votes”.

Wei-Ting Yen, a political scientist at Academia Sinica, Taiwan’s national research academy, said: “Even though local elections are not about China, the outcome of local elections will have huge implications for cross-strait relations.”

Most races are a tight competition between a candidate from the ruling DPP and the main opposition party, the Kuomintang (KMT). The KMT promotes closer ties with Beijing, and its chair, Cheng Li-wun, travelled to China this year to meet Xi Jinping, China’s leader. Xi has vowed to unify China with Taiwan, and has not ruled out using military action to achieve that aim.
Yen said if the KMT loses some of its traditional strongholds, Beijing “may need to reconsider what is the most effective strategy for influencing Taiwanese people”.

One of the most contentious votes is the race for Taipei mayor, an office that has been held by the KMT for three decades. The DPP has selected as its challenger Puma Shen, a national legislator whom Beijing declared a “diehard separatist” in 2024. It is the first time a candidate under sanctions by Beijing has run to be mayor of Taiwan’s capital city. In the neighbouring New Tapei City race, the DPP’s Su Chiao-hui is also proving to be a ferocious challenger to the incumbent KMT.
Shen said in a recent interview that even if he didn’t win, the capital’s mayoral race was “a slap to China” because it proved that “democracy works here in Taiwan”.

Huang Bo-kai, a 23-year-old law student, said his top concern was cross-strait relations and how US-China relations were evolving. “The world’s three major powers are increasingly willing to flex their muscles: the US attacking Iran, Russia attacking Ukraine. I think Taiwan could very well be the next target [of China],” he told the Guardian.

Taiwan’s president, the DPP’s Lai Ching-te, is detested by Beijing and has taken a bolshier stance on cross-strait relations than his predecessor, Tsai Ing-wen, who was admired for her ability to drum up support in Washington while walking a delicate tightrope to avoid angering China.

Lai has pushed for greater spending on weapons to deter military aggression from China. The government has proposed a record 18% increase in defence spending for next year, including for drones and missiles, taking it above 1tn Taiwan dollars (£23bn) for the first time.

But many Taiwanese voters would rather that money was spent on more immediate economic issues. Lev Nachman, a political scientist at National Taiwan University, said the national leaders of the DPP and KMT had been notably absent from the mayoral races, reflecting the extent to which campaigns were focused on local issues.

Going into the campaigns for the 2028 presidential elections, Lai would “try to take advantage of the momentum that [Shen] and Su have built for the DPP,” Nachman said, noting that support for those candidates would not necessarily translate into support for Lai.
Tony Yeh, a Taipei man in his 70s, said: “To put it simply, the authorities should do more to boost the economy and buy fewer weapons.”

Taiwan’s economy has boomed this year, largely thanks to the pivotal role that its semiconductor industry plays in the global artificial intelligence rally. The economy grew by more than 14% in the first nine months of the year, the fastest rate in 50 years. But nearly 70% of workers earned less than the average monthly wage of 49,152 Taiwan dollars (£1,137) in the same period.
Yeh said: “Most traditional industries are having a really tough time.”

William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “The issues that really are going to determine their votes are livelihood issues including the stagnant wage, the astronomically high housing price, the affordability issue, and how the government can better make sure Taiwan’s incredible economic boom fuelled by the global AI growth is going to be distributed more evenly.”
Other voters have more niche concerns. Walking her dog in a park, Kuo Wei-tong, a nail salon worker, said policies affecting pets were among her top concerns.
“People are having fewer children and getting more cats and dogs,” she said. “I think that’s something worth giving serious consideration to as well.”

items.title: From £250 job to £9,000 bill: Inside the rogue trader networks scamming customers at scale
paragraphs: Organised networks of rogue plumbers and electricians have been scamming people on a large scale, a BBC investigation has found.

Nessar Khawaja, who used the online name ThatGuyNess, regularly posted TikTok videos showing his work as a plumber, explaining how he made thousands of pounds from "desperate" customers, and recruiting online to expand his network.
"Me and my team, we're top of the food chain," he said in one video.
The investigation found the 23-year-old is a key figure within an organised group that is systematically ripping off customers and teaching others to do the same.
The BBC put these allegations to Khawaja in writing. He denied any wrongdoing and said his social media posts were intended as light-hearted comedy that did not reflect how he operated in practice.
In a recorded phone call, Khawaja insisted he was an entertainer, was joking and that the BBC had "taken things out of context".
In another video, Khawaja made claims he had electricians working for him who made more than £40,000 a month.
"I've got 100-120 engineers. Imagine how much money I am making them and making from them," he said.
One of Khawaja's associates told an undercover BBC journalist during a secretly-recorded recruitment call that engineers working for them had to hand over 60% from every job to the network.
After being approached for comment, TikTok said it banned the account for "breaching its rules on fraud and scams".
Trading Standards said the average rogue trader call-out scam now costs the victim about £10,000.
Clive, who lives in London, is undergoing treatment for cancer.
He said he had felt forced to pay the rogue trader who came to his home and charged £9,153 for installing an outdoor socket to fit garden lights he already owned.
An independent electrical expert told the BBC the job had not been done properly, was left in an unsafe state and should have cost no more than £250.
Clive said he no longer feels safe in his home.
He explained how he had searched for a local electrician on Google when his usual tradesperson was unavailable and came across Chriss Electrician Ltd.
Clive said the engineer spent about two hours at the property before presenting him with the bill.
He added he had felt pressured into paying as the work had already been completed.
He went to his local bank branch to move money between accounts before returning home and making the payment through the engineer's portable card reader.
Despite his doubts about the costs, Clive said he had feared what might happen if he refused to pay.
"If I hadn't paid him, I thought something might happen," he said.
"When people come to the door now, I think, 'Oh God, who's that?' I don't feel safe any more."
Like Clive, another man, who the BBC has named as Tom, felt he had no choice but to settle the bill when he mistakenly called a rogue trader to his property in Essex after finding a leak.
He says he was initially quoted £49 over the phone after calling a listing at the top of Google purporting to be an established business.
But on arrival, the plumber increased the call-out fee to £250 and the costs kept on climbing.

"He charged us for the first load of repairs, and then the second load with the water cylinder. Basically, he was running my taps constantly saying, 'Look, it's coming out this hot', which caused me to panic."
By the end, the plumber presented a bill for £6,237.60.
"I noticed afterwards that the invoice said Ibby & Co. Ltd. That was when alarm bells started ringing because I had never heard of that company. It wasn't the company I called out, essentially."
Lee, not his real name, spent a year working for Khawaja as a plumber until, he says, his conscience got the better of him.
"It got a bit too much for me," he said. "I didn't like scamming people. So, I left.
"I've worked for London's biggest plumbing company and, no word of a lie, this lot have more jobs. They're giants."
Rather than relying on solid reputations and recommendation, rogue traders rely on search engine traffic.
They either pay to get their details at the top of Google, which means they are seen first, or they mimic the names of reputable companies by making tiny changes to the business name.
Reached by the BBC's undercover journalist posing as a plumber seeking to work with them, one of Khawaja's associates said: "We're a lead company. We'll send you jobs, and then you go to the jobs.
"We sort the jobs through online advertisement. Usually we'll try and get emergencies so we can charge more. You make up the pricing."
The associate told the undercover reporter they had to charge in the region of £400 for every job, regardless of what work was actually needed.
Both Clive and Tom reported what happened to the Metropolitan Police and Essex Police.
Khawaja said he was not a party to the phone call with the undercover journalist and could not comment on its contents.
He said the alleged statements did not reflect how he operates.
He separately told the BBC in the recorded phone call: "You guys should know I am an entertainer and you guys are taking it out of context."
"I am clearly joking and I'm entertaining and I am engaging with the comments, it is not literal," he added.
He said the right of reply sent to him by the BBC contained "false information which has nothing to do with me".

items.title: The young hikers finding friendship and fresh air offline
paragraphs: The wild landscape of Glencoe in Scotland is where Mohannad has found calm

After years toiling all day at a desk as an aerospace engineer in Istanbul, 26-year-old Mohannad Najjar decided to swap his screen for a degree in nature and theology in Cambridge and a volunteering gig as a scout leader.
He walks in the countryside every weekend and has hiked in wild locations in the Scottish Highlands, which he credits with helping him think clearly.
"I just want to see something that's untouched, to be in nature," he says. "When you come in from a hike or a walk, you just feel different."
Najjar is one of a growing number of young hikers in the UK. Nearly 9% of 16-34 year-olds are regular hill walkers or hikers, according to Sport England, up from 2.3% eight years ago.
Watch: Why we're swapping screens for scenery
Many young walkers' groups from Inverness to Nottinghamshire have seen their membership rise over the past two years, according to the Ramblers walking charity.
Demand has nearly doubled for a course it offers teaching map and compass skills to 18-25 year-olds.
Many who sign up want to ditch their phones and no longer rely on a blue dot to navigate, says Alistair Cooper, who leads the Out There Award programme.
"There's a cohort that missed out on outdoorsy, fun stuff during Covid. They want to get out and explore - but often don't know where to start."

Some 83% of people in the UK live in towns and cities, according to the UN, where research suggests noise, traffic, stress and information overload put huge demands on our brains, affecting our mental health.

"Nature is the environment we are adapted to, and being close to it brings benefits such as improved wellbeing, brain function and physical performance," says Dr Danny Longman, lecturer in human evolutionary physiology from Loughborough University.
"There is a theory that simply paying attention to trees and leaves allows our brains to recover," he says.
For Deborah Odutayo, her navigation skills are now one of her biggest achievements
Environmental science student Deborah Odutayo, 24, described going through "an identity crisis".
"I didn't see myself as someone who works behind a desk from 9 to 5," she said.
After solo travelling, Odutayo had dreams of living abroad but didn't know how to finance them. So she decided to change her mindset.
"I just need to be outside, essentially. That's how I started like doing solo hikes and stuff. It feels very therapeutic - mostly for my mental health."
She's since hiked in Kent and the Peak District, among other locations, and camped with an outdoor group in Dorset.
Learning how to get around without using her phone or digital maps is something she is proud of, saying it feels "more intentional and grounding".
No matter the weather, Miranda Chambers-Reid gets outside any time she can
Walking gives people "an instant friend group" when life is in flux, says Miranda Chambers-Reid, who leads a Ramblers' walking group for people in their 20s and 30s in Sheffield.
"They don't want all of their friends to be work friends or old uni friends," she says.
As a mum of a seven-year-old, she made a similar decision when she joined: "I thought, I don't want all of my friends to be mum friends."
Over the last two years, the group has increased from 250 members to 350.
For some it's more about a sense of achievement says Chambers-Reid, who herself covers about 30 miles of walking a week.
"I work in an office and I can't see the sky so whenever possible I will be outside."
For Sej Chauhan, 27, her walking group is about making connections while keeping costs down.
"There's a growing interest in socialising in ways that don't involve drinking alcohol or spending lots of money," she says.
Chauhan set up Girls Who Walk in her home town of Leicester after a lonely year spent studying in Bristol.
To make that experience easier for others, the group's focus is on walking in parks, talking and female companionship. And there's always a stop for coffee.
In two years, the group has grown to more than 300 members - most are 25-35 years old.
"There's no pressure, no barriers with walking," Chauhan says. "Social media can often fill the void outside of work and home, but it doesn't provide the connection that people are craving."
Walking together in Leicester's Victoria Park - the Girls Who Walk group
Not everyone can access green space easily or has the time to go hiking because of work or childcare commitments.
Here are Longman's tips for getting your nature fix as close as possible to home:
Move in nature - an urban park or garden will do
Listen to the sounds of the elements, like wind, rain, birdsong
Smell the distinctive scent of pine forests, breathe in the outdoors
If you are indoors, bring the sounds and imagery of nature into your home using apps

items.title: Met Police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly convicted over attack on UK couple
paragraphs: A Kenyan woodcutter who was wrongly convicted and sentenced to death over an attack on a British couple has told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Police involved in the case destroyed his life.
Somali gunmen broke into David and Judith Tebbutt's beach bungalow on the Kenyan coast in 2011. They shot David dead and abducted Judith, holding her captive in Somalia for six months.
Met detectives flew to Kenya to assist the investigation. Their evidence helped convict Ali Kololo, who spent more than a decade in prison before his conviction was overturned.
Kololo is suing the Met, claiming a senior officer, former Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, gave misleading evidence at his trial and acted unlawfully to secure his conviction.
In his first media interview, he told the BBC about his 15-year ordeal and his fight for compensation, which the Met is challenging in court.
We meet on Lamu, a small island off Kenya's northern coast, once a thriving Swahili port. People and goods are still carted through its narrow stone streets by donkey rather than car.
It was here, in 2013, that Kololo was sentenced to death.
Standing at the jetty, where police once brought him ashore in handcuffs, he relishes being free. But he is struggling to rebuild his life.
"Everything was taken from me. I'm starting from zero. I don't think I'll ever go back to who I was before," he says.

Before his arrest, Kololo lived with his wife and their three young children. He had once worked as a groundskeeper at the resort where the Tebbutts were staying, but by 2011 he earned his living felling trees in a local forest and selling the wood.
"My life was very good," he says. "I was fending for myself, taking good care of my family."
Within 24 hours of the attack, Kenyan police had arrested him.
"I was beaten with clubs and thrown into a car," he says. "They beat me for days, burning me with cigarettes, forcing me to confess to things. They subjected me to torture like no other."
Kololo could not read or write. He says police made him put his thumbprint on a statement claiming he had led the attackers to the Tebbutts.
"I didn't understand anything," he says, calling the statement "a mountain of lies". "I signed it without knowing what it was because of the state they had put me in".
The Kenyan police told us it "at all times strives to work within the law". Kololo is not suing them.

Within days of the attack, a team of Met officers, led by then Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, arrived to support the Kenyan investigation. The UK government had instructed the officers not to accept information from the Kenyan authorities that had been obtained by interrogating detainees.
But Hibberd requested Kololo's statement and later relied on it when giving evidence for the prosecution at his trial.
In court, Hibberd also presented evidence linking Kololo to the attack. He told the Kenyan court Kololo had been wearing a type of shoe that matched footwear marks found in the sand at the resort.

The officer who had arrested Kololo said he was barefoot when he was handed to police. Hibberd did not disclose that the Met's own forensic examination could not establish whether the shoe in question had made the marks.

At the trial, Kololo did not initially have a lawyer. He had to cross-examine all the prosecution witnesses himself, including Hibberd, through an interpreter who spoke Swahili, which was not Kololo's first language.
"I believe I was framed because I am a poor man and I did not have the strength or means to fight for myself," Kololo says.

Kololo was convicted of kidnap and robbery with violence - the only person ever convicted in connection with the attack. He spent three years on death row before his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.
He recalls seeing his prison file. In the space for the expiry date, someone had written "death".
"I was completely heartbroken. I believed I could be executed at any moment, and I would never see my family, my children, ever again."

Years later, the UK's Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) established that Hibberd had omitted significant forensic evidence at the trial. It found that he would have had a case to answer for gross misconduct, but he could not face disciplinary proceedings because he had retired from the force. At the time, his lawyer said Hibberd absolutely disagreed with the report's findings.

In April 2023, Kenya's High Court quashed Kololo's conviction, because of doubts over the prosecution's evidence. This followed years of work by the legal charity Reprieve and a Kenyan lawyer, Alfred Olaba, who represented him for free.
They were supported by Judith Tebbutt, who believed Kololo was innocent. In an interview with the BBC in 2022, she said he had been scapegoated by Scotland Yard.
"He was not there on the night. He was not part of the group that held me. They've put this man in prison without any real evidence."

More than three years after his release, Kololo says he is still living with the effects of his torture and decade in prison. As we walk the narrow streets of Lamu's old town, his thin frame moves stiffly. He is on edge. "My mind is not good," he says. "I have not recovered."
He remembers being kept in a filthy, bedbug-ridden cell with up to eight other inmates, which he thought he would never leave. Twice he contracted tuberculosis and nearly died.
Kololo is now too frail to do the woodcutting he once relied on to make a living. He tries to grow enough to eat on the land around his home, but erratic rain makes it difficult.
"I have nothing. On the days I get food, I eat, and on the days I don't, I endure."

He lives alone in a mud hut. His wife divorced him after he went to prison, and their children went to live with his mother. They dropped out of school because the family could not pay the fees. Kololo says they were not allowed to visit him in prison. When he was released, they barely remembered him, especially his youngest.
"They were too young. Only now are they starting to regain the memory that 'this is our father who disappeared'," he says. "If it weren't for my mother, my children might have died."
For much of our time together, Kololo is remarkably upbeat. He trusts that his lawyers and God will deliver him justice. But when we talk about the Met, his demeanour shifts.
"I am extremely angry with the police," he says. "I'm also angry with the Kenyan Police. They collaborated to incriminate me. What [Hibberd] said destroyed my entire life and my children's lives."
The Met has not apologised to Kololo or admitted wrongdoing. The force is contesting his compensation claim, which his lawyers say could take years to resolve.
"These people falsely accused me. Do I not deserve something?" he asks.

The Met told the BBC that neither they nor Hibberd wanted to comment on Kololo's claim, but it said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Kololo, Mrs Tebbutt, her family and all those who have been affected by this terrible crime. The Metropolitan Police remains committed to supporting the Kenyan authorities in any way that may be possible, in order to get justice for Mrs Tebbutt and her late husband."
Preetha Gopalan, Reprieve's head of UK litigation, describes the Met's behaviour in Kololo's case as "egregious".

"They've spent 10 years trying to evade accountability in every way possible, now dragging him through the courts," she says. "It's possible for them to do the right thing, but they are unwilling, and so this ordeal continues to haunt Kololo and his family."
"Even if I get a billion shillings, I will never be the same," Kololo says. "But if I get the justice I deserve, I can help my children and take care of myself when I am an old man."
