items.title: China extends suspension period for its ban on export of critical minerals to US
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

China has extended for another two months its suspension of a ban on exports of several critical minerals to the United States, a move analysts say roughly aligns with the timing of the current U.S.-China trade truce.

China’s Ministry of Commerce said Tuesday that from November 28 through January 27, 2027, it will continue to suspend its ban on U.S.-bound exports of gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials, which are used in semiconductors and defense systems. It also will keep on hold stricter reviews of graphite exports to the United States. Other export controls on the minerals remain in place.

U.S. officials have repeatedly described critical minerals as a national security priority and urged world economic powers to diversify their supply chains to reduce reliance on China for critical minerals.

Bonnie Glaser, managing director of the Indo-Pacific Program at the Washington-based German Marshall Fund of the United States, told Voice of America in an email that she reads this "as an extension of the suspension of US-specific restrictions, not an elimination of China's export-control regime... General licensing requirements remain, and the separate prohibition on exports to US military users or for military purposes remains in effect.”
Glaser added that “The extension approximately aligns the expiration date with the expiration of the tariff deal. It is only for two months.”

China introduced the export controls on certain “dual-use items” to the U.S. in December 2024. The move was widely seen as retaliation for then-President Joe Biden’s expanded restrictions on exporting chip technology and equipment to China.

China imposed export controls on seven rare earth elements in April 2025, as trade tensions between the world’s two largest economies escalated following President Donald Trump’s announcement of global reciprocal tariffs. Beijing broadened its rare earth restrictions again in October of that year.

After President Donald Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Busan, South Korea, in late October 2025, the two leaders reached an understanding on trade issues. The following month, China announced a one-year suspension of the export-control measures.

Earlier this month, as some of the pauses were due to expire, China’s Commerce Ministry announced a two-month extension. The ministry’s notice on Tuesday extended the suspension of several restrictions outlined in the original 2024 announcement, which had been set to expire Friday.
Washington and Beijing have been negotiating to extend the current trade truce, which is set to expire on January 10, 2027.

On Wednesday, Washington announced plans to levy new tariffs on major trading partners over excess manufacturing capacity, with China facing a 20% tariff. He Yadong, a spokesman for China’s Commerce Ministry, said Thursday that China asked the U.S. to return to the “track of resolving disputes through dialogue and consultations.” He added that China “reserves the right to take necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.”

President Trump met again with President Xi earlier this month in Shenzhen, China, while attending the APEC summit. Xi is expected to meet again with Trump in December when he travels to Miami for the G20 summit, which would mark the fourth face-to-face meeting between the two leaders this year.

items.title: How much of the sharp fall in UK immigration is due to Labour’s policies?
paragraphs: David Cameron was the leader of the opposition when he made a comment on overall migration that was used to interrogate every Tory leader for the next 14 years.

Asked in January 2010 on the BBC by the interviewer Andrew Marr to address comments made by the archbishop of Canterbury calling for the population to remain under 70 million, Cameron said net immigration levels of 200,000 a year were “too much”.
“We would like to see net immigration in the tens of thousands rather than the hundreds of thousands,” he said.

It became a full-blown promise in Cameron’s Tory manifesto that year; and it was there again when he won the 2015 general election, alongside a promise to hold an EU referendum. And the promise was repeated by Theresa May in 2017 as she narrowly defeated the then Labour leader, Jeremy Corbyn.
Both Tory leaders struggled with the actual net migration numbers, which fluctuated between 195,000 and 303,000.

Boris Johnson was pressed on whether he would revive Cameron’s pledge, and his 2019 manifesto said “overall numbers will come down”. Rishi Sunak, five years later, said he would like to see the figures get to tens of thousands but his manifesto promised that “numbers would fall every year”.
It has led to some crowing by Labour – and frustration from the Tories – that numbers have finally dipped below six figures under the current government.
Migration analysts said the Tories struggled throughout the 2010s because the UK was a full member of the EU and had no way of controlling inward EU migration.
EU citizens made up a majority of immigration and net migration in the run-up to the 2016 EU referendum. Since 2022, however, EU net migration has been negative.
As the UK emerged from the Covid pandemic, Johnson opened the doors to non-EU migration and to Ukrainians and people from Hong Kong.

Madeleine Sumption, the director of the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said: “The previous government introduced some relatively liberal policies, including visa schemes for care workers, mid-skilled workers, Ukrainians and Hongkongers, and post-study work visas for international students.”
Several conditions that enabled Labour to achieve net migration of below 100,000 did not exist for most of the time that the Tories were in power, Sumption said.
First, the UK was part of the EU for most of the Tories’ time in office and so it had little control over inward EU migration.

Second, the Office for National Statistics still relied on an older methodology for estimating migration of British citizens under the Conservatives. The new method, introduced last year, has taken “tens of thousands off the net migration figure”, she said.
Third, high migration under the previous government – and particularly under Johnson – has left a temporary legacy of high numbers of non-EU citizens leaving the UK under Labour.
“Non-EU emigration is around 130,000 higher than it was for most of the 2010s, and that is only possible because so many non-EU citizens arrived a few years ago,” she said.
The Tories throughout the 2010s were also under pressure from business and their own party to ensure that they could expand the economy and offer tax cuts, a former cabinet minister said.
“Migration was an issue then but not top of the agenda as it has been for the last few years,” they said.

The Tories claimed credit for the fall on Thursday, after introducing immigration restrictions in the last parliament. But Labour insisted it had been the one to “restore control” at the borders after net migration came close to 1 million under the Tories.
Sumption said the net migration figure could fall further but may also be expected to rise again.

“The lower figures we see today are partly a result of government policy but partly the result of methodological changes and an increase in emigration that is expected to be temporary. The numbers could still have further to fall but there is no reason to assume they will remain below 100,000 ffor ever, even if policy remains the same,” she said.

items.title: Art Mania by Kitty Hauser review – the gripping story of the man behind the Western Desert art movement
paragraphs: In 1971, Geoffrey Bardon, a 30-year-old school teacher and artist from Sydney, arrived at the remote Northern Territory Aboriginal settlement of Papunya, on Pintupi country, to take up a position at the government-run school.

Over the next 18 months, he set up a painting centre for the Aboriginal men, encouraging them to transpose ceremonial designs – traditionally inscribed on the sand or body – on to boards, and started selling the artworks on their behalf.

What occurred under his purview is generally heralded as the origin point of contemporary Aboriginal art, and the nationwide art centre system and multibillion dollar international market that sprung up around it.

There were, of course, already Aboriginal people making art – most famously, Albert Namatjira and the Hermannsburg painters. But the Papunya movement spearheaded the aesthetic of dots, concentric circles and lines that most international and non-Indigenous Australian audiences associate with Aboriginal art.

Like all cultural myths, this story bears close scrutiny – and Kitty Hauser’s Art Mania: Geoffrey Bardon and the Painting Men of Papunya is only the latest in a line of academic and journalistic investigations of the Papunya story.

Hauser focuses on Bardon – specifically his mental health and personal history, and how it influenced the reality and myth of Papunya. She breaks new ground by identifying the key role his brother Jim, an aspiring author, played in shaping the stories of both Geoff and Papunya art.

The subject matter is important, because Bardon became one of the key arbiters of Papunya art and the broader movement that arose around it, known as Western Desert art – often to the exclusion of the artists themselves.

Though the Bardon mythology has been interrogated and partially debunked in the decades since, aspects have proved persistent, including the significance of the paintings, how they are read, and the idea that they represent a uniquely “authentic” kind of Aboriginal art.

Hauser weaves a fascinating and gripping tale, partly because it is cast as a mystery, about something that happened to Bardon at Papunya that dramatically shaped his life thereafter and the stories he told about the painting men and their art.

Bardon and his brother were scions of a once-important family in Sydney’s Randwick, who grew up in a fairly unhappy home. Both had artistic ambitions – Geoff as a film-maker and Jim as an author – though each followed more traditional career paths (Jim was a solicitor).

Drawing on Geoff’s personal archives, his unpublished biography co-written with Jim, and conversations with friends, family and colleagues, Hauser paints a picture of someone who was in some ways well suited to the work he would undertake at Papunya: diffident, affable, generous, curious and enthusiastic. Someone who yearned to contribute something of importance to Australian culture.

Geoff saw his Papunya assignment as a romantic adventure and grist for his artistic mill. But the settlement was a shock to his system: a surreal and alienating environment for someone raised in white suburbia – from the regimented living arrangements and culture of the “welfare” apparatus, to the desert landscape and climate. It was also his first substantial encounter with Aboriginal people and culture, living in proximity to Pintupi, Luritja, Warlpiri, Anmatyerr, Kukatja and Arrernte people.

He was immediately struck by the gravitas of the men he encountered – including now-famous figures such as Tim Leura Tjapaltjarri and Clifford Possum Tjapaltjarri – and their ceremonies, stories and designs. He became wholly absorbed with the heroic notion of fostering a new strain of Aboriginal art.

Working outside his job remit, Bardon set up an ad hoc studio for the men, bought materials with his own money, taught them how to work with different kinds of paint, and gave them feedback on composition. He also started promoting and selling the art, establishing a valuable source of revenue for the artists and their communities.

Geoff’s arrival at Papunya seems to have coincided with a manic phase in his mental health, characterised by preternatural energy, excitement and grandiosity. It fuelled the painting project but was unsustainable and blossomed into insecurity and paranoia – about the settlement’s administrators, his colleagues and local art contacts.

And then came the crash: in 1972 Geoff suffered a nervous breakdown, and Jim had to travel to Papunya to bring him back to Sydney. In the aftermath, he was admitted to a private psychiatric hospital, where he underwent a controversial – and subsequently notorious – treatment called Deep Sleep Therapy, that inflicted lasting psychological damage.

The mania, breakdown and trauma of treatment profoundly shaped how Bardon told the story of Papunya. His diminished capacity also left the path open for Jim, who had his own baggage and ambitions, to take the lead role in Geoff’s various writings about the movement. Between them, they spun a mythology with Geoff at the centre, as a kind of tragic hero; a white saviour and truthteller who martyred himself for Aboriginal art. A narrative that eclipsed the agency of the painting men.

Hauser’s overarching thesis maps Geoff’s experience on to that of white Australia, and it’s true that many aspects of his story are emblematic of a kind of grander narrative of white narcissism and paternalism towards the continent’s First Peoples.
Art Mania also paints a troubling picture of how ignorant many of the people who were promulgating – and often profiting from – Aboriginal art were about the cultures underpinning it.
But Hauser’s book is most convincing and powerful as a cautionary tale: about who gets to tell stories – and the immense amount of personal baggage they bring to the telling.
Art Mania: Geoffrey Bardon and the Painting Men of Papunya by Kitty Hauser is available now (Giramondo; $39.95)

items.title: The Garmin Forerunner 265S is down to $300, its best price of the year
paragraphs: is a senior reporter and author of the Optimizer newsletter. She has more than 13 years of experience reporting on wearables, health tech, and more. Before coming to The Verge, she worked for Gizmodo and PC Magazine.

The Forerunner 265S may not be the newest or flashiest Garmin, but it’s one that I’ve always loved most in testing. For runners with smaller wrists, it fits nicely. The battery life is pretty good thanks in part to its OLED touchscreen. When I reviewed it a few years ago, I called it the Goldilocks of fitness watches at the time, and the only thing that bugged me was its price. But now that it’s down to $299.99 (a $150 discount off its MSRP) at Amazon and Best Buy for Black Friday, I can easily recommend it.
Garmin’s Forerunner 265S is identical to the standard 265, only it features a slightly better battery life and a smaller 42mm build for those with more petite wrists.

The neat thing about Garmins in general is that you really don’t need the latest models to get the most out of the company’s platform. Its watches tend to get firmware updates for several years after launch, which is how long the average Garmin user tends to hold on to theirs. This particular watch is best suited for folks who want something a bit slimmer and smaller, enjoy a pop of color, and want a little extra fitness tracking prowess — but don’t need the whole kit and caboodle that sends the price up by hundreds.

There are a few other Garmin models I like that are also on sale during Black Friday. I wish that I had 10 arms to fully vet every single last one, but alas. That said, here are some others that I have tested and recommend:

items.title: Five lighting designs listed by Marset on Dezeen Showroom
paragraphs: Spanish lighting brand Marset has showcased five of its products on Dezeen Showroom, including a mid-century reissue and a ceiling light that appears like a block of ice.
Marset‘s selection includes the Gambosa table lamp, created by designer Mathias Hahn to reinterpret the classic shade, stem and base as one smooth, glossy sculpture in steel and opal polycarbonate.

Gambosa is defined by its elegant composition, with a round-ended body that looks as if precariously balanced. It also features a considered cable design that sweeps down one side of the lamp like a signature.
It is distinguished by its select palette of colours, with combinations of orange, moss grey, black, pale pink and opal that evoke mid-century style combined with contemporary curation.
With the Lauro collection, Marset has revived a genuine 1970s design classic from its own catalogue, featuring chunky tubes of bent steel.

Created by designers P Aragay and J Pérez Mateo, the Lauro lighting comes in table, floor and wall variants. According to Marset, the range represents the technical achievements of a time when bending steel was a huge challenge.

Another of the highlights from Marset is the Ringo lighting, crafted by designer Joan Gaspar from transparent polycarbonate that is rotomoulded, giving it a dimpled texture reminiscent of a melting block of ice.
Available in flush-mounted or pendant styles, the design has a simple cylindrical shape, with scale and materiality bringing fresh life and visual impact.
Another of Gaspar’s designs is Domus, an angular bollard-style outdoor light that, through simple gesture, recalls a warmly lit house at night.
The design is available in three heights. Units can be optionally combined to create a sculptural look and the illusion of multiple windows.
Geometric glass volumes, metal detailing and glowing bar-shaped lighting elements meet in the Fragile collection, designed for the brand by Jaume Ramírez.
The lights come in pendant, wall and table formats, each made up of spherical and conical shades that lend them a playful aesthetic.
The roots of the Marset brand stretch back to the 1940s, when Francisco “Paco” Marset established a small metal foundry in Barcelona.

His grandchildren Javier and Carlos Marset helped reposition the company as the global design brand it is today when they took over in the 1990s, bringing on board designers such as Gaspar, who is a frequent collaborator.

items.title: The brilliant new iPad mini is $100 off for Black Friday
paragraphs: Apple's had a busy couple of months, releasing headline-grabbing new products including folding iPhones and touchscreen MacBooks. A little lost in the melee was the 8th generation iPad mini – but for some users, this a hugely exciting upgrade.

With a brand new OLED display and a thinner and lighter design, the A20 Pro iPad mini looks and feels incredible. In my testing, I called it almost perfect. And for a limited time, it's currently $100 at Amazon, bringing the price down from $699 to $599.

Performance-wise, that A20 Pro chip (which also resides in the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo) is incredibly speedy and efficient – I managed to eke out around ten hours on a single charge. If it's portability you're after, this might just be the perfect tablet – and at $100 off, it's even more appealing.

items.title: Royal Society for Arts appoints five Royal Designers for Industry
paragraphs: The UK’s Royal Society for Arts has announced five Royal Designers for Industry, who include Durrell Bishop and Bridget Baines, as well as naming an Honorary Royal Designer as it celebrates its 90th anniversary.

The awards, which were established in 1936, recognise outstanding talent across landscape architecture, technology, illustration, fashion and theatre. They are given by Royal Society for Arts (RSA) and can only be held by 200 designers at any one time.

This year’s winners are product and interaction designer Bishop, multidisciplinary designer Harris Elliott, illustrator Laura Carlin, costume designer Tahra Zafar and landscape architect Bridget Baines.
Baines co-founded international practice Gross Max, and her fellow Gross Max founder Eelco Hooftman (pictured in main image with Baines) was given the Honorary Royal Designer award this year.
The winners were chosen for their “joyful” designs,

“Ninety years on, the Royal Designers are still looking forward,” Keeper of the Faculty of Royal Designers for Industry Johanna Gibbons said. “This year’s appointments show how far design now reaches, from public landscapes and picture books to exhibitions, the stage and the objects we use every day.”

“Their work is joyful, and it is serious about making life better,” she continued. “That is what unites Royal Designers across the decades: a living entanglement of disciplines that, with the RSA Fellowship, is a profound force for good.”
Last year’s winners included designer Yinka Ilori and journalist Mona Chalabi, and the award has also been given to designers including Es Devlin, Vivienne Westwood, James Dyson and Zandra Rhodes.
According to the RSA, the winners represent the “sheer breadth of design today”.
“Great design changes how we experience the world, often in ways we barely notice,” RSA programme manager Catherine Joyce.
“For 90 years, Royal Designers have shown what extraordinary creativity can achieve, and how it can make life better for everyone,” she continued.
“These six appointments are a wonderful reminder of the sheer breadth of design today.”
Dezeen also recently celebrated the best designers of this year as part of our Dezeen Awards, including Ilori, Yasmine Ghoniem and Keiji Ashizawa.

items.title: Second court defeat for Trump's deep-sea mining ambitions
paragraphs: The Trump administration's plans to begin deep-sea mining in the Pacific have hit a second legal setback after a federal judge ruled plans to lease areas of sea-floor off the Northern Mariana Islands violated the Endangered Species Act (ESA).
The court's decision follows a similar ruling over a proposed lease sale off American Samoa.
Opposition groups who lodged the Northern Mariana Islands lawsuit said they were concerned deep-sea mining could cause long-term damage to the ocean ecosystem.
The US government has said it wants to start deep-sea mining to enable access to critical minerals and to counter China's growing influence over crucial components needed for electronics.
The administration had planned to put up for sale leases for the Northern Mariana Islands on 16 December 2026.

It is not clear what will happen next as the administration chose not to recognise the first court ruling and went ahead with the sale of two leases covering 13 million hectares (more than 30 million acres) off American Samoa.
Opponents have vowed to challenge that sale.

Ruling on the Northern Mariana Islands case, District judge Jill Aiko Otake said the defendants, the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), which provided the expert opinion behind the lease sales, and Howard Lutnick, who was named in his capacity as head of the department that oversees the agency, had failed to consider the potential effects that could follow once the leases were issued.

The ruling explained that while these leases would only authorise the leaseholder to conduct preliminary surveying activity, they might eventually allow the leaseholder to actually mine the ocean's floor.
The potential impact of that mining had not been addressed in the biodiversity assessment which was used to sign off the lease sales, the ruling said.
Using machines to mine for minerals in the deep ocean is highly controversial.

Some scientists have raised concerns that deep-sea mining could damage little-understood deep-ocean ecosystems, though industry supporters argue the environmental effects remain uncertain and require further study.

Deep-sea mining uses vacuum technology to suck up nodules from the muddy sediment., external However, this process also removes organisms that grow on them, including corals and sponges, many of which cannot grow anywhere else.
In one study of the impact of deep-sea mining, researchers found more than 4,000 animals, 90% of which were new species, living on the seafloor in a remote area of the Pacific Ocean.
Some critics of the industry fear that before we have the chance to explore the full nature of life in the undiscovered deep ocean, it could be endangered.
Norway was the first country in the world to approve commercial-scale deep-sea mining in 2024.
Over 2,000 of the world's scientists met in 2025 to review the data on ocean health and they recommended governments halt deep sea exploration while further research on the impacts was carried out.
More than 30 countries supported this position and called for a moratorium.
Shortly before that meeting, President Trump published executive orders to push ahead with mining and "unleash America's offshore critical minerals and resources".
He said "these resources are key to strengthening our economy, securing our energy future, and reducing dependence on foreign suppliers for critical minerals".
Part of the plan aims to "counter China's growing influence over seabed mineral resources".
Deep-sea mining targets polymetallic nodules, external – potato-sized rocks found over 4,000 metres below the ocean surface.
These contain minerals including nickel, cobalt, and manganese which are used in manufactruring electronics and batteries.
They are also important for renewable energy technologies to tackle climate change, including solar panels, wind turbines and electric vehicles.
The International Energy Agency predicts that demand for the minerals could at least double by 2040., external
U.S. Department of Commerce‘s The National Marine Fisheries Service refused to comment.

items.title: What would happen if Russia detonated a nuclear weapon in space?
paragraphs: ⁠Sputnik-S, a nuclear-enabled satellite, has been assembled by Russia and could be launched in 60 days, reports say
Russia is reportedly preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite into space later this year, in a scenario that could pose a significant threat to global communications.
German media outlets have reported, citing western intelligence agency assessments, that such a satellite could be launched within 60 days and would be operational shortly afterwards.
Here we look at the implications of a nuclear weapon being detonated in space.

A report by the German broadcasters NDR and WDR and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung said western intelligence services, including Germany’s Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) intelligence service and armed forces, had exchanged information showing that a nuclear-enabled satellite, named ⁠Sputnik-S, was assembled several years ago and is stationed in ⁠the Moscow region. It could be launched this year.
A German government spokesperson said it was taking the intelligence reports “very seriously”.

In space, where there is no atmosphere, there is no mushroom cloud. Instead, the energy from a nuclear explosion is released as radiation. A detonation would be particularly damaging in low Earth orbit, or up to 1,200 miles above Earth, where most satellites operate.

Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist and honorary professor at the Durham University Space Research Centre in the UK, said the main effects were twofold: everything within line of sight of the detonation could be zapped by X-rays and other forms of radiation which could knock out or damage satellites within thousands of miles; secondly, radiation particles could be emitted into the lower atmosphere and form a new “Van Allen belt”, the term for two belts of radiation that circle the Earth and shield it from the impact of solar storms.

It would be a replay of an event in 1962 when the US detonated a thermonuclear bomb 250 miles above Earth’s surface – in low Earth orbit – in an event called Starfish Prime. There were many fewer satellites then but it shortened the life of two craft: the Telstar 1 and Ariel-1 satellites.
“Starfish caused severe radiation over a period of months to at least half the satellites then working on orbit, which was not very many at that point,” said McDowell.
Keith Ryden, a professor of space engineering at the University of Surrey in the UK, said low Earth orbit satellites were vulnerable to bursts of radiation.

“Since natural levels of radiation are relatively low in this region, satellites located there are not designed for high radiation levels so they would be vulnerable to unexpected increases,” he says.

There are about 17,000 satellites in lower Earth orbit, including satellites important to weather forecasting, climate monitoring and the military as well as Elon Musk’s network of satellites that form the Starlink broadband network. The latter is crucial to assisting Ukraine’s efforts in repelling the invasion of Russia.
The International Space Station, in which Russia is a partner, is also in low Earth orbit. Musk’s proposed constellation of space datacentres would operate there as well.
Satellites handling TV broadcast, GPS and other communications are in higher orbits that are less easy for a nuclear weapon to affect.
McDowell said the artificial Van Allen belt caused by Starfish Prime was around for five years.

“There will be immediate impacts from a detonation but there are lasting environmental effects that will damage satellites in the longer run. It could take several years, up to a decade, for the trapped particles to diffuse out of the radiation belt,” he said.
Ryden added: “Just as important, the space industry would not have the capacity to rebuild and launch the required number of spacecraft in a short time.”
Hundreds of miles below the Starfish Prime explosion, streetlights in Hawaii were knocked out, burglar alarms were set off in the area, and phone calls were disrupted.
“There might be an impact on computers and electronic systems in the region of earth where the explosion is visible,” said McDowell.
Ryden added that Starfish and other nuclear tests took place over sparsely populated areas so the location of the detonation was key.
“It does depend a lot on where the detonation happens,” he said.
Starfish Prime also created stunning aurora effects as the sky was lit up in shades of green, yellow, red and, according to one report, “tremendous white rainbows”.
“There would be huge auroral effects. It would not be a subtle thing. It’s hard to be subtle with nukes,” said McDowell.

A European security official told the Guardian that they were doubtful that Russia would detonate a nuclear device in space. They said it could cause significant damage to western economies, but that it stood to significantly harm Russia as well. Such an explosion would be hard to control and would probably damage Russia’s own satellites, as well as, potentially, China’s. “It would be shooting themselves in the leg,” they said.

They pointed at Russia’s nuclear blackmail earlier in its war in Ukraine, including when Russia put its nuclear forces on high alert in 2022, followed by movements of troops and weapons. “They were bluffing then – and this looks like a bluff now,” said the official.
McDowell said he was sceptical about Russia detonating a nuclear weapon in space, because it was “such a stupid idea” to commit what would be viewed as an act of war.

items.title: Base Design gives Visa a brand refresh "for the next generation"
paragraphs: Design agency Base Design has created a more compact version of credit card company Visa’s logo and worked with Displaay Type Foundry on a new typeface, as part of a refresh of the brand’s visual identity.

While the 2021 Visa wordmark remains unchanged, the refresh included creating a shortened symbol for the brand, rolling out the new Visa Sans typeface, and creating a blocky hero graphic to market towards a younger generation.
“When you’re working with a brand as iconic as Visa, the challenge isn’t recognition – it’s relevance,” said Base Design executive creative director Min Lew.

“Our ambition was to build on Visa’s extraordinary equity while giving it a renewed sense of energy and expression, one that feels as relevant to the next generation as it does to the generations who have grown up with it.”
As part of this strategy, the studio cut the V out of the existing wordmark to function as its own symbol. It will be used on credit cards and appear across digital platforms.
The studio also wrapped it in colourful bar, which will also be used on graphic elements such as posters, and to frame text.
“More than a framing device, the hero graphic device brings movement, direction, and possibility to the identity,” said Lew.

“This simple gesture becomes the foundation for a visual language that can be energetic at a global sporting event, confident and bold in a B2B environment, or vibrant and elevated for affluent audiences.”
For Visa Sans, Base Design and Displaay Type Foundry also based the design on the existing logo.
The typeface features rounded edges akin to the rounded corner of the Visa V, and overall, extends “the logo’s character across the wider identity”.

Ultimately, the new identity was created to be used across different smaller, touchpoints according to the team, such as at tap-to-pay stations, at checkout, or online, as the brand appears “for only a moment” in day to day life.
“We have deep trust and recognition as a brand,” said Visa chief marketing officer Frank Cooper III. “This refresh gives us an opportunity to build on that.”
A more subtle approach to logo and branding updates has been popular in recent years, such as at Walmart and Google.
In contrast, the US restaurant chain Cracker Barrel recently took a hard swing at a logo update, which was immediately met with online backlash and promptly scrapped in favour of the original design.

items.title: Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos wins race to be next ECB president
paragraphs: Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos has been chosen as the next president of the European Central Bank, to succeed Christine Lagarde, after winning support from the EU’s biggest countries.
The economist and monetary policymaker will become the first Spaniard to lead the ECB, defeating his rival candidate Klaas Knot, the former head of the Dutch central bank.

EU diplomats agreed two other appointments to the ECB’s executive board on Thursday: France’s Laurence Boone and Germany’s Markus Brunnermeier. The trio of appointments was a package deal, after France and Germany converged on choosing Hernández de Cos, who is expected to keep the ECB on the same path.

Following the talks European Council president António Costa confirmed the three appointments, saying: “This will pave the way for the formal appointment of the new ECB leadership by the EUCO [European Council] in December.”
The French president, Emmanuel Macron, also confirmed: “A consensus emerged on the nominations to the European Central Bank.”

The Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, who faces elections this weekend that he is predicted to lose, celebrated the victory of Hernández de Cos and the presence of Spaniards in other big EU roles, by hailing “a Spain that is leading in Europe as never before”.

Spain’s former deputy prime minister Teresa Ribera is one of the European Commission’s executive vice-presidents, with responsibility for a vast portfolio spanning the green transition and EU competition policy. The former Spanish economy minister Nadia Calviño leads the European Investment Bank.

Hernández de Cos, a former Bank of Spain governor, will become the fifth head of the eurozone’s central bank since it was founded in 1998. He is expected to take up his position after Lagarde stands down in February, during a time of political change and economic pressure in the 21-country eurozone.

Europe is entering a big election year, starting with Spain’s elections this weekend, with national votes to follow in France, Italy and (non-eurozone) Poland. European economies are under growing pressure from fierce Chinese competition, US tariff threats and soaring energy prices that are driving up inflation, as well as high debt in several member states.
One of his biggest challenges will be reining in surging prices: inflation in the eurozone hit 4% last month, up from 2.1% a year earlier.
Hernández de Cos, who is now serving as general manager of the Bank for International Settlements, is seen as supporting lower interest rates to boost growth.

Market analysts are closely watching what Hernández de Cos might say about France, where an embattled minority government is struggling to pass a budget. French debt is forecast to hit 122% of GDP next year, more than twice the limit allowed under EU fiscal rules.

Arne Petimezas, the director of research at AFS Group Amsterdam, said Hernández de Cos, who “leans dovish”, was the “continuity candidate”. He added: “Don’t expect de Cos to turn a blind eye to France and its fiscal predicaments. No carte blanche: bond buying will remain contingent on austerity and a path towards a lower debt ratio.”

The ECB’s approach to the French debt crisis will come under intense political scrutiny, especially after calls from the French far-right presidential frontrunner, Marine Le Pen, “to ease the burden of interest rates”.

Hernández de Cos is seen as a central banker in the mould of Mario Draghi, the celebrated former ECB president and Italian prime minister, who is credited with stabilising the eurozone at a pivotal moment in the debt crisis. Matthew Ryan, at the financial services firm Ebury, said Hernández de Cos was “likely to place greater weight on growth, financial stability and fragmentation risk than Klaas Knot, the alternative candidate and a genuine hawk”.
“We do not expect his appointment to alter the near-term rate path. The president sets the agenda but is ultimately one voice on the governing council, and rarely overrides the consensus.”

The contest was set in motion less than a month ago when Lagarde, the ECB’s first female president, announced that she intended to leave her post nine months early to speak her mind about world affairs and confront “the misrepresentation of the truth”.
Macron, who played a decisive role in appointing Lagarde, a former French finance minister, said EU leaders had welcomed her “decisive leadership during her term in office”.
Hernández de Cos’s appointment must still clear the European parliament and the ECB’s governing council, but these steps are seen as formalities.

items.title: The MacBook Neo is receiving a rare $100 discount for Black Friday
paragraphs: While $100 might not feel like much, it brings the laptop down to its original launch price.
While $100 might not feel like much, it brings the laptop down to its original launch price.
is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

If you’re looking for a new laptop or a gift for the student in your life, you can save $100 on the MacBook Neo at several retailers, in both storage sizes and all four colors. The 256GB model is currently discounted to $599.99 at Amazon and Costco, while the 512GB model with Touch ID is available for $699.99 via the same retailers (Amazon / Costco). None of the retailers currently list an end date for the discount, which is the biggest price drop we’ve seen since Apple raised the laptop’s MSRP by $100 in July in response to the ongoing RAM crisis.

Apple’s budget-friendly MacBook leverages the A18 Pro processor, a chip originally found in the iPhone 16 Pro, to keep costs down. Both the 256GB and 512GB models feature 8GB of memory, and my colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto was impressed by the vivid 13-inch screen and speakers, the latter of which are better than those in many cheap (and even midrange) Windows laptops. The Neo isn’t super performant, especially in terms of storage speed and total memory, but it’s great for everyday tasks, casual use, and students.
Update, November 26th: Adjusted pricing and availability to reflect the additional discount that’s now available at both Amazon and Costco.

items.title: Android app developers will soon have to share their address publicly
paragraphs: is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Independent Android app developers are worried about their privacy after Google announced that from next year many of them will be required to share a phone number and address publicly. The policy change is intended to meet European Union regulations under the Digital Services Act, but Google says contact details will be made public worldwide.

Developers have until February 1st 2027 to declare whether or not they’re a “trader” under UK and European law. Broadly speaking, Google says the definition applies if you earn revenue from your apps, especially if that revenue is regular or at high volume. Developers are exempt if their apps are only a hobby or non-commercial, or if they simply don’t publish them in the UK or Europe.

If they self-declare as a trader, developers’ contact details will be shared publicly starting March 1st, including a phone number and address. Google doesn’t accept PO boxes for developer payment profile addresses, meaning many independent developers without an office will either have to share their home address online or pay for a registered agent or other service that provides a business address. One independent developer told The Elec they were considering renting a private office solely to comply with the new rules. We’ve asked Google to confirm why developers aren’t permitted to publish a PO box address, and why details are being shared globally, and will update this article when we hear back.

Apple is subject to the same regulations, but is handling them differently to Google. It will only display developer addresses within the relevant European countries, rather than publishing them worldwide. It’s also allowing developers to supply PO box addresses, so long as they provide Apple with a receipt or bill that links the PO box to their regular address.
Update, November 26th: Added mention of developers’ option to use a registered agent service for a business address.

items.title: The best Black Friday deals we’ve already found
paragraphs: Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 deliver the best noise cancellation and sound quality of any AirPods yet, along with a more comfortable, secure fit and improved water resistance. They also feature built-in heart rate tracking for workouts and support live translations for a handful of languages. Read our review.

You can get an ad-supported Disney Plus and Hulu bundle for $4.99 a month ($8 off) for an entire year. Both streaming services feature a deep catalog of new and classic TV shows and movies, including The Simpsons, Andor, Toy Story 5, and The Fantastic Four: First Steps.

The Nintendo Switch 2 features a 7.9-inch LCD display, magnetically attached Joy-Con 2 controllers, backward compatibility with most original Switch games, and exclusive titles like Donkey Kong Bananza and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Read our review.

Do you ever wish you could turn on your coffee maker or hit the light switch without getting up? The SwitchBot Bot lets you do that. All you need to do is stick the inexpensive contraption on a standard button or rocker switch, which will allow you to control or schedule your pet feeder, garage door, and a wide range of other devices from your smartphone.

An HBO Max Basic subscription provides access to shows like A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, The Last of Us, and The Pitt, as well as films like Superman and Weapons. You can get a year of the monthly, ad-supported subscription for $5.49 a month (about $6 off) until December 1st.
Apple’s latest AirTags feature an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range. Read our review.

Amazon’s last-gen Fire TV Stick 4K Plus streams in 4K and supports Dolby Atmos, Dolby Vision, and Alexa Plus. It also ships with the redesigned Fire OS and, unlike more recent models, still lets you sideload Android TV apps.

Sony’s XM4 noise-canceling headphones were so good, the company brought them back with a few minor improvements. They still offer great ANC, a timeless foldable design, and delivering performance nearly on par with Sony’s newer flagships at a fraction of the cost.

Lego’s miniature bonsai trees can bring a sense of calm to even the most cluttered home. Building each tree — whether it be the black pine, the ginkgo, or the lilac-adorned wisteria — is designed to be a mindfulness practice in itself, centering your giftee as they go. They also make for a great piece of decor once finished, adding a touch of zen to any desk or shelf.

Apple’s most affordable laptop uses the same A18 Pro chip found in the iPhone 16 Pro. It features a vibrant 13-inch display, surprisingly good speakers, and 8GB of RAM, making it a solid option for students and anyone who needs a laptop for everyday tasks. Read our review.

Peacock is a great way to catch up on a wealth of content from NBC’s various networks, whether you plan to rewatch The Office or catch up on all things Bravo. A Premium subscription also grants access to films from studios like Universal Pictures and Dreamworks, along with live sports and a host of Peacock Originals.

Rechargeable AA batteries are handy until it’s time to charge them. Most wall chargers let you refill four, maybe six, at once. Zepath’s clever solution is to ship them in an easy-to-use USB-C charging case that charges eight simultaneously. The batteries themselves are long-lasting, too.

Sony’s DualSense Wireless Controller for the PlayStation 5 features immersive haptic feedback and resistance triggers, which feel great to use. It offers a built-in mic, a 3.5mm headphone jack, and a mute button; it also works with PC, macOS, and mobile devices via Bluetooth or USB-C.
Apple’s 11th-gen iPad is the successor to the previous 10-gen model. It has a new A16 chip and few other changes — and is the only Apple tablet to not support Apple Intelligence.

With 12.4mm drivers, active noise cancellation, and an IP54 rating, the CMF Buds 2A offer high-end features at an affordable price. You can also customize the sound, adjust ANC levels, and find the earbuds using the Nothing X app.

Anker’s durable travel adapter delivers up to 100W of power and works in over 200 countries. It doesn’t support AC plugs, but it does offer a trio of USB-C ports and a nifty LCD display to keep tabs on the charge percentage.

The Apple Watch Series 12 introduces AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, including sound recognition alerts, Live Rewind, and Siri Recap. It can also track your heart rate every five seconds, even when you’re not exercising, and offers faster charging than prior models. Read our review.

007 First Light, a third-person stealth action game from the studio behind Hitman, is arguably the best action game we’ve played this year. It features a wide variety of missions that have you sneaking through enemy territory, engaging in hand-to-hand combat, and taking part in high-speed car chases — you know, classic Bond stuff. Read our review.

Fanttik’s rechargeable electric screwdriver features three adjustable torque settings, a built-in LED light, and 16 S2 hardened steel bits for tackling everything from furniture assembly to small electronics repairs. It also comes with a magnetic storage case and supports USB-C.

No one should have to deal with a rat’s nest behind their desk when devices like Anker’s 2-in-1 USB-C cable exist. The handy USB-C cable splits at the end, giving you the ability to charge up to two devices from a single port. That means you can split power between a phone and tablet or juice a 16-inch MacBook Pro to 50 percent in just 20 minutes using a single port.

The Nintendo Switch 2 has 256GB of storage, but that won’t get you very far if you’ve built up a medium-sized digital game library. Samsung’s P9 256GB microSD express card doubles the console’s available storage.

You likely won’t find wireless earbuds with a more striking appearance than Nothing’s Ear 3A. They also sound fantastic, boast active noise cancellation, and offer robust EQ settings, making them a great pick for the price. Read our review.

Ember’s latest smart mug is designed to keep your coffee at the ideal temperature for up to three hours, with five temp settings between 120 and 145 degrees Fahrenheit. The third-gen version is similar to prior models; however, you can now adjust the heat settings directly on the mug and throw it in the dishwasher, which wasn’t the case before.

Despite being an entry-level variant of the B6 OLED, this model features four HDMI 2.1 ports, a 120Hz refresh rate, a capable processor, and pixel-perfect image quality and contrast for any content you want to watch. Lower brightness is likely the biggest compromise with getting a cheaper OLED.

JBL’s Tour One M3 noise-canceling headphones come with a touchscreen-equipped wireless transmitter that lets you wirelessly listen to audio from in-flight entertainment systems and other devices without Bluetooth. They also offer solid active noise cancellation and last up to 70 hours on a charge.

Hisense’s 2026 CanvasTV is a 4K QLED TV that doubles as wall art when you’re not watching. It features a matte, anti-glare display and runs on Google’s excellent TV software; it’s also a great pick for gamers thanks to its snappy 144Hz variable refresh rate and a pair of HDMI 2.1 ports.

The Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 Combo is a beginner-friendly 3D printer that supports four filament spools. It features an enclosed build chamber, automatic bed leveling, and a large touchscreen, making it easy to produce reliable prints.

Moft’s Trackable Tripod Wallet is a MagSafe-compatible wallet that holds two cards and folds into an adjustable phone stand or small tripod. It also supports both Apple’s Find My network and Google’s Find Hub, offers Qi wireless charging, and includes a detachable shutter remote for taking photos.

Govee’s Table Lamp 2 is way more fun than your average table lamp. The color-changing device boasts built-in scheduling and more than 60 dynamic lighting effects, including preset scenes for various holidays. You can even create custom color combos for when “Dandelion” and other presets just aren’t cutting it.

Birdfy’s metal smart bird feeder features a wide-angle 4K camera that lets you get an up-close look at visiting birds, along with a 1.8-liter seed capacity and a built-in solar panel for charging. It also offers free AI-powered recognition of more than 6,000 bird species.

Bambu Lab’s P2S Combo is a 3D printer that can print in multiple colors and automatically dry its materials to help improve print quality. It also features a 5-inch touchscreen, a built-in camera for monitoring prints remotely, and AI-powered tools that can detect printing problems.

Headspace makes it easier to build mindfulness into your everyday life, whether you’re looking to manage stress, improve focus, or get a better night’s sleep. An annual subscription gives you access to hundreds of guided meditations, breathing exercises, and other tools for beginners and experienced users alike.

The Dreame X60 Ultra is a powerful robot vacuum and mop that does a great job of cleaning carpets thanks to its dual roller brushes and 35,000Pa of suction. It can climb over tall thresholds, squeeze under low furniture, and automatically detach its mop pads when vacuuming carpets.

Saros is a third-person sci-fi shooter in which players fight alien enemies on a mysterious planet trapped in a time loop. The PS5 exclusive features fast-paced combat, a variety of powerful weapons, and challenging boss fights. Read our review.

Bose’s second-gen QuietComfort Headphones build on the original with better sound quality and support for lossless audio over USB-C. They also offer improved noise cancellation and are more comfortable thanks to their lack of “eardrum suck.”
Garmin’s midrange Forerunner watch has an OLED display, a week’s worth of battery life, and dual-frequency GPS for better accuracy. Read our review.

The Matic robot vacuum and mop is ideal for cluttered homes with pets, multiple floors, and a mixture of carpets and hardwood. It offers almost humanlike navigation, tackling high-pile rugs and mopping up wet spills. The quiet bot also requires less maintenance than many rivals thanks to its onboard water tank and dust bag. Read our review.

Azul is a game in which you arrange patterned tiles in order to create the most beautiful tapestry possible. Arranging tiles in a strategic sequence will help you build your score while limiting your opponents’ ability to grow theirs.

The Eufy Omni C28 combines excellent mopping performance with a small self-cleaning dock that’s well suited for apartments and other smaller spaces. It navigates around furniture and into tight areas with ease, while its roller mop does a great job cleaning hard floors.

Arguably the best thing to come out of The Book of Boba Fett was the Mandalorian’s N-1 Starfighter, which Lego has recreated here in miniature. It’s not quite as impressive as the 1,802-piece version, but the cheaper set still packs plenty of detail, including a spring-loaded shooter.

Nothing’s first over-ear headphones have a retro transparent design and high-end features like active noise cancellation, spatial audio with head tracking, and plush ear pads. They also feature a paddle button that allows you to control music playback. Read our review.

Amazon’s 12.3-inch Alexa Tablet 12 Pro runs Android with access to the Google Play Store, unlike the company’s Fire tablets. It also features built-in Alexa Plus integration, a dedicated Kindle reading mode, and up to 16 hours of battery life. Read our hands-on impressions.

Samsung’s last-gen Frame is a 4K QLED TV that displays art on its anti-glare matte screen when not in use. It also supports Dolby Atmos, HDR10 Plus, and popular streaming apps, with refresh rates up to 144Hz on larger models.

TP-Link’s smart smart plug lets you remotely control lamps, fans, and other appliances using your phone or voice commands. It supports Matter, so it works with all major smart home platforms, and lets you set schedules and timers to automatically turn devices on or off.

Google’s latest pair of wireless earbuds features crisp sound, a comfortable design, and solid active noise cancellation, which is great considering the budget-friendly price tag. They even offer built-in support for Gemini and, unlike the entry-level AirPods, a purple option! Read our review.

Roku now makes some of the most affordable, yet feature-packed 4K OLED TVs available for gamers or movie lovers looking for a big TV upgrade under $1,000. The Pro Series LX with better brightness, faster refresh rate, and a polarizer to reduce reflections starts at $200 more.

If you’re on a tight budget, but want spectacular contrast and brightness control that only an OLED can provide, here’s a deal for you. Alienware’s 1440p 27-inch QD-OLED monitor with 240Hz refresh rate is selling at its lowest price yet. Read our hands-on.

Soundcore makes some of the best wireless earbuds you’ve never heard of — and the Liberty 5 Pro may be its best pair yet. The sleek buds deliver powerful noise cancellation, good sound, and surprisingly fabulous call quality for less than Apple’s latest AirPods.

A great first portable music player/speaker for kids. It uses insertable NFC cards (sold separately) to play music and stories to keep kiddos occupied and entertained without zoning out in front of the TV. This model supports Bluetooth and 3.5mm for private listening, too.

The latest entry in the long-running survival horror series returned in 2026, with two different styles of gameplay (tense first-person and guns-blazing third-person perspectives) via its dual protagonists. Read our review.

The latest Powerbeats Pro are a no-brainer for athletes. They pack fantastic sound and thumping bass, along with active noise cancellation, IPX4 water resistance, and heart rate monitoring. Read our review.

The big difference between the Superstrike and other gaming mice lies beneath its main two mouse buttons. It uses haptic actuators instead of mechanical switches, allowing for lower latency and more longevity.

The Nex Playground’s motion-controlled gameplay is designed for ages five and up. It comes with games like Fruit Ninja and Whack-a-Mole Deluxe, but many more titles are available via a subscription. It’s a ton of fun for kids. This is the lowest price so far in 2026. Read our review.

With a 4.3-inch E Ink screen, the Xteink X4 is smaller and more pocketable than any Kindle and Kobo model currently available. It has some drawbacks — it’s limited to TXT and EPUB files — but it’s great for tinkering; it also has a magnetic mount so you can stick it to the back of MagSafe-ready phones.

The Ring 5 is a fantastic entry point for new users. While short on improvements over its thicker predecessor, it’s hard not to appreciate that it manages to deliver similar battery life despite being thinner. Read our review.

Nothing has changed in terms of aesthetics, but the Max 2 deliver better sound and some new features. Not exactly worth upgrading for, but fantastic for those who are considering them now. Read our full review.
It’s hard to find a cooler lamp than Govee’s Uplighter floor lamp at this price. It can light a room, and display a mesmerizing pattern up your wall and onto your ceiling.

The Meta Quest 3S is a battery-powered standalone VR headset that has the same chipset as the pricier Quest 3, but with the same lenses and screen resolution as the Quest 2. In addition to being able to play many games from the Meta Store, it can also be connected to a gaming PC to play VR games like Half-Life Alyx. Read our review.

Nintendo’s latest Switch 2 exclusive is the best way to relive what is arguably the best Zelda game of all time. The revamped visuals look gorgeous, and while the game’s improved controls might annoy some purists who still cling to the heyday of ’98, we reckon most folks won’t bat an eye.

Compared to the last-gen base Kindle model (currently $119.99), the Paperwhite is a much better value. It features waterproofing, better battery life, faster page-turning speeds, and a higher pixel density screen that’s slightly larger (7 inches vs. 6 inches)

The water-resistant Sonos Play sits between the Roam 2 and Move 2, offering a balance of portability and room-filling sound. It delivers up to 24 hours of battery life, with a built-in loop for easy carrying. You can also use it as a power bank and pair it with other Sonos speakers over Bluetooth when Wi-Fi isn’t available. Read our review.

LIFX’s dimmable, color-changing bulbs offer Wi-Fi connectivity, simple setup, and Matter compatibility, so they fit seamlessly into any major smart home platform. Best of all, the smart features come at a price that makes buying multipacks more affordable than other brands.

Iniu’s P55-E2 Power Bank is an ultra-slim three-port USB charger that’s capable of fully recharging an iPhone 16 twice. It supports charging speeds of up to 45W via a USB-C port, which can deliver fast recharging for a range of gadgets.

The Echo Dot Max features a flat design and a redesigned sound system, which delivers nearly three times the bass as its predecessor. It also offers improved conversation detection and better noise filtering, thanks to Amazon’s new AZ3 chip. Read our review.

Donkey Kong Bananza is one of the Switch 2’s first exclusive must-have titles. Its destructible environment allows you to smash your way through each of its 17 levels, and the paths you make will remain intact unless you specifically choose to reset the world. Your companion Paulene’s singing allows you to transform into animals that have abilities that allow you to reach previously inaccessible parts of levels. Read our review.

Whether you primarily drive a car, motorcycle, or a bicycle, the one thing in common with all three modes of transport is the need for a well-inflated tire. This rechargeable 150psi inflator might just save you from a flat (or from being dangerously close to one) when you least expect it.

Google wants to sell you on the Pro’s software features, but it’s the underlying hardware that makes it a stellar Android handset. The build quality is incredible, the larger telephoto sensor is an improvement, and it now supports faster wired speeds and Qi2.2 for up to 25W wireless charging. Read our review.

In Catan, up to four players strategically compete and trade for resources. The iconic board game ends when one player reaches 10 “victory points,” which is achieved by constructing a sprawling civilization of roads, settlements, and cities using sheep, ore, wheat, and wood.

A 10-inch anti-glare touchscreen that comes in a few design options. It’s a frame that features Alexa, and doubles as a smart speaker. It works with Amazon Photos, which offers unlimited storage for Prime members.

Glocusent’s clip-in reading light features five brightness levels and multiple color temperature settings, ranging from a soft, warm glow that’s great for late-night reading to a brighter light that’s perfect for daytime use. The slim USB light easily slips into your pocket, too, so you can read anywhere, from a cozy bed to a dimly lit train.

This innovative new smart lock uses the U1 ultra-wideband (UWB) chip in many iPhones and Apple Watches to automatically unlock your door as you approach. It will also work with the new Aliro standard and be compatible with Android phones for hands-free unlocking.

Roborock’s first roller-mop robot vacuum, the Curv 2 Flow, features flagship specs at a midrange price, including excellent mopping, a retractable mop cover, 20,000Pa suction, AI-powered obstacle avoidance, and a compact design.

Twelve South’s entry-level Bluetooth transmitter delivers up to 25 hours of continuous use and lets you connect up to two pairs of headphones to an in-flight entertainment system, making it a great travel companion no matter where you’re going.

The Chamera is not a good camera, but that’s not the point. Kodak’s charming, keychain-friendly tchotchke lets you snap lo-fi memories on a whim, with an ultra-small 1.6-megapixel sensor, a built-in LED flash, and the tiniest amount of storage.

Sucker Punch’s follow-up to Ghost of Tsushima is everything you could want in a sequel. The open-world revenge epic brims with fluid combat and a host of welcome narrative twists, all set against the gorgeous backdrop of Japan’s Edo period. It’s precisely the type of game photo modes were made for, even if you never use them.

The Wuben G5 flashlight is as small as a Zippo lighter, yet far more versatile, with a bright, rotatable light that can shine in numerous colors. It features USB-C charging and has an adjustable clip.

The last-gen JBL Go 4 has been around for a bit, but the pocket-sized Bluetooth speaker still delivers with up to seven hours of runtime, dual-device connectivity, and an IP67 rating for water and dust resistance. You can also pair it with other Go 4 speakers for bigger stereo sound, if desired.
The Apple Watch SE 3 is a major glow-up, adding an always-on display, wrist-temperature sensor, a more powerful processor, and fast charging. Read our review.

The Insta360 Link 2 offers the same auto-swiveling design as its excellent predecessor, only in a smaller form factor. It also offers a slate of new features, including group tracking and no-follow zones.

items.title: Federal judge blocks the FCC from reviewing ABC’s licenses early
paragraphs: The judge has preliminarily sided with ABC, rejecting the FCC’s efforts to dismiss the case.
The judge has preliminarily sided with ABC, rejecting the FCC’s efforts to dismiss the case.
Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

US District Judge Loren AliKhan has blocked the Federal Communications Commission from conducting an early review of ABC’s broadcast licenses in a preliminary injunction, and rejected its efforts to dismiss ABC’s First Amendment lawsuit. ABC has accused the FCC of violating its free speech rights and claims the agency “waged a retaliatory campaign” against the network over content it broadcast. In her ruling the judge noted that the network was “likely to succeed on their retaliation claim.”

Although Disney, ABC’s parent company, wasn’t set to renew its broadcast licenses until 2028, last April the FCC ordered the network to file for an early license renewal claiming it was part of an investigation into Disney’s policies on diversity, equity, and inclusivity. The FCC’s move came a day after President Donald Trump demanded ABC fire late-night talk show host Jimmy Kimmel following a skit about Melania Trump.

In response to the FCC’s order, Disney and ABC sued the agency in August and accused the FCC of “punishing ABC for its speech” by threatening its broadcast licenses. The preliminary injunction issued by the judge on Wednesday prohibits the FCC from taking any further action in the early review of ABC’s broadcast licenses and noted that the network had shown that the court’s intervention in the agency’s actions was in the public interest.

”No one doubts that the Commission may enforce the law in the manner it sees fit,” the judge wrote. “But in doing so, Defendants may not retaliate against or punish Plaintiffs and other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech.”

items.title: Disney Plus, Hulu, and HBO Max are all over 50 percent off for Black Friday
paragraphs: Black Friday isn’t just a good time to save on a new TV but also a chance to spend less on what you watch on it. The shopping holiday often brings steep streaming discounts, and this year is no exception, with some streamers offering more than 50 percent off. HBO Max, Apple TV, and Hulu are all offering deals, with several plans going for just a few dollars a month. Some discounts even apply to ad-free plans, though there are fewer than last year and prices are generally higher.

Still, you can save big if you don’t mind a few commercials. Right now, for example, you can get a year of the ad-supported Disney Plus and Hulu bundle for $4.99 a month, saving you $96, or sign up for the most basic HBO Max plan for $5.49 a month for 12 months, saving you $66. We’ve rounded up these deals and more below, including what each plan offers and how long you can take advantage of the discounted rate.

With everything from Disney classics and Marvel movies to FX dramas like The Bear and Shōgun, the Disney Plus and Hulu bundle offers plenty for the whole family to watch. For Black Friday, you can get both services with ads for just $4.99 per month ($8 off) for a year via Hulu or Disney Plus, saving you $96 in total. The ad-free bundle is also on sale for $14.99 per month ($7 off) for 12 months, saving you $84. Both discounts are available through 11:59PM PT on November 30th.

Whichever plan you choose, you’ll get access to both streaming libraries. Hulu offers dramas like Furious, Alien: Earth, The Lowdown, and The Handmaid’s Tale, as well as comedies like Bob’s Burgers, Futurama, and It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia. Disney Plus, meanwhile, is home to Disney and Pixar favorites, The Simpsons, and a wide selection of Star Wars and Marvel movies and shows. It’s also a good option for holiday movie nights, with classics like Home Alone and The Santa Clause.

HBO Max is home to some of Hollywood’s biggest releases, and right now, you can watch them for half the usual rate. Now through November 30th, new and returning subscribers can sign up for HBO Max’s Basic With Ads plan for $5.49 a month via HBO Max or Amazon, saving you $66 over the course of a year.

Although the plan doesn’t include live sports, it supports simultaneous streaming on two devices and gives you access to everything from award-winning films like Sinners and Marty Supreme to Wuthering Heights. There’s arguably even more to watch on the TV front, from dramas like The Gilded Age, Lanterns, Euphoria, and Heated Rivalry to comedies such as Hacks and The Righteous Gemstones. Fantasy fans, meanwhile, can immerse themselves in the world of Game of Thrones and its spinoffs, including House of the Dragon and A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, or check out Dune: Prophecy. You’ll also be able to stream new releases, including HBO’s upcoming Harry Potter series.

If you’re looking for an affordable way to catch up on NBC shows, Peacock’s Black Friday promotion offers two ways to save. Through November 30th, new and returning subscribers can sign up for Peacock Select for $2.99 a month ($6 off) for three months or $29.99 ($60 off) for a full year. For access to Peacock’s larger catalog, you can also subscribe to Peacock Premium for $8.99 per month for three months or $89.99 ($40 off) for a year.

The cheaper Select tier is a particularly good value if you mainly watch shows from networks like NBC, Bravo, and Telemundo, including Saturday Night Live, The Office, and Below Deck. Movie buffs and sports fans, however, will prefer Premium, which offers access to a much wider selection of entertainment. Peacock’s catalog includes films like The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, Disclosure Day, and Minions & Monsters, along with shows like The Good Daughter, Dig, and The Paper. A Premium subscription also lets you watch live sporting events, including Sunday Night Football, as well as Peacock originals, such as the various Love Island spinoffs.

If you’re a Star Trek fan or want another way to watch live sports, Paramount Plus is down to $2.99 per month for two months for Black Friday. New and eligible returning subscribers can take advantage of the discount through November 30th, bringing the cost of both the Essential and Premium plans to $5.98 for the introductory period. That makes Premium a particularly good deal, since it normally costs $13.99 a month, compared to $8.99 for the ad-supported Essential tier.

Paramount Plus includes CBS shows like NCIS and Everybody Loves Raymond to Tulsa King and the various Yellowstone spinoffs, including both 1883 and 1923. Movie fans can also browse Paramount’s film library, which includes titles like Arrival, Top Gun, and Interstellar, while sports fans can watch select NFL games, UFC events, UEFA Champions League matches, and March Madness games. Premium also grants you access to Showtime originals and a live feed of your local CBS station, along with ad-free on-demand viewing, though live programming still includes commercials.

Apple TV has built an impressive collection of acclaimed shows, particularly if you’re into sci-fi shows like Silo or thrillers like Slow Horses. Right now, US customers with an Amazon account can subscribe to Apple TV through Amazon for $6.99 per month ($8 off) for six months, saving $48 over the introductory period. Amazon hasn’t listed an end date for the promotion, either.

Six months should give you plenty of time to work through Apple’s other originals, including Severance, Pachinko, The Morning Show, and Pluribus, or settle in for a movie like Arrival or Anchorman. The service also includes live sports, specifically Formula 1 races and Major League Soccer matches.

Anime fans can spend the next six months catching up on shows like The Apothecary Diaries, Jujutsu Kaisen, Black Clover, and One Piece for a lot less thanks to Crunchyroll’s Black Friday sale. Select new and returning subscribers in the US can sign up for the Fan plan for $3.99 a month ($6 off) for six months, saving them $36. The Mega Fan tier is also down to $5.99 a month ($8 off) for six months, while Ultimate Fan is available for $8.99 a month ($9 off) for the same period. Amazon is also offering the same discount on the Mega Fan tier.

All three subscriptions offer access to Crunchyroll’s full anime library without ads, including new episodes shortly after they air in Japan. The Fan tier lets you watch on one device at a time, while Mega Fan increases that limit to four devices and adds offline viewing and access to Crunchyroll’s Game Vault. Ultimate Fan, meanwhile, supports six simultaneous streams and includes Crunchyroll Manga, along with additional store perks.

If you didn’t get a chance to watch the Michael Jackson biopic Michael when it was released earlier this year or just want to catch up on Outlander, Starz is offering a particularly affordable way to stream both on Black Friday. Eligible subscribers can sign up for a year directly through Starz or Amazon Prime for $11.99 ($58 off), which works out to about $1 a month when you pay upfront. If you’d rather not commit to a year, you can alternatively subscribe for $2.99 per month ($9 off) for three months. Either option lets you explore Starz’s catalog of films and TV shows, including In the Grey, Power Ballad, Splash City, and P-Valley.

Amazon is also discounting a wide range of subscriptions through Prime Video, including NBA League Pass, AMC Plus, MGM Plus, and several bundles. Most of the deals below are available through November 30th.

items.title: GTA VI developers vote against unionization
paragraphs: is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Workers at Grand Theft Auto VI developer Rockstar Games won’t unionize, after the vote for a formal recognition agreement failed, with only 25 percent of votes in favor of unionization. The Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB) said that Rockstar workers in the union will continue organizing even without formal recognition.

Voting ran from November 12th through 26th, covering the launch of GTA VI. If successful, the vote would have established a formal framework for collective negotiation with the studio over pay, overtime, bonuses, leave, and pensions, along with a right to consultation over future changes including AI implementation and layoffs. Without it, Rockstar won’t have an obligation to meet union representatives, though workers and union members can still lobby for change informally.

“For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society - this isn’t a sign to retreat, it’s a sign to double down on what we stand for,” IWGB said in a statement sent to The Verge. “Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favour of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognise we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We’re ready to put in the effort to make that happen.”

When Rockstar fired 31 IWGB members last year, the union accused it of “the most blatant and ruthless act of union busting in the history of the games industry.” That case has gone to a UK employment tribunal, with a judgment still pending.

“We are extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we’ve built together and the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI,” Rockstar head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe told Bloomberg News. “This result reflects our team’s strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong. As we look ahead, we’re excited to build on all we’ve accomplished together.”

"Every batch of mohair used by Paul Smith is certified to the Responsible Mohair Standard (RMS), the internationally recognised standard for responsible mohair production.
"If there is evidence that a supplier has not upheld these standards, we will take appropriate action in line with our ethical commitments."
PETA said its investigators had filmed goats being injured during shearing, including at mohair facilities under the RMS.
Allen said: "Hundreds of fashion brands have already ditched mohair, and Paul Smith must do the right thing and follow suit.
