items.title: Why GTA VI’s version of Florida feels so real
paragraphs: There are plenty of reasons why Grand Theft Auto VI is so popular: the 13 years of anticipation, the relatable lead characters and romantic storyline, the sheer level of depth. But another major factor is the sense of place. The GTA series is unmatched when it comes to re-creating the feeling of a bustling, real-world city, and GTA VI’s fictional rendition of Florida is the studio’s most lifelike setting yet. It has functioning buses and trains, plentiful buildings you can go into and explore, residents you can chat with, and huge areas where you can interact with wildlife far away from the bright lights of the Miami-like Vice City. For Emma Fraser, an assistant professor at UC Berkeley who studies urban ruins and virtual cities, the sense of realism has created a unique sensation while playing.

“There’s something about this particular game that is really discombobulating and distracting in a sense,” she says. “Because you have these moments where you think, ‘I’m in a place, I’m experiencing a location.’ You comprehend intellectually that it’s not real or that it’s at best a representation, but you still have this feeling in your brain and you’ll still dream about being in that place.”

Fraser teaches courses on topics including urban geography and virtual worlds and has written papers exploring topics like “mapping in the digital age” and “the virtual spectacle of the end of the city.” She says she started researching video game cities in part because, despite their influence and reach, they’re an underexplored space in academia. “I’m a geographer, and geographers are obsessed with cities,” she explains. “So much of geography is thinking about: How do we imagine cities? How do we navigate cities? How do we build cities? How do we map cities? And video games have all of that, but they’re not taken that seriously as an academic interest.”

Like much of the world, she’s been looking forward to GTA VI for years, particularly because of Rockstar’s on-the-ground approach to research. Before development on the game began, developers from the studio traveled to Florida to get an accurate picture. As GTA VI producer Rob Nelson told me, the starting point for the game was the setting, rather than the story or characters. “We just went around to feel it out,” he said. “Go to the Everglades, go to the Keys, go to the city, as many places as we can, and start thinking about what aspects of the place we want to incorporate.”

While there are plenty of open-world games, many of the most successful — from Elden Ring to The Witcher — are sent in fantastical spaces. GTA stands apart in how its various settings look and feel true to the real world. And Fraser believes that this is one of the key reasons the series has such universal appeal. “You know immediately how to function in a city,” she explains. “You know there’s going to be law enforcement, there are going to be city blocks, there are going to be pedestrians, cars, and buses. It’s this really interesting environment that gives you a lot of possibilities to get a player more immersed in your world, because they already know a lot about a city as a general concept.”
“You can’t hold a whole city in your mind at one time.”

Fraser describes GTA VI’s world as having “implied expansiveness.” It’s not a one-to-one re-creation of the real location. There are plenty of things missing; you don’t see schools or daycares, and parking spaces are relatively sparse. But the game gets enough details right to be recognizable. Fraser explains that as long as certain parts of the city look correct — the lighting, the coastline, the decoration of street corners, the major arterial roads — that’s enough to convince people that they’re in something resembling Miami.

“You can’t hold a whole city in your mind at one time,” she says. “Instead it’s these highlights. What [Rockstar] do very successfully in the game is those snapshots. They’ve got far more content that is recognizable as Florida or Miami than they’ve been able to fit into previous games. So it’s a much more overwhelming sense of being in that place.” The “implied expansiveness” also comes in the form of dialogue, radio programs, and TV shows that suggest a much bigger world by discussing places and moments that exist outside of the game you can actually explore.

This level of verisimilitude — combined with the fact that players can explore the city from multiple perspectives, everything from walking to flying a plane — has led to an experience that Fraser likens to virtual tourism, which can result in all kinds of different playstyles. “Some tourists are going to blow a lot of money on taxis and get to wherever they’re going as fast as they can,” she explains, “and some people just like sitting on a bus or a train and getting to know a place.” Similarly, there are certain players who will just experience the story and play through the main missions, and others who will get lost in side activities like bird watching.
“Some people just like sitting on a bus or a train and getting to know a place”

What’s also notable about GTA VI is how its relationship-focused premise is motivating some players to experience the world in a much less violent way. And that includes how they move through the city. Some people are driving more carefully to avoid killing civilians, while others are exploring spaces while both characters hang out together. “In the first few games, you’re this empty vessel. You’re a criminal, you’re doing criminal things,” says Fraser. “Whereas with GTA VI your motivation and the way you think about your character is really important.”

Now that the game is out and millions of players are venturing through Vice City, Fraser is hoping to use it to research the ways that real and virtual worlds intersect when it comes to how we navigate cities. GTA VI offers a lot of choice in this regard; you can still steal a Lambo and speed through the streets, but you can also hop on a train, put on some headphones, and listen to a podcast while getting where you need to be. “Because this world is so fully furnished, and you have so many options, you might start to import your own real-world practices into the game,” she says.

But at this point, what has struck her most is the attention to detail that separates the universe of GTA VI from its contemporaries. “You can’t just generate a generic city and stick icons in, which is what a lot of games do,” she explains. “You aren’t going to get a sense of a real place if you do it that way.”

items.title: Stranger Than Heaven could be RGG Studio's answer to prestige TV's multilingual period epics
paragraphs: Quick read: Stranger Than Heaven, out 15 January 2027, trades modern Japan for five decades of period crime drama with a multilingual script and a fresh visual style, and it could be RGG Studio's biggest global hit yet.

When it comes to capturing contemporary Japan, no studio does it better than RGG Studio and its long-running Yakuza / Like A Dragon series, to the point that players are drawn in not only by its crime-based, melodramatic narrative and surreal side quests, but also by the chance to engage in virtual tourism. But its upcoming title, Stranger Than Heaven, marks a departure with a more ambitious vision, taking the player on an epic journey across five decades of early 20th-century Japan.

Having had the opportunity to play the game from the start at a recent hands-on event, I can say Stranger Than Heaven's story doesn't begin in Japan but in the US. While RGG Studio has specialised in making games for a Japanese audience, the past decade has seen Sega make concerted efforts to bring the Yakuza series to a global audience, with 2024's Like A Dragon: Infinite Wealth even largely taking place in Hawaii. Stranger Than Heaven also explores Japan during a period of modernisation and Western influence, as shown through its protagonist, Makoto Daito, an orphan with mixed heritage from America and Japan.

I begin with him fleeing poverty, racial discrimination and cops trying to pin a crime on him, as he stows away on a ship in San Francisco that's bound for Japan, hoping to start a new life - almost like a reverse of the immigrant American Dream narrative.

In Makoto, we have a young man whose mixed heritage is made clear by his distinct blue eyes, while English is his first language, a radical change from Yakuza's typically middle-aged Japanese characters, which perhaps also reflects the game being developed by a young team, with game director Mikinobu Abe still in his twenties. Not that this was a factor in choosing a younger protagonist, since we'll also follow Makoto as he ages over five decades.

While RGG Studio's characters have always been societal outcasts as part of the criminal underworld, Makoto and another stowaway, Yu Shinjo, have their mixed heritage also single them out in Japan, as passersby don't hesitate to address them as "keto", an ethnic slur against foreigners that literally translates to "hairy barbarian". It's perhaps how he finds a kind of solidarity with the Black smugglers they have stowed away with, whose charismatic leader, Orpheus, is played by none other than Snoop Dogg.

It's a casting choice that reflects Stranger Than Heaven's ambitions to appeal to a global audience, as is the game's theme song with English and Japanese lyrics performed by pop artists Tori Kelly and Ado respectively, who also have roles in the game. What that also means is that rather than having separate language dubs, the game features a single multilingual audio track, putting to bed any 'subs-versus-dubs' debates, while also arriving at a time when multilingual entertainment is getting more mainstream attention, such as the Emmy-winning Shogun.

"This decision was made to authentically portray Makoto’s dual heritage," Abe clarifies. "The narrative centres on the conflicts and challenges that arise from his identity and cultural background." That's something I was also able to appreciate in the game's opening hours set in Kokura, Fukuoka, in 1915, when Makoto is fresh off the boat and, even as someone who doesn't speak the language, I can hear how he is less confident and fluent in Japanese.

"As the story moves through different eras, Makoto and Yu do not simply grow older; they gradually adapt to life in Japan," Abe explains. "We wanted to express that growth through subtle changes in their body language, mannerisms, and Japanese pronunciation. This meant carefully considering how comfortable they should appear in each scene, so that their adjustment to the environment would feel gradual and natural rather than sudden."

During my hands-on, I also got to explore a couple of other eras, including Kure, Hiroshima in 1929 and Minami, Osaka in 1943. Notably, the passage of time is not presented in one location but in a new city each time. While that does follow a geographical trajectory, starting from the South of Japan and working your way across the country until the story culminates in Tokyo in 1965, the cities picked also serve a narrative purpose.

"Kokura was a major industrial city back then, so it felt natural as the destination for someone who had stowed away on a ship," Abe explains. "We chose Kure in 1929 because it is strongly associated in Japan with yakuza stories, most famously through the film Battles Without Honor and Humanity. It has a particular significance for Makoto, who is conflicted over whether he sees himself as Japanese or American, and entering the world of the yakuza - a distinctly Japanese organisation - intensifies that struggle. At the same time, Kure was a major military port with a significant international population, giving Makoto opportunities to encounter people and experiences that reflect another side of his identity."

With five cities, or rather districts within those cities, it also means a focus on smaller but more densely designed maps closer to Yakuza's Kamurocho compared to the larger, sprawling spaces in the more recent Like A Dragon games.

"Each new city will feel genuinely distinct - not only visually, but also in the way it plays and invites exploration," Abe explains. "Kokura is a dense city where most buildings can be entered, offering players a great deal of depth to explore. Kure is a city built along a coastal mountainside, creating a vertical landscape that encourages exploration across multiple elevations. In Minami, the buildings become taller, and players can enter large multi-tenant complexes."

While there is a challenge in depicting the main cast physically ageing across five decades, it's also expressed through fashion, which really stood out as I played through three of Stranger Than Heaven's eras, with Makoto sporting a different hairstyle and clothes in each one. I also received an answer from art director Daishi Kanaya on these fashion choices, and why, unlike recent Yakuza games, the player won't have free rein to customise them.

"Rather than simply incorporating the fashions of the time, we wanted Makoto’s appearance and clothing to convey his position and situation in life, the relationships around him, and the environment he is living in at that point in the story - for example, what kind of organisation he belongs to and how much financial security he has," Kanaya explains. "We have not made his appearance customisable by the player. We felt it was important for us to present the version of Makoto that is most appropriate to each stage of his life, so that players can more strongly experience his journey as a person."

Stranger Than Heaven's ambitions are also evident in the technical advances made with RGG Studio's decade-old in-house Dragon Engine. While recent games have been made as cross-platform releases, this one is coming exclusively to current-gen, which has allowed the studio to incorporate more complex human behaviour to make the world feel more alive, and to use advanced post-processing and lighting to elevate the visuals. This is especially great during the game's lengthy cutscenes, something the studio already prides itself on doing, which also show its flair and understanding of drama, as these aren't just reserved for bombastic action sequences but really shine during quiet human moments, such as Makoto's first meeting with Tae, played exquisitely by Shogun's Moeka Hoshi.

However, Abe clarifies that he also worked closely with Kanaya to develop a distinct visual style that wasn't just about high-fidelity photorealism. "Kanaya has a background in oil painting, while I come from a filmmaking background, so we brought our respective perspectives together as we searched for a visual identity unique to this title," he explains. "We studied vintage lenses, old films, record covers, and paintings from the period, trying to understand what made those works feel so distinctive - the way they captured light, the softness of their focus, and the texture they created."

As a new game that sets itself apart from the Yakuza series, even if it's still technically in the same universe, portraying what will be the origins of the Tojo Clan, Stranger Than Heaven has been built from the ground up, a change from the studio's approach to efficiently recycling assets for its successive Yakuza titles. That includes a radically different, if at times awkward, dual-limbed combat system that I previously grappled with at Gamescom, as well as many more new bespoke animations, including everyday actions like Makoto eating food from a stall or drinking from a fountain.

"While some motions from previous titles were used as a starting point, they were extensively revised - often to the point that their origins would be unrecognisable. This was necessary because Makoto, his world, and the story surrounding him represent a major departure from our previous games. The way people walk and carry themselves differs from a modern setting, and Makoto’s behaviour and reactions to his environment are specific to his character and era. As a result, we needed to create and adjust the animations accordingly."

In the case of the combat system, while I still found it a bit of a struggle, especially against multiple foes, it's also intentional so that you're not just easily smacking down enemies like Yakuza's Kazuma Kiryu with simple but powerful inputs. "We took a lot of inspiration from Japanese yakuza films and found how raw their action can feel," Abe explains. "The characters are not martial arts masters; their fights are often desperate and unrefined. They grab each other’s clothes, struggle at close range, and use whatever is around them. It is not simply a matter of throwing punches and kicks. In these films, violence often carries a real sense of life-or-death tension - it is a matter of killing or being killed. Creating that tension, and allowing players to experience Makoto’s fear, desperation, and gradual growth firsthand, was at the core of our approach to the tone of the combat."

While a lot of research was carried out to ensure environments were authentic to their time period, the game also carries the disclaimer that it is "in no way a reproduction of actual history", which perhaps also gives it licence to be a little anachronistic, such as having Snoop Dogg rapping a few bars in the title song, which musically also has some hip-hop influences, despite the genre originating in the US in the 1970s outside of Stranger Than Heaven's setting. Snoop himself might also be a bit of a distraction - as has been the controversial casting of the late Tupac Shakur, who wasn't shown during this hands-on - as there's a scene where Orpheus teaches Makoto how to roll his own tobacco (indicative of its time period; smoking in this game actually gives you buffs), though given one of the ingredients is "grass", I couldn't help but be taken out of the moment and think, yep, that's Snoop.

"What mattered to us was depicting a reimagined world and era with a sense of realism to depict what we wanted as a gameplay experience and narrative," Abe explains. "The same approach applied to the casting of Snoop Dogg. Orpheus would teach Makoto how to survive in Japan and how to make money through music and show business, and at the same time, he is a smuggler who brings Makoto from America to Japan. He needed to be someone formidable - someone with musical talent who could also handle emotionally demanding scenes. So from early on, we had the idea that it would be amazing if Snoop Dogg could play the role."

That still leaves the question of setting a story across a period of Japanese history that, while full of cultural change, is also controversial. Considering that Stranger Than Heaven's story depicts racial discrimination in Japan, I can't help but think of the multigenerational drama Pachinko, also beginning in 1915, depicting the treatment of Korean immigrants in Japan during its imperial rule of Korea, which seems entirely absent. You could also argue that the story intentionally skims over more controversial moments in the country's history, notably omitting the 1930s, when it invaded China, and ending before the civil unrest of the late 1960s.

Ultimately, Abe argues that the focus is more on Makoto's personal journey than on recounting history. "The game does touch on historical events, for example, its 1943 Osaka setting takes place during wartime, but the narrative is fundamentally centred on Makoto Daito’s life rather than depicting history in detail," he explains. "Even during war, which profoundly affects the lives of everyone, people still live their own individual lives, and Makoto is no different."

Stranger Than Heaven is then as ambitious as it is contentious, but through its Japanese-Western cultural exchanges and a significant upgrade of visuals and systems, it has the potential to be RGG Studio's biggest global hit to date.
Stranger Than Heaven releases on 15 January 2027 for Xbox Series X/S, PS5, and PC.

items.title: Gérard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged rape of actress in 2018, court rules
paragraphs: French film actor Gérard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.
Arnould, who was 22 at the time, had reported the alleged rape several days after going to his house in Paris to rehearse a play.
She has waived her right to anonymity and her lawyer said Thursday's ruling was a "first" and the forthcoming trial would be historic.

Depardieu, 77, had contested his indictment on two counts of rape. In a letter published in Le Figaro in 2023, Depardieu strongly denied Arnould's allegations, saying "there was never any coercion or violence between us".

Depardieu was for decades a leading figure in French and international cinema for roles in Green Card, The Man in the Iron Mask and the Asterix films. He was awarded France's Légion d'honneur in 1996.

But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc (call out your pig).

Last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation.
He dropped his appeal against the ruling last week and offered "sincere apologies" for his behaviour on the set of director Jean Becker's 2021 film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters).
Depardieu had been a friend of Charlotte Arnould's father and on 7 August 2018 she had gone to his home, where much of what happened was captured on the actor's own CCTV.
Arnould's case was initially dismissed for insufficient evidence, but after she filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation was opened in the summer of 2020.
Speaking outside the Paris appeal court on Thursday, her lawyer Carine Durrieu Diebolt said the ruling was a victory for her client for whom it was "genuinely a relief".
The appeal court said that while Depardieu should stand trial for what took place on that day, he would not be tried for a further alleged rape at a hotel six days later.

Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters that court had partly ruled in his favour: "As soon as we get the ruling, we will look into the possibility of appealing to the Court of Cassation."
Meanwhile, Depardieu is under a separate investigation alongside French author Michel Houellebecq for "allegations of a sexual nature".
French authorities confirmed their inquiry last week, following reports of an alleged "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018.

items.title: Earphones Black Friday deals: 14 brilliant IEMs that punch far above their price
paragraphs: Whether you're a musician who needs accurate monitoring, a designer who wants something better than AirPods for long editing sessions, or simply someone who loves quality audio, Linsoul IEMs make some of the best IEMs (in-ear-monitors) around.
But, other than the best budget IEMs, they usually don't come cheap, so when Black Friday comes around, it's the perfect time to pick up a bargain.

In this article, I've picked out the IEMs I think are most worth your money, running from budget single-driver sets to the best multi-driver IEMs under $500. Many are models I've tested myself, and all of them punch well above their price tags.

I just love this IEM. Billed as the world's flattest IEM, the Reference is built for people who want to hear exactly what's on the recording. Twin 10mm dynamic drivers in a horizontally opposed layout handle the bass, while two Sonion balanced armatures take the mids and a Knowles supertweeter covers the top end. It's the top pick in my best IEMs under $500 guide for a good reason.

This is Xenns Mangird's most premium IEM to date, and it doesn't hold back on hardware: two dynamic drivers and eight balanced armatures per side, split across a four-way crossover. As a result, you get to enjoy a wide, open soundstage with clear, airy treble and loads of detail, while the swirling, abalone-style resin faceplates mean that no two pairs look quite the same.

I'm a big fan of the Tea Pro, which I called "engagingly musical and beautifully built" in my review. Its dual 8mm dynamic drivers and six balanced armatures deliver a full, natural and lush sound, with a sub-bass presence that's always there without ever swamping the midrange. It's not the most analytical, but perfect to relax into for hours at a time.

On a tighter budget? The EW300 packs a lot of tech for the cash, combining three driver types in one compact CNC-machined shell: a 10mm dynamic driver for the bass and mids, plus a 6mm planar and a piezoelectric driver working together on the highs. Swappable nozzles let you tweak the tuning, and overall, the sound from this IEM is warm, punchy and forgiving.

Out of all of ZiiGaat's recent releases, the Horizon is my favourite, earning 8 out of 10 in my review. It pairs a 10mm dynamic driver with two Knowles balanced armatures and two planar drivers, producing a bright-leaning, detailed sound with an impressively spacious soundstage. If you can handle a lively treble, it's an absolute treat.

Launched in 2022, the original Cadenza is a bit of a legend, and it's still the perfect budget entry point into the world of IEMs. A single 10mm beryllium diaphragm dynamic driver, sat inside a 3D-printed resin shell, delivers a balanced sound with rich mids and clear treble, for a low, low price. Light, comfortable and a big step up from basic buds.

Released early this year, the Cadenza II builds on its predecessor with a new 10mm titanium-coated dynamic driver and Kiwi Ears' updated KARS 2.0 bass-tuning system. My review focused on its near-neutral sound and excellent build quality, which includes a CNC-machined aluminium faceplate. If you like your sound bass-heavy, look elsewhere, but if you seek an affordable all-rounder, you're golden.

Billed as the world's first MEMS + 1DD + 3BA tribrid IEM, the Halcyon pairs a MEMS driver, a type of tech also used in hearing aids, with a 10mm dynamic driver and three balanced armatures. When testing it for my review I loved its deep, rumbly sub-bass and well-judged treble; if your playlists lean bass-heavy, it really shines.

The Odyssey pairs a custom 10mm dynamic driver with three genuine Knowles balanced armatures: two full-range drivers for the mids and an ultra-high frequency tweeter. What makes it stand out is its bass: low notes hit like a subwoofer but stop quickly rather than lingering. That keeps the neutral midrange clean and uncluttered, with vocals that sound natural rather than plasticky.

This IEM is a collab between audio brand ZiiGaat and YouTube reviewer Zeos of Z Reviews. Its single 10mm diamond-like carbon (DLC) dynamic driver serves up a hefty 16dB bass shelf, with warm, rich mids and enough treble extension to stop things getting muddy. If you like your music to rumble, this is the one.

The Lush is ZiiGaat's take on a studio monitor and is designed for sound engineers and stage musicians. It pairs a 10mm dynamic driver with four balanced armatures via a three-way crossover, with the bass cut off at 200Hz so it doesn't bleed into the mids. Expect a neutral, coherent and versatile sound in a light, comfortable resin shell.

As the name suggests, Punch Audio is all about big, bold bass, and the Patada gives that tradition a refined twist. Combining a 10mm ceramic diaphragm dynamic driver with a MEMS driver for the top end makes for a smoother, more open treble than you might expect, alongside the usual low-end thump. This is still a basshead set, then, just a slightly more well-behaved one.

The KE4 uses two 10mm dynamic drivers in an isobaric subwoofer arrangement, paired with two balanced armatures through a three-way crossover. It was an early affordable take on the 'New Meta' tuning, and when I reviewed it, I found the bass hefty but the midrange the real star: rich, layered and never boxy or thin. It's comfortable and non-fatiguing to wear, too.

CrinEar's first production IEM, the Daybreak, arrived in 2025 and is built more for enjoyment than analysis. Its combines a dynamic driver, two balanced armatures and two micro-planar drivers in a 3D-printed resin shell with aluminium faceplates. If the Reference prioritises strict accuracy, the Daybreak goes for a more engaging, crowd-pleasing sound that works with pretty much any genre.

It's been a remarkable year for in-ear monitors, and Chinese brands, often lumped together under the "ChiFi "label, are a big reason why. Companies such as ZiiGaat, Kiwi Ears and Simgot are releasing new models at a dizzying pace, and they're no longer just competing on price.
We're seeing genuine innovation, from MEMS drivers to micro-planars, alongside a wave of collaborations with influential reviewers such as Z Reviews and HBB.
The upshot? Sound quality that would have cost a small fortune a decade ago is now available for less than a decent pair of trainers, and the gap with the big established brands keeps on shrinking.

items.title: Sinister signs, suicidal shepherds and a sensational six-hour song: Ragnar Kjartansson’s art is heroically human
paragraphs: Live in the gallery a man in a dark suit and white shoes leans cabaret-style against a piano and sings about his one great love. “Jenny kissed me,” he intones in a voice both melodic and casually conversational. He croons the words of this love song again, and again, and again.

Icelandic artist Ragnar Kjartansson’s durational performance (which means it takes a heck of a long time) is beguiling and beautiful. It’s also a brilliant interpretation of a small masterpiece of English Romantic poetry, Jenny Kiss’d Me, by Leigh Hunt: “Jenny kissed me when we met / Jumping from the chair she sat in.” The poet demands that “Time, you thief” write this down so that he can keep this memory of a perfect moment of love.

Kjartansson’s exquisite theatrical delivery makes you realise this is not so different from Frank Sinatra belting out “No, they can’t take that away from me.” Yet Kjartansson’s lounge singer persona is sweeter and quieter than Frank, and a long way from Vegas, with live piano accompaniment by Kristín Anna Valtýsdóttir in front of a glass wall looking out on winter trees. As he remembers Jenny kissing him, the singer repeats more of Hunt’s poem: “Say I’m weary, say I’m sad … / Say I’m growing old.” You hear the melancholy in his voice, but then comes the triumphant refrain: whatever time may take away, however much he loses, “Jenny kissed me.”

The full performance lasts six hours and will be recorded and shown as a video in this exhibition at Goodwood Art Foundation. The preview I saw was desperately powerful. Kjartansson finds the philosophical nub of Hunt’s poem and ruthlessly emphasises it by seemingly endless repetition: only one moment in this singer’s life matters, the moment Jenny kissed him, and everything else, all the defeat and entropy, is dissolved in the face of this overwhelming fact.

It’s a remarkable piece of performance art, ravishingly conceptual and heroically human. He enacts it in the middle of a gallery hung with four of his big paintings, of Icelandic landscapes with tiny sheep and human figures amid vast gullies and sweeping moorlands. These landscapes belong to a series called Weekdays in Arcadia, which he claims are inspired by his participation in a traditional Icelandic custom in which the community takes part in shepherding flocks down from the mountains. Not that I am doubting his story. It’s just, wow, what a place.

That reference to Arcadia explicitly evokes another landscape painting that meditates on melancholy in the hills and woods: Poussin’s Et in Arcadia Ego, in which Arcadian shepherds have found a tombstone inscription that can be interpreted as Death saying, “I too am here.” One of Kjartansson’s paintings, a sublime and noxious landscape, replaces Poussin’s tombstone with one of Iceland’s natural emblems of mortality, a volcano. Kjartansson’s weekend shepherds – the artist included? – have followed their flock over fields of ash close to its black, mist-wreathed peak.

Kjartansson reveals landscape art as inherently melancholic, full of mortal thoughts. In this gently wooded, pastoral arts centre on the edge of an aristocratic estate he plays with mordant wit on Nordic and English varieties of gloom.

Walk out into the woods and you find his flip homage to Edvard Munch’s Ashes, a painting of despair in the forest: the word NIGHTMARE stands in huge, individual bright yellow letters among the trees. Further along the path, a towering classical monument worthy of a Poussin painting rises in a clearing. Its fake marble grandeur speaks of dignified grief, as if it were mourning a battle or bereavement, but its inscription is comically puzzling: EPIC WASTE OF LOVE AND UNDERSTANDING. These words were actually uttered in a conversation between Kjartansson and his wife – had their relationship all been an epic waste of love and understanding? They laughed at the eloquence and he put it on a monument.

Back inside, in the bigger gallery, there are more monuments, whole shelves of them in neat rows, little porcelain obelisks inscribed in blue: GUILT and FEAR. Are these for sale? Can I buy one? These too come with a nice story: his grandfather was a leading Icelandic ceramicist. There is also a multi-screen film that surrounds you with guitar-playing dancers walking from screen to screen as they strum, their relaxed yet precise choreography and musical synchrony suggesting the same sense of community and mutual caring that makes Icelanders go shepherding together.

Kjartansson’s witty art keeps you guessing about how serious he is. His cinematic Nightmare sign is almost a joke about outsiders’ expectations of dark and sinister Nordic culture, while his monument to wasted feeling may be sad or hilarious. But when he starts to sing about Jenny, you are hit by inexhaustible passion. I could listen for ever. I had to be shepherded away to the press bus.

items.title: Here’s where you can save (a little) on the Ocarina of Time remake
paragraphs: In addition to GTA VI, Nintendo’s stellar Zelda remake is sure to be one of the most popular gaming gifts this holiday.
In addition to GTA VI, Nintendo’s stellar Zelda remake is sure to be one of the most popular gaming gifts this holiday.
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

A lot of people have The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo Switch 2 on their holiday wishlist. In case you haven’t bought it yet, I wanted to share some small but welcome deals happening on the physical and digital versions of the game. Costco members can currently grab the cartridge edition for $62.99, down from its regular price of $69.99 (it’s the only retailer currently discounting the physical version). Both Amazon and Costco are also selling the digital version for $54.99, a small $5 discount.

Ocarina of Time is one of Nintendo’s most groundbreaking titles, having served as its first 3D Zelda game when it launched in 1998. Parts of the original game haven’t aged particularly well — namely some dungeon design and the game’s tricky 3D navigation, since there was only one analog stick at the time — which makes it tough for some to enjoy going back to play the N64 version. Thankfully, the Switch 2 remake introduces several fixes, a host of quality-of-life improvements, and, of course, some lovely visuals that make it a graphics powerhouse by today’s standards.

If you go the digital route, a recent Switch 2 update lets you gift games to players in your family group. It doesn’t have to be your actual family, either, just up to eight people you designate as part of your group. The digital game will then appear gift-wrapped on their homescreen.

items.title: Congo Ebola outbreak reaches 12,000 cases as some responders evacuate
paragraphs: Relatives and healthcare workers prepare to bury a victim of Ebola, in Beni, North Kivu province, Congo, Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP hide caption

BUNIA, Congo — The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has topped 12,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Thursday, as fighting between rebels and the army disrupts efforts to contain the spread of the disease.

It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and nearly half the 12,021 people confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from Congo's Ministry of Health. It is also the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.

The outbreak declared in May is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of people who are sick or have died from the disease. Containing the disease requires quickly identifying and treating patients in isolation, monitoring people who may have been exposed and safely burying the dead.

Fighting between the army and the Convention pour la révolution populaire rebels resumed Thursday morning in Iga-Barrière, a mining town about 25 kilometers (15 miles) north of Bunia in eastern Congo, sending new waves of displaced people toward the city. Bunia is the capital of northeastern Ituri province and a major hub for the Ebola response.

CRP is one of more than 100 armed groups in eastern Congo, where conflict has created one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises. The group was founded last year by former warlord Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International Criminal Court in 2012 of recruiting children under 15 and using them in fighting.

Fighting between the army and the rebels earlier this week had already prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus and left some treatment centers with fewer staff, Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization's Ebola incident manager, said Wednesday.

Smallwood said that about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday after three full days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.

items.title: North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture
paragraphs: In this photo provided by the North Korean government, leader Kim Jong Un inspects a facility the government says is for producing weapons-grade nuclear material at an undisclosed location in North Korea, Monday, Nov. 25, 2026. Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service via AP hide caption
Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service via AP

SEOUL, South Korea — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons, days after ignoring U.S. President Donald Trump's offer to meet during his recent visit to Asia.
Experts say Kim likely wants to show off his evolving nuclear arsenal, the backbone of his authoritarian rule, and reaffirm his rejection of any future talks on dismantling his nuclear program.

The North's official Korean Central News Agency said Thursday that Kim inspected two nuclear materials production factories, one newly inaugurated and the other being expanded. KCNA photos showed Kim and senior military officials walking between dense rows of what appeared to be centrifuges used to produce weapons-grade uranium and touring halls displaying what were believed to be warheads. Some of the images were blurred.
KCNA said Kim visited a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute as well on Wednesday.

North Korea has disclosed a uranium enrichment site a few times since it showed one at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex to visiting American scholars in 2010. North Korea didn't say where the nuclear materials production factories that Kim visited this week are located. In June, when North Korea disclosed parts of a uranium enrichment site while reporting on Kim's visit there, outside experts assessed it was likely an additional uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon.

Kim justifies nuke program by citing threats from US, South KoreaKim said his latest inspection visit was part of efforts to strengthen North Korea's defense capabilities in response to "variable nuclear threats approaching the Korean Peninsula moment by moment." He accused the U.S. of inciting its regional allies to possess nuclear-powered submarines and committing to sharing its nuclear weapons with them, KCNA said.

"The validity and substantiality of our possession of nuclear weapons and the trend of bolstering up its nuclear capability in quality and quantity are an irreversible reality," Kim said, according to KCNA.

Kim also said the deployment of low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons across multiple domains for various missions is crucial and urgent given North Korea's "inevitable reality facing the border with the most dangerous enemy state," a reference to South Korea. North Korea has in recent years focused on developing such tactical nuclear weapons amid heightened animosity with South Korea.

"Trump has talked about a willingness to meet Kim Jong Un, but the basic U.S. position that North Korea must denuclearize remains unchanged. So Kim Jong Un wants to say 'Look at how powerful we are. Don't talk about denuclearization if you want to meet us,'" said Moon Seong Mook, an analyst for the Seoul-based Korea Research Institute for National Strategy.

Moon said Kim's visit to the nuclear facilities was also likely meant to check on how state objectives on the nuclear program have progressed this year and what future goals must be set ahead of a year-end Workers' Party conference.

South Korea's Defense Ministry said it takes Kim's comments on battlefield nuclear weapons seriously and added that Seoul maintains a firm military readiness against Pyongyang's nuclear threats under an alliance with the U.S. South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff declined to share an analysis of the North Korean nuclear facilities reported by KCNA, calling it confidential information for South Korea and the U.S.

Trump still hopes to meet KimTrump reiterated his eagerness to restore diplomacy with Kim as he visited China last week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. But a Trump-Kim meeting didn't happen, with Pyongyang not publicly responding to Trump's overture.

In an interview with the New York Post this week, Trump dismissed the suggestion that Kim had rebuffed his outreach, saying, "No, he didn't ignore it. You know, we had many leaders there … There'll be a time when we meet … It was just not really the right time. It was a very busy two-day period."

Trump also claimed he could revive diplomacy with Kim at any time by restarting the exchange of letters they maintained during his first term, although he acknowledged that the two leaders had not corresponded "recently."

Kim has previously said he could return to talks if the U.S. drops its "hostile policy" against his country and respects what he calls the North's status as a nuclear state. Experts say Kim aims to win international recognition as a nuclear state so that he could demand the lifting of international sanctions.

Last week, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi assessed North Korea has been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon, calling the move "a cause for serious concern."

Nuclear weapons can be built using either highly enriched uranium or weapons-grade plutonium, and North Korea has facilities to produce both at Yongbyon. Last year, South Korea's Unification Minister Chung Dong-young said that North Korea was operating four uranium enrichment facilities and that they were running every day.

items.title: Kids’ tech is a minefield – here's what I’d actually recommend as a parent, design editor and qualified teacher
paragraphs: Like lots of parents, I'm always looking for activities that stop my kids sitting sedentary in front of screens. I use all the tech-free tactics I can, like arts and crafts and board games, but I also value the experiences tech can give them. I just want that tech to be more creative than a tablet or the TV.

Not all kids' tech is evil, and some is pretty darn great. I've found a niche that combines being a parent, my love of design and my years as an early years teacher, and it means I get to test some seriously good products. There are a few I'm firmly recommending, and they'd make great Christmas presents.

I love the Yoto. I can't shout about this enough. We've been using it for the last seven years, I bought one when my daughter was two, and it's going from strength to strength in functionality and design (read my interview with the team who recently redesigned the hardware). The Yoto does have a screen but is very deliberately only using it to display fun pixel graphics, and the time.

If you're not familiar, you play stories and music hosted on cards via the Yoto machine – which comes in a full sized and mini version. Cards are available to buy – but you can also make your own cards, which is the major selling point for me. You can record your own content, or you can put MP3 files onto them. There's also an ever-changing library of podcasts and other audio, accessed via an app.
Yoto is currently up to 30% off – and it would make a fabulous Christmas present.

I bang on about the Nex Playground to everyone – my family adores it. It's an active play system that gets players up and moving through its whole body tracking. In my experience, this console counters the usual effect video games or tablets have on children. It encourages discussion, collaboration with its gentle and imaginative games, which include sports like Bowling (my son's favourite), and big-name titles like How to Train Your Dragon and Bluey. See our full Nex Playground review here.
If you're thinking about a console for your children this Christmas, I really can't recommend this one enough – and it's also currently got 37% in the UK, and 30% in the US off for Black Friday.

If you've got a younger child interested in 3D printing, this is a great option. As I say in my Funbox review, if your child is at the upper end of the 4-12 age bracket, I'd go for a proper 3D printer. My daughter is on the borderline at 9, but my son (5) would get plenty of life from this printer.

It's a fun design, and is super-simple to use via an app. You can draw designs and let the AI print them, or pick from a marketplace of designs (make sure you use the official UGEE designs for maximum effectiveness). Because it's enclosed, it's safer for kids to use.
It's currently got a small saving of $20 at Amazon.

This is the one I'm yet to try, but I'm so excited by the idea. I join a lot of parents in not wanting my children to have their own phones for a long while yet, but I realised that when I was younger I would be phoning my friends on the landline. We don't have a landline, and I gatekeep my own phone for obvious reasons. So I was searching for a solution – and the Tin Can is perfect.

Pitched as a New-School Landline phone, it connects to the WiFi and only phones/accepts calls from approved numbers (controlled via an app). If another child has a TinCan, they can phone each other for free, and other approved numbers can be called if you pay a monthly subscription.

I've got one on its way to me so I'll be doing a review on it soon, but I wanted to put it on your radar as I think it's such a smart idea. It's out in the US, and preorders are open for before-Christmas delivery in the UK.
Want the latest from the world of graphic design?

Georgia has spent the best part of the last decade writing about art, design and tech. After becoming the site's Editor since 2022, Georgia has put her passion and knowledge into steering the site into connecting with the creative community. As well as immersing herself with the industry at events like Adobe Max and the D&AD Awards, Georgia has continued to look out for projects to spotlight, products to test and growing the site. Georgia is also Programme Director of CB's award scheme – the Brand Impact Awards.
