items.title: RSHP centres cantilevered office building Sąvaržėlė around glass atrium
paragraphs: UK studio RSHP has revealed its first project in the Baltic region, a mixed-use office building in Lithuania designed as “a landmark that is unmistakably forward-looking”.
Named after the Lithuanian word for paperclip, the seven-storey Sąvaržėlė is located in central Vilnius, between the UNESCO-listed Old Town and the city’s commercial district.
The stacked building has a cantilevered design and houses office space, a conference hall, a restaurant and a cafe across its 19,000-square-metre space.

“At Sąvaržėlė, we wanted to create a workplace that extends into the city – one that welcomes people, encourages collaboration and contributes new public spaces to Vilnius,” RSHP associate director Jack Evans-Newton said.

“Occupying a unique position between the historic centre and the city’s emerging business district, the building brings these two identities together through a calm and contemporary architectural expression,” he continued.

“Clarity of form, generous public spaces and carefully crafted detailing create a landmark that is unmistakably forward-looking, reflecting the ambition of a growing business district while respecting the scale and character of its historic setting.”
Sąvaržėlė has large, adaptable floorplates, designed to create a flexible interior.

The building has a stacked, rectangular shape and was made from prefabricated steel components that were bolted together on site. On the east and west facades, RSHP placed external ribs that the studio said “echo the tones” of Vilnius’ historic architecture.
Sąvaržėlė is arranged around a central glass atrium with a striking yellow-lined elevator. It can be accessed via a number of different entrances that connect to the surrounding streets.
To enhance the building’s environmental performance, RSHP added a double-skin facade. This uses energy-efficient chilled beam cooling and automated natural ventilation to help reduce energy demand.
In addition, Sąvaržėlė has a 2,897-square-metre fully landscaped green roof.
RSHP has also recently designed a 45-storey skyscraper in Shenzhen and a curved-roof railway hub.

items.title: Veruschka: Striking images of one of the world's first supermodels, who has died aged 87
paragraphs: Veruschka was a distinctive presence on the covers of magazines like Vogue and Life in the 1960s and 70s
Veruschka, the model and artist who became one of the first global fashion stars in the 1960s, has died at the age of 87.
She became known as the striking subject of fantastical photoshoots that helped expand the boundaries of fashion and beauty in the 60s and 70s, appearing on the cover of American Vogue 13 times.

Vogue's obituary, external described her as "the shape-shifting supermodel who defined an era", explaining: "One of the original supermodels, Veruschka was also among fashion's great performance artists."
She also made memorable appearances in classic swinging 60s film Blow Up and 2006 James Bond movie Casino Royale.
Veruschka was born Vera von Lehndorff into an aristocratic family in 1939 in Königsberg, then in Germany, now known as Kaliningrad in Russia.
Her father, Heinrich Count von Lehndorff, was executed in 1944 for his part in a failed plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler.
She studied art in Hamburg and Florence before beginning her career as a model "and soon became a legend", her sister Countess Catharina von Lehndorff wrote in a tribute, external.
"She worked with Yves Saint Laurent, Karl Lagerfeld, and Valentino, but also immersed herself in avant-garde photography projects in which she painted, staged, and deconstructed her body.
"Veruschka was never just a model – she was an artist, a boundary-pusher, a rebel. Her work is considered a feminist precursor to performance art."

items.title: Carlo Ratti and AI assistant to curate Seoul Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism 2027
paragraphs: Italian architect Carlo Ratti has been named the curator of next year’s Seoul Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism, for which he plans to take “an unconventional, AI-based” approach.
Taking place from 24 September 2027, the biennale will be used by Ratti as an opportunity to question the role of a curator today through the lens of architecture.
However, the event’s title, theme and full curatorial team will not be unveiled until 8 December.
What Ratti has revealed so far is that he plans to take “an unconventional, AI-based” approach to the event.
Specifically, he will use an AI assistant, aiming to challenge traditional approaches to developing exhibitions by highlighting emerging tools that can help curators.
“I am delighted to take on the direction of the Seoul Biennale and to explore the future of cities together with the Seoul Metropolitan Government,” says Carlo Ratti.
“Seoul is perhaps the best place in the world to ask how artificial intelligence and the collective wisdom of its citizens might shape the city together,” he continued.
“At the upcoming pre-biennale event, we will begin to introduce the people who will join us, and I think there will be a few surprises – one assistant curator isn’t even human!”
Ratti is an Italian architect and engineer, and director of his eponymous studio Carlo Ratti Associati. He is also a professor at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).
He was appointed by Seoul mayor Oh Se Hoon, succeeding British designer Thomas Heatherwick, who curated the 2025 event.
Heatherwick centred the event on a long, four-storey-high wall displaying images that reflected the ideals of his Humanise campaign.
The Seoul Biennale was established in 2017 by the Seoul Metropolitan Government as a festival of international architecture and urbanism.
“The Seoul Biennale is a place where architects and citizens from around the world think together about the future of cities and explore new possibilities,” said mayor Oh.

“Together with general director Carlo Ratti, who has connected architecture, cities, and technology, we will prepare so that the sixth Seoul Biennale offers a new perspective on cities and architecture and a meaningful experience for citizens.”

Ratti’s previous curatorial experience includes the Venice Architecture Biennale in 2025, for which the theme was Intelligens. Natural. Artificial. Collective. It explored how architecture can be adapted to increasingly unstable living environments through cross-disciplinary collaboration.
At the time, Ratti said, “Dezeen killed the traditional form of the biennale“.
The architect’s other recent projects include the French Pavilion at Expo 2025 Osaka and a proposal for a children’s hospital housed in a one-kilometre “green ring”.

items.title: A vocal cohort of tech leaders celebrates Huang’s Nvidia return, but others are keeping quiet
paragraphs: The phrase “return of the king” rippled across social media on Monday. A vocal subsection of the tech industry was celebrating the resurrection of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. Some called him the “imperial and royal majesty”, others anointed him as “our Jesus” and several simply posted a crown emoji.
“The mistake has been corrected,” said Elon Musk. “Jensen!” exclaimed OpenAI’s Sam Altman.

It had been a whirlwind two weeks that started with the ouster of Huang as Nvidia’s CEO after his admission of an extramarital affair with a woman some in the US government feared to be a Chinese spy. Two more alleged affairs with company employees were later revealed. Silicon Valley engineers and venture capitalists decried Huang’s departure at the time, writing an open letter to Nvidia’s board of directors saying: “Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice.”
Donald Trump also got involved. The president repeatedly said that he’d like to see the return of Huang calling the CEO a “fine person” and “honorable guy”.

In the meantime, Nvidia’s stock tanked, falling more than 10%, and shedding hundreds of billions in value. Nvidia, which designs powerful computing chips used for artificial intelligence, is among the world’s top five most valuable companies.

On Monday, in a stunning reversal, Nvidia’s board unanimously voted to reinstate Huang. The decision came after Trump dialed into the company’s Sunday board meeting to advocate for Huang’s return. In a statement, the White House said: “We have to protect our geniuses.”
Nvidia’s stock rebounded, gaining nearly $1tn in market value. Trump, who owns shares in the chip maker, took a victory lap, making up to $15m with the surge on Monday.

Silicon Valley’s venture capitalists also rejoiced. Jason Calacanis, an angel investor, Nvidia stock-holder and co-host of the tech-centric All-In podcast, wrote a flurry of posts on X. He posted an AI image of a shining long-haired Huang depicted as Jesus holding a graphics processing unit (GPU) in place of the bible, writing: “GPU Jesus has risen.”

Other tech figures took the news personally. Travis Kalanick, the disgraced Uber CEO who was pushed out by his board, was one of the top figures fighting for Huang’s reinstatement. In past weeks, he frequently posted on X, saying “Bring Jensen back”, “LFG” (Let’s fucking go), and “We’ve got your back”.

Kalanick was reportedly among a small group of venture capitalists who lobbied Trump and JD Vance to push Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang, according to the FT. On Monday, Kalanick posted: “I will always sign up to serve him.”
While a vocal cohort of Silicon Valley insiders high-fived Huang’s return, it’s been radio silence from several other of the industry’s top leaders and rank-and-file workers.

The CEOs of Google, Meta and Apple have not weighed in on the debate. When Amazon’s Jeff Bezos was asked at an event last week if he thought Huang should be reinstated, he responded: “I don’t know enough of the details … so I can’t answer that question.” Microsoft’s Satya Nadella had a similar response.

Anil Dash, an entrepreneur with a career in leading smaller tech companies, is one of the few voices in tech who has publicly criticized Huang’s reinstatement. He says it sends the wrong message to the industry – that there are no rules, boundaries or accountability.

Dash pointed to widespread rationale for Huang’s return, which is based on the CEO being singularly crucial in the AI arms race against China. Calacanis, for example, has trumpeted this justification, saying: “We can not [sic] lose the race for super intelligence to China – period, full stop.”

And now, Dash said, Huang could have been compromised by a Chinese asset, and he’s running the biggest company in the industry. “It doesn’t make any sense,” he said. “We’re all being gaslit and we’re at a certain point where we’re like, ‘No, the sky’s not green. The sky’s blue.’”

Dash says the hundreds of thousands of tech workers who live in fear of being swept up in the increasingly frequent waves of layoffs, as the industry pivots to AI, aren’t able to speak up even if they disagree with Huang’s reinstatement. They don’t know if their “boss agrees with these guys”, Dash said.

Alison Taylor, an associate professor at New York University’s Stern Business School, said that mentality extends beyond Silicon Valley to the White House, given that Trump played a part in Huang’s return. “Trump’s whole thing is retaliation,” she noted.

“The message is: if you don’t shut up and go along with it, you’re not going to survive,” Taylor said. “It’s a fuck you to everybody who believes in the rule of law and who believes in anything being fair.”

Huang apologized to Nvidia staff in a company-wide meeting on Tuesday for “some terrible mistakes” he made. The CEO also rejected narratives that he was a “tech bro” who was “above the law”, adding it was “completely untrue” that Trump pressured Nvidia’s board to reinstate him.
“Everything he’s done, it’s just his affection, his admiration, his recognition of the great company that you are,” Huang said of Trump.
In a separate statement, Huang thanked leaders across the industry for their “extraordinary support”.
“I can’t wait to get back to work,” he added.

items.title: The dhow builders crafting giant historic ships in India – in pictures
paragraphs: In the 16th century, the port city of Mandvi on India’s west coast was founded by the rulers of the kingdom of Kutch, and quickly established itself as one of the most dynamic ports in the western Indian Ocean. Its strategic geographical position, along the estuary of the Rukmavati River, which flows into the Arabian Sea in the Gulf of Kutch, and mastery of monsoon wind navigation enabled it to become part of vast maritime networks connecting India to the Gulf, the Arabian peninsula and east Africa.
Mandvi prospered through trade, exporting cotton textiles, indigo, cereals and handicrafts, while importing dates, pearls, Arabian horses and luxury goods.

A stemson, a piece of supporting timber in the bow of a boat, is carved from teak in a Mandvi shipyard under supervision by the master shipwright, or mistri, who designs boats without written plans. All photographs: Frédéric Noy

The city was renowned for its shipyards, which specialised in building huge teak dhows suitable for long voyages across the Indian Ocean. This craft industry was a pillar of the local economy, contributing to Mandvi’s influence far beyond India, and it continues to employ many families of carpenters and other workers today.
The huge teak dhows, traditional vessels suited to long voyages across the Indian Ocean, take about three years to build

Clockwise from top left: a worker cuts a varangue, part of the boat’s frame, from a large piece of teak. This piece connects the two sides of the hull to the keel; a bolt securing a beam to a boat’s frame is tightened; using a chain hoist, a worker positions a stemson inside the hull of a boat; a worker heads home on Thursday evening. The following day, Friday, is the weekly rest day.

It was from the 19th century onwards that Mandvi began to fall into economic decline. The advent of steamships, the need for deep, modern port infrastructure and British colonial rule, which restructured maritime trade to serve its own interests, led to a shift in trade to better-equipped ports such as Mumbai.

After independence in 1947, the creation of the nearby port of Kandla definitively marginalised Mandvi commercially. Mandvi was also affected by the 2001 earthquake in Kutch, which damaged some of the old buildings and accelerated its urban transformation.
Workers in Manvi also maintain and repair modern vessels

The city still clings to its few traditional shipyards, where workers from different religious communities build the boats. While a large proportion of them are Muslim, shipbuilding is also part of a very ancient Hindu tradition.

Each dhow takes several years to build by hand and employs about 25 craftsmen. Apprenticeships begin in adolescence, in a world where teams are related and the trade is as much cultural as it is technical.
Away from the shipbuilding, the city today is known for its neglected architectural heritage and its beaches, which attract Indian tourists and middle-class locals.
The local beach is a popular entertainment spot

items.title: At Albuquerque's Indian Pueblo Kitchen, Native American dishes are the main course
paragraphs: Dishes from Indian Pueblo Kitchen in Albuquerque, N.M., include (clockwise from left) an Indian taco on fry bread, a bowl of atole blue corn porridge with fresh berries, a plate of Pueblo pies with biscochitos and a bowl of red chile beef bone posole. Adria Malcolm for NPR hide caption
There are plenty of kitschy diners and barbecue joints along Route 66, but just a couple of miles off the highway in Albuquerque, N.M., Native American dishes are the star at Indian Pueblo Kitchen.
Late on a weekday morning, the restaurant was already starting to fill up. Most of the tables were taken up by locals, like Merlyn Liberty and Rolf Pendall.
The Indian Pueblo Kitchen restaurant is attached to the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center, which was founded by the 19 Pueblo tribes of New Mexico in 1976. Adria Malcolm for NPR hide caption
"I started with breakfast dessert. The blue corn waffles. And now I'm finishing up my sweetheart's plate of enchiladas and pinto beans," Pendall said.
The restaurant is attached to the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center, a museum and cultural center founded in 1976 by the 19 Pueblo tribes of New Mexico.

The center sits on land where the Albuquerque Indian School operated. Open from 1881 to the early 1980s, it was one of the hundreds of federally funded boarding schools designed to strip Native American children of their family bonds, languages, culture and spiritual practices.
The Indian Pueblo Cultural Center's president and CEO, Monique Fragua, said visitors can start in the museum's galleries and then visit the restaurant to experience Pueblo culture and hospitality.

The Indian Pueblo Cultural Center's president and CEO, Monique Fragua, says visitors can experience Pueblo culture through exhibits at the museum and food in the restaurant. Adria Malcolm for NPR hide caption
"Whether that's through our exhibits, or our food, or in our gift shop, we can celebrate the art of our Pueblo communities," Fragua said.
Museum cafés are not a typical destination for foodies, but this one is.

The menu is all Native American and Southwestern-inspired. Dishes include blue corn enchiladas that you can get "Christmas style," one with red chile sauce and the other with green chile sauce. There's a chile posole with beef short ribs served on the bone, as well as Indian tacos on homemade fry bread. Then there's a dish that's really popular on social media: pickles marinated in cherry Kool-Aid and then deep-fried and served with a green chile ranch sauce.
Patrons dine inside Indian Pueblo Kitchen, which features Native American and Southwestern-inspired menu items. Adria Malcolm for NPR hide caption

Rita Toledo, from Jemez Pueblo, is Indian Pueblo Kitchen's star baker. One of her specialties is biscochitos — fragrant shortbread cookies spiced with anise and rolled in cinnamon sugar that are New Mexico's state cookie. Toledo has made some twists on the traditional biscochito, like making a chile pepper version that has just a little kick at the end with a nice balance of sweet and heat.

Indian Pueblo Kitchen's version of biscochitos is so popular that the restaurant also sells them at its café inside Albuquerque's airport. Toledo turns out at least 48 dozen biscochitos each week just for the airport location.
Pastry chef Rita Toledo says one of her specialties is biscochitos — fragrant shortbread cookies spiced with anise and rolled in cinnamon sugar. Adria Malcolm for NPR hide caption

While we chatted, Toledo was wrestling to open a giant tub of one of her main ingredients — lard. These cookies can be made with butter or shortening, she said, but "lard's the only way to make good biscochitos."
Toledo said that she has been baking all her life and that her favorite part of her work is rolling out dough.

"It calms me. You know, your energy comes out on your dough," Toledo said. "I always tell my bakers, 'Come in happy and in a good mood. That way, your products will come out nice and everybody's gonna love it.'"
Toledo makes hundreds of biscochitos each week to keep up with demand. Adria Malcolm for NPR hide caption

Along with locals flocking to visit, the restaurant is also a hit with tourists like Kathy Allio and Jeff Allen from Pennsylvania. While we chatted, Allio was finishing a bowl of bean chili with elk meat.
"The red chiles are just very flavorful without being hot," Allio said, "so it's delicious."
One thing Fragua, the center's president, is particularly proud of is that the Pueblo community can see itself reflected in the museum's galleries and programming and on the restaurant's menu.

"We're lucky to have that history here on our campus, that we've taken lands that were once created to really change the identity of Native people and change that story of who Native people are," Fragua said. "We've created a campus that's built on resilience, empowering our voices and truly telling the stories of who we are as Native people."
A visitor walks through the "Grounded in Clay" exhibition at the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center. Adria Malcolm for NPR hide caption
Additional reporting by Jeanette DeDios of member station KUNM.

items.title: 'Memories of a Good Meal': How food made a difference during WWII
paragraphs: In a composite of three images, June Hersh (left), Steven Fenves (center) and Alon Shaya (right) flip through a book of recipes. The Fenves family's cook salvaged the book when family members were captured by the Nazis. Denny Culbert; June Hersh and Alon Shaya hide caption
NEW ORLEANS — Chef Alon Shaya believes there's power in a meal.

"It's always been the way that I can start a conversation, build a relationship, disagree about things, but still be able to come together and break bread," Shaya, of the acclaimed Crescent City restaurant Saba, said one recent afternoon. "When you share a meal with someone, a lot of those barriers get broken down."

The Israeli American chef also believes food can be a source of inspiration even in the darkest of times. A few years ago, he spearheaded the Rescued Recipes initiative at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and that got him digging deeper into the role that food played during World War II.
Now, he's collected those stories and the dishes they inspired in a new historical cookbook, Memories of a Good Meal: Recipes of Resilience Inspired by Stories of World War II Survival.
Shaya hopes home cooks use the recipes to inspire dinner table conversations about the deeper stories behind them.
"I want people to gather and cook and eat and put their phones down, and share a meal and recount these miraculous stories of survival, resilience and heroism," he told NPR.

Stories like that of Roddie Edmonds, a U.S. Army master sergeant, whose unit was captured in the Battle of the Bulge and imprisoned in a German POW camp. (Edmonds posthumously won the Congressional Medal of Honor earlier this year for his refusal to turn in his Jewish troops to be sent to concentration camps.)

One of the ways Edmonds and his fellow prisoners distracted themselves from the horror of the camp was to talk about the foods that reminded them of home, be it Sunday spaghetti sauce, hot cakes or cherry pie.

"They're eating up this idea that they were going to go home," Shaya said. "They were going to be free, and they were going to be able to sit around and dig into that filet mignon with creamy mushroom sauce."

The servicemen sketched out detailed plans for a dreamed-of restaurant called the Jolly Chef. There, they would serve all those yearned-for dishes, including candied yams with pecans and whipped marshmallow — one of the recipes in the new cookbook.

Another chapter highlights Polish partisan fighters who lived in underground bunkers and sabotaged the Nazis by derailing trains and blowing up ammunition plants. In a nod to the fire that ensued, a recipe from their chapter also includes smashed potatoes flambéed in vodka.

"Vodka was a form of currency for them," Shaya said. "They would use it to barter. They would use it to celebrate. And so each moment of that recipe helps to really tell the story of what they were going through."

The book has stories from around the world – Hungarian Jews whose non-Jewish cook salvaged the treasured family cookbook as they were being sent to Auschwitz; a French village that took in Jewish children and hid them from the Nazis; Navajo code breakers who changed the course of the war; and Japanese Americans, convicted of no crimes, who were incarcerated in military-style camps in the U.S.

June Hersh, a food historian and writer who worked with Shaya on the cookbook, said remembering and talking about favorite recipes was a form of resistance – turning a tragic situation into something triumphant.

"You can put me in a uniform, you can make me do hard labor, you can shave my head, you can starve me if you want, but I'm not going to let go of my food memory," she said. "It's something you can't take away from me."

items.title: "How did young designers become so convinced of their own powerlessness?"
paragraphs: In the face of planetary collapse, design education and practice need to change to show young designers that it’s possible for them to make a difference, writes Céline Semaan.

The last time I taught a design class, at the School of Visual Arts (SVA) in New York, I remember sitting in my car after the two-hour workshop feeling quite honestly distraught. How had these young designers become so convinced of their own powerlessness?

During class, we discussed the political, ecological and economic infrastructures that make design possible: mineral extraction, exploited labour and the colonial systems sustaining much of what we produce and consume.

Having assumed these conversations had become an expected part of design education, I was taken aback by how little the students cared. Instead, they were far more concerned with securing and keeping jobs in an increasingly precarious industry.
Perhaps the profession needs to reconsider its relationship with obedience
“How do you expect us to make any difference if this is how the industry works?” one asked. Another just wanted to know how to earn a living, without upsetting their employers.

These were excellent questions, particularly as designers now compete with artificial intelligence capable of executing instructions at extraordinary speed. If design is reduced to following briefs and producing outputs, what space is there for a designer to effect any structural change?

Perhaps the profession needs to reconsider its relationship with obedience. Designers are trained to solve problems, yet rarely encouraged to question who defined them, whose interests they serve, or whether they should exist at all. They are commissioned to make products more sustainable without questioning production volumes, or improve services without examining the policies that make them inaccessible.
I often say design is a series of well-informed decisions. Every object, building and service emerges from decisions about resources, labor, budgets and the conditions of life.
Designers participate in these decisions, although they rarely control all of them. So where does their power begin and end?

Imagine a design studio commissioned by a city to address extreme heat in a low-income neighborhood. The brief requests solar-powered cooling shelters and shaded public spaces, with a fixed budget and deadline.

During research, the designers discover that the proposed shelters would be too far from elderly residents most vulnerable to heat, while existing community centers could accommodate cooling facilities at a lower cost. What should they do? Follow the brief, collect their fees and pretend their hands are tied? Refuse the commission, leaving another studio to complete the work, perhaps feeling rebellious for a moment?

There is a third possibility. They could show the city why its proposal would fail to reach its intended beneficiaries and present an alternative within the same budget. Working with residents and community organizations, they could identify accessible locations, compare costs and demonstrate how the alternative better meets the city’s objectives.
The difficult part is to make these commitments part of everyday practice, rather than optional gestures dependent on a sympathetic client

Here we see a tangible expansion of design as a civic responsibility. Designers can use their expertise to bring communities into decisions that affect their lives, improving outcomes while sharing decision-making power.
And if the city insists on its original proposal? The client controls the budget. A junior designer acting alone may have little negotiating power.

But a studio can incorporate community research into its contracts before work begins, negotiate a paid investigation phase and require the client to review evidence and alternatives before approving the design. Of course, this doesn’t guarantee agreement, but it makes critical inquiry a recognised part of the commission.

Design is a practice of applied imagination: understanding interconnected systems to intentionally shape the conditions of life. In this example, designers would examine the relationships between urban planning, public health, housing, energy and community governance. Their value lies partly in identifying what the original commission overlooked and developing viable possibilities with the people affected.

Thanks to the work of people like Victor Papanek, Tony Fry, Ezio Manzini and Arturo Escobar, by now it’s well understood that design has the capacity to shape the world but remains complicit in ecological and social destruction. The challenge today is to translate that knowledge into professional authority, economic leverage and meaningful participation in the decisions that will determine our collective futures.

Likewise, advocates of participatory design have long argued for involving people affected by design decisions. The difficult part is to make these commitments part of everyday practice, rather than optional gestures dependent on a sympathetic client.

Meeting these challenges requires rethinking design education. Designers need to learn to investigate the historical conditions behind a problem, understand ecological and economic relationships, and work alongside communities to develop alternatives.

Design can shape community-owned infrastructure, food systems and forms of local governance as well as products and buildings. These are tangible fields of work requiring collaboration and shared authority.
We should not ask young designers to compensate for structural failures through personal bravery alone

Of course, clients may refuse evidence, and insecure workers cannot always risk confrontation. Already there is too much pressure on Gen Z to save the world; we should not ask young designers to compensate for structural failures through personal bravery alone.

Studios, educators and commissioners must create paid roles and decision-making processes that give designers genuine influence. What if, for example, investigating the risks and assumptions behind a brief became an essential professional service, one that designers were commissioned and compensated to provide?

I keep thinking about those students at SVA, afraid of being considered difficult. We have taught them how to execute decisions without adequately preparing them to participate in making them. If designers are to take responsibility for their role in shaping the systems that govern our lives, they need a say in the decisions that produce those systems.

In the near future, success would mean residents gaining influence over where public money goes, with designers helping turn their priorities into lasting changes in public planning. This is design as a civic responsibility, and a meaningful distinction from machines optimized to execute instructions. To design possible futures, we must grow the agency designers hold, and the collective power they can help communities to build.

Céline Semaan is a Lebanese-Canadian designer, artist, writer, educator and speaker based in New York City, whose work focuses on climate issues and social justice. She is the founder of Slow Factory, a non-profit education and research platform that teaches about regenerative design. Her writing has appeared in The Cut, Vogue, Elle, Refinery29 and New York Magazine, among others. Her first book, A Woman Is a School, was published in 2024, and her upcoming book, Designing Possible Futures, is due for publication in 2027.

If you enjoy reading Dezeen’s interviews, opinions and features, subscribe to Dezeen In Depth. Sent on the last Friday of each month, this newsletter provides a single place to read about the design and architecture stories behind the headlines.

items.title: This stop-motion horror game proves there's something deeply unsettling about handmade art
paragraphs: Stop-motion animation has been a popular aesthetic in indie games, giving creations a more tactile, handcrafted, and personal touch. But while many developers simply emulate this style digitally, two-person indie studio Talha and Jack Co prides itself on making real physical models. For co-founder Jack King-Spooner, creative director of the upcoming game Abide, it's always been what matters most.

"From studying art, I had just so much more affinity for tangible things and seeing what the materials give me as I'm making things," he tells me. "From my first game 15 years ago, I've always been invested in tangible assets. I couldn't really be bothered drawing pixel art when I could just make a little model and then photograph it from different angles, move it a little bit. It was just so much quicker for me."

While Talha & Jack Co's previous two games, the Scottish pagan action-adventure Judero and the chill post-apocalyptic robot-mining adventure Mashina, were sprite-based, Abide is more ambitious: a first-person 3D game, so they're scanning the epoxy clay models with photogrammetry, though cutscenes are still being created as stop-motion animation.

"The models are much, much bigger; they've got so much more detail," King-Spooner says, while bringing up a model in his hand as close up to the camera during our video call so that I can see the latex allowing for very realistic textures of skin pores and lips. "I'm always pushing myself with techniques, and finding new ways to do things. A lot of artists become frozen and immobilised with their craft because they think that there's a right way of doing things, whereas I just like doing things however I can."

Some of that detail nonetheless does have to be reduced, as a larger, more detailed model could be the equivalent of a super high-res model with 500,000 polygons. "We cut down to like 6,000 polygons so that we can hit good frame rates. They're a bit chunky, but for me they only needed to be recognisable as the same character as in the stop-motion cutscenes. I know lots of people love really tight graphics, but I'd rather spend the time on engaging story and engaging gameplay."

There are also additional parts that are made for the stop-motion cutscenes. For example, in a scene that requires a close-up of a character washing their hands, they use a larger hand for that shot instead of zooming in on the model's hands, then cut back to the normal model (something Thunderbirds' Jerry Anderson was famous for).

Even with games like Judero, the devs have noted that their stop-motion style has an inherent creepiness, so given that Abide is an "extreme stop motion horror" that includes prosthetic gore effects, King-Spooner is relishing that by doubling down on it. "There's something very abject and horrific about stop motion animation," he says, "It's got this nostalgia, but it's also got this kind of uncanny movement to it which you project life onto."

To an extent, it also feels like a deliberate response to counter the cosy perceptions people might have of this aesthetic. "A lot of handcrafted games are a bit kind of soft, aren't they? I think with Abide it's really nice that people will think, 'Oh god, a real person, this guy Jack is a real monstrous kind of person that he's made such perverted little dolls doing such horrible things!' I think it adds to the tangibility that it's very much a person's handiwork."

It nonetheless has an idyllic setting on the surface, set in the St Boniface retreat in the secluded countryside with a group of eight residents from different walks of life in some kind of need of them; at night it descends into full-on horror as you start sneaking around and explore parts of the house you probably shouldn't.

"One aspect which is very disturbing is they're all somehow reflections of myself," King-Spooner admits. "I think it's important for a creator to recognise that the work you output is somehow autobiographical of yourself. I'm just rather kind of transparent about it."

In many environments, King-Spooner has also opted to build physical sets or paint textures, such as splattering red paint to make wood textures look bloody or putting on muddy boots and trampling them on white paper to scan.

If there's a downside to creating physical models and objects, it's that there's often no room to keep them, so after production is over, everything is either chucked out or the clay is mushed up to be reused, although King-Spooner isn't especially precious about preservation. As he bluntly puts it, "We're all going to be dirt in the ground."
Abide is coming soon to PC, and you can wishlist it on Steam.

Alan Wen is a freelance journalist writing about video games in the form of features, interview, previews, reviews and op-eds. Work has appeared in print including Edge, Official Playstation Magazine, GamesMaster, Games TM, Wireframe, Stuff, and online including Kotaku UK, TechRadar, FANDOM, Rock Paper Shotgun, Digital Spy, The Guardian, and The Telegraph.

items.title: A dish with a story, Thanksgiving with culinary historian Michael Twitty
paragraphs: You can find the recipe for Michael Twitty's Kush cornbread dressing in his book, Recipes from the American South. NPR hide caption

This Thanksgiving, Morning Edition host Leila Fadel left the studio for her kitchen, where she was met by the two-time James Beard Award winner Michael Twitty, who came with a spice blend, fresh sage, fish peppers and onions from his garden.
His book, The Cooking Gene, planted him as one of the nation's foremost chronologists tracing his ancestry through African American culinary history.

Kush is one of Twitty's most beloved Thanksgiving offerings and one he's been making since he was a teen. The name and the ingredients show the way food became a tool for the enslaved in the Americas to preserve their cultures.

"The name comes from Hausa, the language of West Africa. They are a predominantly Muslim people, but Muslim in the way that West Africans do Islam – which is Islam with a lot of the influence from the traditional culture and spirituality," he said on the origins of the side dish. "And so the name Kush, it's like, couscous," he added.
Michael Twitty is the author of four books including Recipes from the American South. hide caption
The dish is one that connects Twitty to his ancestry.

"There was a time when I couldn't tell you what particular African ethnic groups I came from, but now that I know that I'm part Wolof, Hausa, Fula, and Serer and so many others," he said. "Now, I know this dish has a connection to who I am and my roots and where I came from."
In the making of this dish, Twitty also shared his work documenting the ways African American Jewish people create hybrid dishes in the kitchen.

"It's Matzah ball gumbo, and it's black-eyed peas and quiche," he said of his Black and Jewish identity. "It's a lot of dishes that were from North Africa or from Ethiopia, it's kosher jollof rice and Shito. Shito usually has shellfish in it – we don't put that."
The author of four books tracing the deep roots of the foods he loves says for him it's less about the lore of Thanksgiving, and more about the people the day brings together.

"I have to say that along with a lot of other African Americans, not everybody, but a plurality of us, Thanksgiving, as it's been expressed, means very little," he said of the holiday. "Which means we're not attaching ourselves to the myth of Thanksgiving, we don't really care for that. But we do love tradition, we love cooking, we love food, we love gathering."
And in that spirit, Kush in particular, remains one way for him to taste history.
"It means I haven't forgotten who I come from. And it means I haven't forgotten that I have a legacy to leave," he said.
You can find the recipe for Twitty's Kush in his book, Recipes from the American South.

items.title: Court lets Puerto Rico governor fire firm that runs the island's troubled power grid
paragraphs: LUMA Energy took over the electric grid five years ago. The court's ruling nullifies its contract, and gives the government a year to find a new operator.

items.title: Powerful storms disrupt holiday travel, as Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is postponed
paragraphs: Workers inflate the Spider-Man balloon during Macy's Balloon Inflation 2026 on November 25, 2026 in New York City. Macy's plans to celebrate its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade with a record 100 inflatables, but forecasted high winds are threatening to ground the giant balloons. Adam Gray/Getty Images hide caption

Tens of millions of people are bracing for delays at airports and highways across the country on Thursday, as powerful storms across the United States threatened to disrupt travel for the Thanksgiving holiday.

On the West Coast, high tides have flooded streets along California's shorelines and knocked off a part of Pacifica Pier. The floods have also prompted evacuation warnings. On the East Coast, authorities are preparing to weather the impact of a storm making its way up into New England from the southeast with strong winds and heavy rain. Snow was also forecast in parts of the Midwest.

A firefighter and an official carry a water pump as coastal floodwaters flow in the Sunset Beach community during high tide on November 25, 2026 in Huntington Beach, California. Potentially record-breaking "king tides," combined with elevated surf and a large Pacific swell, are bringing coastal flooding to Southern California during Thanksgiving week, with the greatest impacts anticipated today and tomorrow. Mario Tama/Getty Images hide caption
Some 81.5 million people in the U.S. are expected to travel for the holiday between Thursday and Monday, according to AAA.

Hundreds of flights had already been cancelled or delayed by early morning Thursday, particularly on the East Coast, where authorities have warned people to stay home as the storm barrels through. The majority of people are expected to travel by car for the holidays, and the winter weather could affect their plans due to visibility issues on the road.
Passengers wait at the departure gates at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia on November 25, 2026. DANIEL SLIM/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Richard Bann, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service Weather Prediction Center, told NPR that the East Coast storm remained the main concern, calling it a "multi-hazard" storm.

"It's going to be getting better organized as we go through the day, and it'll be spreading a considerable amount of wind, heavy rain. The real concern with this thing is going to be coastal flooding," Bann said.
Meteorologist Matthew Cappucci with The Washington Post and MyRadar told NPR the storm's magnitude at this time of the year was "unusual."
"We would expect this in deep winter," Cappucci said.
The storm in the East Coast, however, is expected to mostly clear out by Saturday, easing weekend travel for those returning from Thanksgiving gatherings.
Beyond travel, several Thanksgiving parades have also been affected by severe weather.

The incoming storm is expected to cause high winds in New York City, prompting Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Wednesday to delay the city's famous Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade. Organizers were already inflating the iconic giant balloons for the parade on Wednesday when officials announced the decision.

Workers deflate balloons after Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed until Saturday, on November 25, 2026 in New York City. Because of the weather, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade will be postponed to Saturday, November 28, the first time in its 100-year history that it will take place on a day other than Thanksgiving. Adam Gray/Getty Images hide caption

The parade, which is now expected to take place on Saturday, will be the city's 100th, and while it was cancelled before during World War II, this is the first time that it's been postponed in the last century.

The parade's organizers said it took two years to prepare the elaborate celebration, which includes over 11,000 participants and volunteers, thousands of high school marching band musicians from across the country and hundreds of balloon handlers. In previous years, up to 2 million spectators have attended the parade.
"Safety is and will always remain our top priority, and this will be a heavy storm," Mamdani told reporters.

People distribute a Thanksgiving Dinner for commuters on the L subway train on November 25, 2026 in New York City. In what has become a yearly tradition, a group of New York City residents have set up a full Thanksgiving-style meal for commuters on the L train of New York City's subway system. Adam Gray/Getty Images hide caption

He urged the city's residents to prepare for extreme weather conditions. He said the city expected sustained winds between 30 and 40 mph and possible gusts as high as 65 mph, with resulting floods and flash floods.

"Generation after generation has watched Spongebob and Spiderman soar down our streets and has taken in Garfield floating down 6th Avenue. And I know this change of plans will cause inconveniences," Mamdani said. "Yet safety has to come first."
Philadelphia also grounded all balloons for its parade this year due to winds.
Steve Kastenbaum contributed reporting for this story.

items.title: Lucy McRae creates replicant birth bags for Blade Runner 2099 show where "violence and femininity coexist"
paragraphs: Los Angeles-based artist Lucy McRae has created tactile, custom-made designs for sci-fi mini-series Blade Runner 2099 that veer away from the traditionally cold and metallic aesthetic of the films.
The show, which premiered on Wednesday on Amazon Prime, is the latest in the Blade Runner universe and follows Cora, a human fugitive played by actor Hunter Schafer.

She goes undercover as a replicant – a synthetic human – blade runner with veteran replicant Olwen, played by actor Michelle Yeoh, to track down a runaway carrying a secret that could destabilise the city.
McRae joined the production in 2022 as the official futurist of the show, after showrunner Silka Luisa saw her previous work exploring the relationship between emerging technology and human biology.

Her speculative work on body futurism later became direct visual references for the show and McRae was asked to speculate on human consciousness in 50 years’ time, with a specific focus on memory, bio-engineering, replicants’ sensuality, sex and family.
“I created a world-build of those questions, through scale models, building concepts through physical materials,” McRae told Dezeen. “These ideas begin to transpire within the show.”
McRae designed the film’s birth bags, which are incubator-like sacks used to birth or transform replicants.
She also made the crèche set, the facility and replicant birth system that support the birth bags, as well as a skin polymer traction machine that was used for healing the protagonist Cora.

McRae also designed the material and colour palette for replicants, which includes pipes, quilting and industrial materials that fit the interiors of Olwen’s spacecraft and the padding around the traction machine.
The birth bag is a new iteration of McRae’s Compression Cradle, a project presented at the 2019 Milan Triennale exhibition Broken Nature.
It was a machine that offered a simulated hug to a person craving intimacy using an inflatable device.
In Blade Runner 2099, the design scale expanded dramatically, with nine vertical Compression Cradles created inside the Tyrell building where they functioned as birth bags in the show.
McRae often describes herself as a “body architect”. At Future Sensitive, the art-research lab she leads, her work revolves around using the body as a means to speculate on the future.

A few of her recent projects have explored what McRae calls the touch crisis – the idea that, with the rise of technology, digital devices might start to vie for human affection, and physical contact with other humans might suffer as a result.
Her Heavy Duty Love, for example, created for the Venice Architecture Biennale 2021, imagines a machine replacement of a parent’s embrace in a world where humans are grown in artificial wombs.
With The Future Day Spa, meanwhile, she presented a machine that could replace human contact altogether.
McRae’s says her focus on material tactility – such as creases, wrinkles, and squishy textures – adds a femininity to the show.
The series is built on the sci-fi intellectual property that followed from the original 1982 film and its aesthetic was historically labelled as metallic, cold, slick and masculine.
“The physicalisation of the work I do, the texture, achieves the femininity the show was after,” said McRae. “It’s an absolute masterpiece where both violence and femininity coexist.”
She also believes that by domesticating science and rendering technology malleable and wet, it creates a positive future that feels within human grasp and participation.

“It feels positive because it feels within my grasp. I feel I can participate and I can contribute,” said McRae. “Whereas if it’s a future that doesn’t look or feel or belong to something that I understand, then it feels like it’s a closed door.”

The designer said her work for the series, and in general, aims to focus on plausible futures rather than pure fantasy, while raising open-ended questions and encouraging audiences to navigate uncertainty with hope.
“What’s important for Silka and for my work is that anything I’m dealing with is never fantasy,” said McRae.
“I think physicalising possibility allows us to wear it, touch it and be able to get close to something that is far away but then allows us to see if it’s a fit, see if it belongs.”

“What I’m trying to do is create opportunities for people to ask these questions themselves and for me to not answer them. It’s going to be open-ended and unanswered because we don’t live in a world where one answer or many answers fit.”

items.title: LIVE: iPad Black Friday deals on every model start here
paragraphs: If you're a digital artist, you're likely to be looking at the iPad Air and an Apple Pencil Pro. Luckily there are deals on both!
Apple Ipad Air 11-Inch (m4): Liquid Retina Display, 128gb, 12mp Front/back Camera, Wi-Fi 7 With Apple N1, Touch Id, All-Day Battery Life — Blue
Apple Pencil Pro: Latest Model - Device Compatibility Check Required | Pixel-Perfect Precision, Tilt & Pressure Sensitivity, Perfect for Note-Taking, Drawing, and Art. Charges & Pairs Magnetically

Hello iPad fans! It's Editor, Georgia here. As you might know from live blogs past, I use Apple products everyday – and own the iPhone Pro, Apple Watch, AirPods Pro and MacBook Air. Added to that, I've been on these live blogs for eight years now, so I'm very very good at spotting deals, and knowing whether they are good or not.

To be honest, there's not much around on iPads that is spectacularly different from usual. Every Black Friday/Prime Day we get standard discounts – and this year is no different. This makes it a good time to buy, but shouldn't influence you to buy something you don't need.
I'm going to dig into the specifics and I'll be back soon.

Still one of the best deals we've seen in the UK this week is £30 off the 11-inch iPad, bringing it down to £399. Which, in today's world of price hikes and RAM shortages, is a pretty great price for an iPad. The A16 model features a Liquid Retina display, stating storage of 128GB, and Apple Pencil (USB-C) support.

If you're struggling to decide which iPad is for you, you're not alone – the line up can be confusing at the best of times. Gone are the days of choosing between the 'normal' iPad and the iPad mini. Now you've got your Pros, your Airs, your minis and your, er, '11-inch A16's. Good job our handy iPad generations guide is here to see you through, eh?

Normally the choice between an iPad and MacBook is clear-cut: the tablet is generally much cheaper than the laptop. But the advent of the budget MacBook Neo has changed all that, causing us to ask how the heck creatives are supposed to choose between an iPad and MacBook Neo.

For many creatives, the iPad is their weapon of choice when it comes to creating digital art. items.title: Seven beautiful places to visit in GTA VI, from mountains trails to an afternoon at the zoo
paragraphs: As Leonida goes, Mount Kalaga is the top of the world. There are bike trails and hiking trails all the way up the mountain, as well as plenty of hunting opportunities if that’s your thing. Shooting deer makes me sad, so instead I went birdwatching and spotted an eagle.

Yes, Vice City has a zoo. Situated on Waxman Island, it is home to tigers, monkeys, cockatoos and more – a very cute place to wander around on a date. It also has its own lively private beach with a bar.

This little island is home to a memorial sculpture, but Vice City’s party crowd also come here to picnic and take a dip in the ocean. It’s a very short jetski ride from here to Vespucci Island if you want to check out some VERY nice houses (and steal some very nice cars).

Forget Vice Beach, that’s for tourists. The sand dunes around Richard Barebone State Park look more like a Scottish beach than a Floridia one, all driftwood and exposed rock, and a great place to fill out your wildlife logbook with sea birds. On Hardin Island off the coast there is a lighthouse named for Lucia, and from the top you get one of the best views in Leonida.
You know those gummy bears in the water in downtown Vice City? They’re part of the game’s art museum, which also has several other installations and sculptures to look at.

You have to get the ferry to get to this oddly perfect little island (or borrow a helicopter) but it is worth the visit – there’s a big, strange art piece at its centre that I think is going to kick off weeks’ worth of sleuthing. Plus, it’s fun to ride around on a golf cart and annoy the residents in their beautiful apartment blocks.

The story takes you to most of the nightclubs in Vice City – except this one. It’s a blend of strip club and bar, and significantly more high-end than Delights Cabaret. Come here for a dance in opulent and sleazy surroundings.

items.title: BBC Radio 1's Big Weekend 2027 heads to Brighton
paragraphs: Earlier this year the event was held in Sunderland's Herrington Country Park, where about 100,000 music fans basked in the the sun while dancing to a host of major artists.
Grammy and Brit Awards winner Olivia Dean, Swedish pop star Zara Larsson and veteran DJ Fatboy Slim topped the bill across the weekend.
Irish star CMAT, Messy singer Lola Young, former One Directioner Niall Horan and American singer Kehlani were also on the line-up.
The vibrancy of the current electronic music scene led Radio 1 to dedicate day one of Big Weekend to its Dance Party brand for the first time.

It spanned styles, backgrounds and generations - with local lad Max Jones getting the party started on the Introducing stage, and Fisher, MK and Clementine Douglas keeping the party going throughout the day.
Big Weekend tickets are usually significantly cheaper than most major festivals, with a proportion reserved for local residents.
It has not yet been revealed when tickets will go on sale for the 2027 event and at what price.
Details about the line-up will be announced in the coming months, BBC Radio 1 said.

items.title: Adobe isn’t "just ticking a box" – how diversity is shaping its products
paragraphs: I recently had the privilege of attending this year's Adobe MAX, and amidst the flurry of excitement and innovations, what surprised me was the sense of community.

The phrase "finding your tribe" was thrown around profusely during the conference, and while I find the term mildly ickworthy, it bears truth. MAX is a space to connect, network, rant about the state of the creative industry, and, most importantly, a place to show up for your community.

It's no secret the creative industry was, and at times still is, a place of inequality. Be it race, gender, disability or age, while we have made strides to improve things, there are still gaps to be filled – something that Adobe is trying to address.

To learn more, I caught up with Karen Robinson, Vice President, Associate General Counsel, Litigation & Intellectual Property and leader of Adobe’s Black Employee Network, to discuss how Adobe is enacting change with purpose.

I've been at the company for about 14 years. BEN (Black Employee Network) started in the US, and I'm a founding member. Initially, it was an effort to build community, so we slowly started expanding. We had chapters in San Jose, San Francisco, Utah and Seattle, but then we started expanding internationally. Our largest community of Black Adobe employees is actually outside of the US, in the UK – BEN UK is a really strong presence.

I've been the executive sponsor for BEN for probably seven or eight years now, and it continues to be a focused effort that I'm really proud of. What's really interesting about BEN in particular is the allies. It's not just our Black employees – I love that there are so many people who get involved even when it's not necessarily part of their specific community.

It's about intersectionality. So, we have Access at Adobe, Asian/Pacific Islander at Adobe (APIA), Black Employee Network (BEN), Hispanic/Latinx at Adobe (HOLA), Indigenous/First Nations at Adobe (IFNA), Jewish Employee Network (JEN), Middle East/North Africa at Adobe (MENA), Pride at Adobe, Veterans Employee Network (VEN), and Women at Adobe. That's a really lovely thing about our Employee Networks in general, but I'm so proud of BEN. It's something that we put a lot of heart and effort into, and it sustains a lot of us.
We've always looked at inclusivity as something wildly important.

I'm responsible for some of our AI ethics and innovation, and as part of that, we made sure inclusivity is part of it. Looking at AI, how it can be used and what it's being trained on, if you're not focused on issues of inclusivity, you're missing out on large communities. That means the tools you're creating aren't serving those communities, so they're not the best tools you can create.

Our Employee Networks all developed out of a community's desire to be represented – to reflect their culture and the things they found to be important – and reflect them in the Adobe culture. The company really leans into it. It's not just ticking a box, or even just about minority groups getting together to have a sense of community. It's a way to make sure that we're offering the best products that reflect the communities we're serving. It's about empowering creativity for everyone. How do you do that if you're not including everyone?
Sure. You can look at the numbers. I'm not saying anything that's shocking or outrageous. There is still opportunity for more inclusivity within the broader sort of industry.

Something I didn't realise was how much representation mattered. It wasn't until I got to a point where I had people coming up to me and saying, "Hey, I, I didn't even realise that someone like you could exist at a tech company, it makes me think that there's room and opportunity and growth for me."

For a long time, minority communities were being told, "You need to be in science or technology." The reality is, you don't. There are entire swaths of the industry you can be involved in and not have a science or math background, but they needed to hear that and see that. I don't have a technical degree, and yet here I am – the first Black SVP at Adobe.
I look at the numbers, and we're growing. Success breeds success, and representation is a huge part of that.

items.title: ‘When I cut these women out I feel like I’m freeing them’: the feminist collage artists taking scissors to the patriarchy
paragraphs: When Valerie Solanas sold her SCUM Manifesto in 1967 it was priced at 10 cents for women and $1 for men. Artist Justine Kurland considered doing something similar with her “man books”: sell them off cheap to undermine their cultural weight. But knowing that people would just flip the books for a profit, instead she took a knife to what she calls the “problem of language and history and inheritance” in photography. She went through her own library of canonical male photographers, cut up the books and made collages from the spoils. Kurland called the project SCUMB (Society for Cutting Up Men’s Books), after Solanas’s manifesto.

The same idea underpins What Rose from the Cut, a group show at Graces Mews Gallery in south London. Co-curated by Kurland, the V&A Parasol Foundation curator of women in photography Fiona Rogers, and collector Sarah Miller Meigs, the show brings together more than 40 artists working in collage, photomontage and assemblage, across three generations. All the artists share a simple aim: to make something new out of something already there. The result is no one thing: the show is erotic, sentimental, irreverent and sobering, often all at once. “There is something very specific to the idea of what it is to tear something apart,” Kurland says. “There are so many things that collage immediately does right out the door.”

Graces Mews is showing the third version of Kurland’s 99 Nude Collages on the Wall (2026). The work is made up of figures cut from photographer and artist Lee Friedlander’s 1991 book Nudes, collaged into small clusters and pinned to the wall in one big crowd.

For Kurland it’s an act of repair, a kind of vigil. “I have spent more time with those figures than Lee Friedlander ever has. I know every single person’s body by heart. When I’m cutting those women out, I feel like I’m freeing them from Lee Friedlander’s gaze – and probably capturing them in my own lesbian fantasy.” Kurland has cut up hundreds of copies of Nudes, and the work was less punk than she wanted it to be. “I have this teeny little X-Acto [precision knife] and a magnifying glass so I can cut each pubic hair. I’m like a little termite chewing at the foundation of the institution.”

Divine Southgate-Smith’s film I Wore Your Tongue So Loud Against Me (2024), meanwhile, stretches the idea of cut and paste. The artist’s interest in archives started with a childhood devouring films. Split across four frames, I Wore Your Tongue … runs in a “loop in which time is compressed, merging multiple timelines and geographies. The gaze is released from a single point of view.”

The silent montage uses found footage, from wildlife documentaries to films that shaped Southgate-Smith, such as Chris Marker’s Sans Soleil (1983) and Pier Paolo Pasolini’s Notes Towards an African Orestes (1970). The Pasolini was especially important to them: “A record of something unfinished, not quite a film but a film about making a film,” Southgate-Smith says. “There’s a scene where Pasolini, after his return from Africa, shows his footage to a group of African students at the University of Rome, and one by one they gracefully object to the Africa he had imagined.”

Elsewhere, a glass case of political zines, including Spare Rib, Riot Grrrl, Bad Attitude and Shrew, puts the artists alongside activists and grounds the work in protest. Kurland and Rogers reject the split between fine art and everyday image-making, which fits with how they see collage: as something that refuses to rank things as high or low.

Helina Metaferia’s Tapestry (Arokin) hangs from the ceiling next to Lubaina Himid’s playful 16-part series Chatterbox (2018), in front of a case of rare Martha Rosler collages (1966-72). Metaferia’s work pushes back against the systems that have left women and non-binary people out of history. The tapestry features “silk-screen prints on fabric from 1980s Outwrite Women’s Newspapers and Grassroots Black Community News”, taken from the Black Cultural Archives in London.

“In all of the work, I am co-imagining with these archives, facilitating space for Black and Brown femmes to have agency and be respected,” Metaferia says. She also “activates” her tapestries in public performances, wearing them as regalia inspired by her Ethiopian heritage. It takes the histories they hold beyond the gallery walls.

The tactility of the work in the exhibition swings from one extreme to the other. Metaferia’s tapestry hangs next to Tee Corinne’s 1981 book Yantras of Womanlove. In its kaleidoscopic photomontages the cuts are almost invisible. These diagrams of energy (the book’s apt subtitle) look seamless, without beginning or end. It serves as a sharp contrast to Annegret Soltau’s Schwanger [Pregnant] and Auf dem Geburtstisch I [On the birth table I] (both 1978), where the cut is violent and impossible to miss. Even so, the work still feels like repair, in the way it faces up to life in a female body. In this exhibition, no two cuts are the same.
What Rose from the Cut is at Graces Mews Gallery, London, to 30 January.

items.title: Yes, the GTA logo is based on a free font inspired by a game show – here's where to get it
paragraphs: Even if you haven't spent every waking hour of the past seven days immersed in the world of Leonida, you've sure seen a lot of the GTA logo lately. Along with the Vice City palette of pastel pinks, blues and sunset oranges, the logo has been everywhere, from developer Rockstar Games' billboards and murals to those GTA VI brand reactions.

For long-time fans of series, the GTA VI logo is a familiar design with the same core wordmark that's been in use since Grand Theft Auto III. But older readers who have never played GTA might also find it strangely familiar. That could be because it's based on a free typeface that was inspired by a very different kind of game.

The original Grand Theft Auto logo created by The Designers Republic for the first game's marketing featured cartoonish stars and flames for a '70s vibe. It was replaced by a simpler three-letter GTA logo for the second game, in the franchise. It was Grand Theft Auto III in 2001 that introduced the design we know today.

The logo is largely based on Pricedown, a free typeface developed by the Canadian designer Raymond Larabie and published by Typodermic. In his post about the history of the font on the foundry's website, Raymond says his intention was to closely reinterpret Pinto Flare, a display face made for Franklin Photolettering in the late 1960s and best known for its use in The Price Is Right logo.
"I kept the boxy structure and the odd unicase letterforms with swash descenders, but I drew my version harder and more angular compared to Pinto Flare’s softer feel," he writes.

Raymond says he released Pricedown on 30 November 1997. That was just two days after the first GTA came out for windows. And the coincidences don't end there. He says that when the font was later chosen by Rockstar's office in New York, he happened to be working as an art director at Rockstar Toronto. His colleagues weren't aware that someone working at the company had designed the font.

So the world's most expensive video game has a logo based on a free font? And it works: the chunky letterforms with their rounded corners work perfectly achieving easy readability while fitting into the rest of the game's branding.

But it would be a simplification to say that Pricedown is all there is to the GTA logo. Ultimately, Rockstar modified the letterforms and arranged them to make them work as a logo design. The three words of the franchise's name and held tightly in a block that's almost square, the 'r' and 'h' conjoin, and a black stroke provides separation against coloured backgrounds.

An additional touch has been added for each game in the form of the numbering: a pink neon sign-like script for Vice City, tattoo-like blackletter type for San Andreas, the V that recalls US currency design for GTA V.

Considering Grand Theft Auto's satire of US culture and society, it seems fitting for it to have a logo inspired by the identity of one of the country's longest-running TV series (see our pick of the best GTA VI Easter eggs for examples of how the game references pop culture and its own legacy).

Looking for the font? The original Pricedown, now called Pricedown Black is available free for desktop use, and you can download it directly from Typodermic. Raymond later expanded the font into a complete typeface family with other weights. To use those, you'll need to buy a licence. You can find them at MyFonts.
For more on the game of the biggest video game in history, check out our interviews with Rockstar Games' art team on GTA VI's environmental storytelling and the building design in GTA VI.

items.title: DJ gets lucky after finding lost Daft Punk mixtape
paragraphs: DJ Ralph Lawson rediscovered a tape that Daft Punk gifted him in 1997

Daft Punk have become household names after storming the charts with One More Time and Get Lucky - with an intimate set in 1990s Leeds lingering in the memories of attendees. Now, those recollections have been reignited by the discovery of a lost mix by the French electronic duo hidden for several decades.
"It all started when I opened a show for Daft Punk in 1997," says Ralph Lawson, standing on the top floor of the Mint XL club in the city centre.
The 2,500-capacity venue is empty aside from staff testing out a staggering number of lights, bouncing off the spotless floors.
It is a far cry from Ralph's first clubs when he started DJing back in 1991.
He is a co-founding resident DJ at the legendary Back to Basics club - a DIY house music event that became one of Europe's longest-running club nights, hosting global stars until sunrise.
Mint evolved from an intimate Leeds club into festivals, large-scale productions and the new Mint XL club
Ralph is holding up a digital audio tape (DAT) - a discontinued method of recording high quality audio. On its side are the handwritten words: "Daft Punk Mix Feb '97."
"Daft Punk got so big so quickly, they were on such big stages at festivals that they did not really DJ," remembers the music producer.
The French pair were rapidly rising to fame when they were booked for Back to Basics, but they were pipped to the headline slot by drum and bass pioneer Goldie.
Daft Punk were on their rapid rise to stardom when they visited Leeds in 1997, but did not top the bill
By the time the night arrived, Ralph recalls "there were queues around the block".
Despite accidentally jogging one of their records during the set, Ralph got on well with both Thomas Bangalter and Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo - even if the latter only uttered a few words to him.
"I would not say I was best mates with them, but I could get on a guest list," says Ralph.
Whatever their relationship, it was strong enough that Daft Punk sent Ralph a gift in the post - an hour-long mixtape for his radio show on Kiss 105 FM.
This is the only picture Ralph has of Daft Punk playing their DJ set in Leeds
After it was played out on air, Ralph forgot about its existence for decades. He finally rediscovered it during a root around in some old storage boxes, but there was a problem.
"I took it out and there were two bits of tape hanging out."
Despite being in a dry studio, mould had found its way in.
When Ralph tried to play the tape it immediately ripped
Spurred on by his social media followers begging for him to salvage the mix, Ralph found a company that preserves tapes in Bristol.
"The problem with DAT is that it is incredibly fragile," says Adrian Finn, from Greatbear, one of the people tasked with fixing the broken tape.
He estimates the team spent hours across multiple weeks on this "difficult job", carefully disassembling the tape, repairing the rips and getting rid of the mould.
"It's nice to make people happy through this kind of restoration work," says Adrian, who admits he was dancing around "a little bit" while listening back to the mix.
"I thought it was good and glad it played back with hardly any errors."
Adrian Finn from Greatbear in Bristol was one of the people tasked with fixing the mixtape
Back at Mint XL in Leeds, Ralph cannot help but grin as he recounts attempting to play the mix for a second time.
"I was literally floored," he laughs, toppling over in delight once the kick drum blasted out of his speakers.
Ralph had no idea what the first track of the hour-long mix would be, so when it was one of his favourites - Everybody Dancing by the late American DJ Romanthony - he knew it would be "very special".
Ralph dropped to the floor in celebration when he heard the tape for the first time
It is the "rawness" of the vinyl mix - complete with crackles and impressive manual transitions - that Ralph adores.
"It's a testament to the times," he says.
"Not as polished as things are now, where people can see precisely how in time they are and have visual cues."

While the discovery may be a success for the nostalgia and memories of 1990s clubbing, Ralph also hopes the tape and the meaning behind it will inspire the next generation of DJs, music curators and artists.
"I want them to think, 'I could get behind the decks or find the next Daft Punk and put them on at our night', and there's the space for them to do that in Leeds."
Will another French electronic music duo stop by in Leeds on their way to global stardom? Who knows.
But producers like Ralph are adamant that the city's famous club scene can easily foster many more like them.

items.title: Elon Musk pledges to give two SpaceX shares to every child in the US
paragraphs: Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, has pledged to give every child in the US two shares in SpaceX, the space ⁠and AI company he ​runs, worth a total of almost $18bn.

In a brief post on X, the social media platform that he owns, Musk said children will receive one share from the company itself, and one from him personally. SpaceX announced earlier on Wednesday that it would ​contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock ‌to every currently active Trump Account, and that ‌Musk will match the number of shares it donates.

The Trump account program was designed to give every American under 18 a stake in the stock market, to help build wealth from an early age. The White House said last month that it had opened almost 70 million accounts. SpaceX shares closed at $127.44 on Wednesday, valuing the pledge at nearly $18bn.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether Musk’s own donations would also be linked to Trump accounts.

In a separate post, Musk said the company shares will be transferred next ⁠month, with his own to follow later. “The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year,” he wrote.

In October, Musk, whose net worth is around $824bn, announced his intention to give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in America. “This will be the first of many,” he said in a post on X at the time. As of June, he held about 6.42bn shares ​in the company.
Most of Musk’s philanthropic efforts have been conducted via the Musk Foundation, which reportedly holds around $16bn in assets.
In October, SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell ⁠and her husband pledged a share of their SpaceX stock to each of more than 2 million children under ​the Trump account initiative.

Musk and rival AI company Anthropic have recently detailed their sharply different approaches for sharing the spoils of the AI boom. Anthropic, which went public earlier this month, ​said it would commit 5% of its ​shares to a new fund for the “public good”. The company said this initiative, worth around $54bn at current prices, would give it ​more flexibility and scale to ‌make donations for the benefit ​of humanity.

Other major, long-running philanthropy ventures include those of Berkshire Hathaway chair emeritus Warren Buffett, who is reported to have given away $60bn, with the intention of doing the same with most of the rest of his $150bn fortune.
The Gates Foundation has distributed more than $100bn since its founding in 2000, with some of that fuelled by donations from Buffett.

items.title: After the NYT Photoshop ban, there's an obvious way for Adobe to recover trust
paragraphs: We were genuinely impressed with some of the new AI features in Photoshop 2027, from Generative Restyle to Relight. But just a couple of weeks after its release, the latest version of the industry-standard image editing software is facing a reputational crisis.

The New York Times has banned freelance photographers from using the app because of a difficulty in knowing when it uses generative AI. That's just one publication, but the news has made a big impact, and the significance is clear: users may not be 100% sure when they are or aren't using generative AI to edit an image.
There's an easy solution, but will Adobe want to introduce it?

The New York Times wrote in an email to freelance photographers that the newest version of Photoshop “utilizes generative AI in ways that may not be apparent to users. Their use can result in metadata misidentifying photos as AI-generated.” As a result photographers have been told not to use the latest version of the software.

In photojournalism, it's an ethical issue. Images need to reflect reality, so editing is usually relatively limited. The inadvertent use of generative AI also brings with it the risk of an "AI content" tag on social media, which could lead people to question a report, and could severely damage to the reputation of both the photographer and any media outlet reporting news with an image flagged as AI.

The most obvious solution would be an AI-off switch. Digital artists, designers and those photographers who want to use generative AI tools in Photoshop could turn it on. Photojournalists, documentary photographers, and anyone who simply doesn't want to use generative AI or risk being shamed with an AI content tag, can turn it off.

Other software developers have done just that. Canva added an AI off Switch last week, and Maxon has included the ability to turn off its new generative AI features in Cinema 4D and ZBrush. It's a simple mechanism that can be flicked on or off at any time, and the gesture helps offer reassurance to those users who oppose AI.

The question is whether Adobe will be willing to follow this lead, or if it will fear that a switch would call its direction into question or discourage people from using the AI tools it wants to promote.
Adobe didn't immediately respond to an invitation to comment.
