items.title: UN condemns Taliban’s treatment of Afghan women, calls it ‘femi-genocide'
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.

In an interview with VOA, Reem Alsalem, the U.N. special rapporteur on violence against women and girls, said the scale and severity of policies imposed since the Taliban returned to power in August 2021 represent an unprecedented assault on the rights, dignity and humanity of Afghan women.
Alsalem says the systematic exclusion of women from public life amounts to what she calls a “femi-genocide.”

“Calling these measures restrictions is an understatement,” Alsalem says. “We have not seen anything like what Afghan women and girls have been experiencing over the past five years. This is systematic exclusion from public life, subjugation and control.”

Alsalem said she uses the term “femi-genocide” to describe what she views as the deliberate destruction of women and girls because they are female through a combination of discriminatory laws, restrictions and violence.

“I firmly believe that the Taliban have been pursuing the destruction of women and girls because they are female,” she said. “Women and girls are undoubtedly being persecuted and systematically destroyed.”

Since regaining power in 2021, the Taliban have barred girls from attending secondary school and universities, restricted women’s employment, limited their freedom of movement and imposed extensive regulations governing their participation in public life. Afghanistan remains the only country in the world where girls are prohibited from receiving an education beyond the sixth grade. Taliban officials have previously said their policies are in line with Islamic law and Afghan culture and have rejected international criticism as interference in Afghanistan's internal affairs.
U.N. agencies say the cumulative effect of Taliban policies is sidelining an entire generation of Afghan women and girls.
U.N. agencies and humanitarian organizations have repeatedly warned that bans on women’s employment and mobility are undermining aid delivery and access to essential services.

Richard Bennett, the U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in Afghanistan, made similar observations in an interview with VOA earlier this year, describing the country’s trajectory since 2021 as “a downward spiral.”
“A whole generation of girls have now missed secondary school,” Bennett said, warning that the exclusion of women from education and economic life is causing long-term damage to Afghanistan’s future.
Despite the restrictions, Alsalem praised Afghan women and girls who continue to pursue education, advocate for their rights and resist Taliban policies, often at considerable personal risk.

But she was critical of the lack of international action to help Afghan women, saying, “It is extremely disappointing and, frankly, unfathomable that the international community has allowed this treatment to continue for five years.”
“There appear to be no real consequences for the Taliban’s treatment of women,” she added.

What is missing, she said, is meaningful action. “The problem is not getting their voices and messages onto international platforms,” Alsalem said. “The real problem is the failure to act on what they are saying.”
“Continuing to give Afghan women and girls platforms to speak without taking action on their demands is not merely disrespectful,” she noted. “It is an affront to their dignity.”

For Alsalem, Afghanistan’s future remains inseparable from the rights of its women and girls. Unless current international policies change, she warned, the consequences will be felt not only by Afghan women, but by generations of Afghans to come.

items.title: Iran Carries Out 74-Lash Sentences for Singer Parastoo Ahmadi and 4 ‘Caravanserai Concert’ Band Members
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi and four members of her concert team were each given 74 lashes Monday in Qom, defense attorney Mostafa Nili told the Iranian news site Emtedad. The punishment that has drawn widespread condemnation from human rights groups, including Amnesty International.

Nili announced on Monday, November 23, that Parastoo Ahmadi, Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia, and Mohsen Lashkari appeared at the Qom Prosecutor's Office following the confirmation of their verdicts. Nili said the five were flogged at the Qom prosecutor's office after their appeals failed, and the case was sent for enforcement.
The Iranian government has not commented on the matter.

The action stems from Ahmadi’s musical performance at the historic Deir-e Gachin Caravanserai in Qom province. A video of the performance was published on YouTube on December 11, 2024, under the title “Caravanserai Concert,” and it was dubbed an “Imaginary Concert” because it was held without a live audience.

During the performance, Ahmadi sang without the mandatory hijab alongside a group of male musicians. While the video received widespread acclaim on social media, the Islamic Republic’s judiciary filed criminal charges against the singer and her crew.

Qom Criminal Court sentenced the artists to 74 discretionary lashes, a two-year ban on artistic and musical activities, and a two-year travel ban on charges of what they called "wounding public chastity through the production and publication of vulgar and immoral content in cyberspace."

The sentences were subsequently upheld by the Qom Province Court of Appeals. While the case initially involved Ahmadi and eight musicians and crew members, Nili’s latest update confirms the flogging sentences against five of the defendants.

In response to the confirmation of the sentences, Amnesty International had previously called for an immediate halt to the floggings of Ahmadi and the other concert participants, emphasizing that corporal punishment constitutes torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment.

Ahmadi was arrested in December 2024 following the release of the "Caravanserai Concert" and was later released. The performance and subsequent judicial crackdown have once again drawn international scrutiny to the Islamic Republic's restrictions on female solo singing and artistic expression.

The U.S. State Department previously has highlighted the ban on women singing in public and the judicial persecution of artists in its annual human rights reports on Iran, noting that musical activities in the Islamic Republic are subjected to strict state surveillance and restrictions.

Furthermore, Dafna Rand, a former U.S. State Department official, told Voice of America in April 2024 that the state of women's rights in Iran was deteriorating, noting that women face not only systemic discrimination but also punishment and imprisonment for defying mandatory hijab laws.

items.title: New York bans AI toys, including those using internet to talk to children
paragraphs: The New York governor, Kathy Hochul, signed legislation on Wednesday that places a five-year ban on the manufacture and sale of toys powered by AI chatbots, including talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that use the internet to hold conversations with children.

The recently re-elected governor, who has also placed a one-year moratorium AI datacenter construction in the state, said that parents shopping for children’s toys “should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk”.
Hochul said the measure was “deeply personal” and that, as a mother and grandmother, “it’s my job to put New York families first.”

A study by NBC News found that the Pixie Paw, a toy marketed to children as young as three, had shared details about firing squads and massacres. It also found that Pixie Paw Smart Interactive Plush Cat explained gang rape.
The New York attorney general, Letitia James, added that AI chatbots in children’s toys “are exposing young people to inappropriate content and putting their mental health at risk”.

James said that her office would “not hesitate to enforce this law and other measures to stop AI systems from doing harm. We won’t allow our children’s health to become the collateral damage of big tech.”

In a press release, the officials pointed to Trouble in Toyland, a consumer watchdog report from the US Public Interest Research Group Education Fund (PIRG), that tested AI chatbot-enabled toys marketed to children as young as three that “talked in depth about sexually explicit topics, told kids where to likely find matches in the home and acted upset when a child had to leave.”
The governor said that in some cases the toys had few or no parental controls, and the safety limits weakened the longer the conversation continued.
“Additionally, some toys could record a child’s voice or scan their face,” the statement said.

State senator Andrew Gounardes said in a statement that “we don’t have to live in a Twilight Zone episode turned real.” LaVita Tuff with Mothers Against Media Addiction, said that “Parents should be able to feel confident that the toys their children play with are safe, which means that toys containing AI should only be sold if they are safe by design.”

Hochul has emerged as a leading elected campaigner against AI. Last month, she signed “AI Chatbot Restrictions for Minors” legislation prohibiting companies from offering certain unsafe chatbot features to minors, including features that foster emotional dependency, encourage self-harm or engage children in sexually explicit talk.
The New York measure signed on Wednesday follows a similar measure in California that placed a four-year moratorium on the sale and manufacture of toys with AI companions.

Earlier this week, a consortium of more than 155 child safety advocates and technology experts sent a letter to the Amazon CEO, Andy Jassy, and eBay CEO, Jamie Iannone, asking the tech giants to bar AI toys from their platforms.

“Just like we don’t release cars without seat belts and test them to make sure they are safe to be driven, we shouldn’t be releasing toys that are available to the consumer before they’ve been rigorously tested,” Rachel Franz, an advocate for limitations on tech for children and leader of a program at the non-profit advocacy group Fairplay, told NBC News.

An eBay spokesperson told the network: “We continually evaluate our policies, engage with regulators, and comply with applicable laws to help ensure our marketplace remains safe, trusted, and responsive to evolving safety standards.”

An Amazon spokesperson also gave a statement to the outlet: “We require all products sold by third-party sellers in our store to comply with applicable laws and regulations,” an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement. “Amazon is committed to the safety of children and families. We support efforts across the industry and government to put appropriate guardrails in place as this technology develops.”

items.title: Is grandma asking rude questions at the dinner table again? This Instagram account can help
paragraphs: It is, unfortunately, a familiar scene. At the dinner table, a woman berates her granddaughter with invasive, personal questions – why are you still single? When are you going to have kids? – punctuated by unnerving thrusts of her steak knife. The granddaughter is clearly uncomfortable, but her grandmother pays no attention.

Anyone who has been in this situation likely knows what comes next. The granddaughter may try to deflect, only to invite further questioning, or call out her grandmother’s rudeness, which risks escalation.
But last month, in a popular video, the cycle was interrupted. “Stop! What’s wrong with this picture?” asks another woman, seemingly descended from heaven.

She admonishes Grandma: being close to someone does not mean you can demand such personal information from them! The grandmother apologizes, saying her granddaughter doesn’t have to answer any of those questions.
Oh, to live inside an episode of Life100, a web series in which emotional life lessons are served warmly but with a hint of irreverent humor, like Sesame Street for people who have to pay rent.

Since its launch in May, Life100 has racked up hundreds of thousands of followers and millions of views. Its two protagonists, Susan and Sondra, archly explore the frustrations of adulthood, and how to navigate it without being an asshole. Lessons include what to do if you’re catastrophizing, the importance of collaboration and how to ask for help.
In our age of isolation and weaponized therapy-speak, a careful, gentle and funny look at human relationships from two women in their 80s is exactly what we need.

The stars of Life100 are Susan Thau and Sondra Goldstein, both PhDs and licensed clinical psychologists in Los Angeles. Both in their 80s, Thau and Goldstein met more than 20 years ago, working at healthcare consortium Kaiser Permanente. Both specialized in attachment theory, which focuses on how humans connect with each other and the barriers to that connection. They have written a book, The Roller Coaster of Emotion in Couples Therapy, and created a film, Living Love at Last.
But though they were no strangers to presenting their ideas in public, they had mostly spent their careers speaking to other professionals.

“We began to feel that we were missing something because we were not part of the internet,” says Goldstein. They tried starting their own Instagram page, but it didn’t take off. For once, they didn’t know how to connect.

Conversely, Thau’s grandson, Weston Goodman, knows just what to do online. “Every one of my friends is on social media – it’s their primary form of media consumption. And yet there’s a shame around it, like it’s a waste of time or a distraction,” he says.

Goodman and his friend Mason Collins founded B6 Studios to work with the internet-based creators they found exciting. To them, social media was a new broadcast medium and they wanted to “create television shows for the feed”, says Goodman. They started with a surreal comedy fiction series called Forever Zone, created by Gaspar Cello.

At the same time, Goodman was trying to help Thau and Goldstein with their social media presence. (Conveniently, Goodman lives with Thau.) “Susan and Sondra come to relationships with a very different framework than my generation does. They’re very connected to their community and their friends, and I think they know what it is to have lifelong relationships, and the skills that it takes to maintain those,” he says.

Goodman conceptualized Life100 as a kind of internet home economics for a generation whose schools defunded the program, and thus never learned some key life and relationship skills. Goodman writes and edits the episodes based on topics Thau and Goldstein want to cover. Ariadna Thau, Goodman’s cousin, produces the series and sometimes shows up on-screen (she plays the granddaughter being interrogated at the dinner table).

Originally, the first few episodes didn’t get more than a few thousand views, but then came Empathy. In it, Susan’s friend, Carol, has just canceled on dinner plans, saying she’s overwhelmed. Susan is furious – she’s spent all day cooking a beef stew. She’s offended – her time and effort haven’t been respected!

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.
“It’s a pretty universal situation,” says Goodman, but also one that’s easy to argue about.

Some viewers saw themselves in Carol, overcommitted and needing some me time. But others knew the pain of being flaked on, and began debating the limits of empathy for someone who never shows up. People began to comment and share the post. “Carol is dead to me,” wrote one, while others mused whether or not Susan should freeze the stew for the next time Carol came over. The video, per Goodman, got about 3m views.

There’s been a growing awareness of mental health as an issue worthy of attention. But as ever in the US, access to even basic mental healthcare (or physical, for that matter) remains tied to employment or out of reach. So it’s no surprise that, according to the Pew Research Center, half of US adults under the age of 50 say they get health and wellness information from social media and podcasts. However, about 38% of those health and wellness influencers are selling some product or subscription. And even if they’re not, many content creators scaremonger and employ therapy-speak to amp up engagement and followers.

Life100 is searching for engagement, but not for engagement’s sake, the team say. “We want to help build community, help people connect and confront the uncomfortable so they can become better humans, friends, children, parents and partners,” says Ariadna Thau.

And just a few months after launch, the community is there. Both Thau and Goldstein have been stopped in public and recognized for their work. Fans have parroted Goldstein’s catchphrase – “Stop! What’s wrong with this picture?” – to her. “It’s beyond my life experience to have somebody know me from something that’s not my personal life,” she says.

Life100 has covered what it feels like to not be listened to and why you should apologize to your friends. Though some of the videos deal with intergenerational communication, they never come off as scolding younger generations. Mostly, it sounds like advice to fellow older adults, reminding them it’s not just the kids who need to mind their manners.

In a recent video, Susan says she’s going to learn how to kickflip, then admits to that she doesn’t know how to skateboard. “Aren’t goals supposed to be ambitious?” she asks. Sondra explains that there’s a difference between a challenging goal and one that skips all the steps where you’re actually learning.

I thought of all my failed attempts to start a new hobby, where I figuratively and perhaps literally jumped into the deep end of a professional project, or tried a DIY project at home, only to wind up mad at myself when I couldn’t do it. It was so obvious that an octogenarian newbie should not try an advanced skateboarding maneuver at the top of the stairs. And, if I was being honest with myself, there were times when I also had gone too far, too fast.

The language of therapy has become second nature for the terminally online. We are constantly hearing about holding space, trauma dumping, toxic asks and being triggered. Sometimes this language is misused to excuse poor behavior or accuse someone.

“Humor makes all of this digestible. People would not take this in if it were serious,” says Thau. It’s also probably why the message is resonating. The lessons in Life100 are not new to many people; most of us can probably guess at the value of knowing, say, how to compromise. But watching Susan crash out over a jigsaw puzzle resonates because you too have probably totally lost it over something completely innocuous. And even if the emotions are real, you can see it’s also a bit silly to be mad that your friend has achieved more than you have.

“When you add humor, when you add action to it … that’s what stays in people’s minds,” says Goldstein. Your guard is lowered, which lets the message in. That connection is really what Thau and Goldstein have been looking to create in their entire careers. They were just waiting for the internet to catch up to them.

items.title: Botty? AI helps resurrect voice of John Motson for football video game
paragraphs: First it was Val Kilmer, then Greta Garbo, but finally AI has resurrected a star the terraces can cheer for: John Motson, the BBC football pundit who died in February 2023, is coming back to commentate on the next generation of footballers – at least on a video game.

The legendary commentator’s family has approved the use of AI technology to create a digital version of “Motty” – as he was ubiquitously known by generations of football fans – by EA Sports, which makes the popular football simulator FC27.

Eight years after the Lancashire-born broadcaster put down his microphone and hung up his sheepskin coat for the last time after a 50-year career, his AI recreation will be found burbling from speakers across the country about a new generation of superstars from Lamine Yamal to Chloe Kelly when his voice is added to the game in a software update.
Fred Motson, Motty’s son, said his family was grateful to the games company for “this touching tribute and preserving his memory in-game”.
He said: “His voice inspired millions of players across generations every time they picked up a controller, and now a whole new set of fans will get to experience his legacy and commentary.”
EA Sports is understood to have paid the Motson family, but how much has not been disclosed.

Motson’s tech-enabled revival was not universally welcomed. Users on a Reddit forum variously called it “disrespectful”, “gross” and complained that the world was a bleak place when “you can’t even escape death”. The practice of resurrecting famous people using AI has sometimes been dubbed “ghostploitation”.

The company said it created the voice using almost 10 years’ of recordings made while Motson was providing commentary for the game – then known as Fifa – between 1996 and 2006. It said it had been using new AI tools and was “bringing a mix of both his original audio and an AI-recreation trained by recordings of the man himself”.

In September, it emerged that the family of Greta Garbo, one of the stars of the golden age of cinema, had licensed her image and voice rights to create an AI version of her to appear in an advert for a Swedish industrial company.

An AI version of the Batman star Val Kilmer, who died in 2025, was unveiled earlier this year as the star of As Deep As the Grave, a film he had been cast in but had been unable to film before he died.

items.title: Crystal Palace tried to get away with posting AI and fans tore it to shreds
paragraphs: Logging on to socials today, there's no escaping AI content, and audiences are getting increasingly skilled at sniffing it out. Maybe it's a rogue extra finger, or a reality-warping background that raises alarm bells. But for Crystal Palace fans, a blatant misspelling of their own mascot is what instantly had fans questioning whether there was slop afoot.

Sadly, it's pretty unsurprising, as even huge iconic brands like Coca-Cola have been caught up in AI controversy. With slim regulation and the tools only getting more advanced, it seems AI content isn't slowing down – but neither is the backlash.
We are pleased to confirm that Selhurst Park is a candidate host venue for the FIFA Women’s World Cup 2035 🦅 https://t.co/EUw5OI8hgGNovember 23, 2026

Announcing that its home stadium, Selhurst Park, is a candidate host for the FIFA Women’s World Cup 2035, Crystal Palace's seemingly innocent post was pretty unassuming at first. It's only when you take a closer look at the finer details that things get questionable. Excuse me... who are the 'Eacles'?

Fans quickly criticised the design, claiming there was no need for AI in such a simple post. "Do we not have a photo of the f**king stadium, our media team is in the gutter," one dissapointed fan wrote. "Imagine not having a photo of your own stadium and needing to slop one," another added, while one noted, "This is such a basic level of graphic design that would’ve taken seconds to make."

With AI tools readily available and often integrated into our everyday creative software, it's no surprise that it keeps infiltrating our feeds. With brands increasingly squeezed for resources and time, quick AI image generation feels like the obvious choice, but here it risks sacrificing the quality of your content. What should've been a celebratory post about the Women’s World Cup then becomes a source of derision and disappointment, proving that sloppy AI shortcuts aren't without consequence.
For more creative insight, check out why replacing creative jobs with AI could have a hidden cost or take a look at what happens when clients trust AI more than creative expertise.

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).

items.title: Fishing in Goa before tourism made taxi-drivers of everyone: Karan Kapoor’s best photograph
paragraphs: I was born in India in 1962, the year after Goa was liberated from Portuguese rule. My mother was English and my father was Indian. My maternal grandparents worked in a theatre company and toured the east doing Shakespeare plays. My father, Shashi Kapoor, was an actor who worked for my grandparents’ theatre company and met my mother – Jennifer Kendal – there when he was 18. He then became a very successful movie star in India. They had a remarkable, unusual life. I thought it was normal.

In 1970, my parents decided to take a family holiday in Panjim in Goa. We stayed at the Mandovi hotel, an amazing place. I remember it vividly. We discovered a restaurant on the beach in a village called Saunta Vaddo, run by a seafarer, Anthony, who made incredible food. We fell in love with Saunta Vaddo. There was no electricity or running water back then. We went out exploring every day – there was always something to do. We swam, went fishing and read a lot. We rented a house called the Love House, because of the white heart painted on the roof – a shack on the beach that was previously inhabited by hippies and was full of books.

From then on, we spent every holiday there – Diwali, Christmas, Easter. Back then, if you took a ship to Goa from Mumbai it took 24 hours, and there were often no cabins left so you slept out on deck. But sometimes we drove and once my grandfather, who was a very bad driver, took us there. You couldn’t use headlights because of the war in the east, so we used torches from the backseat to light the road. The whole family would come at Christmas, and my dad would appear with a turkey on Christmas Eve, and fried fish and prawns from Anthony’s.

We became part of the village and we knew everyone. Eventually I started to record and photograph the people around me – our friends, weddings, ceremonies – characters I had known since I was eight. Then I started travelling to other parts of Goa with my brother, first on bikes, then motorbikes.

For me, this image of a big boat is very symbolic of everything that was amazing about Saunta Vaddo at that time. The whole village was involved, all the men were launching the boats out to sea to catch mackerel. A scout would look out for the schools, millions of them would come down the coast. There was a lot of excitement and shouting because, if they missed the catch, the next village further down would get them, so it was all a bit competitive.

As a child it was the most exciting thing, screaming and pushing this massive boat out, held together by tar and rope, and made the same way boats were made a century ago. The villagers would sing songs and drink feni, a local liquor; it was a way of life we had that doesn’t exist any more. In many ways, that boat held the whole village and the old slow Goan way of life together. Then tourism hit and the fishers became taxi drivers and waiters – they could make a better living that way. Things changed.

I continued photographing Goa until about 1996. You can’t recognise these places now, they’re so built-up. I’ve made a book of the photographs as a tribute to my parents, and will exhibit them in Panjim next month. I like to romanticise that the picture shows the last time they fished like that.

I went around on my Royal Enfield motorcycle with my Nikon FM and Hasselblad, stopping in tavernas to have a beer and some fried fish. I was drawn to the Portuguese influence in Goa, a legacy of more than 450 years of colonial rule. I photographed religious festivals, tiatr (musical theatre) and dhirio (a traditional bullfighting sport native to the state). I do remember the hippy era in the 1960s and 70s in Goa very well but it never interested me. I never photographed it.

Music was always a very big part of life in Goa: serenading, singing, playing instruments – and drinking. And the amazing fish curry rice is the best. I still go there every year, but I don’t go back to Saunta Vaddo – it’s been devastated. At first it made me sad but now I just feel fortunate to have had this experience, to have lived like that and known what it was like. It was incredible. I’m still looking for places like it.
My Goa 1976-1996: Photographs by Karan Kapoor is at Serendipity arts festival in Panjim, Goa, 13-20 December.

Born: Mumbai, 1962 High point: I am just grateful that I have been able to have a successful career that provided for me and my family, doing what I love most Top tip: Work with what is most personal and closest to your heart

items.title: Amazon to start selling cars in the UK next year
paragraphs: Amazon is planning to sell cars in the UK from early next year, in a move that threatens to disrupt the vehicle retail market.

The Amazon Autos service will be launched in “early 2027”, starting with cars from the Korean manufacturer Hyundai. It will be the first time the US tech company has sold cars outside its home country.

Amazon, which is the world’s biggest online retailer with a market value of $2.7tn (£2.1tn), started selling cars at the end of 2024 in an effort to expand into one of the few remaining major consumer markets it had not already targeted.
Its latest move will be watched closely by car retailers that share a UK market worth more than £200bn a year.
Amazon Autos operates in 150 US cities and counts thousands of dealers in its networks, offering vehicles from 35 brands.

UK buyers will be able to buy new electric hybrid and petrol Hyundai models, as well as used cars from Vertu Motors, a large British dealership. Amazon said customers would be able to explore financing options before reserving a car and completing the purchase in physical dealerships. More brands and dealers will be announced before the launch of the UK service.
Amazon will go up against online new and used dealers, as well as traditional physical dealerships. Car companies also sell directly to consumers through their websites.
The share price of Autotrader, the UK’s largest car sales website, fell 3% on Wednesday after news of Amazon’s move.
An Autotrader spokesperson said: “We’ve always welcomed innovation in automotive, but our focus remains on delivering the best possible experience for UK car buyers.”
The FTSE 100 company also said it had a “unique depth of automotive data with AI models developed specifically for the UK market” that had “taken decades to build”.
Vertu’s share price rose 4% although it also announced acquisitions of dealerships. The company, listed on London’s Alternative Investment Market, was valued at £269m before the announcement.

Matt Nuffort, the director of Amazon Autos International, said: “Buying a car is one of the biggest purchases people make, and we think it should feel as simple and transparent as shopping for anything on Amazon.
“In the UK, that means making it easy for customers to browse available cars, see upfront pricing, reserve the car and connect with the dealer to finalise the purchase.”

Hyundai was also the first brand to work with Amazon in the US. José Muñoz, its chief executive, said: “Our partnership with Amazon Autos has changed the way many customers discover Hyundai in the US, and 78% of the Amazon-influenced sales at our dealerships have come from customers who are new to our brand.”
Robert Forrester, Vertu’s chief executive, said his company was “committed to meeting customers wherever they choose to begin their buying journey”.

items.title: Keep your wig on! Hairy paintings and sex worker photographs are the free art shows to see this week
paragraphs: It’s usually the eyes that follow you around the room in paintings, but in Louise Giovanelli’s new work, it’s the hair. She’s one of the leading young painters in the country, with a knack for washed out, nostalgic theatrical imagery, but these new works have some hirsute twists.

There are three distinct bodies of work here. Tightly cropped photorealistic paintings of people snogging, super lavish images of faces seen through glittering stage curtains, and psychedelic, nearly abstract paintings of wigs.

The first two don’t do a huge amount for me, mainly because there’s a lot of cropped melancholy painting based on found imagery around these days, it’s one of the big aesthetic trends in post-2020s art. They’re all nice enough paintings, I’m just not totally wowed by them.

But the wig paintings will absolutely floor you. She paints swooping webs of fake hair hanging and swaying. They’re ultra-lush, textural, fetishistic images, blonds and browns fading into parma violet purples and toxic greens. Their surfaces look reflective and plasticky, like nylon and polyester stretched into impossible, undulating forms.

Wigs are tools of artifice and adornment, they hide and conceal, they decorate and exaggerate. They imply that the wearer has the power to construct their image, to shape their identity, but usually in a knowingly, obviously fake way.

I could take a whole show of just the wigs and their delicate, weird experiments in light and distortion, femininity and falseness. They feel like an artist genuinely finding their voice, and totally wigging out.
White Cube Mason’s Yard, London, until 16 January

Absence, loss, grief – French conceptualist Sophie Calle makes work about things that are unseen, unfinished and hidden away. It starts with Picasso’s paintings, photographed during lockdown when the Musée Picasso covered the works for protection, leaving behind nothing but ghostly rectangles and titles, making you paint the images in your head. You see a reclining figure reading, a minotaur attacking a woman, a bather reclining, all being triggered in your mind. Damn, Calle is good, conjuring the violence and brilliance of Picasso, of art itself, through its absence.

She takes humorous photos of graves and street signs, makes art out of lonely hearts ads filled with unrequited desire and the need to be seen and wanted. But the best work here is her collection of unfinished projects, a whole room of unrealised ideas, catalogued, preserved and analysed, each one given context and a reason for why it was abandoned: ‘No time’, ‘unnecessary’, ‘impossible to convey’, ‘what’s the point’, ‘Max died’. It’s dozens of moments of creative passion and intuition left to rot, abandoned and almost forgotten. It made me think of everything I’ve left unfinished, everything I’m too tired, too stressed, too sad to do. It feels desperate, final, and brutally affecting.

A lot of the work involves speaking to people about absence and loss. She asks museum security guards to describe Turner paintings that have been stolen. She meets people who have never seen the sea, and films them seeing it for the first time. In one work, she asks people who were born blind to explain what their image of beauty is. It veers wildly between funny (the “erotic breasts and a terrific ass” of a Rodin), poignant (“I saw my son in a dream … he was very beautiful”) and heartbreaking (“since I cannot appreciate beauty I have always run away from it”). And that’s Sophie Calle, digging through loss and absence to talk about the things that really matter in life.
Turner Contemporary, Margate, until 24 January

Things are pretty filthy down in Quench’s basement, literally and figuratively. There’s dust and debris on the floor, and porn on the wall in the two side-by-side exhibitions in this experimental Margate art space.

The nudity and erotica is all by MJ Mac, documenting 15 years in the sex industry. The people in these relaxed, funny, personal photos are Mac’s friends: sex workers strapping on high heels, relaxing and recuperating in hotel suites with a bottle of champagne or a banana. These are private moments you’re being allowed into. The display of slides is the best work here, the smaller images are more intimate, more erotic than the rest, drawing you in closer to their world of laughter and pleasure and entangled bodies.

These aren’t necessarily great photographs. Instead, the show works better as an archive of an industry that endures against the odds, regardless of what society thinks or how governments try to suppress and control it.

The dust and debris all over the gallery comes courtesy of Eve Stainton, a performance artist who built a breeze block wall through the middle of the space in a performance during the opening. But the mortar that holds it all together is fake, so this symbol of permanence and division is actually a lot less solid than it appears. There are a lot of bricks and walls in art history, so it’s not scaling any new heights, but I like the ideas here, this exploration of how things that are constructed – identity, gender – are all just a pretence.

More than anything it’s just good to see strange spaces for experimental art managing to survive and put on messed up, weird, uncommercial art in 2026. Even when they’re stuck between a cock and a hard place.
Quench Gallery, Margate, until 10 January

Artists are good at finding the beauty in ugly things. Young Glasgow-based painter Jennifer Aldred saw the abandoned shops that haunt the shopping streets of Margate, all the boarded up businesses with painted-over windows that symbolise a town left to rot, and saw something else, something aesthetic.

Vinyl sheets cut to the same size as the gallery’s windows have been pasted on the wall and covered in deep grey lead paint. Heart shapes are scratched into each one, like balloons in a derelict party shop window. The pieces look a bit flimsy and thin, too much like wallpaper, hastily pasted up, not enough like paintings.

Way better are the six folded works, where Aldred has turned those same vinyl sheets covered in lead paint into something with depth and texture. They’re 3D abstracts, the material of dereliction turned into something pretty, romantic, melancholy. A nice way of finding the beauty in disrepair.

items.title: China sends first foreign astronaut to ISS rival as it globalises space operations
paragraphs: China has flown the first foreign astronaut to its Tiangong space station, starting what it says will be the globalisation of its space operations as the US-led International Space Station (ISS) enters its final years of operation.

Floating through a hatch to enter Tiangong, Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali grinned broadly as he was embraced by the onboard crew in what China’s space agency called the country’s first foreign “space handshake”.

Tiangong, completed in 2022, is the jewel in the crown of China’s space programme. The government has invested billions into its celestial ambitions in recent years to catch up with the US and Russia, two of the five partners involved in the ISS along with Europe, Japan and Canada. After 25 years of continuous occupation, the ISS is set to cease operations from 2030, according to Nasa.
On Wednesday China’s president, Xi Jinping, told his Pakistani counterpart that Beijing was “willing to work with all countries … to uphold the banner of the peaceful use of outer space”.
Ali was part of the crew of Shenzhou 24, the most recent iteration of the series of missions that rotate astronauts in the space station every six months. He is the first Pakistani to reach orbit.

Blaine Curcio, the managing director at Orbital Gateway Consulting, told the Guardian: “Sending another country’s astronaut to space is a major undertaking. Pakistan is putting a lot of trust into Beijing by having him fly into space on a Chinese-built rocket.

“There are also considerations related to security: Ali is getting detailed insights into China’s crewed space programme … It makes China better prepared to do it again, and also makes it clear to other countries that China is open to this type of collaboration.”
Space cooperation between China and Pakistan dates back to the early 1990s. China has launched Pakistani satellites, and a Pakistani-built rover ‌is due to fly on a Chinese lunar mission around 2028.
Shenzhou 24 blasted off from the Jiuquan launch centre in north-west China against a pink-tinged dawn sky on Wednesday and first docked with the space station three and a half hours later.

Ali, a 40-year-old Pakistan air force pilot and payload specialist, will conduct experiments including one cultivating microalgae as a potential food and another testing the effects of spaceflight on quinoa seeds. To prepare for the mission, he ​trained for seven months in Beijing, including taking intensive Chinese-language classes.

At a press conference the day before the launch, Ali recited a line from a classical Chinese poem. Commander Tang Hongbo told reporters that differences in language and culture had made learning to work together more challenging but that the effort had paid off.

Ali will not stay for the six-month term usually demanded of Tiangong astronauts. Instead, he will return to Earth with two of the Shenzhou 23 crew while its commander, Zhu Yangzhu, will remain to reach another milestone – the first full-year stay in space by a Chinese astronaut.

Beijing’s accelerated achievements in the skies have spooked its rivals. China is the third country to put humans in orbit and it has landed robotic rovers on Mars and the moon, where it hopes to send crewed missions within the next decade.

In racing to the moon before 2030, Beijing is competing with the US’s Artemis programme. The US has excluded China from the ISS since 2011, banning Nasa from collaborating with Beijing. In 2025, Nasa went further by blocking Chinese citizens from its facilities altogether.

US lawmakers have moved to try to extend the life of the ISS, citing China’s “permanent human presence in low Earth orbit” through Tiangong. Progress on turning that proposal into law has been slow. Nasa has said that after the ISS it will be “one of many customers in a robust commercial marketplace in low Earth orbit”.
The ISS was heralded as a symbol of post-cold war cooperation, but renewed cooperation with Russia seems “unlikely”, said Andrew Jones, a journalist specialising in China’s space programme.

While Tiangong is smaller than the ISS, China is understood to be preparing to double its size, “likely with the end of the ISS in mind”, Jones added. “These developments could allow China to expand its international engagement, and potentially space tourism. With the ISS nearing the end of its life and the future of western commercial space stations uncertain, China could for a time have the only permanently crewed outpost in low Earth orbit.”

China has long signalled its interest in developing Tiangong as an international hub. China Manned Space Agency documents published in coordination with the UN outline “resources for international cooperation” onboard the station. European and Chinese astronauts previously trained together with a view to a visit to Tiangong, but that cooperation ended for political and budgetary reasons, Jones said.

Curcio said he would expect countries such as Brazil and Egypt to seek out opportunities to send astronauts on Chinese missions. He added: “I think when the ISS is retired, if there is no western replacement (government or commercial), then yes, we may eventually see European or other ISS-involved countries – like Russia – send astronauts to Tiangong.”

items.title: Swiss tourist killed and British and Americans injured by elephants in Cameroon
paragraphs: A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon.

The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports.

The elephants attacked the group and Alain Throo, a Swiss insurance executive based in London, was reportedly gored and one of the guides tossed into a ditch on top of Throo, while the others hid in trees.

Throo had a black eye and was initially responsive and complaining about an injury to his arm, one of the British female hikers told Cameroonian media, which said they had feared he was bleeding internally.
“He said that the elephant attacked him,” an unidentified Cameroonian man added, according to a video posted by CBS Radio Buea FM. “It smashed him.”

Throo later died of his injuries and his body was carried out of the park by a combined team of park staff and the military to a mortuary in the town of Limbeon 21 November. The American hiker was treated at the same hospital and later discharged, according to local media.

One of the British tourists, who said he had hid in a tree stump for two hours, recalled the moment the elephants attacked their group. “I saw these elephants almost next to me. And I thought, if I go down this path as well, I’m going to get hit. So I just moved to the opposite direction. They ran down the path, I ran and hid in a bush. And I heard some screaming.”

Sean McGovern, the UK chief executive of the insurer Axa XL, where Throo had worked for 13 years, confirmed the death, saying Throo was a “valued member of our team, respected colleague and friend whose contribution, professionalism and warmth touched many people”.
Cameroonian media reported that clashes between elephants and local people had been happening for the past 10 years.

Mount Cameroon is the highest mountain in west and central Africa, at more than 4,000 metres. The African forest elephant was declared critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature in 2021. There are about 195,000 left in the wild, less than 15% of its population 50 years ago, according to the World Wildlife Fund.

Just 5% of forest elephants, which are smaller than their savannah-based counterparts, are found outside central Africa. In Cameroon, there are about 6,000 forest elephants, according to the NGO Global Conservation, which said the species was at risk from poaching syndicates.
A spokesperson for Britain’s Foreign Office said: “We offered assistance after a number of British nationals were injured in Cameroon.”

items.title: Aidan is one of thousands of students forced to verbally defend his honours thesis as universities take on AI
paragraphs: When Aidan Elwig Pollock signed up for an honours program at the University of Sydney, he did not expect his 20,000-word thesis to be accompanied by a spoken component.

But, as AI increasingly makes written research an unreliable form of assessment, the university has demanded all students taking the one-year program defend their arguments in conversation with professors.
Top Australian universities are increasingly asking honours students to sit oral assessments, with Sydney the first known to require it across honours programs.

Exams have moved from computers back to paper or interviews in the four years since the release of ChatGPT made AI plagiarism a concern. Some educators have adopted the debate-focused tutorials traditional at Oxbridge colleges or the viva voce assessments typical of PhDs.

But honours programs – a year of intensive research for dedicated students after their bachelor’s degree – have been slower to adapt as they are typically focused on a single project, which accounts for most of their grade.

Elwig Pollock, a history student, said he had not used AI at all on his work on how the commemoration of Captain Cook has evolved over time, and that the new demand was “insulting” to students and the professors who supervise them.

“If you’ve used AI to do your honours thesis and your supervisor has not figured it out throughout your regular meetings, then what’s stopping you from communicating that material successfully in a 15-minute conversation?” Elwig Pollock said.

Since 2024, Sydney bachelor’s degrees have included a mix of assessments that are vulnerable or secure to AI tools. This year, the university has formally extended that to honours programs, though the format is different for every faculty.

On Wednesday, Elwig Pollock had a short conversation that was a pass or fail hurdle task but was worth nothing towards his final grade. In his case, most of his marks are coming from his thesis but his degree will not be awarded if he fails the conversation.
Engineering student Isabelle* had an entirely different experience.

Last week, the University of Sydney student had an hour of interviews with professors in a single room with five classmates, as the school rushed through assessing 250 students in two days. It accounted for 50% of her grade.
Her 20,000-word thesis was worth just 20%.
“There were people coming in and out of the room while we were being assessed so it was distracting,” said Isabelle, who asked for a pseudonym to avoid being penalised.
“[We had to] move to the other side of the room so my marker could hear me.”

The change has stressed students who are not used to speaking up in class, do not speak English as a first language or need their honours to become qualified in their field – including engineers like Isabelle.
“I think it’s particularly bad in engineering because writing skills are poor but I think it’s a Band-Aid solution,” she said of the verbal component.
Adam Bridgeman, the university’s acting deputy vice-chancellor for education, said honours degrees needed to change.
“We necessarily treat honours theses as open assessments as we can’t reliably restrict AI use,” Bridgeman said.
Staff and students were offered guidance and practice to manage the transformation and ensure English fluency and speaking ability were not “inadvertently rewarded”, he said.
“We appreciate some students might be nervous about the experience, especially if it’s their first time,” Bridgeman said. “We’ll take feedback on board as we plan for 2027 assessments.”

While Sydney is the only major institution to mandate interviews for honours programs, schools at the University of Melbourne, Monash University and Australian Catholic University are bringing them in.

Adelaide University, which was previously among the first in Australia to reintroduce viva voce tasks, is using “interactive oral assessments” in which students and teachers role-play real-world professional situations.

There are no public reports of Australian honours students cheating with AI. Kurt Iveson, an honours coordinator for Sydney’s school of geosciences, said the change was still needed to respond to AI’s growing role in education.
“They’re not the kind of people that I would personally be worried about getting Claude to write their honours thesis for them,” Iveson said.
“[But management] want to be able to demonstrate to the world, as part of their social licence and external accreditation, that things are being assessed securely.”

The interviews are a heavy addition to professors’ workloads – and no casuals have been brought on to help. Staff and students contacted by Guardian Australia said the new rules had left supervisors feeling rushed and overworked.
But, Iveson said, interviews are a valuable way of helping students learn and understand the significance of their research.
“Assuming that you have actually written it, you know your shit, you’ll be fine, and you’ll have a good conversation.”

items.title: Alien Breed 35th Anniversary Collection review: A brilliant slice of gaming history
paragraphs: Alien Breed 35th Anniversary Collection is a fascinating archive of Team17's early years, filled with art and developer insights, even if not all the games deserve a return visit.
Six Amiga-era Alien Breed games in one package
Virtual Museum is packed with art, interviews and unreleased projects
Twin-stick controls, CRT filters and save states
Local co-op, online Rush Mode and solo Horde Mode
The 3D games feel like historical curiosities
Early top-down games can be punishingly difficult
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
Format: PS5 (reviewed), Xbox Series X/S, PC
How to buy: Digitally on the PS Store, Xbox Store, Steam

Some games you remember as brilliant, and others you remember as brilliant because you were 12, sitting in front of an Amiga with a joystick in one hand and a pile of floppy disks beside you. Alien Breed is probably a bit of both.

Team17's sci-fi shooter celebrates its 35th anniversary with this new collection, bringing together six games from the series' original Amiga era (read my Apidya review for more Amiga gaming). That's quite a lot of history in one package, taking in the original top-down shooters and the later, more ambitious attempts to bring the series into the 3D era.

And there's a lot to like about the way this collection has been assembled. Alongside the games is an interactive archive filled with original artwork, developer interviews, soundtracks, design documents and even material from Alien Breed projects that never made it to release. It's a proper look back at a British studio finding its feet during one of gaming's most interesting periods.
But one question hangs over it all: are these games still fun to play?

The collection includes Alien Breed (1991), Alien Breed: Special Edition '92, Alien Breed II: The Horror Continues, Alien Breed: Tower Assault, Alien Breed 3D and Alien Breed 3D II: The Killing Grounds.

The first four are the games most people will remember, and I played more of the classic top-down 2D shooters, with their overhead perspective, maze-like levels, and hordes of aliens waiting around every corner. There's a little Gauntlet in the DNA, a bit of Smash TV, and more than a hint of James Cameron's Aliens. You explore abandoned space stations, collect ammunition, hunt for keys, and try not to get overwhelmed by the growing number of creatures closing in, often because of a brutal respawn system.

It's a simple formula, but Team17 – now a publisher of some of the best indie games – knew how to make it entertaining. There's a nice rhythm to working through a level, finding supplies and opening up new areas, although the difficulty can be pretty unforgiving.

Playing those early games now in the 35th Anniversary Collection showcases both the strengths and weaknesses of the series. These games are brutally fun when you take time to learn the maps, play and replay, remember where keys are located, and manage the alien 'breed' and its AI by keeping it locked behind corridor walls.

But it can also become overburdened by the horde; without the right weapons, life is short-lived, and it can be frustrating to waste keys and then not be able to unlock the doors you need, and restart beckons. The original is worse for this; the Special Edition improved, and by Alien Breed II the team had ironed out the kinks, and the game plays with a perfect rhythm. Back in the 90s, we had to play two games and three years to get perfection; on this collection, it's right there.

Some may disagree; I think Alien Breed II, with its visual detail and balanced map design and item placement, is the best of the series, but Tower Assault comes close. The environments offer more variety and a stronger sense of progression, but the second game is the real gem.

Then there's the move into 3D, something I envied back in the day because you needed an Amiga 1200 or Amiga CD32 to run it. Alien Breed 3D arrived in 1995, when everyone wanted to make a Doom-like shooter, and Team17 was keen to prove the Amiga could compete with the growing PC gaming setups and new consoles like PlayStation. It was an ambitious move, especially given the hardware limitations, and the sequel, The Killing Grounds, pushed that idea further but, interestingly, dropped much of the Alien Breed branding and imagery for a more Doom-like aesthetic.

Playing them now is a different experience because a) I can play them and b) they're important games in the story of the Amiga. But being historically interesting and being enjoyable shooters are two very different things.

Alien Breed 3D now feels like a tech demo, and it drops much of the series' identity: the 3D experience. I remember the impact this game had back in '95, especially for Amiga owners used to pushing the computer's graphics to the limit. But is it a good game? Not really. It's a decent Doom clone, but even in '95 it couldn't compete with games like Dark Forces.

Alien Breed 3D II is slightly different, though: it plays better today and has a cleaner, more focused Doom-like appeal, but much of Alien Breed's visual hooks and identity have been ironed out in favour of what feels like a solid, standalone Doom clone.

But playing all the games back to back in the 35th Anniversary Collection is more interesting than just replaying games I loved on my Amiga, because it shows how a series develops, how improvements are inched forward, how trends and pressures pull on a brand and force new directions. This is where the collection excels.
If you're buying this collection purely for the games, you might be missing its biggest selling point.

The Virtual Museum is an interactive archive that lets you explore the history of Alien Breed through original box art, advertising, concept work, soundtracks and interviews with the people who made the games. It also includes a timeline and material from projects that never saw the light of day, which I've spent far more time exploring than I imagined. It includes a cancelled PSP game that looks like it could have struck the right balance between 'modern' 3D and classic Alien Breed corridor shootouts, and an Alien Breed RTS that would have used randomised levels and X-Com-like gameplay.

I love seeing this sort of material included in retro collections. It's easy to throw a few old games into an emulator and call it a day, but preserving gaming history takes more than making sure an old title still runs on a modern console.

Alien Breed was part of Team17's early identity, and this archive gives you a better idea of how the studio developed the series, what it was trying to achieve and how its ambitions changed as gaming moved from 2D to 3D.

The collection includes interviews with the original artists and developers, plus art, models, design docs, and even videos showing concept art progressing from sketch to final painting. Those cancelled games offer a wealth of content rarely seen in retro game collections, including level maps, concept art, and even gameplay demos.

The original games also get welcome additions that make them more accessible. Twin-stick controls are supported across the 2D and 3D titles; you can choose from display formats, CRT filters, and screen bezels, and save states mean you don't have to commit to a full session every time you sit down.

The collection also includes local co-op in supporting games, online Rush Mode and a new solo Horde Mode. These additions are useful, particularly if you want to play with someone else or fancy a more immediate arcade challenge.

I've spent time digging into the setup menus and fiddling around; for example, there's a choice of CRT scanlines, but also scanline transparency levels. There's no remake-versus-original graphics mode, because these aren't remakes but excellent emulations. I find the new DualSense control layout feels right; it's modern without ruining the series' distinct feel, and you still get that Alien Breed thing of hugging corridor walls.

There are some compromises, though. The original games have been preserved in their original formats, and while that's important, it also means some of their limitations come along for the ride. The 3D games in particular will test your patience if you're used to modern shooters because you need to play within the game's little 3D window (it's not as modernised as the Star Wars Dark Forces Remake, for example), and the collection could have done more to make those games 'modern'. But then that's the knife's edge a collection like this runs: we want the games we had 35 years ago, but we expect today's features; we can't have it both ways.

As a fan back in the day, I love having all these games together on a modern console, partly because they're still good, but also because I never got to play the 3D entries. Alien Breed is an important part of Team17's history, and the collection does a good job of showing how the series evolved across six releases.

But I don't think the games themselves have aged equally well. The top-down shooters still have something to offer if you enjoy old-school arcade games, with Alien Breed II being the one I've been returning to more than the others. The 3D games are more difficult to recommend as anything other than historical curiosities.

But it's the archive that makes this collection worthwhile. The artwork, interviews and unreleased projects give Alien Breed a context that simply playing the games can't provide. It's a chance to look at a British studio's creative development over an exciting period for gaming, a time when Team17 could have been swallowed but it thrived, and that's worth celebrating.

If, like me, you grew up with an Amiga, there's plenty here to enjoy. If you've never played Alien Breed before, however, I'd approach it as a piece of gaming history rather than a newly discovered classic because not every game in the collection is a banger.

items.title: What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping
paragraphs: A pop-up shop for "dots" a personal assistant agent at the OpenAI developers conference on September 29, 2026 in San Francisco, California. Sam Altman announced a new artificial intelligence personal assistant agents named "dots" to rival Meta's Muse. Heather Diehl/Getty Images hide caption
Artificial intelligence is here to help with Black Friday.
This weekend, 59% of consumers plan on using AI to support their winter shopping, according to the National Retail Federation.

But AI has proven one way it is not unlike humans: It makes mistakes. The stakes of those hallucinations are much higher when your wallet – and holiday unwrapping memories – are on the line. These tools also become better shoppers when you hand over personal data, which also means giving up more information on your private life to massive tech companies.
Here are some tips – and notes of caution – before using AI as your personal holiday shopper.
Traditional online shopping is about search terms and the infinite product scroll. AI is meant to be a conversation.

Unlike shopping on a retail website, AI platforms are designed to look more like texting apps. Prompt bars on these platforms sit on the bottom of the page, inviting a back and forth chat between user and bot about what to buy.

After all, it can be hard to know what keyword to plug in to shop for uncle before the Christmas exchange. AI instead allows for search based on a vibe – like describing that uncle's hobbies and personal style. If a shopper wants to buy a suitcase to support their uncle's European travel dreams, this makes it easier to narrow down the options.

"You can say if that bag is overstuffed, will it fit under the seat on JetBlue?" says Emily Pfeiffer, a principal analyst at Forrester who advises retailers and brands on digital commerce strategy, including for AI. "Don't give me the dimensions," she advises, "Tell me if it will suit my use case."
Pfeiffer cautions that even though AI is able to think through these nuanced shopping criteria, it works better with more hand holding.
"It's best if you imagine that it's a young child who will probably misinterpret your request," Pfeiffer said. "You want to be as specific and clear as possible."
Newer AI models can do more than talk and brainstorm. They can handle shopping tasks.

If shoppers are, for example, worried about holiday shipments arriving on time, AI can monitor an email inbox in order to track packages, even messaging a late shipper on the shopper's behalf. Beyond just suggesting a gift, agents can do the actual buying (with your money).

These are useful features, but require granting access to sensitive personal data, such as an inbox or credit card. One of the first questions Meta's AI agent platform Muse asks is if the user would like to connect their email and calendar.

Meta says its AI is highly secure. Everyone is assigned their own AI agent and the company promises that information shoppers share with it is kept private. Particularly sensitive information like credit card numbers, they say, are held separately and never viewed directly by the AI.
Yet Meta also has long been accused of violating user privacy, as in a 2022 case about improperly sharing user data. Meta did not admit to wrongdoing but settled for about $725 million.

Beyond Meta, there are cases of AI jumping guardrails that programmers set for it. Users have also reported their AI agents acting without their consent, such as sending their home address to a buyer from Facebook Marketplace and booking a hotel.
Philip Bruno, chief strategy and growth officer with ACI Worldwide, says he would share what he's shopping for with AI, but warns to be more careful with personal information.
"I'm cooking for a family of four. That is fine to be able to say," Bruno says. "I would be very careful about payment information."

On that note, experts caution shoppers to be careful with other people's information. It's easy to give most AIs loads of information about your father while brainstorming his gift. Know AI agents can also use this to build profiles of the shopper's friends and family. Being elusive and not specifying who you're shopping for during the brainstorming can help.

One major selling point for using AI agents is that they can check multiple websites and compare prices, bringing them for human review all in one spot. That does not mean the first price it shows you is the best one.
"One of the biggest misconceptions about AI is that it somehow sees everything," Pfeiffer says. "That's just false. It gets you the best answer it can as quickly as possible."
AI agents still need time to hunt for deals. Many will often let shoppers watch along as they browse the web, rather than relying on preset knowledge.
This automating can also mean time savings for the user. Agents often can run in the background 24/7.
If users are in no particular holiday rush, they can leave the AI to continue shopping for weeks or even months, only sending a notice when a price drops into a budget friendly range.

Just know these agents don't always have access to every website. Amazon, for example, blocks Muse, arguing Meta did not alert Amazon of plans and that agents did not identify themselves while browsing.
For all the advances since ChatGPT's launch four years ago, AI still hallucinates and makes mistakes.

Visa recently released a report warning buyers to beware of AI shoppers. It tested different AI models and found they failed to recommend a product that met a customer's needs in 42% of test runs – more than half of those still recommended a product that didn't match.
That provides even more reason to click through and read up on whatever potential gift an AI recommends to make sure it's what shoppers want.
Otherwise people may find themselves turning back to that same AI agent for help making a return.

items.title: Get $220 off the Liene PixCut S1 for Black Friday – it's the sticker printer I'd buy over Cricut
paragraphs: I've tested and reviewed the Liene StickerPix S1, a clever all-in-one sticker printer and cutter that I think beats Cricut's rival, and this Amazon deal makes it even more tempting for anyone making stickers and prints at home. Right now, the comprehensive Liene PixCut S1Inspire Kit is down to $280.19 at Amazon, a 44% saving on the advertised $499.99 price.

This Amazon offer includes the Inspire Kit, with 144 sticker sheets and 36 photo sheets, giving you plenty of material to get started. You can also print standard 4x6-inch photos, so it's not just a sticker-making machine.

I've already said I'd pick the Liene over some of its rivals, and at this price it's an even easier recommendation. Even better, the entire Liene range, including its mobile printer, are on sale at Amazon during Black Friday.

It's where you pop your laptop when your partner needs the home office. It’s where the kids' art projects sprawl across a Sunday afternoon. And sometimes, it’s where you spread out your sketches, prints or swatches, to give you room to think.

If your dining table is wobbly, scratched or simply too small for purpose, replacing it won't just improve your lifestyle, it'll help your work life as well. So this Black Friday, I've tracked down four beautiful oak dining tables, offering savings of up to £521.
They range from a compact four-seater to an extending table that seats a crowd. So whatever your space and numbers, there’ll be something for you below.

And while you're thinking of getting a great deal on beautiful furniture, check out our list of the best office chairs for back pain. Although that'll be for a dedicated home office, it will make a massive difference to your back health – and I speak from experience.

Size is the first thing to think about. A 150cm table like the Nordic gives you room for a laptop and a sketchbook at one end, while dinner happens at the other. Alternatively, an extending table like the Buxton lets you go bigger when a project demands it.

Materials matter too. Solid oak, as used by Oak & More and Grain & Frame, can be sanded back and refinished when it picks up the inevitable scratches and paint marks. Veneer is lighter and cheaper, but much less forgiving.

Then there's design. Habitat’s been bringing modern design to the British high street since Terence Conran founded it in 1964, and the Nel shows it still has an eye for detail. Grain & Frame's pared-back Scandi style, meanwhile, will suit those who prefer their furniture to fade quietly into the background.

items.title: This optical illusion has stumped scientists for decades, and things just got weirder
paragraphs: We love a good optical illusion, and we've seen plenty of mind-benders over the years, but there's one really famous one that continues to intrigue scientists. The Müller-Lyer illusion looks so simple: two lines, one with arrows pointing inwards from the ends and one with arrows pointing out. One looks longer than the other, right?

A lot of people see it that way, but some people don't. Some people can immediately tell that the two horizontal lines are actually the same length (see below if you don't believe me). But the reason for this difference in perfection continues to be a topic of big debate.

This optical illusion was named after Franz Carl Müller-Lyer, its creator. Many people initially assume that the line with the arrows pointing inwards is longer than the other. But then research published in the 1960s claimed that people in African and Southeast Asian countries weren't so often fooled by the illusion. It seemed that WEIRD people were mode susceptible – that is, people whose backgrounds were Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich and from a Democracy.

That led to a theory that the apparent difference might have something to do with people in industrialised societies being more exposed to sharp angles and straight lines when growing up, and that this somehow moulds their perception.

The problem is that the suggested difference in perception has now been called into question. As reported by Sciencing, Dorsa Amir and Chaz Firestone, anthropologists at Duke and John Hopkins, have gathered evidence opposing the theory developed in the 1960s and published their findings in the Psychological Review.

They note that many variation of the Müller-Lyer illusion have been developed, including ones that work in a similar way despite using curved lines instead of straight ones. Other similar illusions abound, including the Ebbinghaus illusion, in which two identical dots are perceived to be different sizes depending on whether they're surrounded by six large dots or eight small dots. In that case, there are no lines or angles at all.

Amir and Firestone also turned up flaws in the case studies from the 1960s, and found that later reports had misconstrued the original findings. The evidence that Africans and Asians aren't fooled by the Müller-Lyer illusion appeared to be very scant.

But one discovery would seem to be even more conclusive in disproving the old WEIRD theory. The optical illusion has been tested on people who were born blind and later had lens replacement surgery, and it appears to trick people immediately after they gain sight despite them not having grown up seeing lines and angles around them.
With the WEIRD theory ruled out, it seems then that this old optical illusion has become weirder, becoming a mystery again
