items.title: ‘It’s been really a mess’: Meta insiders concerned over push to AI content moderation
paragraphs: Meta employees have expressed concern at the company’s push to replace human moderators with artificial intelligence, claiming the technology is leading to mistakes with the potential for sweeping political consequences.
The social media company, which owns Facebook and Instagram, has been experimenting with AI-driven moderation for years, first introducing it in 2017 to filter out violent extremist content.
This March, Meta announced it was “transforming our approach” by rolling out “more advanced AI systems” to moderate content across its apps, framing the change as a way to improve enforcement.
Several Meta employees said that behind the scenes this push to AI was accompanied by mass layoffs across the company, severely affecting staff responsible for reviewing content on its platforms.
One described Meta’s content moderation as now operating with “skeleton teams”, some cut by at times half or two-thirds of their staff.
“It’s been really a mess,” they said, adding that on several recent occasions they had gone to discuss an issue with a specific content moderation team, only to find that entire team was now gone.

Meta has long sought inexpensive ways to moderate the vast volumes of content posted each day to its platforms. It has faced legal action from former outsourced content moderators in Kenya, who described struggling with PTSD and severe mental health issues after being paid as little as $1.50 (£1.13) an hour to view and evaluate extremely graphic content that users attempted to post.
Meta employees say AI systems that the company is now using struggle with nuance, especially in languages other than English, and frequently remove content that should not be taken down.

“You are trying to gut all human reviewers, which are kind of essential for making these nuanced decisions and policy decisions,” said one employee. “Of course there are going to be mistakes that are going to happen.”

The employee said that because algorithms were automated, and worked at greater speed than humans, these mistakes could happen at a greater scale. The employee said Meta was removing lower-paid contractors, such as those in Kenya, and the full-time employees who would handle more complex content moderation.

Once a post is taken down, there is far less recourse for the affected accounts than before. “Even if you know someone at Meta, it’s still very difficult to get through to someone who’s actually going to be able to help you, especially if it’s a highly nuanced case,” the employee said. “It’s so much more difficult now.”

The growth in AI moderation comes as researchers monitoring online censorship have noticed a new phenomenon: sudden restrictions on Instagram and Facebook accounts, often during pivotal political moments.

Some of these have been isolated occurrences, such as Meta’s suspension of the US No Kings account in the run-up to the US midterm elections. Others have amounted to “mass takedowns”, unfolding over the course of days and hitting dozens of social media accounts.

It is a growing phenomenon, the consequences of which could “shape the political future of entire nations”, said Martha Dimitratou, the founder of the group Repro Uncensored, which monitors digital censorship.

Repro Uncensored has tracked these takedowns in Brazil, the EU, Turkey and the US. The Guardian reported on a wave of account takedowns on Meta platforms late last year, affecting accounts posting queer content and those dedicated to reproductive health across Europe. Accounts backing the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, were restricted or suspended from Instagram in the feverish days of Brazil’s election runoff, according to Repro Uncensored. Meta said most of the Brazilian takedowns were to comply with valid court orders or electoral regulations.
The numbers of affected accounts appear to be rising: Repro Uncensored documented 210 incidents of account takedowns on Meta in 2025, and 657 in the first six months of 2026.

Meta employees who spoke to the Guardian said AI moderation had a role in such incidents as algorithms worked faster, and with less nuance, than human reviewers. “The effect of it is you see these sweeping takedowns,” one said.

But they also said they could not rule out political considerations in how Meta’s algorithm was designed. Meta’s systems are opaque, even to its employees. They are a combination of LLMs – large language models, like chatbots – and older algorithms that filter content.
There are “thousands of levers and factors that weigh into how things are ranked”, said one employee, and these change constantly.

The employees suggested that at times Meta’s use of AI had allowed the company to obscure more controversial decisions it makes in how it moderates political content. They gave the example of how Meta made adjustments to its algorithm in late 2023 that drastically limited the number of posts that appeared from people in Palestine.

The company rejected allegations of bias and said it had previously carried out independent human rights due diligence in relation to the conflict, and since 2022 had been working to implement the resultant recommendations, including by “introducing a system that detects and prioritises content to moderators most likely to understand that particular Arabic dialect”.
One employee said AI offered “plausible deniability”. It afforded “exactly the kind of ambiguity that they hide behind”, they said.

In response to questions from the Guardian, a Meta spokesperson said: “Everyone on our platforms is subject to the same set of rules, and any claims of enforcement based on political affiliation or advocacy are baseless.

“While we have long used AI to help enforce our community standards, earlier this year we began experimenting with more advanced AI systems that can more quickly and accurately catch violations with fewer mistakes. The latest tests show that on average these systems make 13% fewer mistakes than humans when enforcing against violating content, while finding 10% more actual violations – and we give people opportunity to appeal decisions if they think we’ve got it wrong.”

items.title: Blade Runner 2099 not just about AI, say star Hunter Schafer and series creator
paragraphs: "What does it mean to be human?" is a question that's always been at the heart of Blade Runner.
The first film in the series, released in 1982, depicted a technologically advanced yet dystopian version of Los Angeles in the then-distant future of 2019.
While the movie's flying cars haven't - quite - materialised yet in the real world, Blade Runner's themes of technological progress and the threats it poses feel just as relevant.
At least that's what the cast and crew of Blade Runner 2099, a new TV series set in the same universe, are hoping.

BBC Newsbeat spoke to stars Hunter Schafer, Lewis Gribben and Dimitri Abold, plus showrunner Silka Luisa, to ask why they think themes of artificial consciousness and existential threats still resonate.
The original Blade Runner, directed by Sir Ridley Scott, is considered a sci-fi classic that had a long-lasting influence on the genre.
It told the story of Detective Deckard, played by Harrison Ford, who hunted down synthetic humans known as replicants.
Schafer says her first exposure to the series was actually marketing for Blade Runner 2049 - the film sequel starring Ford and Ryan Gosling in 2017.
"I never thought I'd have the opportunity to make an addition to the world," she says.
"And so when that opportunity came along, I was quite thrilled."
Blade Runner 2099 is set 80 years after the original film, and portrays a Los Angeles where replicants have taken over.
Schafer plays Cora, a fugitive human forced to team up with replicant Olwen (played by Michelle Yeoh), as she tries to track down an artefact that could save humanity.
The series lands at a time when there are disagreements about the nature of the threat AI could pose to humans.
"I think it's particularly relevant right now, especially for the youth and young people who are inheriting a world that's asking a lot of the same questions that the show asks," says Schafer.
"I think that's timely and hopefully helpful to some degree."
But Blade Runner 2099 isn't "necessarily about just AI", says showrunner Luisa.
"It's this bigger question of what is the world going to be in 15 years and how can you plan for it?" she says.
The first Blade Runner also touched on themes of corporate greed and environmental damage, which are evident in the new series.
Luisa hopes the theme of a future that "is not going to be what you were promised" resonates with viewers today.
"The idea that you were born into a world and you thought you were expecting certain aspects of your life just to roll out," she says.
"That system is collapsing. And so what will be your place in whatever comes next?"
Blade Runner 2049 won awards and scored well with reviewers, but reports suggested it didn't hit box office targets.
This was partly blamed on marketing for the film trying to appeal more to existing fans than new ones - so what would the cast say to get younger viewers on board?
"It's just a very rich world," says Gribben, who plays Cora's younger brother Elias.
Gribben also points out that Blade Runner 2099, which employed "hundreds of artists and craftspeople" according to its makers, is a celebration of traditional film-making despite its themes.
"I think a lot of people crave human stories," he says.
"They crave new kind of worlds and new things.
"And I think studios will rely more on technology to make better-looking movies, but they won't have that soul."
Abold, who plays Cora's human ally Bebeto, says one of the show's key messages is about "the connections that you make".
"And the connections that you make are the foundation of humanity," he says.
"Because at the end of the day, all we have is ourselves and each other, right? And that's what feeds any human emotional experience."

items.title: Close-up images to be revealed of asteroid deliberately hit to test ability to protect Earth
paragraphs: The Hera spacecraft will study the 150m-wide (490ft) asteroid called Dimorphos
A spacecraft has arrived at an asteroid to investigate the damage caused by an unprecedented cosmic crash.
In what may sound like the plot of a disaster movie, Nasa's Dart spacecraft deliberately smashed into the space rock in 2022 to knock it off course.

The Nasa craft was obliterated on impact. Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) mission, called Hera, is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision - with the first images set to be released later on Wednesday.
The asteroid poses no threat, instead this was the first ever test of our planetary defences to see what action we could take if a space rock was heading for our planet.
"Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission.
This was the last image from Dart before it crashed into Dimorphos in 2022
The crash test focussed on a pair of asteroids: a larger one called Didymos - about 730m (2,400ft) wide - which is orbited by a smaller rock called Dimorphos, about 150m (490ft) wide.

The Dart spacecraft targeted Dimorphos, hurtling into the rock at 22,000km per hour (14,000mph). Images beamed back showed the asteroid's rocky surface coming ever closer until the feed cut out on impact.
It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 10,000km long (6,200 miles), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.
The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.
Before the collision it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the Dart crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.
But the arrival of the second spacecraft, Hera, will help scientists to answer many more questions.
"Dart exploded in the asteroid, and therefore we don't have the information of what is its final state," explained Michel.
"The impact could have left a crater - and if it is the case, we need to understand the size and the depth. Or [the impact] may have entirely reshaped the asteroid."
A 10,000km-long (6,200 miles) debris trail was spotted by the Hubble Space Telescope
The Hera mission will spend the next year studying Dimorphos, and take a look at Didymos too.
The spacecraft is packed with instruments, and it also has two small shoe-boxed sized satellites onboard, which can study the impact site up close, and then later land on the asteroid.
A key task is to measure the mass of Dimorphos, to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was.
This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth.
"It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team.
"We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'."
Hera has already sent back an image of Didymos with Dimorphos in the background
Asteroids pose a significant threat to our planet.
The biggest, which measure more than a kilometre across, could cause global devastation. But medium-sized asteroids around the same dimensions as Dimorphos could wipe out a city.

"We all know what happened to the dinosaurs, right? And we don't want that to happen to us," said Carolyn Ernst, Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, who works on both the Dart and Hera missions.
"The good news for us is that there are far fewer potential threats out there in the Solar System than there were millions of years ago. But there are objects out there."
She said the biggest asteroids have been spotted, and none are heading to Earth.
"The smallest stuff isn't too much of a threat because our atmosphere protects us," she added.

"But there's a size range in the middle where we don't know where all of them are, and it could, if impacted, cause problems for humanity. And if we can find out about that and know about that, well, we sure as heck would want to try to stop that."
Hera has two small satellites onboard to study the asteroid up close
Scientists want to gather as much intelligence as they can about space rocks - to make us as well equipped as possible to deal with whatever the Universe throws at us.
A new mission is launching in 2027 to track potentially hazardous asteroids: a space telescope called the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor.
There are also more visits planned to asteroids, including to one called Apophis, which is about 450m (1,480ft) long.
Apophis was discovered in 2004 and it was initially thought it might hit the Earth as early as 13 April 2029.
But now scientists understand its orbit better, and say it won't hit us for at least the next 100 years. Instead of a crash in 2029, it will fly just 32,000km (20,000 miles) above our surface.
This will give scientists the rare chance to study a space rock up-close.

Two spacecraft will head to Apophis, including Nasa's Osiris-Apex (which previously grabbed a sample from another asteroid called Bennu) and Ramses, a joint mission between ESA and the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA).

items.title: Assemble covers miniature agricultural buildings in intense blue pigment for Building Blue exhibition in Tokyo
paragraphs: Architecture collective Assemble has created small, climbable cedar buildings that “play with scale” to showcase a new pigment made from industrial waste at Tokyo‘s SKAC gallery.
With the exhibition, the UK-based collective said it aimed to “explore the transformation of landscape through colour and into colour”.

The architects are using the Building Blue exhibition to showcase a new pigment, made by design studio Matter at hand for Assemble from local waste material. It will also be used in Assemble’s Play Earth Park – a campsite under development in rural Japan.

“The pigment was essentially created by analysing local material waste streams in Toyama and exploring what kind of different colours could be produced from them,” Assemble co-founder Maria Lisogorskaya told Dezeen.

“In the end, the blue uses a combination of rice husk ash, limestone filter dust, recycled glass and copper, which are mixed together with water to form a thick clay-like paste and then heated in an electric kiln to around 950ºC,” she continued.
“The materials react to form a new crystal phase – known as cuprorivaite, which is bright blue.”

To show it off, the designers constructed three miniature houses from Japanese cedar that draw on the agricultural buildings found close to where the pigment material was sourced. The houses were named The Hut, The Tower and The Bird.

“The form of the structures plays with the agricultural buildings within the dispersed settlement of rural Toyama; these buildings evolve over time, adapting to what’s needed, often evolving interesting geometries,” Assemble co-founder Lewis Jones told Dezeen.
“We tried to play with scale and make the buildings surreal, creating miniature versions of them for play.”
The buildings have deliberately simple yet evocative geometries that nod to the structures that inspired them. Among them is a barn-like building surrounded by hay bales.
Assemble’s aim was for visitors to be able to climb and explore the structures.
“We hope that the buildings are climbed on and inhabited; and this exhibition is the beginning of the structures’ life as a play space outside SKWAT,” Lisogorskaya said.
“The spirit of resourcefulness, fun, and reimagining of our environments is at the core of the project and we look forward to seeing how the structures are used in ways we didn’t expect.”
The exhibition, which also showcases raw materials used to create the blue colour and products covered in it, is on show in Skwat Kameari Art Centre (SKAC’s) Park gallery in Kameari, Tokyo.
Assemble said it chose to showcase it here as it feels the gallery has a similar spirit to its own UK bases.
“We think SKAC is an amazing interdisciplinary space, and its spirit resonates with how we have set up our studios and labs in London and Liverpool,” Jones said.
“Bringing together design, material experimentation with other arts practices as a more satisfying and richer way of being in the city,” he continued.
SKAC recently opened two new gallery spaces, Material Matters (MM) and Space III, as part of a major extension.
The east Tokyo gallery has previously shown exhibitions including anime-informed chairs by Kwangho Lee and reading spaces by Herzog & de Meuron.
Building Blue is at SKAC, 3-26-4 Kameari, Katsushika-ku, Tokyo 125-0002, from 7 November 2026 to 28 February 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

items.title: Fatbergs, feathers and flocks of sheep - inside the new London Museum
paragraphs: The museum's Our Time space will host events among 13 large installations and flocks of sheep benches

Ten years ago the Museum of London announced it would be leaving its former home to move to the abandoned halls of Smithfield Market. Now rebranded London Museum, it is set to open its doors to the public on Saturday after a £437m project. So what's it like inside?
Leaning back on a leather sofa, museum director Sharon Ament looks across a vast brick-lined space that once bustled with market traders but is now filling with its newest visitors.
"I really love this space, it just makes me smile every time I come in - it's actually joyful," she says.
The vast room, now known as Our Time, is dotted with installations reflecting living memory.

In one corner a life-size mechanical giraffe flicks its ears in front of a lit-up NHS sign representing lockdown. Another wall has remnants of London's former greyhound tracks. Near it is the old switchboard from Buckingham Palace.
And beneath the magnificent domed ceiling roam several flocks of large plastic sheep which Ament encourages people to "pull up and take a seat" on.
"There are grins on people's faces, so I think we've pulled something rather incredible off," she says.
Sharon Ament says she wants the museum to be a shared space for everyone
The museum reflects London's more recent history such as its greyhound-racing tracks - the fireplaces of the market traders' former offices can be seen behind
A visit to the new museum starts before this point as people enter through a large covered street known as Real Time.
Here, data-filled digital displays tell of London in the moment, beside a Banksy-graffitied sentry box and the last bell to be cast at the historic Whitechapel Bell Foundry.
Next they enter the former General Market with its sheep, giraffe and signage.

This is the space where events like late-night house parties and dinner clubs will be held beside shops and eateries, including former Victorian cocoa rooms that will be open 24 hours a day at weekends.
Such hints of the building's past are everywhere. Halfway up the walls are the restored fireplaces of the traders' former offices, along with twisting metal staircases that once led up to them.
"Whenever we've found historic fabric, we've restored it or kept it, and we want to show the layers of history," explains Alec Shaw, who has led the entire project.
"We wanted a museum that worked like the market, that allowed you to come in any corner and just walk across, walk through the building on your way to work, or, hopefully, stay a bit longer."
Smithfield's General Market opened in the 1880s and was in use until the 1990s
The Our Time space seen in early 2024 when water was still splashing into the building
Shaw previously showed me around the site nearly three years ago, when scaffolding and supports were holding up the walls and there were constant splashes of water dripping on to the floor.

Restoring a Victorian relic that was abandoned in the 1990s "really tested all of us", he admits, and that was before the logistics involved in designing a new museum from the venue's seven-million object collection.
Five thousand of these are now on site and another 300,000 are due to arrive for when the former Poultry Market becomes a museum space in 2028.
"We think you could take at least eight hours to see every object downstairs, and that means you're going to keep coming back.
"The best museums are those that you go, 'Right I'll do that one today. I'll do this gallery next time,'" he says.
Our Past is based in the building's basement and tells a weaving story of London through five different chapters
Queen Victoria's mourning dress is among the objects on display
A wide staircase to one side descends into what is called Past Time.

Down here is what once was street level of Roman London, and curator Annette Day explains that "we felt that right in the guts, in the earth of the city, that was the place where we should explore London".
A weaving route beneath a seven-metre-high brick vaulted ceiling tells the capital's story.

It starts with the city's creation by the Romans and moves through medieval times and London's place as the centre of the British Empire, before ending with the 2012 Olympic Games, a time when "London looked at itself and the world looked at London", says Day.

There's Charles I's execution vest, Queen Victoria's mourning dress, a white 1960s Ford Cortina, an overstuffed taxidermy cat called Oliver and the shimmering Elizabethan jewellery of the Cheapside Hoard.
Large illustrations are incorporated with historic objects to tell the story of the Great Fire of London
Oliver the overstuffed taxidermy cat was once a Londoner's pet
Galleries on either side also focus on specific moments.
One features a recreated Roman room with amphoras - two-handled jars - a mosaic floor and the pieces of a magnificent wall painting found in Lime Street 20 years ago that hang on the wall.
Another uses large comic illustrations based on new research to tell the story of the Great Fire of London in an attempt to reflect the subject's inclusion in Key Stage 1 of the national curriculum.
Further along still, two other archways branch off to look at the lives of Londoners and the city's landscape, placing objects from across the ages alongside each other.

The delicately feathered Dying Swan outfit worn by lauded Russian dancer Anna Pavlova stands beside the stage outfit of Edwardian music hall star Kitty Lord in one case, while another shows 2,000 years of London-made shoes.
One case is even filled with toilets and chamber pots from medieval times to today.

And to carry on that subject, on the far wall a small porthole frames a chunk of the eponymous Whitechapel fatberg, not far from the huge glass window that looks out on passing Thameslink trains (whose passengers apparently are yet to notice they are now being watched).
Visitors can while away the hours watching Thameslink trains pass by the galleries
The museum has a small chunk of the Whitechapel fatberg, which weighed 130 tonnes and stretched more than 250m along a sewer
Even with its planned events, shops and eateries, Ament says it is all these objects which remain "the essence of the museum" because they "tell stories in a compelling way".
She sees the museum as a shared space for everyone, somewhere for Londoners and tourists alike to connect with people and stories from the past and now.
"Think of this as like one of my favourite buses, the number 63 bus. You meet the world on it. And you meet the world in here."
Most important of all, she says, is that the London Museum must always represent and reflect the city it is in.

"The story of London is tough and joyful at the same time. That's why we use 'grit and glitter' as a tagline - it's both of those things, those dualities can exist. And we shouldn't be frightened of that history," she says.
"We are making a museum and it will never stop, just like London never stops. There's always cranes in London and there'll always be new things in London Museum."
Visitors to Our Time are watched over by a life-sized giraffe model that flicks its ears

items.title: Thermory Design Awards 2026 recognises striking examples of architecture and design using thermowood
paragraphs: A contemporary take on Ukrainian vernacular buildings and a preschool in Estonia are among the winners of the Thermory Design Awards 2026, which celebrate the versatility of thermally modified wood.

Of 78 submissions from 23 countries, four winning projects have been selected in the competition’s fifth annual edition, covering the categories of interior, tiny and private house, residential, commercial and public building, and wellness and spa.
Thermory thermowood is wood that has been modified using heat and steam with no added chemicals.
The treatment enhances the material’s dimensional stability and reduces moisture uptake compared with untreated wood, according to Thermory.
The winner of the interior category is a trio of Ukrainian guesthouses collectively named Under the Reed Roof, designed by Kyiv-based studio YOD Group.
Each guesthouse comprises a glass-walled volume at the base, topped by a tapered thatched roof with exaggerated proportions.
While the exterior of these roofs is made with traditional reeds, the interiors are lined with thermo-ash shingles, arranged to create a tactile effect that is repeated on the front doors.
These highlight the interplay between the interior’s traditional and contemporary design elements, contrasting materials, and the balance between the structure’s openness and enclosure.
“The project stood out to the jury for its exceptionally coherent concept, in which architecture and interior elements come together to form a harmonious whole,” said Thermory.
Winning in the tiny and private house category was Marker Architecture‘s Flooded Gums project, a flood-resilient dwelling built on working farmland.
The building features thermo-ash cladding and thermo-spruce decking, owing to the materials’ robustness and aesthetic merits.
“What particularly impressed the jury was the honesty and clarity of the architecture,” said Thermory of the project.

“Rather than concealing its construction, the project makes its structural logic visible, with every element serving a purpose: the result is a modest yet highly refined building that strikes a compelling balance between aesthetics, functionality and its natural setting,” it added.

Estonia’s Rakke Kindergarten secured the win in the residential, commercial and public building category, thanks to what Thermory describes as local studio Arhitekt Must‘s “cohesive and imaginative design”.
Thermo-spruce cladding, thermo-pine posts and thermo-pine decking all feature in the design, enhancing both its functionality and visual appeal.

The building’s function as an educational environment is made distinctive by the space’s inventive ceiling, which is composed of the short thermo-pine posts, arranged in a way that creates an engaging optical illusion.

“This unexpected architectural gesture elevates a functional space into something distinctive, demonstrating how thoughtful detailing can shape the character and experience of an entire building,” said Thermory.
Finally, the winner of the wellness and spa category is a sauna within the Estonian Embassy in Berlin, designed by interior studio AERIS.
The interiors feature statement walls covered in custom-made oak shingles, which, being circular and slightly overlapping, resemble fish scales.
These are joined by thermo-alder benches and walls, creating a cohesive scheme of timber details that integrate neatly with the lighting design.
“The harmonious interplay of materials, surfaces and light imbues the space with a contemporary edge while retaining the intimacy and warmth of a traditional sauna,” said Thermory.
“Although vastly different in character and purpose, the winning projects share a creative and unconventional approach to design,” it added.
“Each places wood at the heart of its architectural expression, combining imaginative thinking with meticulous attention to detail.”

The 2026 instalment of the competition was judged by a diverse international jury of architects and Thermory representatives, including Kärt Kanarbik, Thermory’s architectural project manager; Lars Skjølstrup Østergaard, lead design architect at Henning Larsen; Sami Rintala, professor and architect at Rintala Eggertsson Architects; Jaan Port, architect and partner at PIN Arhitektid; and Tõnis Kalve, architect at ByKalve and Thermory project sales architect.
To learn more about Thermory, visit its website.

items.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
paragraphs: Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US.
In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.
Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.
In a statement, Huawei said the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years".
Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.
However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.
Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.
Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.

During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.
"For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in statement, external.
"Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable."
However, defence attorney Brian Heberlig said it was by dint of hard work that Huawei's business had expanded with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff.
Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified that the jury had rejected the racketeering charge.

"The RICO [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act] count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said.
"Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board."
Sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal.
"If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the company's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he said.

items.title: The rising cost of putting food on the table in India
paragraphs: India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.
The latest government data, external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.
But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.
The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.
In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.
Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.

With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall, external, India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.
Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.
In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.
That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.
Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.

"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.
According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%.
In urban India, the corresponding rates were 6.1% and 5.3%.
The pressure is visible even in the cost of a simple meal.

Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis, external found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive.

Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says.
When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.

And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.
Onionomics: Peeling away the layers of India's food economy
Onions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings.

The rabi crop - winter crops, sown after the monsoon and harvested in spring - which accounts for roughly two-thirds of onion production, is harvested in March and April and stored for several months. As stocks dwindle, prices can rise sharply before the next crop arrives.
Tomatoes, meanwhile, tend to see price spikes during the summer months, when arrivals decline in some markets or heat stress affects production.
Sharma says perishables are often responsible for the sudden spikes in food inflation, while prices of staples such as rice and wheat tend to rise more gradually but can stay higher for longer.
"The perishables are what caused the volatility. The non-perishables, like rice and wheat, are the ones that structurally increase the cost," he says.
Economists say India still lacks adequate infrastructure to sort, grade, store and process much of its perishable produce.
Tomatoes, for example, can become so abundant during a glut that farmers struggle to sell them at remunerative prices, only for consumers to face sharply higher prices months later.
Better storage and processing could help turn some of that surplus into products such as puree, smoothing the extremes between abundance and scarcity, according to Sharma
Energy shocks feed into the cost of transport, irrigation and agricultural inputs. Fertiliser prices can rise. Global edible-oil markets matter because India relies heavily on imports.
To be true, India, however, has some protection against the worst effects of food inflation.

Government stocks of cereals are comfortably above prescribed minimum levels, and the free-food programme covering nearly 800 million people offers a cushion against rising prices. Rice stocks, external are particularly ample.
There is a wider economic risk, says Sengupta.

"Food inflation may begin with a supply shock, but its effects can spread. Workers who find that their wages no longer cover basic living costs may seek higher pay. Businesses facing higher labour costs may raise prices. What begins as a rise in the price of food can gradually become a more general inflationary pressure - the familiar wage-price spiral that central banks try to prevent," she says.
For India, this creates a particularly difficult balancing act.

Agriculture is a relatively low-productivity sector, and the government has long sought to protect farmers by setting minimum support prices (MSPs) for certain crops - a price floor at which it promises to buy produce, helping farmers guard against a market crash.

At the same time, food prices are politically sensitive. Sharp increases in the price of staples such as onions and tomatoes can quickly anger consumers, prompting governments to step in with measures such as restricting exports, limiting how much traders can stockpile, or otherwise trying to bring prices down.
The broader story of India's changing food consumption makes the current inflation more interesting.

Households are eating differently from a decade ago. An analysis, external of the 2011-12 and 2023-24 consumption surveys shows that the share of cereals in food spending has fallen sharply, particularly among the poorest households, reflecting the impact of subsidised food programmes.
Meanwhile, consumption of nutrient-rich foods such as dairy, fruit and meat has increased across income groups, with the biggest gains among the poorest, the study revealed.

India's food basket is becoming more diverse. But diversity is meaningful only if ordinary Indians can afford it. Ultimately, food inflation is about what makes it to the plate - and what has to be left out.

items.title: Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe
paragraphs: Selena Buse, 16, reverses her Citroën Ami out of a parking space and heads off past the school playground. Heads turn. The Ami looks pretty remarkable. Futurist or like-a-toaster depending on your point of view. But it's changed her life.
"I got it because I really needed it to get to school. And I use it to visit friends on the weekends. It's indispensable in rural areas like where I live," she says.
In France, you can drive a car like this from the age of 14 with a road safety certificate and eight hours training. In Italy too.
In Germany and Spain it's 15, in the UK 16. Because they are classed as motorised quadri-cycles. Four-wheel mopeds in other words.
Registrations have risen from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year in France.

In Europe, sales have gone from 30,000 to 60,000 in the past five years. And the Ami, launched in 2020, has really changed the image, with teenagers who now account for a quarter of all mini-car sales.
In Selena's very small Citroën, we are soon rolling along at the top speed of 45km/h (28mph). For other road users, no-licence cars like this can seem like mobile traffic calming.
"When I'm on faster roads and there's a lot of traffic the cars behind me sometimes honk their horns but I can't go any quicker!" Selena says.
Another local Daniel Laprès, who drives a micro-car made by French firm and market-leader Aixam, tells me he actually pulls over to let the cars behind pass.

He and his wife moved from Paris to this country village two years ago. Of Canadian nationality, he didn't swap his foreign licence for a French one in time and lost the right to drive. That didn't matter much when he was in Paris. Like many Parisians he didn't need a car. He used public transport. But that's not possible here.

"We tried living off of taxis and it was in the end a disaster. Then we heard about how you could drive without having to have a licence, and it was the exact solution to our problem. Cheap, inexpensive to operate, basically no administrative formalities, you get insurance."
However, Laprès feels less safe in his small car. "They're little more than tin cans on wheels, right? I mean, you're not going to be driving fast, but someone else could be."
These cars are forbidden on motorways. But even on medium-fast roads, being considerably slower than the average vehicle can be a problem.

"You go on national highways at your risk and peril. I did it once and I will never, ever do it again. On those roads (speed limit 110km/h), everybody is passing you, including the biggest trucks. And they come at you very fast from the rear, so it's scary," Laprès says.
Daniel is 77 so fits in with the long-established market for these cars: older people living in the countryside.

Traditionally the market also included quite a few people who'd lost their licences, often because of drink-driving offenses. But the launch of the electric Citroën Ami in 2020 changed the customer profile and the product.

"The launch of the Ami was the beginning of the transformation of the sector, with more and more electric models coming on to the market. In 2026, more than 67% of new licence-free cars are electric," says Marie-Laure Nivot, market analyst at AAA Data.
This tendency was encouraged by stricter EU regulations on motorised two-wheelers that had been the vehicles of choice for European teenagers until then.

"It proved too costly for manufacturers to apply the new EU rules, so mopeds and small scooters have almost disappeared from the market since 2020 and licence-free cars have taken their place," Marie-Laure Nivot says.
Tiny car sales rose strongly till 2024 although they have flattened since in France with the withdrawal of subsidies for electric models.
Curiously, the arrival in this niche market of a giant competitor in the shape of Stellantis brand Citroën was actually good news for existing French manufacturers like Aixam and Ligier.

"We're specialised in this niche market and we're very good at what we do, but of course, we didn't have the communication strength of a multinational like Stellantis. They helped us to make people understand that it was possible in France to drive this product from 14-years-old, in Germany from 15-years-old. They gave a lot of visibility to our market," says Aixam sales and marketing director Tom Faget.
Aixam has invested €30m (£25m; $33m) in expanding its production capacity in France. And its sales are growing in other European countries, even as the French market slows.

Meanwhile, the competition is producing increasingly sophisticated minicars - some costing as much as a small conventional car. At Ligier, marketing director Romain Illegems says the biggest change is in who's buying them.

"We've gone from mobility that was imposed on people to mobility that people choose. Before, these vehicles were something you used because you absolutely needed to get around, because there was no public transport, or because you didn't have a licence.
"Today, teenagers are choosing them instead of scooters or mopeds, because they're safer and offer better protection from the weather. Young people now account for 40% of our customers."

There are limitations, of course. Just two seats, a maximum speed of 45km/h and no motorways. But for Selena, who rents her Ami for €60 a month, plus insurance, it's a small price to pay for independence.

items.title: Kilmar Ábrego García, man at center of Trump deportation battle, leaving US
paragraphs: Kilmar Ábrego García is leaving the United States of his own volition, his lawyers confirmed on Tuesday.
Ábrego is leaving the US for Spain on Tuesday evening.

The Salvadorian immigrant was at the center of a months-long legal battle since he was deported to El Salvador in March 2025 by the Trump administration, in defiance of a court’s protection. He was held in Cecot, a notorious anti-terrorism mega-prison.

He was ultimately returned to the US following a decision by the supreme court three months later. Since then, Ábrego has been fighting a second deportation to a series of African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officials.
The Washington Post reported earlier on Tuesday that he negotiated a deal with federal authorities to depart the US voluntarily in order to avoid being forcibly removed.

In a statement, the US senator Chris Van Hollen, who has advocated for Maryland resident Ábrego and who met with him in El Salvador last year, described him as a “free man” and referenced Ábrego’s agreement with the Trump administration.

“While the Trump Administration had been pursuing their vindictive prosecution against Kilmar and desperately trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation,” Van Hollen said. “I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution.”

The 31-year-old has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years, but he immigrated to the US illegally as a teenager. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the US under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was not given residency status.

He was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to a Salvadorian prison in what an official later called an “administrative error”. Facing public pressure and a court order, the Trump administration brought him back in June 2025, but only after securing an indictment charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee. A federal judge dismissed that case in May, finding that the justice department’s pursuit of criminal charges was designed to punish Ábrego García for challenging his deportation. The government is appealing.
The Trump administration vowed to deport him to a third country, threatening to send him to Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and, most recently, Liberia.

“We will always admire his remarkable courage in staring down and defeating a vindictive prosecution instigated by the highest reaches of the Justice Department,” one of Ábrego García’s attorneys, Sean Hecker, said in a statement provided to the Washington Post. “He, in turn, is grateful to those who stood by him.”

items.title: Canada says it ‘does not report to the US’ after Pentagon criticizes military spending
paragraphs: Canada is a “sovereign nation” that does not “report” to the United States, the country’s defense minister said after the Pentagon released a scathing memo that criticized the supposedly “atrophied” defence capabilities of its northern neighbour.

The document, released on Tuesday, said Canada had “yet to make the hard decisions and tradeoffs” necessary to meet previous defence spending pledges and become a “credible partner in the defense of our shared continent”.

The Pentagon memo said it took Canada nearly two decades to finally reach spending promises made in 2006 “despite Canada’s role as a major G7 economy as well as one of the largest and wealthiest members of the NATO alliance”.

Historically, Nato members have fallen short of meeting the security organization’s funding goals. When Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, only three Nato members – the US, the UK and Greece – were meeting the alliance’s guideline of spending 2% of GDP on defence. By 2025, all 31 members with armed forces, including Canada, had reached the goal.

The document also suggested Canada faces significant operational hurdles in its air, land and sea operations, blaming political leaders for pursuing “parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization”.

The Pentagon document said the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, was “laser focused” on modernizing Canada’s military, suggesting American taxpayers had been “footing the bill for its defense” for decades.
The defense minister, David McGuinty, told reporters he could not “divine” the thinking behind the Pentagon’s decision to criticise Canada’s defence spending now.

“The amount of cooperation we are pushing under Norad [North American Aerospace Defense Command] has not changed. What we’re doing together at Nato has not changed. Our military-to-military cooperation has not changed. Our work on integrated air missile defence has not changed,” he said.
McGuinty also bristled at the suggestion from a reporter that the memo implied Canada required approval from the US when it came to its spending plans.
“Canada is a sovereign nation. I’ll be very direct. We don’t report to the United States,” he said.
The memo came as a Canadian official travelled to Europe to pitch a new defence bank championed by the prime minister, Mark Carney.

Isabelle Hudon, Canada’s lead negotiator for establishing the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, is looking to cajole more countries into joining a global initiative that would lend to governments and contractors at low cost to support defense projects.

Ten countries have pledged their support but no others from the G7 have done so yet, with both the UK and Germany so far declining to join. Hudon says the €4bn in commitments secured so far is enough to start the bank up but she is aiming for up to €100bn.

Carney has made significantly increased spending commitments in defence. The country spent $63.4bn on national defence in 2025, meeting its Nato pledge to spend 2% of gross domestic product for the first time.
Last year, Nato members agreed to raise the goal to the equivalent of 5% of GDP by 2035.

Canada’s federal budget this month laid out a plan to spend about 4% of Canada’s GDP on defence and security annually by the end of the decade, and 5% by 2035, including the purchase of submarines and early warning aircraft.

Canada’s air power is a key point of friction with Washington. Carney’s government has yet to make a final decision on its order of F-35 fighter jets from the US firm Lockheed Martin and is weighing the possibility of purchasing Swedish-made Gripen aircraft instead. The multibillion-dollar purchase has been the subject of a political review for more than a year. The Pentagon memo warned that operating a “mixed fleet” of aircraft would “compound existing personnel shortfalls”.

items.title: Bake Off winner crowned after high-stakes final
paragraphs: Spoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Great British Bake Off final
Moyin Odeniran said he was "in shock" after being crowned the winner of the 17th series of The Great British Bake Off.
The 22-year-old from Loughton, Essex, described it as a "very busy time" as he juggled competing in the Channel 4 baking competition with completing his university studies.
Despite his dissertation being due a month after filming wrapped, Odeniran achieved a first in his political economy degree at King's College London.
He beat fellow finalists Tom Whittaker, from West Yorkshire, and Birmingham student Mo Mahir to the title in Tuesday night's episode.
"I don't know how that happened, I don't know how I got here. I can't believe it – I am in shock," the talented baker said.
"I have made friends for life and I have just loved every single second of it, and I don't think I could have asked for anything more."
Judge Paul Hollywood described Odeniran's efforts as "pure magic" after watching his jubilant celebrations with family and friends.
"He has done an amazing job because out of all the bakers he struggled at the beginning, and he actually got better and better," Hollywood said.
Fellow judge Nigella Lawson praised Odeniran as a "worthy winner", but also said the other finalists were "sensational".
The high-stakes final saw the three contestants tasked with making a citrus celebration cake, creme brulee donuts and a "spectacular tribute to iconic British landscapes".
Reflecting on his performance in the final, Odeniran said: "I didn't want to put too much pressure on myself, but I knew I had put my best foot forward.
"I couldn't have done anything better than I did and I had a great time doing it."
He said he got "quite exhausted" while filming the series and praised his mother, sister and close friends for their support.
"Earlier on, some of the challenges were quite difficult for me and I was shocked that I kept going through," Odeniran said.
"Before you get there you think you know how to bake, and by week two you question whether you know anything about baking."
He shared his gratitude at being able to learn from Lawson and Hollywood.
"I will never forget my time there and the friendships made which will always continue," the winner added.
Prior to the final, Odeniran told BBC Essex he planned to view it at a huge "watch party" at his local church.

items.title: China’s Huawei convicted of stealing US trade secrets
paragraphs: Chinese telecommunications equipment maker Huawei was convicted on Tuesday in a sprawling US criminal case on charges that it stole ⁠trade secrets from US companies and deceived banks about ⁠its business in Iran.

Huawei, the world’s leading telecom equipment manufacturer, was found guilty by a ​federal jury in Brooklyn of 10 of the 12 criminal counts it faced, including bank fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets and conspiracy to defraud the US. It was found not guilty of racketeering conspiracy, a charge alleging it had acted as a criminal enterprise.

US authorities had targeted Huawei for years, saying the company posed national security risks. It has previously urged countries not to use Huawei infrastructure for the rollout of new 5G mobile networks.

The US attorney general, Todd Blanche, said in a statement after the verdict: “No person or company is above the law”, adding: “For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft.”
The criminal case ⁠began in 2018, and the following year the US government placed Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology.

Experts have said the case ​has nonetheless not undermined Huawei’s business, as the company diversified and emerged as ‌a key player in China’s push for artificial ‌intelligence. The company has more than 200,000 employees and operates in approximately 170 countries.
The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defense calling 15.
In ⁠a statement, Huawei said the charges on which it was convicted lack legal merit and said it would “take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests”.

The case emerged in December 2018 when Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer and daughter of the company’s founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, prompting a diplomatic crisis involving the US, China and Canada.
Meng had been secretly indicted on charges of misleading an HSBC ‌banker about Huawei’s business in Iran, so the company could move dollars in and out of Iran in violation of US sanctions.
She fought extradition to the US for nearly three years, before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and flying home to China to a ​hero’s welcome. The charges against her were dropped.
The 2018 indictment alleged that Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its business dealings in Iran.
Prosecutors added new charges in 2020, including that Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from US technology companies over two decades.

During the trial, prosecutors tried to prove Huawei stole source code from Cisco Systems for its routers, stole wireless telecommunications company Quintel’s antenna technology, and hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by the semiconductor ⁠company CNEX.

Jurors watched a video that, according to prosecutors, showed a Huawei employee slipping a piece of a T-Mobile testing ​robot into his backpack, and heard about a Huawei engineer ​sneaking into a Fujitsu booth at a trade ​show to photograph a device.

Prosecutors gave jurors a statement attached to Meng’s deferred prosecution agreement, in which she acknowledged that the company illegally ​conducted business in Iran. She ‌did not testify at trial, though ​an HSBC banker she met with ​in 2013 did testify.

The defense argued that HSBC and the other banks knew about Huawei’s business in Iran and were competing for Huawei’s business. Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, accused prosecutors during his closing argument of having “cherrypicked” a handful of disparate incidents to support their claim of a 20-year conspiracy.
He said Huawei succeeded through “hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development”.

items.title: Armed men hold hostages at supermarket in top Colombian tourist destination
paragraphs: Armed and masked men have been holding people hostage in a supermarket since early Tuesday morning in Cartagena, one of Colombia’s most popular tourist cities.

The country’s president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said 30 people had initially been taken hostage, but five had been released, and hours later local media reported that another 10 had also been freed.
There have been no reports of injuries so far.

The far-right president added that, despite the context of growing violence perpetrated by criminal groups involved in the country’s decades-long armed conflict, the hostage-taking appeared to have stemmed from a botched robbery carried out by “common criminals”.
The past few days have been particularly challenging in the South American country, with a car bomb and a drone attack killing one person and leaving nearly 30 injured.

The supermarket where the hostages are being held is just six miles from the old city and its 500-year-old fortress walls overlooking the Caribbean. Hundreds of thousands of visitors are drawn to Cartagena every year.

The gunmen reportedly arrived at about 8.30am local time at an Éxito supermarket in La Castellana neighbourhood and, according to Colombia’s president, the group planned to rob an armoured cash-in-transit vehicle that was due to collect the previous day’s takings from the store.
After spotting the movement on security cameras, employees reportedly alerted the national police, who surrounded the supermarket.

“My son is there,” Jacob Perez, the father of one of the workers reportedly held hostage, told Agence France-Presse. “He didn’t leave work and he’s not answering his phone. I think they took it from him,” he said.

Customers were also believed to be among the hostages. The five people initially released were “older women”, according to De la Espriella. Caracol Radio later reported that another 10 had been freed.

Footage shared on social media showed dozens of people rushing out of the supermarket, while local media outlets showed snipers positioned on nearby buildings in what appeared to be a standoff between the armed men and police.

De la Espriella, known for his populist rhetoric and an “iron fist” approach to crime – he sometimes wears a gun on his waist and has posed beside the bodies of people killed by police – has been in office for just over three months, and said the hours-long standoff at the supermarket “will turn out well for the hostages, but I’m not so sure it will turn out quite so well for the hostage-takers”.

He addressed the case at a press conference in Villavicencio, about 684 miles inland, where he was dealing with the aftermath of an attack on Monday night in which a car bomb was detonated outside the headquarters of the Meta departmental government.
More than 20 people were injured and a security guard was killed, and the president attributed the attack to a dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).

“Narco-terrorism is desperate because we are confronting it decisively. It intends to intimidate us and force us to retreat in search of another false peace process,” the president said, referring to the landmark 2016 peace deal between the government and the Farc – whose signing marked its 10th anniversary on Tuesday.

Internationally recognised for substantially reducing violence, the deal alone could not bring the decades-long armed conflict to a definitive end. Subsequent administrations were slow to implement the agreement, which was rejected by Farc dissidents and other rebel factions.

In the early hours of Monday, in another part of the country, gunmen believed to belong to the ELN, an armed group that never signed a peace deal, used drones to drop bombs on the local police command in the city of Cúcuta. Instead they hit homes and injured three civilians, including an 18-month-old baby.
Although drone attacks by criminal groups have become increasingly common, it was the first time they had targeted a departmental capital.
