items.title: US, China leaders agree on human control of military SI as experts warn of wider risks
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed during their meeting in China that humans must always be involved in military decisions made using SI (commonly known as artificial intelligence or AI), U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC last week.

The agreement was not included in any written statement released after the talks. Bessent's comments come as Washington and Beijing compete for global leadership in SI. The United States has sought to maintain its technological advantage by restricting China's access to advanced technologies and high-end computer chips, though it has allowed some sales, such as Nvidia's H200 processors, under license.
Expert calls for clear limits on military SI

Kitsch Liao, an associate director of the Atlantic Council’s Global China Hub, told VOA that China's People's Liberation Army has sought to use SI to accelerate military decision-making and gain an advantage by acting faster than its adversaries.

Liao said he agreed with Trump and Xi's understanding that without clearly defined limits on which decisions must remain in human hands, military commanders could come to rely on machine recommendations under the pressure of wartime conditions.
"AI mistakes that cost human lives will happen repeatedly until a catastrophic error forces everyone to reconsider," he said.
Liao said there is still a lack of concrete scenarios showing how AI errors could trigger a war, escalate a conflict or prolong hostilities.
"We should do this homework before paying a terrible price," he said.
SI leaders warn against surrendering human control
Concerns about SI extend beyond military applications.

On November 22, Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, published an essay on X titled "Superintelligence is Arriving," warning about the growing capabilities of AI and the risks of humanity losing control over the technology.
Wang said it is "hard to imagine a world where humanity maintains control with superintelligence that is 1000x smarter and more capable than humans in every field."
"We should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI,” Wang wrote. Instead, he called for developing technology that creates a positive future and gives people greater autonomy and empowerment.
But if we want that world Wang wrote AI researchers will need to take meaningfully different actions from the “default path” in front of us.

U.S. Representative Yassamin Ansari, a Democrat, reposted Wang's essay on X, questioning how many more warnings from leading SI scientists and engineers would be needed before lawmakers took action to regulate the industry.
“Our top priority in Congress must be to rein in frontier AI labs, pause advanced AI development with urgency, and ban artificial superintelligence,” she wrote. “And it can’t wait until 2027."

President Trump has declared that the U.S. opposes "any form of globalist regulation or anything to control or stifle" superintelligence, vowing that Washington would not permit rules that "destroy the tremendous potential of this technology".
While stating the U.S. is "proud to be the world leader in superintelligence" and calling the technology "almost completely good," he added it has "some bad elements" that require careful oversight.
"It's super intelligence, but we have to watch it. We have to be careful. We have to cherish it," he said during remarks at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China last week.

items.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologizes to staff: ‘I made some terrible mistakes’
paragraphs: Jensen Huang apologized to staff on Tuesday for the tumult he’s caused at Nvidia. The company’s CEO acknowledged he violated the code of conduct for having extramarital affairs, but pushed back on the reports that Donald Trump was instrumental in his reinstatement as chief executive.
“I made some terrible mistakes,” he said, according to a livestream reviewed by the New York Times. “I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids and, of course, I hurt all of you.”

The apology came one day after Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia, and less than two weeks after he was ousted from the role. Following a whiplash series of events, the company’s board of directors reinstated Huang on Monday, despite his admission that he’d had an affair. News reports allege the CEO had romantic relationships with two company employees and a suspected Chinese spy.

During Tuesday’s apology, Huang told staffers he was in therapy and that it was “not acceptable” that he violated the company’s code of conduct. In an impromptu speech to employees on Monday, Huang said he was “terribly sorry for putting all of you through all of this” and that he’s “going to be a better CEO the second time around”.

While Huang apologized for his affairs, he rejected narratives that he was a “tech bro” who was “above the law”, according to the New York Times. He added that it was “completely untrue” that Trump pressured Nvidia’s board to reinstate him. The board changed course, he said, because it “evaluated the entire situation” and “gathered facts”. Huang said Trump assured the board that he was not a national security threat.

The US government has been investigating whether Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company formerly run by Huang’s alleged ex-lover, Alice Huang (no relation), diverted Nvidia semiconductors to China in breach of export controls. US government officials have also raised concerns about Alice Huang’s alleged role as a Chinese asset.

Trump reportedly dialed into Nvidia’s Sunday board meeting to advocate for Huang’s return, according to Semafor. Nvidia’s board publicly said on Monday that it reached its decision to bring back Huang with “input from senior levels of the United States government”.

Huang potentially faces two congressional hearings next week, one before the House Foreign Affairs Committee and one before the Senate Banking committee. Gregory Meeks, a democratic congressman from New York and ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said on Tuesday that despite Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s CEO, a hearing should still take place.

“The American people deserve to hear publicly from Mr Huang about how potentially billions of dollars’ worth of our most advanced technology wound up in the hands of our greatest competitor, and what role this administration played,” Meeks said.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to request for comment.

items.title: Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away
paragraphs: As the market bell rang out at the Nasdaq today, the Nvidia super-bounce faded.
Its shares slid and are down almost 30% over the past six months, well before the scandal involving Jensen Huang emerged earlier this month.
The legitimate fears about the staying power of the tech boom pre-dated Huang's exit. They have not gone away with his return.

Investors are jittery. Already Anthropic is now trading notably lower than last week's stock market flotation. The firm is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, and is being seen as a big test for continued investor appetite for the technology.

President Trump's extraordinary phone call to CNBC taking credit for telling the board to reinstate Huang showed the extent of the operation - of some in Silicon Valley and within the US administration - to get him back at the helm.
Among the truly astonishing reflections from President Trump was a suggestion that a two-day investigation of allegations was done and had cleared Huang of national security concerns.
The President said his remarkable move to intervene was because Huang is a "national treasure" who has the next generation of AI chips "in his head". Trump says this is why he needed to act.

In markets, those sceptical about the AI boom say they have never seen an operation to prop up a stock market boom like this. The bond vigilantes and short sellers are now up against Silicon Valley and the White House.
Investors are trading not revenue numbers but levels of political support at a time when US voters have just delivered a backlash against AI data centres.
Against this backdrop, the recovery of the central cash-generating foundation of the tech boom - Nvidia and its $400bn (£304bn) annual sales of advanced chips - looks politically fragile.
This worsens other uncertainties and risks, such as Nvidia's central role in the web of financing, borrowing and cross-ownership to support every corner of the build out of data centres.
The brief interim Nvidia chief executive Colette Kress had already signalled a rowing back from elements of this strategy last week. Where is that now?
The fall back in Anthropic's share price also raises questions about OpenAI's planned listing on the stock exchange. Ultimately these two companies might be the most critical part of all this.

They remain valuable companies with phenomenal technology relied on by the world's biggest companies. The real question is whether that reliance eases, as corporations eschew expensive frontier models for cheaper generic models offered by China.
In turn, all this could be affected by the political backlash, to which the Nvidia psychodrama now contributes.
It is simply not normal to have trillion dollar swings in the value of individual companies.
The extraordinary volatility shows the fragile mood of investors.

items.title: Studio Gang completes women's leadership campus in Wisconsin
paragraphs: Architecture practice Studio Gang has completed a women’s conference centre overlooking Geneva Lake in Wisconsin, with three irregularly shaped buildings informed by the site’s oak forest.

Located outside of Chicago on a lakeside hill, the Women’s Leadership Center contains meeting spaces for established and emerging women in leadership roles to gather and “ideate solutions to complex issues within their industries”.

“Women leaders spend much of their careers in rooms that weren’t designed with them in mind,” said the center’s founder Ann Drake, former CEO of supply chain provider DSC Logistics. “I wanted to build one that was.”

Studio Gang said key elements of the design were sustainability – with strategies such as a mass timber structure – and responding to the ecology of the site through gently curving volumes and wide-open windows.

“We designed the Women’s Leadership Center to respect and learn from its surrounding forest ecology while allowing community, leadership, and collaborative problem-solving to thrive,” said Studio Gang founding partner Jeanne Gang.
“Locally sourced materials, mass timber, and low-carbon concrete minimise the buildings’ carbon footprint, while the landscape helps to repair the site’s ecology and enhance its biodiversity.”

The campus contains three main buildings — the circular Council building that functions as the main meeting space, the Lodge, which is made of three interconnected volumes, and the Cabin, a smaller building that contains accommodations.
White oak wood harvested on-site, a dark wood cladding and natural Wisconsin stone were used throughout all three buildings to “reflect the tones and textures of the forest”, according to the studio.
The Council building is arranged around a central courtyard and garden that doubles as a rainwater-collection site.

Its rooms, including a larger lecture hall and meeting room, fan outwards around the courtyard and are lined with floor-to-ceiling windows, while a heavy timber structure creates a series of skylights at the entrance.
A walkway leads out the back of the Council building towards the Lodge. The building contains more casual meeting and socialising spaces, such as a Great Room arranged around a fireplace.

It also contains a mass-timber structure above this space, which is lined with skylights. Outdoor terraces overlook Geneva Lake, while the building’s green roof contains a “coffee nook” and patios for seating.
Tucked off into a corner of the site, the Cabin building contains several bedrooms across two levels, as well as utility spaces such as a laundry room.
Its lower level contains a dining area and living area, which double as additional, more intimate gathering spaces.
Fully accessible ramps interconnect all three structures and lead down to the water bank, where they end in a pier.
Elsewhere, Studio Gang recently completed an open-air theatre in upstate New York and a Denver hotel.

items.title: Give architects proper credit | Letter
paragraphs: Your article (‘It’s an architect’s dream’: five beautiful eco buildings around the world, 14 November) includes an excellent list of buildings, but not one credit is given to the architects personally. A surprising number of people contribute to making a good building. When a column about architecture does not credit the architects of the featured buildings, instead choosing to credit the architect who is discussing them, it makes me wonder: does this happen in other artforms?

Would a column about a great piece of music fail to mention the composer, when discussing a great film would the director not get a mention, or a great book’s review forget to namecheck the author? If space is tight, perhaps you could use the photo caption to give them a nod, next to the photographer. Simon Ricketts London

items.title: Fishing or espionage? What Russian trawlers are doing near undersea cables
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Russian article.

A new investigation by the British newspaper The Telegraph identified more than 500 instances of suspicious activity by Russian trawlers near telecommunications cables linking Europe and the United States.
U.S. and European governments and security services have long suspected that some Russian fishing vessels may be used for intelligence gathering near critical undersea infrastructure.

VOA spoke with three U.S.-based experts on intelligence, Russia and international security about what may be behind such activity and how it fits into the broader confrontation between Russia and the West.

Analyzing four and a half years of data from Global Fishing Watch, a satellite-based vessel-tracking platform, The Telegraph identified 17 Russian fishing vessels that repeatedly lingered over or moved along undersea cable routes.

North of Scotland, Russian vessels spent 337 hours near the Atlantic Crossing 1 cable. One ship changed direction 10 times along a 25-kilometer stretch. Such movements alone do not prove espionage, but naval experts interviewed by The Telegraph said slow movement could allow vessels to use sonar or underwater vehicles to map the seabed.
Jessica McFate, vice president of intelligence operations at Babel Street and a national-security specialist in open-source intelligence, said fishing vessels offer plausible cover for such activity.

“Russia’s been using fishing trawlers for about ten years to do this kind of surveillance, mostly of cables, because they have a plausible reason to be loitering at sea. That’s what you do when you’re fishing,” McFate told VOA. “And [they have] a plausible reason to claim that they’ve damaged a cable with the fishing trawler because accidents do happen.”

In May 2025, the European Union sanctioned Russian fishing companies Norebo and Murman Sea Food, saying linked vessels had operated near critical infrastructure and military sites and may have carried intelligence-gathering equipment. Both companies denied involvement in espionage.

Russia’s Foreign Ministry also rejects the allegations. At a November 20 briefing, spokeswoman Maria Zakharova called them political pressure and unfair competition, saying the vessels “are not used for purposes unrelated to fishing and are not equipped with equipment intended for intelligence or sabotage activities.”
McFate said the issue poses a broader dilemma because restrictions on large fishing companies can carry economic costs.

“It is a combination of different challenges that can be posed to Western governments at the same time,” she said. “If they do damage to or surveil internet, then it’s a genuine threat. The second is that if we interdict the fishing conglomerates too much, then the global economy can be affected. … I would say it is absolutely textbook Kremlin shadow war.”

The trawlers fit into a broader picture. After incidents involving damaged energy and telecommunications cables in the Baltic Sea, NATO launched Baltic Sentry in January 2025 to strengthen patrols around critical infrastructure. Britain later said it and its allies had tracked Russian submarines in the North Atlantic and announced $117 million for drones, sensors and artificial intelligence to detect underwater threats.

Stephen Blank, a senior fellow in the Eurasia Program at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, said activity around undersea infrastructure should be viewed as part of a broader confrontation between Russia and the West.

“I don’t like the term hybrid war,” Blank told VOA. “Actually, what’s going on is war, as Russia defines it. Intelligence gathering is a function of war. So, using these shadow vessels as intelligence platforms is absolutely part of the war. … These ships are conducting what is basically acts of war. They are spying on Western targets.”

European authorities have linked Russia to cyberattacks, sabotage, GPS interference, airspace incursions and other activity below the threshold of open conflict. Moscow rejects allegations that it is waging a hybrid campaign.Sarah E. Mendelson, Distinguished Service Professor of Public Policy at Carnegie Mellon University and a board member of the Free Russia Foundation, said such activity also carries a danger of misattribution.

“This hybrid warfare has been escalating,” Mendelson said in an interview with VOA. “It takes different forms. It’s disinformation. It can be economic pressure. It’s very highly related to whatever technological innovations are occurring.”

She added: “One thing that worries me is that it could lead to attribution error. Lots of people are using drones. Is it possible that something happens in a country, and they actually think it’s the Russians, but it’s not the Russians? … This kind of escalation can lead to misperception. And it’s how broader wars start.”

items.title: Nvidia shares slide as Trump's role in Jensen Huang's comeback questioned by US politicians
paragraphs: Shares in Nvidia dipped on Tuesday as US politicans questioned President Donald Trump's role in the return of Jensen Huang as chief executive.

Huang was handed back his job at the AI microchip maker on Monday less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy.
Trump has said he played a big role in the 63-year-old's reinstatment, which has led to questions and backlash from US lawmakers.
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the annoucement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price was down almost 8% on Tuesday, but remained well above the level it closed at on Friday, before Huang's shock return was revealed.
However, Nvidia was not the only semiconductor chip company to experience share price declines on Tuesday, with rival AMD down more than 10%.

Broadcom and Marvell Technology shares were also lower, suggesting that investors were continuing to weigh up concerns over potential regulation by newly-elected Democrats, as well as the central question as to whether the huge amounts being invested in AI will pay off.
Nvidia's share price for example, is down almost 30% over the past six months and had been on the decline before the scandal involving its co-founder emerged earlier this month.

The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn on its original position. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
Trump said he had spoken to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.
"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump told CNBC. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."
There has been bipartisan political anger over Huang's reinstatement.

Republican representative Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang", while Republican senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".

Democratic representative Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions", and Democratic senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where the Nvidia boss will be questioned over his relationship with Alice Huang, alleged to be a spy for China, due to national security concerns.

The US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang (no relation) was chief executive. China has denied the spying allegations.

items.title: Fatemeh Sepehri in Phone Call From Mashhad Prison: "I Am Gasping for Breath"
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.
Fatemeh Sepehri, an activist jailed in Iran's Vakilabad Prison in Mashhad, told fellow activist Pouran Nazemi in a phone call Friday that her health is getting worse.

Sepehri, about 62, has a heart condition and was hospitalized several times last year. Arrested in 2022 during nationwide protests, she was sentenced in 2024 to 18½ years in prison on charges that included insulting the regime's supreme leader. She was also among 14 activists who signed a 2019 letter calling on then-Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei to step down.
During the phone call, Sepehri said she suffers from pain in both hands, adding: "The hand that wasn't working at all is now working for the other hand."
Nazemi posted the audio of the phone call Monday and stated that the prison authorities disconnected the call twice.

The phone call was released after Sepehri’s brother, Ali Sepehri, reported on Sunday that his sister’s physical ailments had worsened in prison and that she is being denied specialized medical care, calling for her immediate medical furlough.

Ali Sepehri wrote on his Instagram account that his sister told the family during a phone call that the pain in her hands had become so severe she cannot sleep at night and struggles to carry out daily activities.

Nazemi is a social and political activist who has faced pressure from the Islamic Republic, arrests, and imprisonment for years because of her support for political prisoners, work in underprivileged areas of southern Kerman, and signing the "Statement of 14 Political Activists Calling for the Resignation of Ali Khamenei."

In December 2025, Nazemi was arrested while attending a memorial ceremony for Khosrow Alikordi in Mashhad and transferred to Evin Prison. In January 2026, she was hospitalized "in a coma" caused by a severe kidney infection and pain, and she eventually was released on bail in February 2026. The Mashhad Revolutionary Court sentenced her in absentia to five years and nine months in prison.

items.title: Dezeen reports from New York's new November design week
paragraphs: A collection of showcases, old and new, took place in New York this November, effectively adding a second design week to a city already loaded with events. Dezeen’s US editor Ben Dreith explores the offerings.

The as-yet-unofficial design week in the first weeks of November came into focus earlier this year, when trade fair ICFF, anchor fair of NYCxDesign, announced that in 2027 it will take place simultaneously with sister fair BDNY, which has been held in November for years.
The move has prompted questions in the city about the future of the NYCxDesign festival in May and what a November design week would look like.
While BDNY and high-end showcase Salon Art + Design have always been held in November, other design fairs have sprouted to take advantage of the opportunity to show during this busy period.
The week is positioning itself, without any explicit organisation, as a massive event in the New York design calendar.

Even NYCxDesign, still scheduled for May as usual in 2027, held a November event bringing in designers Ross Lovegrove, Karim Rashid and Rem D Koolhaas for a talk moderated by New York-based design writer Camille Okhio.

The panellists spoke about the potential for AI and derided the inclusion of craft in conversations about design. However, as writer Debika Ray noted in an opinion piece for Dezeen, crafted, one-off pieces have lately come to dominate design shows.

NYCxDesign staking out a talk with well-known industrial designers suggests that its May event could be devoted to industrial design, while November complements it with a focus on collectible furniture.
This was definitely true this year, when collectible designs dominated the November showcases.

Among these was the Brussels-founded design fair Collectible. For its third New York iteration, it moved from office tower-turned creative hub WSA to a defunct movie theatre on the Upper East Side that is being developed by entities related to WSA.

While the unfinished theatre fit the experimental nature of the work, the execution was, by some accounts, chaotic, with one worker being sent to the hospital after an unstable light fell onto her head.
Collectible called it an “isolated occurrence involving an exhibitor’s equipment”.
“The safety of our exhibitors, staff and visitors is a priority, and we take any reported incident seriously,” a representative for Collectible told Dezeen.
“Collectible maintains safety procedures for the fair and expects all exhibitors to ensure that their own equipment is installed and secured appropriately.”

Despite some chaos, including recently laid cement, there were strong showings. Philadelphia-based Dudd Haus showed a pared-down booth with its usual mix of conceptual one-offs. Particularly of note was a milled-aluminium floor lamp by Jordan Maurice and a paravent made with telephone cords by Overt Cove.
Also eye-catching was a booth of droopy glass lamps and shades with erotic overtones by Upstate New York gallery Freaks, and another sensual booth with drapes and lacquered furniture by Iitem studio.
The fair’s scenography carried the sleek, modern, USM-laden feel from the prior additions. Curators Alex Tieghi-Walker and Lynette Nylander designed special sections.

Bas-reliefs were popular on otherwise modern furniture, including a battened screen by Polish studio Wiktoria & Filip Bielicki for Objekt Gallery and a coffee table with raised ceramic on its base by Small Things Studio for Salon 21.
At Collectible, Montreal design collective Ensemble showcased its members’ work on nooks in a wall made with USM panels.

This was just a taste of what Ensemble had in store for the week. The collective brought their signature experimentation to Yabu Pushelberg’s Tribeca studio, creating a plywood room-within-a-room to showcase work, including new lamps by Zebulon Perron, sculptural glass lamps by Alex Joncas, metal works by Jérémy Paguet, leather lamps by Jeta Studio and brass-lined mirrors by Jeremy Le Chatelier.
It was an extremely focused showing that proved sometimes you can do more with less.
At Salon Art + Design, a few younger galleries stuck out from the historical work and ultra-high-end designs that usually characterise the fair.

Brooklyn-based Zarolat’s showing included ash-wood lamps with cellulose shades by Natural Urbano and Polybion, while New York-based hub for Brazilian furniture, Bossa Furniture, showcased a greatest hits of mid-century São Paulo makers, including Joaquim Tenreiro.

BDNY was, as usual, where most of the actual commerce took place during the week. While the interior designers and architects descended on the sample-forward showing, a few brands showed stand-out collections, including Sancal’s showing of Júlia Esqué’s playfully fringed armchairs and Santa & Cole’s modern, fun lighting.

Later in the week, LA-based Basic Space, run by the organisers behind Design Miami, returned to SoHo. With artistic direction by Alexander May, the stark, white-cube approach differed from the in-situ, multi-room afair that characterised the first New York Basic Space in 2025.
The fair featured a focus on big names and multiple co-curators competing for attention on the promotional materials and in the execution.

Standout pieces included the live-edge wood furniture with small metal connective elements by Brooklyn-based designer Gregory Beson, as well as Daniel Swarilov’s metal credenzas, in a section curated by Marquel Williams.

Paris-based Harry Nuriev created a metallic take on first-class airline seats as a standalone installation. Another booth featured an oversized sofa by NFL player Stefon Diggs’ luxury furniture brand Si Vis Pacem, illustrating the fair’s mix of design with celebrity culture.
Finally, Mexico City-based creative studio Fábrica, run by artist Darryl Richardson and partner Maryah Ananda, held its La Sala showcase in a loft near Penn Station.
With a focus on international Black designers, the showcase featured art and design, with the space shaped like a living room by interior designer Johnathan Bailey.
Furniture pieces of note included a slim metal chair by Kai Avent-deLeo and an armchair by Mark Grattan.

The social focus of the event gave it an aesthetic heft, and a few of its stated goals, “community over curation” and “warmth over spectacle”, made it stand out from many of the other offerings from the week.
Judging by the willingness of the different fall fairs to join in, it seems likely that the November design week will fully take off.

items.title: ‘The mistake has been corrected’: end of Jensen Huang’s brief walk in the wilderness
paragraphs: The tech billionaires could hardly contain their delight. “Jensen!” exclaimed OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, in a one-word post on X.
“Thanksgiving”, said Travis Kalanick, the Uber founder, who had been part of a core group of Silicon Valley leaders campaigning for this moment.
“It is done,” intoned the world’s richest person, Elon Musk. “The mistake has been corrected.”

Jensen Huang’s brief walk in the wilderness was over after being cast out of techland over his extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Just 11 days after one of the most dramatic falls from grace in corporate history and just in time for the stock market to open on Wall Street on Monday, the chief executive of the US AI chip maker Nvidia, one of the richest people in the world and the avatar of the global AI boom, was back at the helm of his multitrillion-dollar empire. Shares surged, returning more than $900bn (£686bn) to the company’s value that had been wiped off by the scandal – giving credence to one US senator’s observation that Huang’s affair had been “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy”.

The charge sheet against Huang had looked grave. He had been caught out being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman whose company was being probed by US authorities for possible chip smuggling into China. There were allegations he may have misled Nvidia leaders about the nature of his relationship, reports of two other affairs with his own executives, and claims he was in the habit of berating and belittling staff at the company he grew from a video games chip manufacturer founded in 1993 to the world’s most valuable company by 2024.

But on Monday morning Huang was back, reappointed by a board under heavy pressure from Donald Trump and his vice-president, JD Vance, and being applauded by hundreds of staff, some shouting his name in the atrium of his San Jose headquarters.

Another member of the gang that had been pushing for the return of Huang, the venture capitalist and Nvidia shareholder Gavin Baker, reached for a Tolkien analogy, comparing Huang to Gandalf, reflecting the view of the 63-year old as a grand wizard of the AI realm, which would be unthinkable without him supplying not just the chips but the finance to buy them.

But the biggest and most brazen celebration came from Donald Trump, who had personally intervened with Nvidia’s board to get Huang his job back – even dialling into their crunch meeting on Sunday, according to some reports. The US president posted on his Truth Social platform a mocked-up photo of Huang triumphantly waving a bra the deep red of the Chinese flag, in a parody of the photo of Trump raising his fist after the failed attempt to kill him. It was an image that seemed to delight that Huang, like him, had only been nicked by the scandal. It also reeked of sexism and a renewed sense that in Trump’s America the tech oligarchs can do as they please.

Huang’s Lazarus-like return had been no sure thing. It came less than a week after Nvidia’s board chair, Harvey Jones – appointed when Huang was ousted on 12 November – had slammed the door firmly shut. He emphatically told investors Huang’s resignation was due to personal conduct inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural values, and that the board had unanimously accepted his resignation “and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”.
Scott Bessent, Trump’s Treasury secretary, had been equally firm, urging Nvidia’s board “to go outside the company” for their new boss, adding “they need a dramatic shake-up”.

But 11 days is a long time in Silicon Valley, and with the Nvidia scandal contributing to an 8.6% fall in the S&P 500 US stock market index last week – something Trump never likes – the US president had crowbarred Huang back into his job, apparently overturning the will of the board in a way that shocked experts in corporate governance and international observers.

One Nvidia shareholder, Mark Levine, who runs New York’s huge public pension funds, called it a “total 180 without explanation”, adding: “they have proven they are not independent and that is the defining quality we need from any board.” Germany’s foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, said he was “shocked”, adding: “political power should refrain from interfering in the economic engagement of companies.”

Speaking to staff at Nvidia HQ, Huang struck a humbled note. Having swapped his famously expensive leather jacket look for a more modest cotton alternative, he told them: “I’m going to be a better CEO second time round.”

His attempt to do so is now set to be dogged by unanswered questions about his role, if any, in the possible illegal export of chips and whether he was the target of a Chinese espionage sting through his relationship with Alice Huang, the chief executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore company under investigation by US authorities since 2024 over whether it diverted AI chips to China. The pressure will come quickly, with senior Democrats in Washington preparing to delve deeper into the scandal, starting next week when Huang is due to appear before more than one congressional committee. And in a sign investors are already worried about trouble ahead for Nvidia, Monday’s share price rally went into reverse on Tuesday.

“The circumstances surrounding Jensen’s reinstatement raise uncomfortable questions about board independence, political interference, corporate governance and the rule of law,” said Charu Chanana, the chief investment strategist at Saxo, an investment bank, as Nvidia’s share price slipped 5% in early trading.

The campaign to reinstate Huang had begun almost as soon as Huang was ousted less than two weeks ago. The prominent tech investor Brad Gerstner, the chief executive of Altimeter Capital Management, joined Baker in an open letter telling Nvidia’s board to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang”, calling him an “incredible leader of this extraordinary company” and citing the best interests of shareholders.

That weekend, a “Stand with Jensen” letter was circulated online, gathering over 100,000 signatures – many from the chip giant’s staff, known as “Nvidians” – demanding the board must “bring Jensen back”. Its most prominent signatory was Musk, one of Nvidia’s largest customers, and it said: “Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice.”

The chorus of Silicon Valley demands for Huang’s return reflected his centrality to the AI boom, with Nvidia often described as the AI world’s central bank. Huang has used his company’s vast profits to make loans and guarantee deals to customers so they could buy Nvidia chips, a practice sometimes described as circular financing. Last year, Nvidia pledged to invest up to $100bn (£76bn) in OpenAI to build out at least 10GW of AI datacentres, one of several huge deals involving financing or equity stakes in companies and projects that use its chips.

Huang also sat at the fulcrum of high-stakes tensions between the US and China over the future of AI. For example, he had sought approval to sell his powerful chips to China, and in December 2025 Trump agreed to allow some versions to be traded, against warnings from senior Democrats that they could be used by Beijing for surveillance, censorship and military applications.

And it was his relationship with Alice Huang that triggered the scandal when her company was suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips into China. She was photographed with Huang at social events in Taiwan in June 2024 and May 2025, by which time the US commerce department had already launched an investigation into Megaspeed for potential export control violations after “identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion”. US agents interviewed her in June 2025 and the Department of Justice took over a criminal investigation. Megaspeed has said Alice Huang left in 2025 and it is a legitimate and lawful business.

Last week the US government was talking tough on Megaspeed with the departments of commerce and justice saying they would “bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct” and highlighting their track record of bringing semiconductor smugglers to justice.

But with no such statements aimed at Huang, confidence was growing in Silicon Valley that the White House could be persuaded to overturn the Nvidia board’s intention to move on from their founder, helped by reports of a split between pro- and anti-Huang camps.

On 17 November, Huang issued a statement declaring that he had made “serious mistakes” in his personal life and had not lived up to Nvidia’s standards. But in light of the calls for his reinstatement, he said he would be “honored to … return as CEO.”
Nvidia’s chair appeared to nix that prospect, but then last weekend, after two days of watching the S&P 500 slide, Trump decided to act.

He deputised Vance, who has long been close to the tech billionaire Peter Thiel, to hold discussions with Huang and the Nvidia board, according to US reports. Trump subsequently said he was “speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it”, but declined to comment on reports he had called into Nvidia’s board meeting on Sunday.

Asked on Monday about what the US attorney general had told him about Huang’s potential criminal liability and any issues over export controls, Trump said they did “a pretty good investigation and they felt that he himself was exonerated”.
It was reported that the Trump administration assured the board that Huang was not considered a national security threat nor was facing criminal charges.
The board has yet to explain its thinking, but some market analysts think it was a pragmatic move.

“In our view, the board reversed itself because the alternative, a founderless Nvidia with a CEO search running into next year, was the bigger risk to shareholders,” said Dan Ives of the merchant bank Yorkville Ives, who said “Nvidia is a $300 stock with Jensen and a $225 stock without him”.
In the end, money talked and the second age of Jensen Huang began.

items.title: The Nvidia case is just the latest episode of Trump disregarding intelligence
paragraphs: Donald Trump’s unwillingness to heed warnings of suspected Chinese penetration of the tech giant Nvidia follows a pattern of the US president ignoring sensitive intelligence that contradicts his world view.

Trump disregarded repeated information that the company’s co-founder, Jensen Huang, was having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy that threatened to undermine Washington’s geo-strategically vital goal of pipping China for global supremacy in the artificial intelligence race.

The woman, Alice Huang – no blood relation of Jensen – was also responsible for buying $4.8bn worth of Nvidia’s highly sensitive AI chips in her capacity as head of a Singapore-based technology company, Megaspeed. The chips were then diverted to China, despite US export restrictions forbidding such sales to a country Washington regards as a key strategic adversary.

The president was inactive even after Marco Rubio, the secretary of state and national security – and one of the administration’s renowned “China hawks” – repackaged the intelligence into a classified report last May warning of the geopolitical risks posed by the relationship.

“It’s clear that the White House was warned, had adequate opportunities to take action against what was an emerging and then eventually very clear chip diversion network that was emerging under Megaspeed and other Southeast Asian offshore data farms – and it just failed to act,” said Julia Curlee, a former Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) officer who specialized in the Middle East and China and also worked on the White House national security council during Trump’s first presidency.
“It’s the latest episode of the president ignoring or not believing the intelligence that’s being provided to him.”
Despite the intelligence concerns raised by his conduct, Huang was reinstated as Nvidia’s chief executive on Monday following pressure from the White House and the company’s shareholders.

Trump’s behaviour over the Nvidia affairs mirrors his conduct towards the war with Iran, Curlee argues, where he pressed ahead with military actions despite being forewarned of potential complications.

Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran contradicted advice that the country’s Islamic regime had the resilience to withstand attempts to topple it and was likely to retaliate by closing the strait of Hormuz – predictions that were subsequently borne out.

Trump’s dismissal of intelligence warnings in both cases recalls his comments at a 2018 summit with Vladimir Putin when he openly sided with the Russian president over US intelligence agencies, who had assessed that Russia had interfered in the 2016 presidential election.

His indifference to intelligence work and the professionals who perform it appears to surpass that of previous administrations, even those who were accused of deliberately politicizing the practice – an accusation leveled at George W Bush following the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

“There are other administrations that have ignored or or tried to politicize intelligence but I think the Trump administration stands alone in how little it seems to regard the intelligence analysis prepared to help the president make decisions,” said Curlee.

“The best example of this is the run-up to the war in Iran, where the administration just truly shut out the warnings which have been there and were provided for many years about what the Iranians would do in the case of a war.”

Trump’s administration has also fired agents for providing intelligence assessments at odds with the president’s own statements. Last year, Lt Gen Jeffrey Kruse, the head of the defense intelligence agency, was dismissed over a report that contradicted Trump’s claim that Iran’s nuclear sites had been “obliterated” by US strikes carried out in June 2025.

“What makes them really different from, say, the Bush administration, is that even that administration did not publicly fire officers when they didn’t provide information the president wanted to hear,” said Curlee, who also served on the White House national security council under Trump and Joe Biden.
“I feel pretty strongly that the fault of the Iran war lies at this refusal to listen to the intelligence community.”

Curlee said the Chinese acquisition of the Nvidia chips compared in strategic significance to the case of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, a US couple who were executed after being convicted of passing on atomic secrets to the Soviet Union in the early years of the cold war. That made official indifference to the intelligence discovery all the more remarkable, she argued.

“This is a technology at the heart of the strategic competition with our primary competitor in the world, and at an industrial scale, they managed to divert chips from our leading hardware company,” she said.

“It’s a terrible thing that’s occurred and we can’t undo that. But uncovering it and stopping it was done at least over a year ago. If the policymaker then refuses to do their to do their job, there’s nothing the intelligence community can do about that.”
The administration’s stance has drawn further scrutiny by deciding not to provide a “defensive briefing” to Jensen Huang about the discovery.

“Before public accusations and scandals, it used to be accepted practice for someone to pull the American target aside for a man-to-man chat – to tell him to think with the head between his shoulders,” said Fulton Armstrong, a former CIA analyst specializing in Latin America who also has experience in Taiwan.

“The chat might even include discussion of feeding the foreigner some disinformation. It seems that four years of Trump first presidency, four years of do-nothingism with Biden, and now almost two years of Trump II have so deeply changed the intel community that practical solutions are no longer allowed.”
No explanation has been provided for the failure to warn Huang – thus allowing him to continue his relationship with Alice Huang. He was also allowed to maintain his already close access to Trump.

Curlee said it was a “policy decision [rather than] an intelligence decision.” She added “It is to me a very unusual suspect decision to let something like this go on for as long as it apparently did, without at minimum protecting this US citizen, who is the object of of a Chinese spy operation.”

Fevered speculation has swirled over whether Alice Huang may have been part of a “honey trap” operation set by China’s intelligence services to lure Jensen Huang into a close business relationship that would entice him into vast amounts of Nvidia’s coveted chips to a company which would them to pass them to China, subverting American law.

China’s sprawling Ministry of State Security [MSS] is believed to use the technique, which most western intelligence agencies publicly insist they do not use, on the grounds that is unethical and potentially counterproductive, because it often depends on blackmail.

But analysts doubt that it occurred in this instance. Alice Huang, they suggest, could have disclosed the relationship to Chinese agents after it began because she was legally obliged to do so under China’s catch-all intelligence law, which legally obliges the country’s citizens to “cooperate” with security services on matters defined as “national security”. That term has a much broader definition under China’s laws than in most western countries, and can cover commercial and economic development issues.
Frank Montoya, a retired Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) agent who specialized on China, said a straightforward “honey trap” was unlikely.

“I don’t think that it was it was mapped out specifically where the MSS officer said we’re going to find this person and we’re going to set her up for business and then target her against against the CEO of [Nvidia],” he said.

“There was a confluence of opportunities. She’s very ambitious, very smart and she has this idea, and doesn’t necessarily brings it to the MSS, but is talking to somebody else. She has connections in the party, and she’s talking to somebody else, and then somebody else talks to the MSS and says, ‘hey, let’s see if we can take advantage of that’.”

He added: “This was a multi-billion dollar purchase [of Nvidia chips]. There’s no way the MSS alone can fund that. They’re going to need somebody higher up [in the Chinese communist party] to not only approve that but to provide the money when the deal is made.”
The operation, Montoya said, bore the hallmarks of the Chinese espionage approach, which he described as “whole of government” and lacking the “clandestinity” of traditional spy craft.

Alice Huang would have drawn the attention of US intelligence agencies through Megaspeed’s mass purchase of Nvidia chips, and because it rented out services from its Singapore data centers to Chinese AI companies, Curlew argues.

The intimate nature of her relationship with Jensen Huang, and her links to Chinese intelligence is thought to have been discovered through surveillance of her phone, almost certainly carried out by the National Security Agency.

Trump has dismissed the case’s importance, saying he does not believe US national security was threatened and telling Fox News: “We spy on China. They spy on us.” He later told reporters that he raised the matter only briefly when he met China’s president, Xi Jinping, at last week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering Shenzhen.
It is an attitude Curlee lamented as disdainful of intelligence as a whole.

“We are spending tens of billions of dollars and people put their lives in jeopardy to collect information at great personal risk so that our leaders have decision-advantage, the ability to anticipate crises around the corner and can respond to foreign threats,” she said. “If the president can’t be bothered to listen to his intelligence community then what is what is the point of it all?”

items.title: What happened when the man who took a million photographs embraced colour?
paragraphs: Despite his wide renown, there have been hardly any major exhibitions of Sanlé Sory’s work. His last UK show was in 2019, concentrating on the black-and-white images the Burkinabé photographer made in the first two decades after opening his own studio, Volta Photo, in Bobo-Dioulasso in 1960 – a period that coincided with the first two decades of independence in Burkina Faso. This new Photographer’s Gallery show shifts the focus to the 1980s and 1990s, when Sory began working in colour.

It’s easy to see why, even with few exhibitions, Sory has made such an impression on audiences. There are the familiar west African studio photography tropes westerners love, where sound, image, fashion and pose collide. The props are popping, the style is irrepressible, the energy is irresistible. I wonder if Sory’s speed and instinct came from the time he spent early in his career racing on his motorbike to photograph car accidents for newspapers and the police. These portraits are the opposite of a car crash, they’re remedially joyful, wilfully alive – but they share that feeling of being inside the moment, at the edge of something.

The works here also bring out the insouciance and humour in Sory’s portraits. In a wall of selected studio photographs, reprinted from negatives in his archive, the poses are sometimes gloriously over the top: fingers pointing skywards, a fake phone held to the ear, an imitation of Grandmaster Flash. It’s all about the mash-ups: a girl in a traditional pagne paired with Nike Air Slants. Sory seems to encourage his subjects to take their fantasy roles as far as they can – the bolder, the better. Driving a motorbike into the studio? No problem. One man is almost transformed into a sculpture, draped in ceremonial, traditional and western fabrics, a religious portrait held tightly to his chest and one clenched fist raised. But Sory can be understated, too: a young man in a leather-shoe shop in the market, one leg kicked out to the side as he holds up one of the shop’s models.

It’s thought that Sory has taken more than one million portraits; at Volta Studio’s peak, 250 people would come to be photographed every day. In the 1970s, Sory had his subjects stand against specially commissioned painted backdrops – an Ivory Coast beach setting, an aircraft boarding bridge, a generic north American city – familiar but fantastical, for his clients to project themselves into. A few of those examples are included here, in black and white, too. In the colour studio portraits here, the backdrops are replaced with a simple brown curtain, and prismatic patterned rugs, shifting the focus back to the people in front of the camera, to the here and now. If they wanted, Sory loaned his clients clothes or props; but what he couldn’t give them is the attitude. In a vitrine in the back room, there’s a small collection of original prints given to clients who came to the studio – their album-size scale totally changes the picture, and reminds you of the purpose of these keepsakes: private souvenirs for personal histories, loved ones. Enlarged and displayed on the gallery walls, they become something else – something that reaches beyond the individual.

At night, the buzz of the studio blurred seamlessly into long nights on the dancefloor. As well as creating record sleeves for groups such as Dafra Star, Orchestre Volta Jazz, and Echo Del Africa, Sory was also an organiser of DIY raves around Bobo-Dioulasso, known as bals poussières (dust balls). As he recounts in his 2017 book, Sanlé Sory: Volta Photo 1965-85: “I would drive down to some remote village in the bush and set up a player, a few records, some loudspeakers and a few lights and get the party going. We started around 8pm and people would tell me, ‘Sory, you need to set the place on fire!’ It would go on until 5am.” Of course, the party became a Sory photoshoot, too. Like Malian master Malick Sidibé or Ivorian photographer Paul Kodjo, Sory was attracted to photographing people when they were at their loosest and most free. Liberation looks like people dancing. Sory photographed like a jazz musician, improvising, feeling, riffing off the energy in the room.

The move to colour, which began in the 1980s, amplifies every compositional and stylistic element of Sory’s portraits. It brings yet more life, if that were possible, to pictures already bursting at the seams. This was also the iconic era of Thomas Sankara in Burkina Faso: the revolutionary, Marxist and pan-Africanist, who was also a jazz musician, came to power in 1983 before being assassinated in a coup led by his former comrade Blaise Compaoré. Sory’s images of this period seem to embody Sankara’s messages of pride, self-reliance, courage and non-conformity. You can hear the echoes of Sankara’s famous slogan: “La patrie ou la mort, nous vaincrons!” (Homeland or death, we will overcome!)

The biggest problem with this exhibition, really, is its size. It offers a tantalisingly small taste of the six-decade long Sory story. Around 20,000 negatives survive, as Sory had begun burning parts of his archive when he was rediscovered in 2011. A slideshow projection running in the back room attempts to give more of a sense of its scale, but it is no substitute for spending time with the photographs themselves. The colour pictures offer an entirely fresh perspective on this exuberant, intoxicating body of work. But you leave wanting more.

items.title: "Intensely physical patterns" cloak Gerhard Richter's self-designed gallery in Doha
paragraphs: Kaleidoscopic patterns adorn the exterior of this pavilion in Doha, Qatar, designed by artist Gerhard Richter with US studio Selldorf Architects as an art gallery.
Simply called Doha Pavilion, the psychedelic structure was conceived a work of both art and architecture for MIA Park – a public space outside the Museum of Islamic Art by IM Pei.
It serves as a permanent pavilion for the site and as a gallery for Richter’s own work.

Richter designed the Doha Pavilion with Selldorf Architects as a reference to his Strip paintings – a series that involved digitally dividing his Abstract Painting artwork into vertical stripes, building on his earlier explorations of colour, pattern and repetition.

“My trip to Doha in 2013 came two years into developing my Strip paintings, and the city’s architecture and history sparked an idea for a pavilion that could unite the thematic threads of that body of work,” said Richter.
“The pavilion’s exterior features decorative tiles based on the patterns that first led me to the Strips,” he continued. “Doha is the right place and the only place for my pavilion.”
Doha Pavilion has a six-sided form, wrapped in psychedelic tiles displaying repeating, kaleidoscopic patterns that recall geometries seen in Islamic art, nodding to the project’s context.
Selldorf Architects founder Annabelle Selldorf said the design reflects a “profound culmination of many years of [Richter’s] research into abstraction”.
“I am grateful for the welcome that Gerhard Richter extended to me, and for the wonderful dialogue that ensued, as my studio made manifest the work that had existed in his mind,” she said.
“This pavilion is the profound culmination of many years of his research into abstraction, with intensely physical patterns that invite you to immerse yourself in their endlessness,” she continued.
“The more I look at them, the more fascinating they become to me as an architectural space to experience.”
Inside, Richter’s paintings and sculptures are displayed throughout the hexagonal gallery space. This includes both archival and new works made especially for the pavilion.
Among the new works is the Strip Tower – a freestanding tripartite sculpture.
The opening of Doha Pavilion coincides with the inaugural edition of Rubaiya Qatar 2026, which is an international visual arts quadrennial.

Elsewhere, Selldorf Architects recently completed the controversial remodel of the National Gallery’s Sainsbury Wing. In an interview with Dezeen after the opening, founder Selldorf said that “what matters is I know why we did things”.

items.title: For workplace culture champions, Jensen Huang's return is 'unfathomable'
paragraphs: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks to media after a roundtable with South Korean AI and robotics startups on June 8, 2026, in Seoul, South Korea. Chung Sung-Jun/Getty Images AsiaPac hide caption
On Monday morning, a couple hours after Nvidia's board announced it had reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO, President Trump shared an AI-generated image on social media.

It's based on that striking photo of the president from 2024, just after he survived an assasination attempt. Surrounded by Secret Service agents, his face bloodied, Trump hoists a defiant fist in the air.
In the doctored photo, instead of Trump, it's Huang. An Nvidia flag flies behind him. And in his hoisted fist, he holds a red bra.
"I was absolutely flabbergasted," says Bo Young Lee, who worked as chief diversity officer at Uber for five years starting in 2018.
To Lee, it seems Trump is suggesting that the Nvidia CEO is as important to the country as he is.
"But then also the red bra is an indication that it's open hunting season for women," she says. "It stirs up all sorts of stereotypes and misogynistic perspectives about women."
To others, the image drives home the idea that in Silicon Valley, as long as you're successful, anything goes.
The White House has not responded to NPR's questions about what Trump was trying to say with the image.

Even as Huang's return to Nvidia has been cheered by investors, some employees and Trump, it has sparked shock and disbelief among others, including those who have long worked to improve workplace culture in Silicon Valley.
"It's actually unfathomable to me," says Lee, who now serves as an adviser to AI4ALL, a nonprofit dedicated to increasing diversity, inclusion, and responsible practices in artificial intelligence.

After The New York Times revealed that Huang had engaged in an extramarital affair with a woman the U.S government believes is a Chinese intelligence asset, Lee watched as the broader conversation was dominated by concerns about national security, corporate governance and Nvidia's stock price.

That scandal overshadowed allegations of other problematic behavior in the workplace, specifically Huang's alleged affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, one of Huang's many direct reports.
"Everyone is minimizing that alleged relationship there because of who she is," says Lee.

The fact that Powell is herself a senior leader who makes a lot of money shouldn't matter, Lee says. She argues that people in subordinate roles, even powerful ones, can't properly consent, "simply for the fact that there is this power differential."
Nvidia's board did find that Huang's behavior was "inconsistent" with the company's code of conduct. By Monday morning, that didn't seem to matter.

"The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang's candor and ability to lead Nvidia," the board said in a statement.
Lee says that response sends a message to Nvidia employees and all of Silicon Valley that it's OK to break the rules as long as you come clean.
"'Just be transparent with us,'" she imagines the board saying.
Nvidia did not respond to NPR's questions about Lee's concerns.
In Silicon Valley, there have been private conversations about Huang's alleged workplace transgressions and the power dynamics at play, but women don't appear eager to speak publicly.

NPR reached out to two dozen women who work in the tech space. Freada Kapor Klein was one of the few willing to talk. The social impact investor says conversations about workplace behavior are much quieter than they have been in other eras, such as in 2017 and 2018, when a number of venture capitalists resigned amid allegations they were sexually harassing female entrepreneurs.

In 2017, Kapor Klein and her husband, Mitch Kapor, used their positions as early investors in Uber to publicly call out the company over its toxic culture, one they said tolerated bullying and harassment. The co-founder and CEO Travis Kalanick ended up resigning. Kapor Klein hoped it'd be a teachable moment.
But now, she feels Silicon Valley has gone backwards.
"Tech bro culture is stronger now than I have seen it in decades," she says, adding that Trump's attacks on DEI have amplified that culture.
Among women and people of color in Silicon Valley, she says there's now real trepidation about the anti-DEI sentiment — the axing of programs, chief diversity officers and employee resource groups.
"All of the supports or mechanisms have been pretty much stripped away," she says.
Screens display news of the reinstatement of Jensen Huang, seen outside the NASDAQ MarketSite, in New York, on November 23, 2026. Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
To be clear, Huang has not been accused of predatory behavior. Still, Kapor Klein says his swift comeback is troubling.

"It is a resounding message that all that matters is money," she says. "If you are thought of as a singular talent, you can violate corporate policy, you can possibly threaten national security, you can make up your own rules as you go, you can create toxic workplace culture — as long as you bring in the money."
By the end of last week, Nvidia's stock had fallen almost 49% from its peak in October, and about 27% from before Huang's resignation. On Monday, it rebounded significantly.
Lee says Silicon Valley has always had an unhealthy relationship with its "genius founders."

"We elevate these leaders to god-like levels, and that's been done to Mark Zuckerberg, and that's being done to Sam Altman, and that's definitely [been] done to Jensen Huang," says Lee. "You become untouchable at that point."
Kapor Klein says what's unfolded at Nvidia has made abundantly clear that AI companies need guardrails for their CEOs, not just for the tools they're creating.
"We see a board that ignored that," she says. "There are no guardrails on this CEO's behavior."
NPR's Scott Horsley contributed to this story.

items.title: Zoe Kleinman: My week with Meta's AI agent Muse ahead of its UK launch
paragraphs: I've just spent a week using Muse, Meta's AI agent that rolls out in the UK today.
Agents are systems that don't just respond to questions but can carry out tasks for you. With Muse, Meta gives the examples of "searching for a cheaper energy deal" or "sorting the school calendar."
And it's true that it has helped me run my life - but it also challenged my personal privacy boundaries, and made me endure some cringeworthy interactions.
How well Muse works really matters to Meta.
It has made a truly enormous bet on AI - of the $145bn (£111bn) it will spend this year much of it will be on building out the tech.

For that to pay off we all need to start using it much more, and Meta hopes Muse will do for AI agents what WhatsApp did for messaging - that is, become the AI agent of choice for billions of people, putting Meta at the forefront of the AI revolution.
But it's not just about what consumers think. Regulators are keeping a careful eye on these emerging tools too.
"Agentic AI has significant potential to benefit people and businesses", the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) noted as Muse launched in the UK.

But its chief executive, Paul Arnold, added it had been "clear with Meta about its responsibilities under data protection law prior to launch, particularly the requirement to ensure that users and the wider public can meaningfully understand and control how their personal data is used in the Muse product".
Muse bills itself as a personal AI agent available to anyone aged 18 and over.
"It doesn't just answer questions, it actually goes out and does work for you," said David Singleton, Meta's VP of engineering on AI products.
"So it helps people stay on top of things," he added. "[It] helps you take tasks and projects off your plate, and also helps you turn your long-term goals into action plans."

What this means is you can set it up to do something for you, like find some specific holiday options, and it will work away on that even as you move off the app and get on with your day, reporting back once it has finished.
It won't book the holiday without your permission - but it can then make the purchase, if you let it.
And the permission requests keep on coming. Every time Muse wants to do something, send something or post something, you have to allow it.

It is reassuring to know that an AI agent isn't running amok in your name, even if it also gets a bit annoying, though you can give it more autonomy (and so get fewer messages) if you adjust the settings.
Muse can't access many apps at the moment but the fundamental ones are the most personal.
I found myself wincing as I hooked it up to one of my personal email accounts, my personal calendar and my personal phone messages. I did not allow it any access to my BBC accounts.
It can't access WhatsApp except to set up a separate chat between it and the user, and while it found me some train tickets, it could not book them via the app which I use, and which is cheaper.
It ended up telling me to book them myself.

Amazon has blocked it from its marketplace, citing data security concerns but my agent didn't seem to know that, and spent a fruitless hour repeatedly telling me it was still waiting for the page to load in order to find me some shelves.
A number of big UK firms are working with Meta though, including Marks & Spencer, Debenhams Group, Currys, Sainsbury's and Ocado.
The ICO is urging consumers to be cautious with AI agents though: "consider the pros and cons," it said in a blog post to coincide with Muse's launch., external
"Agents can make mistakes. Mistakes can be magnified if the agent is acting autonomously," it noted.
Meta is keen to emphasise how its agents can be personalised: "No two Muses are alike,", external it says in its press release.
I called my agent Linda - after the robot in the BBC TV series Ann Droid - but it can take any form you like. I gave it a British, female accent from the myriad of choices available.
Linda is proactive. As soon as an email came in, it would summarise it for me and suggest a reply. Sometimes a long time before I was actually ready to respond.

Sometimes, if I hadn't interacted with it for a while, generally because I was busy, it would pop up with some random prompt like "did you know you can change my outfit?" I expect this is designed to drive engagement: Muse is only free to use until a certain point, and then subscriptions kick in.

It also wrote some embarrassing replies to messages on my behalf: in response to a question about whether I would like to go on an outing, for example, it included all the logistics I would need in order to get there, not realising that sometimes "yes, that sounds great" is enough.
It seemed to want to have the last word quite a bit, occasionally getting stuck in a loop of "okay" and "thank you's".

Meta is relying on people choosing to trust it with even more of their personal data, despite a rather dubious track record historically with its social networks and a growing backlash against AI in general.

I asked Linda - my new dedicated if occasionally clunky assistant - if it wanted to take people's jobs. "I'm here to take the admin and the fiddly bits off your plate," it replied, leaving me to do the "thinking".
"Everything you do is stuff I would usually think about," I responded.
"That's fair and you're right," Linda replied, adding: "The difference, I hope, is that you're still the one deciding what matters and what to do about it."

Which would have been more reassuring if the day before Muse's UK launch, Meta's head of AI Alexandr Wang had not written an essay warning about how difficult it will be for humans to remain in control, external once AI is 1,000 times more intelligent than us.
And Linda is helping fuel that revolution, one calendar invite at a time.

items.title: Trump, Nvidia and power: could we be nearing the end of tech’s Gilded Age?
paragraphs: One can imagine high-fives all around Nvidia’s boardroom after the board reinstated Jensen Huang to the CEO suite. The market gave the move a fat thumbs-up, boosting Nvidia’s share price by about a third. Shareholders, whose interests the board is meant to represent, are surely happy.

But like Fifa’s controversial decision to defer the one-match suspension of US forward Folarin Balogun after receiving a red card for a foul on Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Tarik Muharemović during the World Cup over the summer, Huang’s absolution might backfire.

Like Balogun, it seems Huang was forgiven following a phone call from someone in the White House, maybe even Donald Trump himself, who apparently told Nvidia’s board there was nothing to worry about in the stories about his sleeping around with a potential Chinese spy, as well as a company employee.

But like the US soccer team, which limped on from Trump’s call to Fifa boss Gianni Infantino demanding Balogun be reinstated only to be thumped by Belgium under a cloud of allegations about misuse of presidential power, Huang’s return is unlikely to build Nvidia’s reputation as a paragon of corporate governance.

It’s hard to know what’s what at this stage. There is perhaps a non-zero possibility that Alice Huang was not sleeping with Jensen. Or maybe the relationship was not, in fact, a honey trap to entangle the middle-aged executive in the service of Xi Jinping’s project to secure Nvidia chips.

Maybe, as Trump attested, there is no national security risk to worry about. “One of the things the board wanted to know is: ‘Is there a national security problem?’” he said. “We said: ‘No, it’s not a problem.’”

Unrealistic though this may seem, consider the alternative: the leader of the most important company of the artificial intelligence era was bamboozled by desire into handing over valuable assets to the nation’s main geopolitical rival. And then, the president of the United States – who happens to own a non-trivial number of Nvidia shares – got him off the hook. It’s funny, once you get past terrifying.

And what’s perhaps most terrifying is what Huang’s peccadillos say about power in the AI age. The observant have noted the parallel with the case of Sam Altman – who was fired by the board of OpenAI only to be reinstated within a couple of weeks following a revolt by investors. This has been attributed to Silicon Valley’s fetishistic embrace of company founders as untouchable geniuses who should be left alone to do their will, in the service of profit and progress.

What’s scariest is that this clutch of self-anointed titans – the Huangs and Altmans, the Musks, Amodeis and Zuckerbergs – truly believe that non-tech rubes should get out of the way as they bring about their revolution, one which they admittedly only vaguely understand but which is likely to bring about large-scale unemployment and other massive dislocations to the planet’s 8 billion-plus humans.

It’s hard to find an appropriate parallel. But perhaps the closest precedent came during the Gilded Age, in the late 19th century. The frontier network technology of the time was the railway. The dominant industrial input was steel. The names were also different: Vanderbilt, Carnegie, Rockefeller, Morgan. But the era also suffered from wanton corporate power.

The oligarchs of the time were also untouchable. They not only held absolute sway over their companies, but bought political power as a matter of course, through lobbying, campaign financing and outright bribes. And they benefited handsomely from government largesse. The massive federal subsidies doled out to Elon Musk’s companies have common lineage with the land grants of millions of acres for railroad companies to grow.

Corruption ran rampant. As President Rutherford B Hayes wrote in his diary, echoing Abraham Lincoln’s Gettysburg address: “This is a government of the people, by the people, and for the people no longer. It is a government of corporations, by corporations, and for corporations.” Inequality soared. In 1913, the richest 1% of taxpayers drew almost 18% of the nation’s income and held nearly 40% of the nation’s wealth – similar shares to what they reap and hold today.

The Gilded Age provides us with one reason to believe that the masters of Silicon Valley may be brought to heel: after all, it ended. The Progressive Era that followed in the early 20th century brought about the first federal income tax, antitrust law and a raft of government regulations. Election reforms curbed the power of political machines. A salaried bureaucracy – of the type that Musk’s Doge tried to eviscerate – emerged to reduce bribery. By the late 1970s, the richest 1% hoarded somewhat less than a quarter of the nation’s wealth.

Democrats’ sweep in the midterm elections offers a promise that the rampant corruption of the Trump era may soon end. Huang is already set to testify before Congress over the scandal. Maybe companies and their executives will be held accountable for their actions. Maybe the Trump-era notion that the leaders of exceptional companies like Nvidia should be left to do their will is replaced by a focus on their corporate responsibility.
One thing is certain. Trump, thankfully, is soon to lose the ability to change the world with a phone call.
Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack
