items.title: Take me to the fatberg! The £437m new Museum of London is an astonishing sight
paragraphs: ‘All the grit and the glitters,” trumpets a big illuminated sign on the roof of the old Smithfield general market, beaming out as if advertising a raunchy burlesque show. It is the jazzy tagline of the new-look London Museum, which has gone from being marooned on a roundabout in an armpit of the City to taking over this prime Victorian market complex, following an arduous decade-long transformation.

The slogan is fitting for a museum that displays everything from priceless Tudor jewels to a lump of congealed fat and rags dredged from a Whitechapel sewer. Just as the colossal fatberg was scraped from the murky depths, so has the former market hall (and its extensive warren of basement vaults) been meticulously scoured and scrubbed up. London’s centre of butchery for 800 years, which Charles Dickens found “all asmear with filth and fat and blood and foam”, has been lavished with a £437m glow-up, reborn to tell the story of the capital in all its gritty, glittery glory. And the finished result is an astonishing sight.

It may be hard to remember now just how off-putting the museum’s previous home was. Since 1976, it had been imprisoned in a windowless brick bastion, throttled by traffic and accessed by a couple of elevated bridges, like a fortified keep. “We still got 700,000 visitors a year,” says Alec Shaw, director of transformation. “But they wouldn’t come back.” It was a dingy ordeal, somewhere you went because your school dragged you there, not for the active pleasure of spending time.

Now it is hoped people will drift in off the street, possibly without even knowing they’re entering a museum. “We’re essentially wrapped with 250 metres of high street,” says Asif Khan, one of the architects involved, alongside Stanton Williams and conservation specialists, Julian Harrap Architects. The 44 shop units that used to ring the market, where grocers and butchers hawked their wares to the street, have been converted into 12 outward-facing “houses” for the museum and its partner organisations, “making it more like a coral reef than a singular organism”, says Khan. Encrusted with these retail barnacles, which will range from cafes and pubs to galleries and shops, the museum hopes to lure in passersby who might never have thought of going.

Inside, they will find a place that is light years from the city museum stereotype of a dusty, fusty repository. Opened in 1883, the general market was the last of Smithfield’s three market halls designed by City architect Horace Jones, also the author of Tower Bridge. Jones concocted a dazzling cathedral of commerce: a majestic dome rises above the vast former market hall, where decorative iron “phoenix columns” support a lattice of trusses that hold up a roof of vaulted skylights.

Around the edges, dilapidated shops have been stripped away to reveal the building’s raw brick shell, with iron fireplaces left hanging surreally halfway up the walls. The former shop of James Burden Ltd, purveyors of premium meat, now houses a stepped theatre for educational programmes. Another unit has become the museum store, where the wares of London artisans will be on sale.

In every nook, historic architectural details have been lovingly preserved, making the building itself, and its accrued layers of history, a prime exhibit. Bucketloads of fragments in the museum’s collection – known as “bulk archaeology” – have even been cast into the polished concrete floor, forming a sort of archaeological terrazzo from bits of old pots, pipes and tiles. “It’s a gesture to our primordial reflex to dig, to find,” says Paul Williams, co-founder of Stanton Williams. Kids will love searching for curious fragments.

Thirteen displays are scattered around the perimeter of the main hall, loosely themed around “Our Time”. Topics range from greyhound racing – there’s a rotating “totalisator” contraption used to calculate betting odds at Harringay Stadium – to an altar of shop signs, where the likes of Morley’s fried chicken and Topshop glow like neon relics of the British high street. A stack of hefty speakers teeters in one corner, dedicated to carnival sound system culture. Shaw promises the space will come alive with DJs on Friday and Saturday nights, when the museum will open until midnight.

In tune with the neighbourhood’s 24-hour culture, it will open again at 7am with a ring of the last bell to be cast in the Whitechapel foundry , just as the meat market traders clock off next door, and revellers stagger out of Fabric night club, perhaps accidentally stumbling into the museum on their way home.

“We will be flowing out on to the streets and going right into the night,” says museum director Sharon Ament, who wants it to retain the energy and bustle of a market. With at least four entrances and no ticketing or bag checks, it is aiming to redefine how a museum meets the surrounding city, as a truly porous public place. “You might even slip on a piece of old chicken skin on the way,” she adds, “and we love that.”

The main former market hall feels quite sparse (left empty with corporate hire in mind) but its sheer scale means that pleasingly chunky objects can be displayed. Syd’s coffee stall, a century-old east London institution run by three generations, stands on one side, near an Italian knife-grinding van parked precipitously up on a mezzanine balcony. Syd’s, which will serve tea on Tuesday afternoons, was donated by the family on the proviso that it wouldn’t be used to serve “posh coffee”. It makes a refreshingly earthy foil to Clerk’s House, the museum’s restaurant, where you can dine on a Smithfield chop for £34.

The hall feels as if it will be a lively place to loiter, with the energy of a station concourse, but the main event is buried underground. A cut in the floor leads visitors down, past theatrical layers of pigmented concrete suggesting sedimentary earth, to the stygian realm of “Past Time”. Here, in the atmospheric former goods depot, the museum’s trove of 5,000 objects are displayed in five loosely chronological chapters, charting London’s 2,000 year history from Roman Londinium to the fatberg.

Designed by Atelier Brückner, it is a well-paced romp through neolithic axes, medieval glassware, royal robes and rock guitars, culminating in the museum’s most startling feature. At the far end of the vaults, a big picture window opens on to a tunnel where you can marvel at the Thameslink trains swooshing by. Few museums have ever managed to convey the thrill of infrastructure quite so viscerally. Delight in the startled shock of commuters as they see your ghostly face peering back at them from the shadows.

It goes on and on. (Shaw estimates it would take eight hours to see everything.) A series of side rooms, like chapels along a nave, contain displays dedicated to Roman mosaics, the Great Fire, women’s suffrage, and the Cheapside Hoard, a bounty of Elizabethan and Jacobean jewellery discovered in 1912.

Along the way, the museum made some momentous discoveries of its own. A set of vaulted chambers was uncovered, which will become an additional exhibition space set to open next year with items from the Bloomberg collection, which were found during construction of the megalithic media company’s HQ. Back upstairs, one of the shop units was revealed to contain a miraculously intact tiled interior of Lockhart’s Cocoa Rooms, a temperance movement cafe from 1875. It will operate as another living exhibit, serving hot chocolate late into the night – a touch of Victorian abstinence fitting for gen Z’s sober social habits.

These discoveries, along with Covid and inflation, are part of the reason the project budget rocketed from an initial £150m, as the scope grew ever larger. A second phase is now under way, due in 2028, which will see the neighbouring 1960s poultry market transformed with conservation labs, open collection storage and a large temporary exhibition space beneath Ove Arup’s soaring concrete dome. As Williams notes, wholesale markets make ideal venues for museums: “Where else in London could you find a world-class exhibition space,” he asks, “with a loading bay purpose-made for articulated lorries?”

The project is one of the most accomplished and complex transformations of an existing building the capital has seen, but it almost didn’t happen – twice. Behind all the grit and glitter is the fact that this magisterial complex almost became a soulless office development, as so tragically happened to the bulk of Spitalfields market in the early 2000s at the hands of Norman Foster. Save Britain’s Heritage (SBH) fought two public inquiries, with English Heritage in 2007 and the Victorian Society in 2014, against the City of London Corporation, which would have happily seen most of the market bulldozed for offices in the name of growth.

items.title: Iraq completes Kirkuk oil smuggling probe amid widening crackdown
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.
A committee formed by Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to investigate alleged oil smuggling from Kirkuk province has completed its fieldwork.

A member of parliament's Security and Defense Committee told VOA that its findings confirm information in a classified intelligence report alleging that oil from Kirkuk was smuggled through the Kurdistan Region into Iran and on to Afghanistan.
The committee's final report has not been released.
An Iraqi security source told VOA that five military officials are expected to face questioning within the next 10 days over suspected negligence in the case.

Mazin Gharib, a Kurdish politician serving as a member of Iraqi parliament's Security and Defense Committee, confirmed that the investigation was complete and said government measures are expected within two weeks.

"According to intelligence reports, Kirkuk has also been identified as part of this case, and reports have been submitted about it. The committees have completed their work, and I believe the government will take measures regarding oil smuggling within the next two weeks,” Gharib told VOA. “Beyond Kirkuk, several other locations are involved, beginning with areas around Mosul."
The identities of those suspected of involvement and the full extent of the alleged smuggling operations remain undisclosed.

The Kirkuk investigation comes amid a nationwide campaign against oil smuggling following Iraqi forces' entry into Jurf al-Sakhr, south of Baghdad, on Friday, ending 12 years of de facto control by Iran-backed armed groups, primarily Kata’ib Hezbollah.
Iraqi Army units, Federal Police and state-funded Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) deployed to the town under an arrangement for Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah to gradually withdraw its fighters.

The operation followed a leaked Iraqi Intelligence Service report alleging that the group had been involved in oil theft there since 2021. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi subsequently described Jurf al-Sakhr as the starting point for extending state authority and combating smuggling elsewhere.
On Sunday, Iraq's Supreme Judicial Council announced that an investigating judge had inspected a breached oil pipeline near the border between Dhi Qar and Basra provinces.

Preliminary investigations uncovered an organized crude oil smuggling operation involving tanker trucks, according to the council. One suspect and several Energy Police officers responsible for protecting the pipeline were detained.

Separately, an Iraqi court on Saturday ordered the arrest of a Najaf Provincial Council member who heads its energy committee and his brother. Eight Energy Police personnel also were detained over suspected smuggling through another breached pipeline in Najaf province.
Authorities have not established whether the separate cases are connected.
Meanwhile, Kirkuk faces a financial crisis that has halted public construction and infrastructure projects, prompting contractors to protest unpaid government obligations.
Nawzad Anwar, head of the Kirkuk branch of the Iraqi Contractors Union, said contractors had invested their own money in public projects without receiving payment.

Speaking at a news conference Sunday, Anwar said, "Contractors have fulfilled their responsibilities and spent their own money to implement these projects, many of which were carried out on trust. Today, contractors are demanding their financial entitlements, which are their legal rights. We call on all parties to support Kirkuk so that these projects can be completed. Unfortunately, projects across all sectors including health, education, roads and infrastructure have come to a standstill, and none have been put into service."
No direct connection has been established between the alleged oil smuggling and Kirkuk's inability to finance public projects.
VOA contacted the chairman and members of the Kirkuk Provincial Council about the investigation.
The chairman declined to comment, saying he did not want to interfere with the investigative committee's work. Other members said they were unaware of its activities.
The government's anticipated measures could clarify the responsibilities of security officials and whether further individuals or locations will face investigation.

items.title: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
paragraphs: The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.

The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.

When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.
Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.
On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.
On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".
The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years.
The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China.
China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.
Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China.
Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers.
Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist.
Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry.

Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools.
That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House.
Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%.
Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too.
Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take.
The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal.
In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations.
Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

items.title: World Children’s Day highlights growing challenges facing Afghan children
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.

As Afghanistan continues to face one of the world’s largest humanitarian crises, child rights advocates and U.N. agencies say millions of Afghan children remain vulnerable to hunger, malnutrition, displacement and barriers to education, underscoring the urgency of protecting children's rights and investing in their future.

These concerns were highlighted this week as the world marked World Children’s Day, observed annually on November 20 to promote children's rights and well-being. This year, the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) marked the day under the theme “My Day, My Rights, My Future,” emphasizing that children should be included in decisions affecting their lives and futures.
World Children’s Day commemorates the adoption of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, the landmark international treaty ratified by Afghanistan in 1994.

“It’s a fun day with a serious agenda,” former UNICEF Afghanistan Representative Adele Khodr said during a World Children’s Day event in Afghanistan. “We need to give children the chance to speak up. Today is a day for children to ‘take over,’ express their hopes, highlight their challenges and hold us as adults accountable for the promises and commitment we have made to them.”
Khodr said Afghan girls and boys are often “largely invisible as citizens” and urged adults to listen to children and act on their concerns.

According to UNICEF, an estimated 3.7 million children in Afghanistan are suffering from wasting, including about 1 million children with life-threatening severe acute malnutrition. Dr. Tajudeen Oyewale, UNICEF's representative in Afghanistan, has warned that growing needs and funding shortages are placing increasing pressure on health and nutrition services.

Hospitals and treatment centers in several provinces are struggling to cope with rising admissions of malnourished children, while some nutrition facilities have reduced services because of funding constraints, according to UNICEF.
The World Food Program (WFP) also has sounded the alarm about worsening food insecurity.

“A visit to a health center in Afghanistan is a highly distressing experience, where we are practically witnessing the next generation waste away,” said John Aylieff, WFP country director in Afghanistan. “This is not simply heartbreaking, it is unacceptable.”
WFP estimates that approximately 3.7 million Afghan children could experience acute malnutrition this year, alongside 1.2 million pregnant and breastfeeding women.
Humanitarian organizations say poverty and displacement are amplifying the risks faced by Afghan children.

A recent report by Save the Children, based on interviews with more than 800 children and caregivers in seven provinces, found that more than half of displaced children reported eating less after leaving their homes. Forty-one percent said their health had worsened, while caregivers reported a 33% decrease in access to education.
Nine out of 10 children surveyed said they needed food assistance.
According to Vanessa Frazier, the U.N. special representative for children and armed conflict, economic hardship can also leave children vulnerable to recruitment by armed groups.

“If there is poverty and families are finding it difficult to feed everybody in their families, they might even encourage a boy child to join the army because there would be some form of security, food and a salary because it's a job,” Frazier told VOA.
She said recruitment is not always forced and is often linked to worsening economic conditions that leave families with few options.

Frazier said the United Nations continues to engage Taliban authorities regarding the recruitment and use of children, emphasizing that international law defines a child as anyone under the age of 18.
“The problem that we have is that the distinguishing element used in the edicts is signs of puberty and not the age of 18, which comes out of the Convention on the Rights of the Child,” she said.
“It is important for us in our conversations with the de facto authorities that they understand that signs of puberty are not a legal milestone. The legal age under the Convention is 18.”
Frazier noted that Afghanistan remains a party to the Convention on the Rights of the Child and therefore remains bound by its provisions.

She also said U.N. monitoring has documented instances in which boys have been used in a range of military-related roles. “We see boys being used in many roles, including carrying weapons, fighting, serving as border guards and other functions.”
According to Frazier, the Taliban remain listed in the annex of the annual report of the U.N. Secretary-General on Children and Armed Conflict because of continuing violations against children.
Along with concerns about nutrition and child protection, access to education remains a critical issue.

A joint assessment by UNESCO and UNICEF found that 53% of primary school-age children in Afghanistan remain outside formal education, while more than 2.6 million girls have been deprived of secondary education since 2021.
“Nothing can replace in-person schooling and substitute for their fundamental human right to formal education,” the report said.
After returning to power in August 2021, the Taliban banned girls’ secondary and tertiary education in Afghanistan, with primary education the only level of formal schooling accessible to girls.
Frazier described the restrictions affecting Afghan girls as a form of “gender persecution” and called for girls to be allowed to participate fully and equally in society.

As Afghanistan marks another World Children’s Day, U.N. agencies and humanitarian organizations say ensuring that Afghan children have access to education, healthcare, nutrition and protection will require sustained commitment from both Afghan authorities and the international community.

items.title: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO as US probes alleged chip exports to China
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original Mandarin article.

Nvidia has reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as president and chief executive officer, less than two weeks after resignation earlier this month. The reinstatement comes amid alleged violations of U.S. export controls and Huang's reported relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of having ties to Beijing’s intelligence agency.

The company's board voted unanimously Monday to restore Huang to the top position, saying it was satisfied with his explanations and leadership. Nvidia said the board had also received input from senior U.S. government officials and concluded that his return posed no national security risk. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who had taken over after Huang's departure, will return to her previous role.

President Donald Trump applauded the decision in a Truth Social post, calling it “the correct and proper decision” and emphasizing that Huang’s leadership is essential to the success of the company and the prosperity of the American economy.

The development comes as the Trump administration continues investigating whether Nvidia improperly supplied advanced super intelligence (commonly known as artificial intelligence or AI) chips to Chinese entities in violation of U.S. export restrictions.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that the administration had yet to receive the explanations it requested from Nvidia about the company's compliance practices.

In an interview with CBS's Face the Nation, Bessent said administration officials had been in contact with Nvidia's interim management, to determine whether potential violations reflected isolated misconduct or a broader failure of the company's compliance culture.

“We will see which level of the business knew about this. Was it at the lower levels? Was it the middle levels? Did it go all the way to the top? And I have confidence that the Nvidia committees are moving very quickly on this and will come up with some very fulsome and robust answers,” he said in the interview.

Bessent had previously raised concerns that Nvidia might have pursued questionable sales to increase revenue. He emphasized Sunday, however, that a possible culture of noncompliance remained a matter to be investigated, not an established conclusion.

Asked about reports that some Nvidia business deals were sealed through informal handshakes rather than written contracts, Bessent said investigators should still be able to trace large transactions through financial records and other evidence.

Bessent also distinguished the company's potential compliance failures from Huang's reported relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le. He said he assumed Jensen Huang did not know she was suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence.
Bessent said the administration was investigating Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company formerly led by Alice Huang.
“We will see if Megaspeed was indeed a pass-through company, a front company based in Singapore, to get the high-end chips to Chinese entities,” he emphasized.

He said the Treasury Department and other agencies had supported placing Megaspeed on the U.S. government's restricted-entity list. Nvidia had removed the company from its customer or sales list in August 2025.

Separately, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton confirmed Sunday that investigations involving Alice Huang and Megaspeed were continuing. He said Nvidia's board was also expected to examine the matter and that the American public would eventually receive answers about the potential national security risks.

The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security announced new rules November 16 to tighten controls on remote access to advanced SI chips and computing services through overseas data centers. The measures are intended to prevent companies and entities in restricted countries from circumventing U.S. export controls by accessing American technology through third countries.
The rules, which took effect November 19, also introduced additional licensing requirements for advanced semiconductor exports to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

The investigation has intensified scrutiny of Washington's efforts to prevent advanced American technology from reaching China's military and artificial intelligence sectors, while maintaining the global competitiveness of U.S. technology companies.

items.title: Nvidia shares up nearly 33% and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns
paragraphs: Nvidia shares skyrocketed after the tech firm reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive with immediate effect.

His shock reinstatement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy, a period in which shares in the chipmaker have also fallen significantly.
Nvidia shares had risen by nearly 33% by midday ET (17:00 GMT), boosting its market value by about $1 trillion and also lifted stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq up by nearly 7%.
Tech stocks more broadly have also rallied following large falls on Friday, with much of the rally starting in pre-market trading before Huang's return was announced.
Live updates: Jensen Huang returns as CEO following affair with alleged spy
Amazon shares were up by nearly 4% and Microsoft shares were up nearly 3%, while other major tech firms including Apple saw more modest gains, up less than 2%.
Other chipmakers also experienced large increases. Micron Technology jumped 19%, and Intel shares climbed nearly 13%.
While the surge in Nvidia shares was large, the firm's share price remains about 21% down from a month ago.
A sharp drop occurred on 4 November, after the Democrat's midterm election victory sparked fears of tougher AI regulation to come led to a broad tech stock sell-off.

On Friday alone, Nvidia shares fell by 13.7% as tech stocks more broadly fell, and as Reuters reported - unconfirmed by the BBC - that the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) over its accounting practices.
Nvidia is a key firm at the core of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with the chips it makes central to the industry.

Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate the firm's co-founder following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him, the company said - but US President Donald Trump has claimed he "convinced" the board to reinstate Huang.
Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage firm XTB, said Huang's return showed Huang was the "godfather" of AI, and "has a talismanic influence over the sector".
"Barely two weeks ago this man was ousted from the company that he founded due to serious misconduct and potential national security issues," she said.
"Even though Huang did not hold special voting shares on the board, Nvidia's directors cannot see a future for the company without him."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said Huang's reinstatement was an astonishing about-turn for Nvidia, particularly given reports of an as-yet unconfirmed SEC investigation.

"This is the biggest corporate U-turn in living memory. To go from being embroiled in a spy scandal to being reinstated as the head of one of the world's most valuable companies in less than a fortnight is nothing short of remarkable," he said.
"Today's stock market rebound represents a massive sigh of relief by investors. However, one cannot rule out a more conservative approach by Huang going forward.
"His every move will be scrutinised by the market, and he may wish to tread more carefully to protect his integrity and ensure that Nvidia is being run responsibly."
Politicians are also demanding greater scrutiny.

Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said Huang's reinstatement "reportedly at the encouragement of Trump Administration officials and without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation."
She added: "What is abundantly clear is that the AI industry requires guardrails and oversight."

items.title: Nvidia’s humiliated board should resign out of embarrassment | Nils Pratley
paragraphs: What was it that Nvidia’s board was saying about there being no chance of Jensen Huang coming back?

The position – a mere six days ago – was supposed to be definitive. The exit of the co-founder came after “disclosure of personal behaviour inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms”, said Harvey Jones, who had been rapidly installed as chair of the chipmaker. The board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” after he “voluntarily resigned”, added Jones.

The contribution of the US treasury secretary was equally forceful. Scott Bessent was already focused on the need for a new-broom external hire to replace Huang amid the scrutiny over Nvidia’s compliance with US export controls. “They need to go outside the company,” he said, calling for “a dramatic shake-up”.
Those statements are now inoperative, in the famous phrase of Ron Ziegler. The board says it has “every confidence in Jensen” and his “candor and ability to lead Nvidia”.

What prompted this humiliating U-turn? At least Jones and his fellow directors didn’t bother to disguise the fact they’d been lent on. There was “input from senior levels of the United States government”, which can only mean somebody above Bessent. Sure enough, Donald Trump said he convinced the board to reinstate Huang, calling him “a great patriot and national treasure” and adding that the US government had no reason to think his return posed a threat to national security.

The most jaw-dropping detail is that Nvidia’s board hasn’t even completed its investigation into reports that Huang was “the target of a foreign intelligence effort”, the only formal reference to his alleged affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former boss of a Singapore-based company suspected by US officials of smuggling Nvidia chips into China.

Why even bother continuing the inquiry when we can safely guess that it will conclude that the boss did nothing seriously wrong? As for Huang’s two alleged affairs with Nvidia subordinates – relationships that would usually be a sackable offence at a US company – the board will probably never reference them again.

Huang, with his big tech petition-signing crew shouting their support, has proved too big to fire. At Open AI in 2023 Sam Altman was fired and reinstated four days later. The process has taken only slightly longer at Nvidia.

The clinching factor, one can speculate, was the fall in AI share prices after Huang’s resignation. From Trump’s standpoint, a bursting of the AI valuation bubble represented a danger to the last two years of his presidency, so best to give investors (or most of them) what they wanted and get the “godfather of AI” back at the wheel of the circular financing carousel. After the hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off Nvidia’s valuation in recent days, $1tn was instantly wiped back on.

The gamble won’t necessarily work for ever, of course. Bessent, before starting his own U-turn on Huang’s position in recent days, was asking the right questions. Congressional scrutiny of Nvidia’s export controls won’t stop just because the company has belatedly formed a committee to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. One trusts Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, will still be pressed for details of the famous intelligence memo he reportedly circulated in the spring identifying Alice Huang as a Chinese spy. Huang himself can no longer be taken seriously on the subject of export controls.

But it is Nvidia’s board that emerges looking idiotic. The directors have reversed the biggest decision they had to make. They have done so under political pressure, forfeiting any claim to independence. And, even as Huang returned, there was no real signal that his powers will be checked to create a semblance of conventional governance. The patsy directors should resign out of pure embarrassment.

items.title: What collapse of COP31 talks reveals about an increasingly divided world
paragraphs: Some have hailed the lack of consensus as a sign of a positive shift, despite the Turkey summit failure
Some may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.
Yet that is what happened in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday.
The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.

Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines".

Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase".
And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all.
Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then?

The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai.
Co-leader of the negotiations Chris Bowen blamed the failure to reach an agreement on "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory"

Normally, it is difficult to establish exactly who has said what at these conferences. Much of the bargaining takes place behind closed doors, and governments are often reluctant to admit which proposals they have opposed.
This time, some of the opposition was public - mostly from oil-producing nations.

Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking on behalf of the 22 Arab League countries, argued that Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical greenhouse gas emissions. It was wealthy industrialised nations, he said, that bore the overwhelming responsibility for the problem.
He defended the Arab countries' right to choose how to tackle climate change according to their national circumstances.
Russia's delegate Sergei Kononuchenko went further. Cutting oil and gas supplies before demand fell, he warned, would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty.
"For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he said.
The wider political backdrop was still more revealing.

The US, which in previous rounds of talks had helped broker compromises - sometimes working alongside China - had no official delegation in Antalya. President Donald Trump has rejected the entire international climate process.

And while delegates argued over fossil fuels in Turkey, Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products.
The priorities of some of the world's most powerful governments appeared very different from those being discussed in the negotiating rooms.
The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, said a deal that did not mention fossil fuels was "unconscionable"

Yet, perhaps, the picture is more optimistic than it first appears. About 130 governments backed a demand for explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels - roughly two-thirds of the countries represented in Antalya.

Christiana Figueres, who led the UN negotiations that delivered the Paris Agreement, argued that countries were right to walk away rather than endorse a weaker political commitment that might undermine the progress already made.

Looked at this way, the collapse is not evidence that the world has lost its appetite for climate action. Quite the opposite - a substantial majority of governments were demanding more ambitious action.
So why not simply find a way for them to move ahead without waiting for the countries determined to block them?
The difficulty becomes clearer when you look beyond the dispute over fossil fuels.

Kononuchenko had another target in his sights: climate finance. Much of the money wealthy countries provide to poorer nations, he complained, comes as loans rather than grants. He said that developing countries ended up repaying more than they received.
"This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner," he declared.

Then, in a striking moment, he leaned towards the microphone and switched from Russian into English to address his criticism directly to the Europeans: "First of all distinguished representatives of the EU."

Russia has its own reasons for attacking Europe, but the complaint about finance is one that many developing countries share. They argue that they are being asked to pay for damage they did little to cause while receiving too little help to adapt to climate change or build cleaner economies.

The EU had ruled out significant new funding before the negotiations began. Mohamed Adow, the Kenyan campaigner who heads Power Shift Africa, accused Europe of rejecting a flawed deal while refusing to acknowledge its own responsibility for the failure on finance.
The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the COP process
So is it possible for a majority of countries to outvote those blocking progress?

The UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, has acknowledged the need to "improve, modernise and reform" the process. Some governments have proposed introducing voting when consensus proves impossible. Others want countries prepared to move faster to make their own agreements outside the formal talks.
But there is a reason the UN climate process depends on consensus. International climate co-operation is largely voluntary.

Voting might produce more ambitious agreements on paper, but would it persuade the governments that had been outvoted to act? Consensus also offers some protection to smaller and poorer nations that might otherwise find themselves overruled by the most powerful countries.

Meanwhile, the failure to agree a summit declaration does not mean climate action stops. Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles are becoming increasingly competitive, while the upheaval in global oil and gas supplies is giving countries another reason to generate their own electricity rather than depend on imported fossil fuels.
The energy transition is moving forward, whatever happens in the UN negotiating rooms. The problem is that it is not moving nearly fast enough for the climate.
What’s next after no deal at COP31 climate talks?
Perhaps the most poignant aspect of the failed Antalya Pact is what the countries had apparently been prepared to accept.

The final draft expressed "deep concern" that global warming was expected to exceed 1.5°C in the next few years. It warned that further warming would cause increasingly serious damage, some of it irreversible, and called for urgent action to limit how far temperatures rose above that threshold.

This remarkably strong language had survived into the final version, apparently without provoking the opposition that sank the agreement. Even countries bitterly divided over fossil fuels and finance seemed prepared to acknowledge the scale of the danger.
Yet they couldn't agree on how to respond.

And that, perhaps, is what Antalya tells us about the state of international climate co-operation. The problem isn't simply finding the right words or changing the voting rules. It is persuading countries with very different interests to take action that no international authority can compel them to take.
That was always going to be difficult. In today's divided world, it looks harder than ever.

items.title: How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
paragraphs: Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.
That central position prompted questions, in the aftermath of Huang's departure over revelations of extramarital affairs, over how important he was to the wider AI industry and US economy.
The fact he has been handed his job back after just 11 days in a U-turn by Nvidia's board implies the top brass believe Huang is irreplaceable.
Shares in the company have surged on the news of Huang's shock return, following a period of sharp declines.
While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.
The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.
Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.
It is now one the most valuable firms in the world and its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.
Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on it, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.
Some suggested his departure, which was sparked by the emergence that Huang had an affair with a woman alleged to have been a spy for China, posed a risk to the wider AI industry.

That was because it was unclear whether Nvidia would change strategy and potential rein in spending - a move could have had wider implications for the US economy, but which looks unlikely now Huang has returned.

The fears were sparked due to Nvidia being a key source of finance for many firms, as well being a microchip supplier. On its journey to the top of the AI industry, it has, through Huang, created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".

Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.

The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?
That risk was perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, had called for Huang's reinstatement.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, and backed a campaign, along with shareholders and supporters, to "Bring Jensen Back".
Following the announcement of Huang's return, Musk posted: "The mistake has been corrected."
Kathleen Brooks, research director at investment platform XTB, said Huang's return suggested he was "the godfather" of AI and has the status to shift "the dial for corporate finance".

"Is Jensen Huang the most valuable man on the planet? His return suggests more of the same when it comes to circular financing and the rapid AI infrastructure build out, and the market loves it," she added.
However, Huang's return to Nvidia does not solve the wider issues rattling the tech stock markets in recent weeks.
Investors had taken fright at Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms.
Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will actually pay off.

However, investment in AI is still expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, who said the technology would remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.
The value of the shares in Big Tech companies have cushioned the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs, buoying investments and pensions for people worldwide.
President Donald Trump hailed Huang as a "great patriot and national treasure" after his reappointment and pointed to the chief executive's wider impact.
"The country needs Jensen's leadership at Nvidia in order to ensure the success and prosperity of not only the company, but the American economy," he wrote on Truth Social.
Nvidia said its leadership had received input from "senior levels of the United States government and was "confident that Mr Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk".

items.title: Trump claims credit as Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia
paragraphs: Jensen Huang is back atop Nvidia after the chipmaker's board reinstated him as president, chief executive and board director. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," Huang said in a statement. Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images/Getty Images Europe hide caption
Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images/Getty Images Europe
Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO of the world's largest chipmaker on Monday, sending the company's stock soaring as President Trump claimed credit for brokering his close ally's return.

It was a stunning reversal of fortune for Huang. He resigned less than two weeks ago, following news reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of being a Chinese spy.

In a statement put out just before the market opened, Nvidia said its board voted unanimously in favor of bringing back Huang after a series of conversations and meetings, as well as input from people at "senior levels" of the U.S. government. "Based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk," the board said.
Nvidia's stock price shot up more than 30% on Monday, helping buoy stock indexes after last week's losses, which were driven by the tech sector.

Trump endorsed the board's move, calling it the "correct and proper decision" in a social media post. He said Huang's leadership was needed "in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy."

The president had repeatedly urged Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang as CEO in public comments and on social media. In a lengthy interview with CNBC Monday morning, Trump claimed his influence helped Huang get his job back.
"I don't want to say, but basically I was represented at the board," the president said, in response to a question about a report in Semafor that he had called directly into the NVIDIA board meeting.
"I spoke to them. Let me just put it that way. And I convinced them," Trump told CNBC. "And I must tell you, it was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week and a half ago."
He later added: "When the stock starts dropping forty, fifty percent, it was a lot easier for me to do it yesterday than it would have been."

Nvidia, which Huang co-founded and has run for the past 33 years, dominates the market for the chips used to train and run artificial intelligence. Trump and Huang have grown close during the president's second term in office, with Huang becoming one of the most influential business leaders with the president's ear on AI policy. He has successfully lobbied the U.S. government to allow chipmakers to sell some chips to China, although Nvidia's most advanced chips are subject to export controls.

Huang resigned from Nvidia on Nov. 12 after news reports that he had affairs with multiple women, including an Nvidia executive who reported to him. But the most explosive allegation was that he'd engaged in a relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that was buying Nvidia chips, whom U.S. officials believed had ties to Chinese intelligence.

The Justice Department has said it is conducting a criminal investigation of Megaspeed for potential chip smuggling. In a statement sent to NPR on Nov. 15, Megaspeed said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business," and that Alice Huang left the company in 2025, but that it is conducting an internal investigation.

Nvidia's board said as recently as Nov. 17 that it did not intend to reinstate Huang, though Huang publicly said he would return if the board allowed it. On Monday, board chair Harvey Jones said in a statement: "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."

The board said on Monday its turnaround followed a series of meetings with Huang that left them satisfied with his "candor and ability to lead" the company. It said its investigation into Huang and the allegations he had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort continues and that Huang is "committed to cooperating with it."

"I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement on Monday. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment."

On Monday, Trump said that the government has "no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security," and that Attorney General Todd Blanche says the U.S. "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."
Last week Nvidia's board said it had formed a committee to oversee the company's national security policies, compliance with U.S. export controls, and risk management of global trade.
Huang is expected to testify before congressional committees next week.
To explain why it was so important that Huang remain at Nvidia's helm, Trump told CNBC he feared China attempting to bring his expertise to their country.

"I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen, 'Hey, how would you like to come to China?' He's got a little blood in him, you know. He's got a little blood there. 'How would you like to come to China and head up Huawei, okay, and head up one of our companies?'" Trump said. "And you know what? If Jensen was angry enough, if he was treated badly, maybe he could do that."
When CNBC asked Trump if he wasn't worried after he was alerted that Huang was in a relationship with a potential spy, Trump demurred, saying, "I won't get into it."

Following the CNBC interview, Trump celebrated Huang's reinstatement on Truth Social by posting a doctored image invoking a famous photo of the president after the assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, in 2024. In the posted image, Huang is in President Trump's place with blood spattered on his face, raising his fist — holding a red bra — as an Nvidia flag waves in the background.

items.title: ‘A fight to demand that humans are worth investing in’: Theaster Gates on taking over America’s last porcelain factory
paragraphs: “The worth of hand-painted china depends mainly upon the hand,” reads an advertisement dating from 1910 and displayed just inside the entrance of the Pickard China factory, a sprawling, 60,000 sq ft brick building just outside of Chicago. “Most of the large staff of artists at the Pickard studios have been trained in the great art centers of Europe, and each piece of Pickard is painted from start to finish by the same master craftsman.”

Those statements are a distant echo from another age. These days, Pickard – the last operational porcelain fine china factory in the US – is in a shocking state of disrepair, its 12 remaining employees struggling to fulfill longstanding orders for the White House (Pickard began producing official White House china in 2008 when the company was commissioned by Laura Bush), Williams Sonoma, US embassies, private golf clubs and anxious brides-to-be.

Inside the building, decommissioned machines the size of school buses remain frozen in their final moments of functionality, collecting dust, cobwebs and slip splatter. The roof is patched by a checkerboard of blue and green tarps strung from rafters and draped into makeshift troughs, water trickling into large commercial garbage cans. The doors to some rooms have remained locked for decades in an attempt to contain the toxic mold spreading inside. Thousands of pieces of porcelain plates, cups, pitchers and bowls sit stacked on ancient wood shelves, languishing in various stages of incompletion. Some lights are functional, most are not, casting the whole eerie scene into semi-darkness.

The lights are about to be flipped back on. In September, Theaster Gates, the celebrated artist and radical urban interventionist, became the new owner of Pickard China – its client roster, its design archive, and this massive, crumbling factory surrounded by cornfields in Antioch, Illinois, 50 miles north of Chicago.

I visited the factory on a damp, early fall morning, a few days after the staff had learned of the ownership change. Just five employees were on site, stamping, trimming and lining individual pieces among the battered machinery and crumbling walls. I was instantly struck by the magnitude of what the new owner was up against. “It feels like I was slowly building the muscle and aptitude to be ready for a project like Pickard,” says Gates, a ceramicist, sculptor and art world heavyweight who is best known for transforming sections of his South Side Chicago neighborhood by buying up abandoned buildings and deftly turning them into inspired spaces of community, art and learning. “It’s like I’ve been preparing for a decathlon for 20 years.”

Gates was formerly professor at the University of Chicago and an urban planner, but when his star began to rise in the art world he used his earnings to become something of a real estate Robin Hood, scooping up old buildings, businesses and archives on the brink of extinction. In 2013, he purchased the Stony Island Bank for $1 from the city of Chicago, transforming the derelict 113-year-old Neoclassical behemoth into a thriving cultural center that includes a cinema screening Black films, the personal vinyl collection of the pioneering DJ Frankie Knuckles, the full archive of Ebony and Jet magazines and a Korean-inspired tea salon. Just last year, Gates opened the doors to The Land School, a 40,000 sq ft former parochial elementary school that, following his $14m reimagining, now serves as a center for experimentation in art, music, and community engagement.

But Gates admits that this latest acquisition is on a completely different scale. While his other projects have been bought, renovated and run by his arts nonprofit, the Rebuild Foundation, his purchase of Pickard marks the first time Gates is taking over a floundering business and hoping to make it profitable. And he’s doing so at a moment when the sustainability of American manufacturing and the perceived value of human labor is in free fall. In other words, it is the quintessence of a Theaster Gates project.

“The way that I’m approaching this is that, first, you have to make the choice that the human hand is worth investing in,” says Gates, who has spent his artistic career examining entrenched, often exploitative systems and doggedly burrowing alternative routes, showing the world that another way is possible. “From the turn of the century, big business has been trying to figure out how to need humans less and how to make more money. AI is just the newest face to what has felt, for me, a very consistent ambition of a certain kind of business practice. So, on one level, this is a civil fight to demand that humans are necessary to creative and manufacturing acts.”

Which is why his first action item upon being named the new owner and president of Pickard was not to fix the leaks or start tinkering with the ancient kilns, but to shore up the emotional health of the skeleton crew of employees.

“We were left with a building that needed a lot of care, and a staff that needed to know that their jobs were important and that they were safe. The first thing I wanted to do was really work on the mental health of my staff, to show my humanity and my willingness to make the investments that were necessary,” says Gates, who has long been interested in the question of labor, studying thinkers from John Ruskin to John Calvin. “Those things are no longer theoretical or conceptual, they’re very, very practical right now, and I’m enjoying it.”
Gates purchased the company for an undisclosed sum from Andy Pickard Morgan, a fourth-generation Pickard family member who had been at the helm since 2006.
“I’m not on eBay looking for companies,” says Gates, when asked how he ends up with fixer-uppers that no one else will touch. “The first criteria is that it lands in my lap.”

Up against slumping sales and deteriorating infrastructure, Pickard Morgan was quietly preparing to sell or shutter the 130-year-old family business when Gates cold-called him, inquiring about partnering on a homewares project he was leading for Prada. Gates quickly discovered that Pickard, once the pride of Chicago and an employer of hundreds – including a cadre of plate painters imported from the Wedgwood factory in Stoke-on-Trent – was on life support.

“I’m really proud of the decorative legacy that Pickard’s had, but I have an opportunity to bring a new philosophical position to it,” says Gates, whose own ceramic practice references myriad cultural influences, from the ancient practices of Japanese pottery to the work of 19th century enslaved ceramicist David Drake. “First we assess deeply what we know how to do, and what we’ve done for the past 130 years, and then do a remix and an edit before we start throwing anything out. There has to first be a logic, a philosophy, a cultural root, before you touch a thing.”

Gates mentions the company’s two remaining line painters, who were brought over from Wedgwood more than 25 years ago, revered for their steady hands and the delicate, uniform gold circles they paint on china bound for Air Force One or the White House dining room.

“I’ve been thinking a lot about the possibilities. What if our liners made other lines besides edging a plate? What are the other kinds of lines that they might be interested in, or might know how to do? I don’t know if anyone’s ever asked them,” says Gates, who plans to host drawing workshops for employees where they can create more freely, perhaps inspiring the next generation of Pickard designs and motifs. “If they can move between skilled artisan to free independent thinking artist back to skilled artisan, can we grow what’s able to happen on a plate?”

As he is known to do, Gates is focused simultaneously on both the small details and the big ideas. Adroit and deeply experienced with restoration projects, he promises that if we return in a year, we will see a gorgeous building and a humming artisanal manufacturing business. He is also unbound in his artistic pursuit to conceive of a better world, with a hope that something grander will emerge.

“If we’re going to try to imagine some kind of scaled celebration of people’s labor and their efforts to make things, it’s going to have to be bigger than what I can produce in one little studio,” says Gates. “Why is it art? Because the factory will become a conceptual example of what’s possible. The plates and cups and bowls – that’s just the byproduct of trying to offer our humanity back. Not only does it feel like art, it feels like the biggest conceptual project I’ve ever done.”

items.title: Apple iPhone Duo review: the most novel and interesting iPhone in almost a decade
paragraphs: Apple’s first folding phone has upended the usual order of things with some interesting choices about how you use a iPhone – for better or worse.

The Duo sits atop the pile as Apple’s most expensive smartphone – at £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,499) it costs more than most of its folding Android rivals and as much as the iPhone 18 Pro Max and the latest iPad mini combined.
It is designed as a pocketable device that replaces your phone and tablet but it is neither a regular iPhone when closed nor an iPad when open, it’s something else entirely.

The Duo is a squat, wide and weighty device, flying in the face of eight years of folding Androids that have generally been tall and thin. The outside 5.4in screen is bright, crisp and smooth. Open the Duo like a book to reveal its fantastic 7.6in folding OLED screen with a matt finish similar to the company’s high-end iPads, MacBooks and displays. This eliminates glare and hides the crease down the centre where it folds.

Like all folding screens, though, it is not made of regular hardened glass and so must be treated with care. Press hard enough with a fingernail and you will leave a permanent mark. And there have been multiple reports of faulty devices with broken screens.

The Duo is short and squat when closed because Apple has used the same 1.4:1 ratio for the outside and inside screens, just at different sizes, which is mathematically beautiful but does present some usability challenges.

The closed Duo is a very wide device measuring 84.1mm across – 6.1mm wider than the giant iPhone 18 Pro Max – which makes it almost exclusively a two-handed device for typing or reaching anything across the screen even with a PopSocket on the back.

The display is short, which does not leave much room for your messages or content when you use the keyboard. Apple has altered iOS for the first time in a decade to try to make the most of the restricted vertical space by moving what would be at the top and bottom of the screen to the right.

The dock has been moved to the right, while the status bar has been condensed into a circle under the selfie camera. The right bar is home to controls, such as the back button and tab bars, but shoves the main body of the app to the left, making it harder to reach when held in your right hand. With the Touch ID fingerprint scanner on the right side, it will be tricky to use for the left-handed.

The inside screen and stereo speakers are well suited to landscape video, photos and other widescreen content. Old TV shows shot in 4:3 ratio fill it almost exactly, while modern 16:9 TV shows have narrow black bars top and bottom and wider films are letterboxed. Browsing, reading and certain apps are better turned to portrait for a longer view.
Main screen: 7.6in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (430ppi)
Cover screen: 5.4in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (460ppi)
Camera: 48+48MP rear; 12MP+4MP selfie cameras
Connectivity: eSIM-only 5G, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Satellite, UWB and GNSS
Water resistance: IP68 (6 metres for 30 mins)
Dimensions unfolded: 117.8 x 164.6 x 5.2mm
The Duo runs iPhone apps in broadly three classes: those that haven’t been updated, those that have been updated for iOS 27.1 or later and those that have been redesigned specifically for the Duo.

Most apps are in the first or second class. The first is a standard iPhone app in the middle of the Duo’s screen, which doesn’t look too bad on the outside screen, but is comical on the inside, similar to the early days of the iPad.
The second class will stretch to fill either screen of the Duo, but will not use the right panel at all, leaving it as black wasted space.

The third class are the best, making use of the full screen and the side bar. Apple’s apps mostly have the best layouts, but there are a rapidly growing number of third-party apps that make decent use of the screen with dual-panel views. Google Maps was recently updated to expand the map across the full screen with small tools for navigation and the compass in the bottom right. Simple but effective.

Other app redesigns have been less successful, ending up with information obscured by the status bubble and dynamic island. Instagram’s boss, Adam Mosseri, recently admitted on Threads “it’s a bit of a tricky form factor” and that it will be “pretty challenging” to make the best of the Duo. Even Apple hasn’t got it all right: moving the equals button from the bottom right corner on the calculator app is particularly irritating.

The hinge of the Duo can hold the phone open in multiple forms. For example, you can stand the Duo like an A or a greetings card to show iOS’s standby clock and widgets when locked. Partially open the inside screen, and iOS neatly pushes app icons, the clock, playback buttons and other elements away from the central fold. You can use the Duo like a mini laptop with the keyboard on the bottom or play media with video pushed to the top half and controls on the bottom. Netflix even has a nice immersive effect that projects some of the colour from the video on to the bottom half of the screen.

The inside screen supports up to two apps in split screen for multitasking, but only when in landscape orientation. You can’t resize them, but you can pin the apps as a pair to launch them together. Some apps, such as Safari, allow you to open more than one window, so you can split-screen two websites.

In portrait orientation, you can pin a video to the top half of the screen with an app open below it, but that’s it. Any video app that supports picture in picture should work, including YouTube, Netflix, BBC iPlayer and other streaming apps.

The Duo has the same A20 Pro chip as the iPhone 18 Pro and performs very well. But it also has surprisingly good battery life, lasting almost two days between charges with the screens actively used for about 3.5 hours each for apps, browsing, messaging and photos.

The battery lasts longer when predominantly using the outside screen, while gaming drains it much faster. It should outlast most heavy days with some left in the tank, with most people needing to charge the Duo every other night.
A full charge takes about 82 minutes hitting 60% in 30mins using a 60W or greater USB-C power adapter (not included) or longer using 25W Qi2/MagSafe wireless charging.

The battery will last more than 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity and can be replaced for £209. Out-of-warranty screen repairs cost £389 for the outer display and £999 for the inner display. The nano-texture display layer can be replaced for £49.
The specialists at iFixit awarded the phone five out of 10 for repairability, the highest score for a foldable but far behind the best traditional slab phones.
It contains 35% recycled material. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.
The Duo has four cameras: a 12MP selfie camera on the outside screen, a 4MP camera hidden under the inside screen, and two cameras on the back.

The regular selfie camera is decent and supports Apple’s Center Stage tech to automatically reframe the shot but it is a small step down from regular iPhones. The selfie camera under the inside screen is only good enough for video calls and only in bright light.

The rear camera is one of the biggest compromises for the folding form. The Duo lacks a telephoto camera similar to the base-model iPhone 17, having only the main and ultra-wide 48MP cameras. They shoot good photos and video in most scenarios, but are noticeably worse than the iPhone 18 Pro in low-light conditions.
The Duo has one big advantage: you can use the main cameras for selfies with the outside display as the viewfinder. It is a bit awkward, but the results are better than any selfie camera.

The camera has a few other tricks. You can show your subject what they look like in the outside screen, or display animated characters to capture the attention of children. You can prop the Duo up half-folded and activate Smart Take to automatically capture photos and video of you in front of the camera.
The iPhone Duo costs from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,499).

For comparison, the iPhone 18 Pro costs £1,199, the iPhone 18 Pro Max costs £1,299, the iPhone Air costs £1,099 and the iPhone 17 costs £899. The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 costs £1,699, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra costs £1,899, the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs £1,799 and the Honor Magic V6 costs £1,300.
The Duo is the most interesting and different iPhone in almost a decade, changing the way Apple’s ubiquitous smartphone works.

The folding form opens up many new possibilities. The inside screen is brilliant and the matt texture eliminates glare, while hiding imperfections. It is a great size and shape for content – watching TV on a public-transport commute is a delight – but less ideal for multitasking with multiple apps, which feel a bit short and cramped.
The short and wide outside screen takes some getting used to, particularly for messaging, and requires two hands to type on. This isn’t the device for small-phone aficionados.

The app situation is rapidly improving with 100s of developers deploying updates to better make use of the Duo’s shape every day. But you’ll still run into some jarring app experiences, which are eased a little by lots of slick software touches built into iOS.

Shifting the dock to the right felt logical after a day of use and I really like the new condensed status icon circle. But it will be tricky to use for the left-handed, as will Touch ID on the right side, which works well but is a step back from the convenience of Face ID.

The folding form brings many compromises. It is extremely expensive. The dual camera on the back is decent, but not the best on an iPhone and lacks a telephoto option. The Duo is heavier, thicker and not as robust as a regular iPhone. The inside screen must be treated with care. The performance and battery life are good, however.

The Duo is far from perfect, and there are better folding phones on the Android side. But it is the most fun I’ve had with an iPhone in quite some time, and for those locked into Apple’s ecosystem but craving a different experience, this is it. For everyone else, there are better and far cheaper options available.

Pros: phone and tablet in one, fabulous matt tablet screen, top performance, good battery life, novel software, a different iPhone experience, fast Touch ID sensor, water resistance, decent dual cameras, great speakers.

Cons: extremely expensive, heavy, hard to use one-handed, squat shape not ideal for messaging when closed, no Face ID, bit of a learning curve, more fragile than a regular device and costly to repair, no telephoto camera, tricky for left-handed users.

items.title: Why Nicola Coughlan's new drama might leave viewers uncomfortable
paragraphs: I Am Helen is the latest project in writer and director Dominic Savage's I Am... series, female-led stories focusing on themes like mental health and relationships.
The two fully-improvised episodes, devised in collaboration with Coughlan, follow a relationship spiralling after Steve tries to choke Helen during sex without consent.
"We never realised how incredibly timely it would be," Coughlan tells BBC Newsbeat.
"It feels incredibly relevant right now, and specifically right now, because pornography that includes strangulation has just been outlawed in the UK."
Earlier this month, the government made it illegal for anyone to possess or publish porn that shows strangulation or suffocation.
That decision followed a review last year that found choking was "rife" on porn sites and had become normalised, particularly among younger people.
Coughlan and Cole say they were keen to make everything about their characters and the setting as relatable as possible to emphasise the shocking fallout.

"We needed one inciting incident that felt like something that could really plausibly happen between a couple, that it just goes slightly too far without consent, and it just blows everything up," Coughlan says.
"It's really important we see Steve's perspective in it because it makes him a normal guy.
"He's not this evil guy who's attacking Helen. He does bad things, but he's complicated. And hopefully you see them both as real people."
Filming the series from a script without dialogue meant the actors were fully immersed in their characters, making them real not just for viewers but for themselves too.
"I'm not playing myself, but there's far less, let's say 'character' here than anything else I've ever done because a lot of this is about just reacting," Coughlan says.
She and Cole would film long takes, some lasting about an hour and often with heated exchanges, which might need to be shot multiple times.
Coughlan describes I Am Helen as "the most challenging thing in terms of material that I've ever worked on", adding for the first time in a role she needed counselling.
"You literally would be physically and mentally quite exhausted," she says.

"There were times that I said to Dominic [Savage] if he wanted to do a third take for example - and I've never said this before on set - but I actually don't think I have that in me because you hit a wall.
"When you're given that freedom, things happen and I think you can get some really interesting and also quite shocking stuff," he says.
For him, that came when he damaged a fridge on set with a punch.
But it's that authenticity of emotion which, while difficult for the actors, is what Coughlan thinks makes the series so engaging.
"When people watch the 'I Ams', they feel quite truthful," she says.
"I think that's a big reason as to why, to be honest."
Cole researched the manosphere online while developing his role and says he could see how people like Steve "quickly become lost in this quite simple ideology".
"The more interesting thing was the lower level, the kind of 'bro influencer' type people, who a lot of what they say is actually quite good," he says.
"You know, 'go to the gym, be healthy, look your best'.
"But occasionally they veer into comments on male and female societal roles and how a woman should stay at home."
For someone like Steve, who Cole says wants a traditional relationship and a family, those ideas left him "completely lost".
The characters quickly "get caught in a cycle", he says, as they find it harder and harder to understand each other.
"It starts off as a question, which becomes a debate, which becomes an argument, which becomes a huge bust-up, which becomes forgiveness, an apology, tears."
Coughlan says viewers have told her they expected the series to end with serious violence, perhaps even with Steve killing Helen.
But she was determined to avoid a shock factor so the characters didn't tip into being unrelatable.
"There's some very extreme moments in this, but some of them are not extreme," she says.
"It's better that he didn't [kill Helen] because as a viewer, you don't want people to go, 'well, if he does X, then that's the moment to leave'.
"From my perspective, you watch it and you go, 'you don't need to hit a threshold'.
"If you feel scared and uncomfortable, that's enough reason to get out of a situation."
If you have been affected by the issues raised in this article, help and support is available via BBC Action Line.
