items.title: 'It gives me the ick': Can you cheat on someone with a video game?
paragraphs: The relationship between the two main characters, Jason and Lucia, is at the centre of Rockstar's latest Grand Theft Auto title
Imagine your partner spending hours flirting with someone else, trying to hold their hand and taking them on dates. Most people would have questions.
But what if that someone only exists inside a video game?
The latest instalment in Rockstar's blockbuster Grand Theft Auto franchise has already set sales records, making $3.8bn (£2.9bn) in its first day alone.
At the heart of the game is the relationship between its two main characters, Jason and Lucia.
Rockstar says the Bonnie and Clyde-style duo do not have to maintain a full romantic relationship to progress the game.
But their connection can grow by spending time together outside of the main crime and life-on-the-run storyline – through shopping, visiting bars and restaurants and working out together.
Smaller interactions like holding hands and quickly responding to each other's texts can help build a bond.
The idea has restarted a debate almost as old as gaming itself: if you are that invested in a fictional relationship, is your real-life partner entitled to be upset?
In September, polling company YouGov put that question to more than 4,000 British adults.
About 6% said they would regard it as cheating, while a further 19% said they would "not be okay with it". Women were considerably more likely than men to take a dim view.
Alli Franco, a 30-year-old Texan who posts anime and gaming content to more than a million followers, external on TikTok, says she felt "dismayed" watching the debate unfold online.
"If your partner is insecure about a fictional character, then there needs to be some serious reflection," she told the BBC.
"It's similar to having a crush on a TV star, but even further removed from cheating since there is no other actual person involved.”
After Franco posted a video on the subject, hundreds of commenters appeared to agree with her, although some did have reservations.
"To be honest, it depends," wrote one. "If you're cancelling plans with your significant other or directing your intimacy towards a fictional character, then that is a little odd."
"It's very odd and it really gives me the ick," another woman told us.
Can you cheat on your partner in a video game character?
For decades, video games have allowed players to build relationships with non-player characters, or NPCs.
Gamers could marry villagers in Harvest Moon in 1996, shape emotional storylines in Final Fantasy VII and pursue more complex romances in role-playing games like Baldur's Gate II.
In life simulator The Sims, they could flirt, date, marry and have children with computer-controlled characters.
But all those interactions were tightly scripted, based on rules and storylines written in advance by game developers.
GTA 6 offers something more dynamic, allowing players to shape the relationship between Jason and Lucia through a wider range of open-world interactions and choices.

"The more sophisticated games get, the less likely it is that players get pulled out of the experience," says Arienne Ferchaud, an associate professor at Florida State University who studies how people form connections with fictional characters.
"Games are doing a better job of mimicking reality and mimicking social relationships."
Rockstar has said players do not have to build a romantic connection in the game
Grand Theft Auto 6 may represent the current cutting edge of game design, but the next leap forward could come from artificial intelligence.
Nvidia, Ubisoft and other huge tech companies are already experimenting with generative AI systems that allow players to hold more natural conversations with NPCs.
Future characters could remember past encounters, react to a player's actions and build relationships that change over time rather than following a pre-written script.
Ferchaud believes that could make games feel even more immersive.

"You could have relationships that feel more solid or more special," she says, although she argues AI as it exists today would still be creating "a stronger illusion" rather than a genuinely meaningful connection.
Whether that is exciting or unsettling may depend on the player, and there has been some resistance to the wider use of the technology in gaming.
Franco says she is already seeing adverts for AI chatbots that let fans talk to their favourite anime characters.
"I can definitely see AI integrating into games and making it a more realistic experience," she says.
"But should that happen I would still see it as just a game. At the end of the day you can't cheat with lines of code."

items.title: Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules
paragraphs: A Ukrainian FP-1 long-range attack drone is launched at an undisclosed location in Ukraine, Aug. 16, 2026. Efrem Lukatsky/AP hide caption
GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."

After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.

Bleary-eyed negotiators insisted the agreement was better than nothing and showed the U.N.'s disarmament process could still function. But for many humanitarian organizations and many countries, the deal falls far short of what they had hoped for.

Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo.

Their concerns stem from the kind of warfare we are now seeing. In Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza, civilians are being killed by semi-autonomous drones. This year in Sudan, 80% of civilian deaths were caused by drones according to the U.N.

Humans remain, albeit very remotely, in control for now, but humanitarian organizations fear we are on the verge of seeing artificial intelligence-assisted weapons make the decision to kill entirely on their own.

"There is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm," said ICRC legal adviser Georgia Hinds. "That's not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross."

No one went into the negotiations thinking they would be easy; some of the world's most powerful countries, among them the U.S., Russia and Israel, had already indicated their reluctance to agree to binding regulations.
On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting's agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

"They're just kicking the can down the road," said one frustrated delegate. As the clock ticked on and the weekend approached, diplomats scrambled to get some kind of result from negotiations that had been billed as a last chance to regulate weapons whose technology and decision-making capabilities we may not even fully understand.
Finally, at 4:30 a.m. on Saturday morning, they emerged from the negotiating room to announce their compromise: no to a deal within a year, maybe to legally binding rules, or maybe not.

The ICRC immediately said it regretted the move and renewed its appeal for a binding treaty. Other campaigners were less polite, calling the deal "a real disappointment" and a "nothing burger." "I am concerned people will die because of this," added another.
A key worry is that, with two years to talk about possible rules that might only be optional, the technology will race ahead, uncontrolled.

"We're likely to see the systems proliferate," said Anna Hehir, an expert in military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute. "They're not like nuclear weapons in that they're inaccessible. There are autonomous weapons that are easy to purchase or even to create for all kinds of actors: individuals, nonstate actors, criminal groups."
There are also big questions about how our existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – can be upheld if those doing the killing are not humans, but machines.

"These rules are the bare minimum that militaries and states have developed and agreed to adhere to," said the ICRC's Hinds. "The commander remains responsible for making sure that the use of force is lawful. The commander remains accountable. You cannot hold a machine accountable for a violation of the law."

But in the race to develop new weapons, no country wants to come second. Although most U.N. member states do agree there should be some controls over autonomous weapons, the compromise in Geneva means that, for the next two years at least, weapons that can use artificial intelligence to make life-and-death decisions will remain unregulated.
Meanwhile, weapons technology is developing at pace, while diplomacy is struggling to keep up.

items.title: The AI boom had a really bad week — and it's raising loud alarms
paragraphs: Stocks got hit hard this week amid fears that the AI trade could be buckling. Spencer Platt/Getty Images hide caption
A yearslong AI boom showed signs of unraveling this week in spectacular fashion.

AI-related stocks have powered markets to record highs and helped support the broader economy. But investors now fear that a potential bubble in the sector could be bursting, which could spark wider financial repercussions.
Here's what to know about the week in AI and why alarm bells are ringing

Investors were hoping the stock market debut of AI giant Anthropic this week would provide a boost to the markets. Instead, the entire stock market got pummeled on Friday, sparking one of the worst weeks that Wall Street has seen in quite some time.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 10% for the week, its worst performance since the onset of COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns in March 2020. Even Anthropic, which gained 17% on its debut, ended up slumping more than 8% to close near its IPO price on Friday.
Meanwhile, both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average entered a correction as of the close of trade on Friday, meaning a drop of 10% from their recent highs.
It's the culmination of weeks of fears that have been building up about the sustainability of the AI trade.

Back in September, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in over three years. That poses a big challenge to AI companies because they still need to borrow billions of dollars to do things like build out data centers that power the growth of their technologies. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for them.

Democrats also took over both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, vowing to take a tougher regulatory approach toward the AI sector and slow down the build-out of data centers, which have been unpopular with voters.
Democrats were also elected as governors in states that have been key to the data center build-out, like Texas, where Gina Hinojosa stunned the political world by winning her race.

And then there's the turmoil at Nvidia, the top AI chip company. Its CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned this month after being suspected of having had an affair with a woman who's believed to have been spying for China.
All this has exacerbated investors' worries about the sustainability of an AI trade into which investors have sunk billions of dollars.
Hank Smith, the head of investment strategy at Haverford Trust, thinks it's unlikely the markets will recover quickly, the way they have previously bounced right back after AI shares dropped.

"I think it has taken the market the better part of the last two or three weeks to realize it is not going to be like the previous sell-offs," Smith said, adding that AI could fall "out of favor" through next year.
"It's just going to take a little bit of time to heal," he said of the tech market.

Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO this month, throwing the company's leadership into turmoil. Here, Huang delivers a keynote address at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas on Jan. 6, 2025. Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
That has been a big source of debate on Wall Street.

Some people fear that the AI sector could be in the middle of a bubble that is bursting, just like tech stocks did during the dot-com bust of 2000. At the time, investors had sunk money into tech companies that often had no profits — and not even revenues — and were wiped out in the bust.

Smith, though, argues that this time around the AI trade is being powered by top companies such as Meta and Apple, and he doesn't see them as likely to go out of business, the way many dot-coms did. Nvidia — despite its leadership shake-up — still posted strong results this week.
The future prospects for AI, Smith said, are "not based on a pie in the sky."
That said, Smith continued, there is still a question about whether investors will see the sizable returns they are hoping to get.

And there's another big fear: how interconnected AI companies have become. Nvidia, for example, not only owns shares in other big AI companies like Anthropic but is also lending a lot of money to them. In turn, they are buying chips from Nvidia.

This circular system of financing also involves lesser-known companies, such as CoreWeave, that are borrowing heavily to build out data centers. Nvidia is a major investor in CoreWeave, in another sign of the interconnectedness.
This close-knit ecosystem is raising concerns that if one or two companies run into trouble, it could kick off a chain reaction that could lead to something like a financial crisis.
It could be potentially significant. The U.S. economy has effectively become an AI economy.

Building out data centers, for example, may be unpopular with voters, but construction creates jobs, which is why some parts of the U.S. have courted the centers. In fact, AI investments helped the economy grow at an annual rate of 3.4% in the most recent quarter.

Not only that, but AI-related stocks have become an integral part of the broader markets, accounting for a substantial portion of the S&P 500. That means many investors hold these stocks as part of their portfolios, including as components of index funds, pensions or retirement funds like 401(k)s.
So if the AI trade unravels, it could have a ripple effect far beyond the high-tech world.
Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.

items.title: Who will be Robert Pattinson's 'Bond girl' - and does the role need to change?
paragraphs: No actress has yet confirmed they're in the running - but stars who have been bandied about the internet include Zendaya, whose name shot to the top of the list after Pattinson's casting.
The duo have already shared three films together this year and make a "really exciting pairing," says Ivan-Zadeh.
Rose agrees that as one of the most recognisable actresses in Hollywood, Zendaya is "definitely someone I'd be thinking about now".
But her Euphoria co-stars Hunter Schafer and Sydney Sweeney could give her a run for her money.

There have been rumours about Sweeney getting the role for months, and you can see why, says Dr Llewella Chapman, a film historian at the University of East Anglia. "She has sex appeal and an ability to take on tougher roles too," she tells the BBC.
Sweeney was given a boost last month by former Bond girl Trina Parks, who told the Telegraph she would fit the role well because Bond needed a woman with "ownership over her sexuality".
The way the films have treated Bond girls "hasn't always aged well", says Rose.
Some scenes from 1960s Bond films are "basically rape", and "wouldn't fly today", said No Time To Die director Cary Fukunaga in 2021, external - referring to Thunderball and Goldfinger.
In reality, we have come a long way since then.
Over the years, producers have taken steps to usher the franchise into the modern era.
These days, the women of Bond are now much more likely to be sharp, capable equals to 007 - and what's defined as "attractive" has also evolved.
Belluci's inclusion in Spectre as a "Bond woman" aged 50 was widely praised for spotlighting a different type of sex appeal (even though she was only four years older than Daniel Craig in real life).
We've also had other powerful women in Bond, such as Michelle Yeoh's Colonel Wai Lin and Lashana Lynch's MI6 agent Nomi, who also made history as the first black female 007.
Rather than fitting the traditional Bond girl mould, both of them were competent women who could give Bond a run for his money.
"We've moved away from the role being someone with a silly name and for Bond to pat on their bottom," says film critic Ivan-Zadeh. "It's moving in the right direction".
Many people say, however, there is still further to go.
Having more female Bond villains, as well as love interests, could be one way to make it more equal, suggests Rose. "That's what I'd want to see."
"They can be romantic interests, villains, spies, allies or even the person who ultimately outsmarts Bond. There's room for all of those roles,” agrees showbiz journalist Nikki Onafuye.

Another way the roles could evolve is by bringing in "a queer or sexually fluid Bond woman," suggests Ivan-Zadeh. "Someone whose desires don’t simply revolve around Bond. That would create some genuinely interesting chemistry.”
Others are hoping to see more diverse actresses cast from film markets such as China, India or Nigeria.
“There have been a number of women of colour in the past, but I'd like to see more," says Be Manzini, writer and filmmaker.
"I'd like to see an Indian Bond girl," agrees Chapman. "Aishwarya Rai was touted for the follow up to Die Another Day but never got there."
More broadly, there is an appetite to see Bond girls have their own lives.
“For me, it's about giving these women proper storylines,” says Onafuye. "They should have their own motivations and their own ambitions.”
None of this is to say we should do away with the traditional Bond glamour.
"No-one wants to see Bond girls slumping around in their PJs," says Ivan-Zadeh.
But the important distinction is that "being sexy shouldn't be the only thing a female character has to offer,” says Onafuye.

“To those arguing that it's fine for Bond's women just to be sexy and hot, I'd say there's nothing sexier or hotter than a woman (or man) with a brain and a wit,” adds entertainment journalist Caroline Frost.
Ultimately, whatever direction the new producers go in, most agree the "Bond girl" or Bond woman is a key part of the Bond universe.
But continuing to evolve is crucial, says Chapman. "It's about retaining the humour and history of Bond but also recognising - this is 2026."

There are, of course, lots of other women within the films, and for Frost, the key is to have a range of different Bond women on screen, "all well matched with 007 in terms of strength, resources and, above all, wit".
"Bond has always had fascinating women," agrees Rose. "I'd just love the next film to give them the space to be as interesting as the man in the tuxedo."

items.title: Trump, Takaichi discuss Indo-Pacific security as Japanese leader reaffirms Taiwan policy
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original Mandarin article.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi says she spoke to President Donald Trump on Thursday, discussing regional and international issues following Trump's meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Speaking to the press afterward, Takaichi said the two leaders also discussed the Indo-Pacific and the war in Ukraine during the roughly 20-minute call. “I will further elevate Japan’s relationship with the United States to a higher level,” Takaichi told reporters.

But Takaichi acknowledged differences with Washington over the International Criminal Court, which the U.S., China and Russia criticized in a joint declaration in Shenzhen. She said Japan has consistently supported the court and that Trump is aware of Japan’s position.
Earlier Thursday in Shenzhen, Takaichi told reporters there was “absolutely no change” in Japan’s position on Taiwan, as stated in the 1972 Japan-China Joint Communique.
Takaichi added that Japan would continue close communication with Washington to strengthen the bilateral alliance and consult on a range of international issues.
VOA reached out to the White House for comment on the call but didn't receive a response at the time of publication.

Yu-Hua Chen, an associate professor in the Global Studies Program at Akita International University (AIU) in Japan, told VOA that U.S.-Japan relations under Takaichi have been particularly close. Tokyo has been using multiple institutional channels to maintain the relationship, with post-summit phone calls serving as one example.
Trump also spoke with Takaichi by phone after meeting Xi in Beijing in May.

Akita International University's Chen said Takaichi's latest remarks were considerably more moderate than her earlier comments in November 2025. This time, she returned to Japan's traditional approach of strategic ambiguity on Taiwan, he added.
"Takaichi's aim was probably to prevent tensions between Japan and China from escalating further," Chen said.

In November 2025, Takaichi told parliament that the use of military force by China on Taiwan, such as a naval blockade, would likely constitute a “survival-threatening situation” that would force Japan to respond.

Her remarks triggered strong protests from Beijing and contributed to a prolonged deterioration in bilateral relations. China subsequently increased pressure on Japan through measures including restrictions on exports to Tokyo, warnings against travel to Japan and tighter controls on strategic materials such as rare earths.

Takaichi's appearance at the APEC summit also underscored the difficult state of Japan-China relations. According to Japan's Kyodo News, Xi and Takaichi had a brief encounter at the summit's opening ceremony. Takaichi approached Xi, but he did not respond.

China also sent retired former ambassador to Greece, Zhang Qiyue, to receive Takaichi at the airport, rather than having a senior leader greet her. The reception contrasted with Xi's personal welcome for Trump and senior Communist Party official Cai Qi's reception of Putin.
Takaichi's visit had been viewed in Japan as an opportunity to restart high-level dialogue with Beijing. However, Xi did not hold any formal meetings with her.
Chen said the Japanese government had likely anticipated the relatively cool reception, but that Takaichi chose to attend the summit, nonetheless.

"This shows that Takaichi's approach to foreign policy is considerably more flexible than many observers expected," Chen said. "It also shows that Takaichi as prime minister can be very different from Takaichi as a member of parliament."

Takaichi has nevertheless reiterated her willingness to maintain communication with Beijing, saying before returning to Japan that she was not concerned that Trump's meetings with the Chinese and Russian leaders would undermine Japanese interests.

items.title: Iran’s Supreme Court Upholds Death Sentences of two protesters
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

Human rights sources this week reported that the death sentences of Navid Najjaran and Milad Armoon had been upheld by Iran’s Supreme Court, and that the cases of the two young protesters had been referred to the sentence enforcement branch.

The case dates to the 2022 nationwide protests, when Arman Aliverdi, a member of the Basij militia, was killed in Tehran’s Ekbatan neighborhood. A criminal court first sentenced Armoon, Najjaran and four other defendants to death for murder, but the Supreme Court overturned those sentences. In a retrial, Armoon was sentenced to prison and ordered to pay blood money, while Najjaran was acquitted for lack of evidence.

Earlier this year, Branch 15 of the Tehran Revolutionary Court, presided over by Abolghassem Salavati, sentenced Armoon and Najjaran, along with two other defendants, Mehdi Imani and Seyed Mohammad Mehdi Hosseini, to death on a separate charge of “moharebeh,” or “enmity against God.”
Rights groups say the convictions relied on forced confessions.

The Dadban Legal Training Center reported Thursday that the Supreme Court had upheld the death sentences of Armoon and Najjaran, and that their cases had been sent for enforcement. Citing an informed source, Dadban said the court overturned the death sentences of Imani and Hosseini and sent their cases to another branch of the Revolutionary Court for retrial.
The United States sanctioned Salavati in 2019 for imposing harsh sentences, including death sentences, on political prisoners and peaceful protesters.

The Hengaw Organization for Human Rights also reported that Shamim Ettehadi, a Baha’i resident of Yazd, was arrested after intelligence agents raided his parents’ home and searched the property. He was taken to an undisclosed location.

The Baha’i faith is Iran’s largest non-Muslim religious minority, with an estimated 300,000 followers, but it is not recognized under the Islamic Republic’s constitution, and its members have faced arrests, property seizures and bans on higher education since the 1979 revolution.

According to Hengaw, government forces searched the home during the raid and confiscated several books and other items related to the Baha’i faith, along with electronic devices belonging to family members. Ettehadi had previously faced arrest and judicial action because of his religious beliefs and related activities. Authorities have not disclosed the reason for his arrest or his whereabouts.

The U.S. State Department has also documented the persecution of Baha’is in Iran, reporting that government forces have raided their homes, arrested them, and seized their personal belongings and electronic devices. The department says Baha’is face charges such as “propaganda against the state,” national security offenses, imprisonment, and other government-imposed restrictions because of their religious beliefs and activities.

items.title: Iraqis cautiously optimistic as government forces enter Iran-backed militia stronghold
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.
Iraqis expressed cautious optimism Friday after government forces entered Jurf al-Sakhar for the first time in 12 years. There were no reported clashes.
Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi described the entry as a return to state control over a strategic town long dominated by an Iran-backed militia.

The deployment, carried out under al-Zaidi’s direct supervision, followed days of tension and threats of confrontation with Kataib Hezbollah, the powerful militia that has controlled the area since 2014.
The operation involved federal police, two brigades of the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), energy police and counterterrorism units.
For some residents, the peaceful deployment offered hope that years of insecurity and displacement might finally be coming to an end.

“So far, everything is good. The situation is calm,” resident Wissam Daghiri told VOA. “The security forces have arrived; they understand the situation and have adapted to it. Our relationship is good. There is no sound of gunfire, thank God, and that is exactly what we want.”
Daghiri said residents also hoped the operation would pave the way for displaced families to return to their homes and communities.
Another resident, Mazen Mahmoud, welcomed the security forces' arrival.

“We thank our security forces. They have been very cooperative and friendly with us, and there have been no disagreements between us,” Mahmoud told VOA. “We hope, God willing, that peace will return.”
Iraqi officials portrayed the deployment as a significant step toward restoring government authority over territory controlled by armed groups operating outside the state's effective command.

“Today is a historic moment in which the Iraqi army proves that it is the protector of the country and its security,” said Sabah al-Numan, spokesperson for Iraq's commander-in-chief of the armed forces.
He described the operation as an ongoing replacement and redeployment of personnel, adding that a new phase focused on public services would follow.
In a video statement after the deployment, al-Zaidi declared that “no force should remain outside the state.”
Jurf al-Sakhar, southwest of Baghdad, has been under the control of Kataib Hezbollah since Iraqi forces and allied militias recaptured the area from Islamic State militants in 2014.
Its status has become a test of Baghdad's ability to assert authority over powerful Iran-aligned armed factions, some of which operate within Iraq's official security structures.

The government has also been investigating allegations of illegal oil trafficking throughout the area. Iraqi officials have reported identifying suspected oil-smuggling operations using satellite imagery, although the full extent of the alleged activities remains unclear.

Despite the peaceful entry of government forces, some observers question whether the arrangement represents a genuine transfer of authority or merely a reorganization of armed factions under official command structures.
The agreement reportedly involved Hadi al-Amiri, head of the Badr Organization, and an influential figure within the PMF.

Critics fear that militia-linked networks could retain influence through PMF units or their connections within the federal police, allowing the same armed groups to maintain effective control under a different administrative arrangement.
The United States has also called on Baghdad to confront Iran-aligned militias.

“The United States expects Prime Minister Al-Zaidi to hold Iran-aligned militias accountable for engaging in violent and destabilizing activities throughout Iraq and the entire region,” a State Department spokesperson told VOA earlier this week.
The spokesperson accused the militias of undermining Iraq's sovereignty, weakening its economy and diverting Iraqi resources through corruption for their own benefit and that of Tehran.
Beyond the immediate security arrangements, the future of Jurf al-Sakhar's displaced population remains a major unresolved issue.

Thousands of residents have been unable to return since 2014. Estimates of the displaced population vary, with some local accounts citing 120,000 people and other assessments placing the figure substantially higher.
Elizabeth Tsurkov, a researcher on Iraqi affairs who was abducted by Kataib Hezbollah in 2023, told VOA that Jurf al-Sakhar's problems extend far beyond allegations of oil smuggling.
She pointed to allegations of sectarian targeting, enforced disappearances and other serious human rights violations against its Sunni population by the Shiite militia.

Tsurkov called for genuine government control, investigations into suspected mass graves and weapons-storage facilities, and the return of displaced residents, whose number she estimated at between 120,000 and 180,000.

items.title: NYU Launches a Ukrainian Studies Initiative
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Ukrainian article.
New York University has launched a Ukrainian Studies program, making it the latest college to join this fast-growing international network of universities studying Ukraine.
Since its founding two years ago, the Global Coalition of Ukrainian Studies, backed by the Ukrainian government, has expanded to more than 100 institutions in 28 countries.

Universities join the coalition by signing a memorandum of understanding. Each school runs its own programs, while the coalition, fronted by First Lady Olena Zelenska, connects them with Ukrainian scholars, conferences and shared resources.

Anastasiia Vlasenko, head of the Ukrainian Studies initiative at NYU, says students have been among the main advocates for the program. “We have a very large Ukrainian student association... They were the ones who wrote the largest number of letters to the university administration calling for Ukrainian Studies to be established,” Vlasenko told VOA.

At NYU, Vlasenko teaches a new course, “Governance and Politics of Ukraine”, which covers "a vast part of Ukrainian history, which is known for its democratic movements... We also look at Ukraine’s political situation, protests, corruption and anti-corruption efforts, and the various scandals that are a constant feature of Ukrainian political life,” Vlasenko notes.

Some students admit that they knew little about Ukraine before taking the course. “I've seen a lot about the war in the news, and I don't really know much about it. So I chose this class just to learn,” says NYU student Raihan Alam.

Atticus Sambar Landa studies economics at NYU and is especially interested in the transition from communism to a capitalist society. “We just talked about corruption today, and I think the transition of specifically state-owned enterprises into the private sector are very fascinating and how that's played out for the people, for the oligarchy,” the student says.

Some students, like Daria Kalinichenko, were born in Ukraine and want to learn more about their homeland. “This is the first semester that NYU has offered this particular course, and it’s a great opportunity to learn a little more about Ukraine in the context of America and international politics," Kalinchenko said.

Anna Ivanenko attends the Stern School of Business and says, “I hadn’t planned to take anything related to politics, but when I saw that Ukrainian politics was being offered as an elective this semester, I thought it would be great to take a course related to Ukraine.”

Vlasenko believes the knowledge students gain in the classroom may prove useful after Russia’s war in Ukraine ends. “Ukraine’s reconstruction will create investment opportunities for major American businesses and will be important for U.S. policymakers. NYU can help provide them with the expertise and perspective they need...,” she said.

items.title: Grade I interiors, gold bars, cost fears: Bank of England faces headache over £160m revamp
paragraphs: Andrew Bailey may spend his days closely watching developments in the strait of Hormuz or US stock markets for signs of shocks to the global economy – but the Bank of England’s governor has a £160m problem brewing much closer to home.

A secretive major revamp of the Bank’s historic headquarters in the heart of London’s Square Mile presents a huge test of Bailey’s project management skills. The central bank, with its reputation staked on carefully counting the nation’s pennies, will be keen to avoid delays, budget-busting or any echoes of the expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that left his former peer Jerome Powell awkwardly clashing with Donald Trump on camera.
Bailey and his senior managers believe they can modernise the Bank’s Grade I-listed structure and interiors while 3,500 staff are still busy at work on site.

By the summer of 2028, 1,400 Bank staff who work in a nearby office at 20 Moorgate will be relocated to Threadneedle Street, have taken voluntary redundancy or have been offered an alternative job in a new outpost in Leeds, also being refurbished.

It appears a unique project for Britain’s struggling building trade: overhaul a site with a globally recognised exterior; preserve its Roman mosaic floors, stone columns and vaulted, ornate ceilings while keeping exact floorplans under wraps, for fear of terror attacks.

The Bank itself began in rented premises in 1694, moving to Threadneedle Street in 1734. Nicknamed the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street after a satirical cartoon of William Pitt the Younger, it has been refashioned and remodelled – first by Sir John Soane between 1788 and 1833 and then again in the 1920s when the interior was largely demolished and rebuilt.

The building is owned by the Bank, which was given independence to set interest rates by Gordon Brown in 1997, and, after the 2008 financial crash, it was later handed responsibility for regulating the banking sector by George Osborne.

Cash to fund the scheme will come from an estimated £100m of savings each year for three years that the Bank says will accrue from 450 redundancies and other cost savings. As one member of Bank staff told the Guardian: “It’s like there is a leaving party every week.”
What the Bank wants to avoid is a repeat of the delays and cost overruns that dogged the Federal Reserve in Washington, which led to Trump threatening the US central bank with court action.

Over the life of the Fed’s renovation project, construction costs have soared. The initial budget of $921m (£696m) in February 2020 was revised several times before December 2024, when it hit $2bn. Construction was supposed to be completed in mid-2024 but is now expected to run until December 2027. The final cost is likely to be nearer $2.5bn.
The Bank’s scheme is on a much smaller scale, and pales against the possible £60bn it will cost to renovate the Palace of Westminster. It is more akin to the £80m Elizabeth Tower restoration.

What Bailey will want to avoid is joining the Elizabeth Tower, which houses Big Ben, as the subject of parliamentary scrutiny after its budget doubled and then rose by a further 20%, giving ammunition to critics who have long accused the Bank of mishandling its core purpose of helping to manage the economy by setting interest rates at the appropriate level.

The Bank project was first announced in July 2025 and work was due to start this month, but it was only in October, with a month to spare, that the construction company Sir Robert McAlpine was awarded the building contract.

Described as an “incredibly complex project”, it aims to transform the neoclassical building, which sits opposite the Royal Exchange and adjacent to the Mansion House, into what some staff hope is a Google-like workplace of friendly office spaces, breakout rooms and in-house cafes.

The Bank says there will be no delays, citing the appointment of architects last November. A project manager, a cost consultant and a firm of engineers were also signed up, and they have already begun evaluating budgets and timescales.

A Bank of England spokesperson said: “As part of our plans to preserve our historic Threadneedle Street office we are considering how best to renovate the site and optimise our running costs. All our procurement processes aim to deliver value for money.”

Bailey’s team – based in a grand part of the Bank known as the Parlours – will need to judge the cost implications of meeting new regulations on fire safety, accessibility, electrical testing – with the fire at Notre Dame mid-renovation still fresh in the memory – new plumbing and the need to have a more environmentally friendly building with heating based on renewable sources.

And that’s not to mention the security of the building while all this goes on. Bailey will be concerned that the 400,000 bars of gold, worth more than £200bn, and £100m of bank notes in the vaults are safe from terrorists and thieves.
A further complication is the fate of the Bank’s museum, which is now open to the public and tucked away in the side of the building, facing on to Bartholomew Lane.

Some senior staff had wanted to relocate the museum into the central quad and have the 100,000 visitors a year – mainly schoolchildren – march through the main entrance. Others wanted to have cafe space near the entrance to make the Bank appear more modern and appealing to visitors.

Vivienne Grafton, the executive director of central operations, told the Architects Journal: “This is an opportunity to breathe new life into a legacy building, not through radical reinvention, but through thoughtful, intelligent transformation.”

But architectural plans have yet to be agreed with the local authority – the City of London Corporation – and Historic England, which must sanction the proposed work on a building considered a cornerstone of Britain’s financial district.

Anna Joynt, a senior architect and heritage expert at the London practice of Allies and Morrison, said it was common for large, complex historic building projects to begin preparatory works before full consent has been given.
“There may be bones of the future scheme in place but the wider scheme may not be developed enough to submit for listed building consent – which needs a lot of detail,” she said.

“It’s fairly common to split out simpler early enabling works and get permission for them in advance of a main scheme. It means work can start earlier and save money as the longer you wait the more things cost.”

There has been some tangible progress on the scheme. The roof of the main portico is clad in scaffolding to allow for repairs. And last year the Bank secured planning permission to overhaul one small section – an area known as the former governor’s secretaries’s offices, which will have their plasterboard walls taken out and the space opened up and modernised.
As for the rest of the 1.4-hectare (3.5-acre) site, staff must wait and see.

items.title: Apple MacBook Pro M6 review: probably the last of its generation
paragraphs: Apple’s base-model MacBook Pro gets a solid speed bump, offering most of the features from its top-level siblings but in a design that has just been superseded and may soon be phased out.

It is the starting model in Apple’s popular MacBook Pro line, but that doesn’t make it cheap. Costing from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199) it is £300 or equivalent more than its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to jack up prices. It is, at least, £500 cheaper than the other new MacBook Pros.

The laptop’s solid aluminium body, look and feel are identical to its predecessors, using the design first introduced in 2021. With five generations of the machine having been and gone, it is a bit of a known quantity, but the 120Hz miniLED screen is still brilliant, as are the first-class keyboard and trackpad. The port selection is also solid and the MagSafe charging cable remains a delight.

The M6 model only comes with the smaller 14.2in screen, which is still the sweet spot for portability and productivity. It reaches a sustained 1,000nits brightness for standard content and working – double that of the MacBook Air – and hits 1,600nits to make HDR content pop. It is only really beaten by the OLED screen on the new MacBook Pro design, which costs considerably more.
Screen: 14.2in mini LED (3024x1964; 254 ppi) ProMotion (120Hz)
Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, 3x Thunderbolt 4/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, SDXC, headphones

The M6 is Apple’s latest generation chip and was first used in the Mac mini to great effect. Compared with the M5 generation of chips, including the current MacBook Air, the M6 MacBook Pro is about 11% faster for day-to-day usage and 24% for more intensive multi-core tasks. The extra performance wasn’t that noticeable in day-to-day tasks, but just like the M5 version, it absolutely flies during use.

However, it also has up to 57% faster graphics performance, beating many of Apple’s older M-Pro chips. That makes the M6 quite a leap from older machines with more than enough power for many creative work tasks.

The MacBook Pro also has fantastic battery life, lasting about three days of light work between charges using the browser, messaging, notes and word processing apps. That makes it one of the longest-lasting laptops for general use, but even for more intensive work, developing and editing photos, the battery still lasted about two days.

The MacBook Pro is made of 45% recycled materials, which Apple breaks down in its environmental impact report. The battery should last in excess of 1,000 full-charge cycles and can be replaced for £225 by Apple. Apple makes repair manuals available. The company offers trade-in and free recycling schemes.
The MacBook Pro M6 costs from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199).

For comparison, the 14in M5 Pro MacBook Pro costs £2,499, the 14in OLED MacBook Pro costs from £2,899, the 13in MacBook Air costs £1,299, the Dell XPS 14 costs from £2,038.45 and the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra costs £2,599.
The M6 MacBook Pro is a potent machine for general use that is let down by its high price, mostly thanks to the scourge of RAMageddon.
But it is also likely one of the last iterations of its design, having been superseded by the new thinner, lighter and OLED-equipped MacBook Pro.
The M6 is a great laptop with fantastically long battery life and a quality screen, keyboard and trackpad, built on the foundations of the many great MacBook Pros over the last five years.

But at £1,999 or equivalent it is also a difficult pill to swallow, primarily aimed at Apple buyers who want a nicer screen or more ports than a MacBook Air and are prepared to pay £700 more for it. For everyone else, there are better models available with more grunt or a cheaper price.

Pros: great performance from M6 chip, minimum of 16GB memory and 1TB storage, super-long battery life, great ProMotion screen, great Centre Stage camera, plenty of ports and an SD card slot, great speakers, Touch ID, top-class keyboard and trackpad, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support.
Cons: no Face ID, no USB-A, RAM or SSD cannot be upgraded after purchase, very expensive, not a big upgrade on M5 version, no OLED screen, heavier than newer design.

items.title: Art psychotherapists are already regulated | Letters
paragraphs: We welcome the discussion about public protection, professional accountability and the importance of appropriate regulation within counselling and psychotherapy (Letters, 5 November). However, we feel it is important to highlight a distinction that may be helpful to readers.

Art psychotherapists are already a statutorily regulated profession in the UK, regulated by the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC). The HCPC regulates 15 health and care professions, including arts therapists (art psychotherapists, art therapists, drama therapists, music therapists) and the titles art therapist and art psychotherapist are legally protected. Practitioners must meet HCPC registration requirements, standards of proficiency, conduct and ethics, and continuing professional development requirements.
This means that art therapists occupy a different regulatory position from counsellors and psychotherapists, whose professional registration is currently voluntary.

We do recognise the importance of extending statutory protection across professions where it is currently absent, but would appreciate recognition that we, along with drama therapists and music therapists, are a statutory regulated profession. Elizabeth Donnelly Chief executive officer, British Association of Art Therapists

items.title: Participating in art and culture has measurable benefits on our wellbeing | Letter
paragraphs: Reading Emma Brockes’ response to a recent Art Fund study, I felt the significance of the research may have been lost in its packaging (Art is good for your health? Allow me a quick eyeroll, 5 November).

The language of “prescribing” art has its roots in social prescribing. I understand why this might make people uncomfortable, particularly if it suggests that culture is being instrumentalised rather than enjoyed for its own sake.

Yet these findings matter for two reasons. First, they provide evidence for what many of us know intuitively: that participating in and experiencing art and culture are not only enriching, but also have measurable benefits for our health and wellbeing.

Second, with budgets for culture under pressure, this evidence strengthens our case for public investment. Surely that’s another argument for keeping our national museums free and ensuring everyone can access their wellbeing benefits.

Rather than viewing this study cynically, we should recognise the opportunities it presents. As Daisy Fancourt, who is quoted in Brockes’ article, explores in her excellent and insightful book Art Cure, the evidence extends far beyond visiting galleries and museums.

In the London borough of Ealing, we’re piloting a free creative health programme bringing residents and council staff together through activities ranging from clay workshops to Islamic geometric drawing. Almost all participants have reported improved wellbeing following these sessions. But beyond the evaluation, conversations have shown me how even an hour spent being creative can positively change the course of someone’s day, while regular participation can have a lasting impact on their lives.

Art shouldn’t have to justify its existence through its health benefits. But understanding those benefits strengthens the case for everyone to experience, participate in and benefit from art and culture.

And if the thought of visiting a museum makes Brockes’ eyes roll, I’d happily invite her to one of our workshops. She might leave having learned a new skill, but I suspect she’d take away rather more than that. William Rees Culture officer, Ealing council

items.title: Apple MacBook Pro review: lighter, thinner and a stunning OLED touchscreen
paragraphs: Apple’s MacBook Pro has been redesigned for the first time in five years, getting slightly slimmer, significantly lighter and adding a fantastic new OLED display with the first touchscreen on a Mac.

The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display comes in two sizes, 14in and 16in, but rather than replacing the standard MacBook Pro they sit alongside them as an even more expensive option. The OLED machines start at £2,899 (€3,299/$2,899/A$4,599) – a £400 or equivalent upgrade on the matching spec LCD models – serious prices for serious work machines, not helped by significant cost increases driven by RAMageddon.

Shut, the new OLED MacBook Pro looks almost identical to its predecessors: a little smaller in every direction but with the same aluminium body, combination of ports and overall profile. But pick it up and the weight loss is immediately noticeable. The 14in version is 14% lighter than its predecessor at 1.38kg, which makes it only 150g heavier than the 13in MacBook Air, and the 16in version is 15% lighter at 1.82kg.

The new touchscreen is the biggest change, complete with the dynamic island around the web cam like a modern iPhone. The screen on the LCD MacBook Pro was already fantastic, but the switch to OLED has several benefits. The screen is even brighter, hitting an incredible peak of 2,000 nits for outdoor or HDR content viewing, making it one of the brightest laptop screens available.

OLED displays have individually lit pixels, which gives them dramatically better contrast with the deepest blacks and eliminates any blooming effects. That makes the new screen one of the very best on any product and a genuine joy to use to create or watch content. It is super crisp, vibrant and smooth, and makes the most of dark mode.
14in screen: 14.2in tandem OLED (3024x1986; 254 ppi) ProMotion (10-120Hz)
16in screen: 16.3in tandem OLED (3472x2266; 254 ppi) ProMotion (10-120Hz)
Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, 3x Thunderbolt 5/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, SDXC card, headphones

The OLED MacBook Pro isn’t the first laptop with a touchscreen – they’ve been common on Windows laptops since 2012 – but it is the first Mac with one. For the most part the touchscreen mirrors mouse clicks, so you can single tap on just about anything or tap and hold for right click on most things.

It also supports most of the gestures available on a trackpad, including swipes, pinch to zoom and rotate. Three-finger swipes trigger mission control so you can switch between windows, while flicking them left or right snaps them to the screen’s edge – though unsnapping them requires a mouse for some reason. Swipe in from the right side of the screen for notification centre, down from the top right for control centre and from the dynamic island for Spotlight or Siri.

The Mac is not touch-first like an iPad and there is no touchscreen keyboard. But Apple has built new touch systems that third-party app developers can use to do unique things, such as tools that fan out around your finger or scrubbing dials. Those are few and far between at the moment.

That leaves touching the screen an optional extra. Like Windows machines, it is handy to have direct interaction with something using your finger sometimes. Pinch to zoom or rotating a photo is a lot easier directly on the screen than the touchpad, as is tapping the screen to pause video. The touchscreen is also useful for performing various gestures if you use a mouse rather than a trackpad.

The OLED MacBook Pros come with the same M5 Pro or Max chips and memory choices as the regular MacBook Pros with essentially the same performance in benchmarks and during general use. They also have similar battery life, lasting for about two days of office work while mainly using the browser, writing, messaging and note-taking tools.

For more intensive workloads, such as developing and editing photos or other mid-level creative apps, the 16in version with M5 Max still managed to end the day with 40% left in the tank. If pushed to the limit, the battery lasts about two hours, which is still long enough to get a solid task or two done when away from the charger.

The MacBook Pro OLED is made of 55% recycled materials, which Apple breaks down in its environmental impact report. The battery should last in excess of 1,000 full charge cycles and can be replaced for £225 by Apple. Apple makes repair manuals available, offers trade-in and free recycling schemes.
The MacBook Pro with PROLED starts at £2,899 (€3,299/$2,899/A$4,599) for the 14in version or £3,399 (€3,899/$3,399/A$5,499) for the 16in version.

For comparison, the 14in M6 MacBook Pro costs £1,999, the 14in M5 Pro MacBook Pro costs £2,499, the 13in MacBook Air costs £1,299, the Dell XPS 14 costs from £2,038.45 and the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra costs £2,599.
The OLED MacBook Pro might be the first touchscreen Mac, but touch is the least interesting part about it.

The reduced weight, slimmer body and absolutely stunning new screen are meaningful upgrades that will no doubt see the MacBook Pro through another five years as one of the very best pro laptops you can get.
The light-up Apple logo on the lid is a welcome blast from the past, while the dynamic island at the top of the screen takes up less space and is more useful than the notch it replaces.

The touchscreen is best thought of a value-added extra that is useful on occasion or for certain types of tasks. This isn’t a touch-first laptop, it’s more like one that just happens to have a touchscreen similar to many of the best Windows rivals, which is just fine.

I still wish the dynamic island contained Face ID like it does on an iPhone. The Touch ID fingerprint scanner is fine, but face recognition on a laptop is better. And no matter how you slice it, any of the new MacBook Pros cost a lot of money, part of which can be blamed on RAMageddon.

As crazy as it might sound, if you’re currently hoping to replace an older machine with a new high-end M5 Pro or Max Apple laptop, the extra £400 or equivalent for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR is worth it over the regular LCD MacBook Pro.

Pros: stunning OLED touchscreen, dynamic island with great Centre Stage camera, thinner and lighter, choice of extremely potent M5 Pro or Max chips, long battery life, plenty of ports and an SD card slot, brilliant speakers, Touch ID, first-class keyboard and trackpad, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support.
Cons: extremely expensive, no Face ID, no USB-A, RAM or SSD cannot be upgraded after purchase, touchscreen only occasionally useful.

items.title: Apple iPad mini A20 Pro review: the best small tablet but with a big price
paragraphs: The new iPad mini takes Apple’s fan-favourite tiny tablet and upgrades just about everything about it, including giving it a new OLED screen, serious performance, speakers embedded into the display and even water resistance, all with a big new price tag.

The eighth-generation iPad mini costs from £699 (€749/$699/A$1,099), which is £200 or equivalent more than the original price of its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to bite. That makes it uncomfortably expensive, costing £270 more than the base model iPad (A16) and only £50 cheaper than the bigger 11in iPad Air M4.

The new mini reads like a wishlist from small iPad owners. The tablet is about 1mm thinner, 38g lighter and slightly smaller compared with its predecessor, but still manages to fit in a 0.2in larger screen. The mini is the first iPad to have IP67 water resistance, which means trips to the beach or pool are less fraught with danger. Even the video call camera has been moved to a more sensible position in the landscape edge of the tablet. It lacks Face ID, though, making it reliant on the Touch ID fingerprint scanner in the power button.

The new 8.5in OLED screen is the star of the show: bright, vibrant and with inky blacks to make the absolute most of your content. But it lacks the “ProMotion” display technology Apple uses on many of its other devices to keep scrolling and interactions super smooth. It is particularly jarring when you move from a modern iPhone with its 120Hz screen back to the iPad with its relatively slow 60Hz display.

The new speaker system has a pair of tweeters that fire out of slimline gaps between the screen glass and aluminium body with woofers that play directly through the screen. They sound really very good for something this slim, with direct, powerful audio you can’t block with your hand while holding the sides of the tablet.
Screen: 8.5in Super Retina XDR OLED (326ppi)
Processor: Apple A20 Pro (5- or 6-core CPU)
Connectivity: wifi 7 (5G eSim-only), Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Touch ID
Water resistance: IP67 (1 metre for 30 mins)

Inside the new iPad is the A20 Pro chip from the iPhone 18 Pro and Duo, which absolutely flies. It comes in two versions depending on storage, with all but the most expensive model having one fewer CPU cores and half the NPU performance. Most will not miss it.

The battery lasts a solid nine to 10 hours of active screen use for lighter tasks such as browsing the web, answering emails, taking notes, watching movies or viewing photos. Playing games dents the battery to more like six to eight hours. The tablet charges to about 50% in under 30 minutes using a 35W or greater USB-C power adaptor (not included) and reaches 100% in about 100 minutes.
The battery will last more than 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity and can be replaced for £115. Other out-of-warranty damage, including screen repairs, costs £519.
It contains 35% recycled material. The company breaks down the tablet’s environmental impact in its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.

The iPad mini A20 Pro costs from £699 (€749/$699/A$1,099). For comparison, the iPad costs £429, the iPad Air 11in costs £749, and the iPad Pro 11in costs £1,199. The iPhone Duo costs £1,999 and the Lenovo Legion Tab 5th gen costs £649.

The iPad mini is the best small tablet available. That was true for previous models and is doubly true for the new one. Almost everything about it has been upgraded – the screen, the body, the camera, speakers and chip – yet it feels and works very similarly to the last few iPad minis.

The mini has a loyal following for whom the bigger screen than a phone and the portability of a compact tablet are the sweet spot. They are typically public transport commuters, people who fly a lot or those that have turned to it for a notepad replacement. They will love this revamp.

But you also see a lot of them in the workplace. Minis are used on building sites, as payment systems in stores, check-in terminals for greeters, by waiting staff in restaurants or in universities used for handwritten notes and marking up scientific papers.

The iPad mini isn’t quite the perfect small tablet. The screen should be faster and it is jarring that it isn’t, particularly at this very high price. It still lacks Face ID. And for most people the cheaper basic iPad or iPad Air is a better buy.

Pros: compact and light design, top performance, 10-hour battery life, great OLED screen, water resistance, landscape camera, USB-C, great speakers, full multitasking and external display support, long software support, recycled aluminium, Apple Pencil Pro support.
Cons: very expensive, screen not 120Hz, no Face ID, small size is cramped for some uses.
